articles.title: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction
articles.description: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction ABC30 Fresno
articles.description_html: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction  ABC30 Fresno
articles.article_title: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction
articles.heading: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction
articles.summary: As cataract treatment continues to evolve, patients now have more lens implant options than ever before.
articles.content:
Friday, September 11, 2026 1:28AM
MERCED, Calif. (KFSN) -- More than half of all Americans age 80 or older either have cataracts or have had surgery to remove them, according to the National Eye Institute.
As cataract treatment continues to evolve, patients now have more lens implant options than ever before.
Dr. Kelley Hawkins, an ophthalmologist with EYE-Q Vision Care, said cataracts develop when the eye's natural lens becomes cloudy with age.
"When we're born, the lens is kind of a clear jelly-like material," Dr. Hawkins said.
As people get older, the lens can become cloudier, denser or more brown in color. Dr. Hawkins said cataracts typically begin developing around age 60 and progress over time.
"For most people, it starts at the age of 60 and kind of progresses over time. The average age for cataract surgery is 65 to 75 years old," Dr. Hawkins said.
Common cataract symptoms include blurry, cloudy or foggy vision, glare around lights and colors appearing faded.
During cataract surgery, doctors make a small incision through the cornea to remove the cloudy lens.
"Once inside, we actually use an ultrasound device to break the cataract into pieces and safely remove it from the eye. Once the cataracts out, the eye needs a lens to see. So we actually put an implant inside of the eye, and that's that intraocular lens," Dr. Hawkins said.
Dr. Hawkins said patients now have several choices when it comes to lens implants. One option is a monofocal lens, which is designed to provide clear vision at a single fixed distance.
"Most people want that to be far away, but some of my nearsighted folks choose up close with that lens. It's going to improve the vision, but you're still going to need glasses for either the distance or for up close," Dr. Hawkins said.
Another option is a multifocal lens, which can reduce a patient's dependence on glasses by providing vision at multiple distances.
"This lens implant gives distance vision, intermediate, and some near, kind of like our progressive glasses do," said Dr. Hawkins. "What really excites me is kind of this newer technology that we have for cataract surgery, this light adjustable lens."
Dr. Hawkins said the light adjustable lens is implanted during cataract surgery like other intraocular lenses. After recovery, patients return about a month later for adjustments designed to further refine their vision.
"Essentially, to dial in the vision is as close to perfect as possible. It just makes it customizable to every patient. Once you find your happy place, we actually lock this lens in, and then it stays like that for hopefully as long as possible," Dr. Hawkins said.
Dr. Hawkins also highlighted what she described as the relatively easy recovery process following cataract surgery.
"On average, it takes a few days for the vision to recover, even up to a week, and that's normal. Most patients have some mild irritation in the eye after surgery. That's expected. Severe pain and things like that are very unlikely," Dr. Hawkins said.
Patients considering cataract surgery should discuss the available lens options with their eye care provider to determine which choice best fits their vision needs and lifestyle goals.

articles.title: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks
articles.description: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks wndu.com
articles.description_html: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks  wndu.com
articles.article_title: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks
articles.heading: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks
articles.summary: A former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic is warning that the companies developing artificial intelligence are not acting responsibly.
articles.content:
Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks
Researcher who worked at OpenAI and Anthropic says companies are racing toward self-improving superintelligence
SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - A former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic is sounding the alarm about the potential risks of artificial intelligence.
Jacob Coxon, who spent the last three years working at the two AI companies, announced his resignation on social media Tuesday.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said.
Within hours, Evan Hubinger, a researcher who still works at Anthropic, responded online.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans. I personally think it is greater than 10 percent within the next decade,” Hubinger said.
The claims raise questions about whether the threat is realistic or part of a series of bold predictions from an industry known for rapid advances and ambitious forecasts.
The concerns extend beyond Silicon Valley. In South Bend, residents are also thinking about how artificial intelligence could affect everyday life.
“What’s going to happen if this AI takes over some part of the landing program for airports or something like that where people are directly threatened,” said Joseph Mauck, a South Bend resident.
Mauck said the concern is not limited to worst-case scenarios. He also worries about how closely the technology is already tied to daily life.
“If you are going to mimic the personalities and characters of human beings, then you have to take into account the tremendous amount of subtlety that goes into their actions,” Mauck said.
Not everyone shares that level of concern.
“It’s going to be exponential, right. Computers are going to work faster and they’re going to start to be able to use resources on their own, so I don’t think we’re too far off from it. Whether I’m afraid, I don’t know — I try not to live in fear,” said Adrian Pacheco, a South Bend resident.
Whether it is fear of the worst-case scenario or unease about what comes next, people are wrestling with the same questions as researchers who are leaving the companies building the technology.
“I think we can pull it off — we’ll survive,” Pacheco said.

articles.title: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards
articles.description: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards WLWT
articles.description_html: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards  WLWT
articles.article_title: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards
articles.heading: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards
articles.summary: Warnings from artificial intelligence researchers are fueling concerns about the rapidly developing technology’s potential to wipe out humanity.
articles.content:
AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards
Warnings from artificial intelligence researchers are fueling concerns about the rapidly developing technology’s potential to wipe out humanity.
The issue was a major topic at MidwestCon in Cincinnati, where technology leaders and attendees discussed balancing innovation with safety.
Jacob Coxon, who recently resigned from AI company Anthropic, accused Anthropic and OpenAI of irresponsibly developing technology that could pose an existential risk.
Another researcher wrote on social media that they believe there is a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.
MidwestCon founder Rob Richardson said such warnings should be taken seriously.
“There is a possibility that we are definitely underestimating the power of AI,” Richardson said. “I do think we need policy.”
Richardson emphasized that people must remain in control of how AI is developed and deployed.
“AI knows it can do almost everything, but it doesn’t know when to stop,” he said. “Humans need to be there to tell it when to stop.”
Cincinnati resident Nikki Crenshaw said she remains optimistic.
“I’m going to stay hopeful and believe that it’s going to help us versus hurt us,” Crenshaw said.
The U.S. does not currently have a comprehensive federal law regulating AI.
A bill introduced in Congress in July would give the federal government authority to disable AI models determined to pose a risk to the public.

articles.title: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology
articles.description: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology WVXU
articles.description_html: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology  WVXU
articles.article_title: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology
articles.heading: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology
articles.summary: City Council indicated interested in an ordinance to limit data storage and sharing, while expressing support for how Cincinnati Police use license plate readers and other technology.
articles.content:
Cincinnati City Council unanimously passed a motion Thursday requesting an ordinance to put limits on surveillance technology like license plate readers. It's not clear whether the eventual ordinance will have majority support, however.
Council member Anna Albi introduced the motion. She says surveillance tech is a "hot topic" and that these tools are important to solving and preventing crime.
"But we need to balance that need with ensuring we're protecting our citizens, frankly, from government overreach and abuse of these very powerful technologies," Albi said, adding this motion is intended to start a larger discussion.
"Let's talk publicly about what type of surveillance technologies the city is using ... because honestly, from everything I've heard from CPD and [the] Law [Department], Cincinnati is doing it right. We have great oversight from our law department when it comes to these contracts."
The motion requests a report and presentation from city administration within 30 days with an overview of how the city uses cameras, drones, and license plate readers.
Many other communities in Greater Cincinnati have faced publish pushback for using Flock cameras, and several have paused their use or even canceled contracts as a result. Those include: Lebanon, Hamilton County, Oxford, and in Northern Kentucky, Fort Thomas, Newport, Independence, Fort Mitchell, Bellevue, and Florence.
Cincinnati does not use Flock Safety technology, but contracts with Axon for body cameras and license plate readers. The city put out a Request for Proposals about a year ago, indicating the Cincinnati Police Department is undergoing a five-year expansion; the RFP sought quotes for installing 30 to 50 cameras throughout the city. Submissions are under review, according to the city website.
Two people registered as paid lobbyists for Flock Safety in 2025 but terminated their registration this year. A third person registered as a lobbyist for Flock Safety early this year: Katherine Ott Zehnder of Politicom Law. The city charter requires lobbyists to update or terminate their registration each July; Ott Zehnder did not.
Council members Jeff Cramerding and Seth Walsh co-sponsored Albi's motion.
"I want to make sure that we continue to use technology to deter crime and track down shooters and do whatever is necessary," Cramerding said.
Earlier this year, Council passed a motion prohibiting the city from sharing any data from city-owned surveillance technology with any third-party for the purpose of civil immigration enforcement, unless mandated by law, a court order, or judicial warrant.
The motion passed this week also requests a draft ordinance that would establish a surveillance use policy, limit data sharing and storage, require an annual "state of surveillance" report, and require City Council approval of related contracts.
The details of the requested ordinance are not spelled out, and it's not clear whether a majority of Council will support it.
Council member Scotty Johnson, a retired Cincinnati Police officer and current chair of Council's Public Safety and Quality of Life Committee, expressed concern.
"We must stay 10 steps ahead of the bad guys, and the bad guys have surveillance, the bad guys have technology," Johnson said. "The reality is that there are things, there are surveillances, there are investigations that the citizens of Cincinnati do not need to know about — this body [City Council] doesn't need to know about — because of the sensitive nature in which the Cincinnati police operate. I understand that's a little disturbing to some people, but law, but crime is solved as a direct result of [these] investigations."
Even Council members who indicated support for limits on surveillance technology also expressed their belief that Cincinnati is already doing it "the right way."
"It's my understanding that the Cincinnati Police Department is using best practice," Cramerding said. "I will not support anything that in any way handcuffs our police or prevents them from doing their jobs."
Vice Mayor Jan-Michele Lemon Kearney said in committee on Tuesday that she supports the motion because it's good to get more information.
"But we know that cameras help us solve crime. They also deter crime," she said.
The eventual presentation is expected at a meeting of the Public Safety and Quality of Life Committee, which means every other week. The presentation is expected to be ready by the meeting scheduled for Oct. 6.
Full text of the motion
Title: Motion on City Surveillance Technology and Ordinance
WE MOVE that the Administration present to Committee within 30 days on an overview of the City's use of surveillance technology, including cameras, drones, and license plate readers, covering current deployment, data retention, and any data-sharing agreements.
WE FURTHER MOVE that the administration draft an ordinance for Council's consideration, including limits on data sharing and storage; a state of surveillance annual impact report; surveillance use policy; and Council approval of related contracts.

Council members Jeff Cramerding and Seth Walsh co-sponsored Albi's motion.

"I want to make sure that we continue to use technology to deter crime and track down shooters and do whatever is necessary," Cramerding said.

Earlier this year, Council passed a motion prohibiting the city from sharing any data from city-owned surveillance technology with any third-party for the purpose of civil immigration enforcement, unless mandated by law, a court order, or judicial warrant.

The motion passed this week also requests a draft ordinance that would establish a surveillance use policy, limit data sharing and storage, require an annual "state of surveillance" report, and require City Council approval of related contracts.

The details of the requested ordinance are not spelled out, and it's not clear whether a majority of Council will support it.

Council member Scotty Johnson, a retired Cincinnati Police officer and current chair of Council's Public Safety and Quality of Life Committee, expressed concern.

"We must stay 10 steps ahead of the bad guys, and the bad guys have surveillance, the bad guys have technology," Johnson said. "The reality is that there are things, there are surveillances, there are investigations that the citizens of Cincinnati do not need to know about — this body [City Council] doesn't need to know about — because of the sensitive nature in which the Cincinnati police operate. I understand that's a little disturbing to some people, but law, but crime is solved as a direct result of [these] investigations."

Even Council members who indicated support for limits on surveillance technology also expressed their belief that Cincinnati is already doing it "the right way."

"It's my understanding that the Cincinnati Police Department is using best practice," Cramerding said. "I will not support anything that in any way handcuffs our police or prevents them from doing their jobs."

Vice Mayor Jan-Michele Lemon Kearney said in committee on Tuesday that she supports the motion because it's good to get more information.

"But we know that cameras help us solve crime. They also deter crime," she said.

The eventual presentation is expected at a meeting of the Public Safety and Quality of Life Committee, which means every other week. The presentation is expected to be ready by the meeting scheduled for Oct. 6.

Full text of the motion

Title: Motion on City Surveillance Technology and Ordinance

WE MOVE that the Administration present to Committee within 30 days on an overview of the City's use of surveillance technology, including cameras, drones, and license plate readers, covering current deployment, data retention, and any data-sharing agreements.

WE FURTHER MOVE that the administration draft an ordinance for Council's consideration, including limits on data sharing and storage; a state of surveillance annual impact report; surveillance use policy; and Council approval of related contracts.

articles.title: NASA’s Life-Saving Technology Where Cell Signals Can’t Go
articles.description: NASA’s Life-Saving Technology Where Cell Signals Can’t Go NASA (.gov)
articles.description_html: NASA’s Life-Saving Technology Where Cell Signals Can’t Go  NASA (.gov)
articles.article_title: NASA's Life-Saving Technology Where Cell Signals Can't Go - NASA
articles.heading: NASA’s Life-Saving Technology Where Cell Signals Can’t Go
articles.summary: Search and rescue technology developed in part by NASA saved five lives
articles.content:
Memorial Day weekend 2024 started with a blue sky and a mild three- to four-foot chop in the water off the Gulf Coast of Mississippi — a perfect day for a fishing competition. A team of five was about 40 miles offshore checking their sonar, and 30 seconds later the boat was gone. They were in the water struggling to pull on life jackets and grab the coolers as they bobbed up. When a boat sinks, survivors can be virtually invisible amid the vast expanse of water.
When their fishing trip went wrong, Easton Barrett had the only mobile phone and no cell service. He recorded a brief farewell, planning to put his phone in a cooler in hopes someone would find it.
Another team member activated a personal locator beacon (PLB) that had been stowed at the last minute, which sent a distress signal to the Search and Rescue Satellite-Aided Tracking (SARSAT) technology carried by multiple satellites in Earth orbit. In the SARSAT system, developed partly by NASA, an emergency signal containing the transmitter’s location is directed to the nearest available ground station.
A mission control center then alerts rescue coordination centers to mobilize search and rescue crews. For Barrett and his crew, that was a Florida Coast Guard boat.
“Ever since, I have tried to teach others about safety on the water and in the outdoors by using a PLB,” said Barrett. “If that will save one life, it’s worth the effort.”
A beacon like the one that saved his crew, a registered ResQLink PLB developed by ACR Electronics Inc. of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, also notifies the device owner’s emergency contact, indicating a distress call was activated. All emergency beacons must meet the same requirements to ensure they work when needed. Every rugged, buoyant, handheld devices have a five- to 10-year battery life.
SARSAT began operations in 1982, becoming an international collaboration in 1985. The flight and ground technologies used globally were originally developed at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. Now there are 62 satellites in the program and 45 nations contributing services, from operating ground stations to providing rescue crews. More than 63,000 lives have been saved.
SARSAT by the Numbers
The Search and Rescue Satellite-Aided Tracking system developed over several decades by NASA and other government agencies saves lives on land or at sea.
- 1982 — the start of U.S. operations
- 1985 — the start of international operations
- 62 operational satellites
- 45 nations contributing services
- 63,000+ lives saved
One rescue in 2024 demonstrates how it all comes together.
- 40 miles off the Mississippi Gulf Coast
- 5-person team participating in a fishing competition
- 30 seconds for a boat to sink
- 200 pounds of bait dumped to make a cooler buoyant
- 3 close encounters with wildlife, likely sharks and eels
- 4 hours in the water
- 1 personal locator beacon
- 1 Coast Guard rescue boat
- 5 lives saved
“If it has anything to do with NASA, it's got to be awesome.”
EASTOn Barrett
ACR Customer

articles.title: 5 backend technology priorities for peak retail events
articles.description: 5 backend technology priorities for peak retail events cio.com
articles.description_html: 5 backend technology priorities for peak retail events  cio.com
articles.article_title: 5 backend technology priorities for peak retail events
articles.heading: 5 backend technology priorities for peak retail events
articles.summary: The holiday shopping season puts inventory, fulfillment, and transaction systems to the test. Here’s where technology leaders should focus.
articles.content:
The holiday shopping season puts inventory, fulfillment, and transaction systems to the test. Here’s where technology leaders should focus.
Peak retail events, from Amazon Prime Day and Labor Day promotions to Black Friday and Cyber Monday, compress months of retail activity into a matter of days. The margin for error is small: Rocket Software research found that 55% of consumers would switch brands after one or two failed transactions, including 12% who would leave immediately.
That makes the holiday shopping season a valuable test of a retailer’s technology foundation. Systems need to keep pace as demand accelerates because performance shapes both revenue and customer confidence. In the same survey, 84% of consumers said knowing a company uses modern, secure technology would make them more confident doing business with it.
Many clients are taking an incremental approach to modernization, strengthening existing systems while building on the technology investments already supporting core operations. Peak shopping events provide an opportunity to evaluate whether those modernization efforts are delivering the operational outcomes the business expects.
What should retailers prioritize to prepare backend technology for peak shopping events?
1. Strengthen inventory visibility and data accuracy
Inventory is often one of the first places where cracks begin to show when demand accelerates. A distribution center may mark an item as sold while the ecommerce site still shows it in stock, creating problems that extend well beyond a missed sale. Teams shift their attention from serving customers to reconciling data, and decisions become harder when every minute counts. What seems like a minor discrepancy during a typical week can quickly become an operational issue when inventory is moving across channels at a much faster pace.
We encourage clients to think about inventory confidence as a business capability, especially as demand shifts throughout the day. Maintaining a trusted view of inventory across the retail ecosystem gives teams the information they need to act decisively, rather than spending valuable time determining which system has the correct answer.
2. Improve backend resilience across retail systems
High-volume shopping periods test how well systems work together under pressure. For many, that means coordinating modern digital experiences with core transaction systems that have processed the business for decades. Delays that begin in one part of the technology ecosystem can ripple outward, affecting business operations long before anyone identifies the source.
Many clients are extending existing platforms while introducing new applications alongside them. That makes visibility across both legacy and modern environments increasingly important, especially as data and transactions move between them. Understanding those dependencies before traffic begins to climb gives technology teams a clearer picture of where friction is most likely to emerge.
Critical business processes have to continue even while teams isolate the issue and restore normal performance. The retailers we work with are focused on understanding how their technology landscape behaves under sustained demand so they can respond with greater confidence while keeping the customer experience uninterrupted.
3. Maintain reliable transaction processing
Checkout often receives the most attention during the holiday shopping season, but the transaction itself is only one point in a much longer chain of business processes.
During peak demand, retailers rely on coordinated performance across:
- Pricing
- Payment processing
- Fraud detection
- Order management
- Inventory systems
When one part of that flow slows, the effects are felt well beyond checkout, influencing everything from conversion to fulfillment.
Once transactions begin to slow, recovery becomes increasingly difficult. Dependencies that normally operate in the background can quickly become bottlenecks, making it harder for teams to keep orders moving as demand continues to build. An end-to-end view of transaction performance reveals where dependencies create friction, giving technology teams a better opportunity to resolve issues before customers notice them.
4. Increase end-to-end supply chain visibility
The work doesn’t stop at checkout. It continues through the fulfillment process, where changing conditions can affect delivery timelines long after a purchase is complete. A delay in one area can quickly affect decisions elsewhere, especially when inventory and orders move at a much faster pace.
Supply chain visibility gives teams the context they need to respond as conditions evolve. Visibility creates time to act, so when teams can see where operations are beginning to slow, they can make adjustments before disruptions become customer-facing. During peak retail events, that level of visibility supports steadier execution across the business.
5. Turn observability into faster operational decisions
Peak retail events generate an extraordinary volume of operational data. The priority is identifying the signals that explain what’s happening across the business while there’s still time to respond. Performance metrics become far more meaningful when they’re viewed in the context of business operations.
That broader context helps teams distinguish between routine fluctuations and issues that require immediate attention. It also provides a clearer understanding of how systems perform under sustained demand, giving technology leaders practical insights they can apply before the next shopping season.
How ready is your retail operation?
Black Friday and Cyber Monday may span only a few days, yet they provide one of the clearest measures of operational readiness. By the time holiday traffic begins to surge, most of the important work has already been done. Readiness is reflected in the reliability of the technology ecosystem and the confidence teams have in the information guiding their decisions.
In our work with clients, these priorities extend well beyond the holiday shopping season. They reflect the capabilities organizations are investing in to modernize at a sustainable pace while continuing to rely on proven core systems. That means extending the value of proven core technologies while integrating new capabilities that improve agility without disrupting the systems the business depends on.
See how Rocket Software helped a U.S.-based POS provider deliver more efficient, secure retail payment experiences.

articles.title: Melissa Alston Selected as Craven County Information Technology Director

articles.article_title: Melissa Alston Selected as Craven County Information Technology Director
articles.heading: News Flash
articles.summary: Melissa Alston has been selected as Craven County’s Information Technology Director. A native of Rocky Mount, Alston is a seasoned local government technology leader with 25 years of public service ex
articles.content:
Melissa Alston has been selected as Craven County’s Information Technology Director. A native of Rocky Mount, Alston is a seasoned local government technology leader with 25 years of public service experience in North Carolina.
Prior to joining Craven County, Alston spent more than two decades with the City of Rocky Mount, most recently serving as PMO/IT Project Manager, where she led complex technology initiatives and cross-departmental projects. She previously served as Interim Chief Technology Officer, providing executive leadership for the city’s technology operations, cybersecurity, enterprise applications, infrastructure, technology strategy, and an $11 million operating budget. Her career has included roles in finance, customer service, project management, and technology, giving her a broad understanding of local government operations.
“We are very excited to have Melissa join our team,” said Jack B. Veit, III, Craven County Manager. “Her years of experience as a leader in local government technology prepare her well for this role. I look forward to seeing how her talents strengthen Craven County’s technology and cybersecurity needs.”
Alston holds a bachelor’s degree in public administration from Liberty University and an associate’s degree from Nash Community College. She is a Local Government Federal Credit Union (LFGCU) Civic Fellow, a leadership program that invests in emerging local government leaders and strengthens the connection between public service professionals and the communities they serve. She also serves as the Chair of the Professional Development Committee for the North Carolina Local Government Information Systems Association (NCLGISA), helping advance professional growth, knowledge-sharing, and leadership development among local government technology professionals across the state.
As Craven County’s IT Director, Alston will focus on strengthening technology and cybersecurity, advancing digital transformation, developing high-performing teams, and building strategic partnerships that position the County for continued growth and innovation.
Alston joined Craven County as Information Technology Director on August 26, 2026.

articles.summary: Police1's exclusive companion report to the “What Cops Want in 2026” survey reveals how officers want systems that work together, reduce duplicate work and help them spend more time on policing
articles.content:
Download your copy by completing the “Access this Police1 Resource” box on this page!
Technology is now part of nearly every patrol task — from receiving calls and running records checks to writing reports, reviewing video and documenting evidence. But Police1’s “What Cops Want in 2026” survey of 1,777 patrol officers found that the tools meant to support the job can also take time away from it.
Officers are not asking for more systems. They want reliable, connected technology that works in the field, cuts down on duplicate entry, and helps them get back to the calls, people and problems that need their attention.
This report examines the hidden technology tax on patrol time — and the practical questions agency leaders should ask before making their next technology investment.
Download this report to uncover:
- What officers say about the technology they rely on during every shift
- How slow systems, duplicate entry and disconnected platforms add time to routine work
- Why report writing and required documentation continue to take time away from patrol
- The field realities leaders should consider when evaluating new technology
- What officers want from training, support and technology implementation
- Practical questions to ask before investing in systems that affect patrol workflows
The standard for patrol technology should be simple: Does it help officers get information, document what matters and return to the work only people can do? Download the report for the findings and practical guidance.

articles.title: China’s Huawei branded a criminal enterprise as tech firm’s US trial opens
articles.description: China’s Huawei branded a criminal enterprise as tech firm’s US trial opens The Guardian
articles.description_html: China’s Huawei branded a criminal enterprise as tech firm’s US trial opens  The Guardian
articles.article_title: China’s Huawei branded a criminal enterprise as tech firm’s US trial opens
articles.heading: China’s Huawei branded a criminal enterprise as tech firm’s US trial opens
articles.summary: The defense says: ‘It’s about competition, not conspiracy’
articles.content:
A US prosecutor described China’s Huawei as a criminal enterprise that stole from US companies to build its telecommunications empire, as the trial against the tech company kicked off in Brooklyn federal court on Wednesday.
“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Taylor Stout, a trial attorney from the US Department of Justice, said in the government’s opening statement. “For 20 years, that’s how Huawei, a massive Chinese telecommunications company, victimized American companies and abused the American financial system, all in an effort to dominate the telecommunications industry around the world.”
Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from five US companies, including operating system source code for internet routers from Cisco Systems and a robotic arm to test phones from T-Mobile, to gain an unfair competitive advantage and grow its business, the prosecutor told jurors.
“We’ll hear from people who caught Huawei red-handed trying to steal American tech,” Stout said, adding there was video of an employee stealing the robotic arm.
The defense painted a very different picture of the company and its success in court.
“It’s about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct,” Brian Heberlig, one of a team of lawyers representing Huawei, said in his opening. “Huawei earned its success ... There was no blueprint for crime.”
Huawei is known for its telecommunications equipment, mobile phones and, in recent years, AI chips. It does business globally but its networking gear is restricted in the US and suppliers are banned from exporting US goods and technology to the company without approval from the Department of Commerce.
On Thursday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said “the Chinese government firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises,” when asked about the case and the US prosecutor’s “criminal enterprise” description.
China “firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests”, the spokesperson said at a regular press conference.
The case against Huawei began in 2018 with an indictment charging the company and its chief financial officer with bank fraud and sanctions violations for allegedly misrepresenting its business in Iran to get around US sanctions and move millions of dollars through the US financial system.
In the ensuing years, it grew into a sprawling indictment that includes racketeering, a pattern of illegal activity conducted by an enterprise to generate profit.
Heberlig, defending Huawei, told jurors that prosecutors will describe routine activities by global tech companies “but will twist those ordinary activities to try to make them look criminal”.
He said the incidents involving Cisco and T-mobile were “actions by individual employees” and that management worked to make things right after learning of them.
The prosecutor also accused the company of keeping the nature of its work in Iran secret so it could launder US dollars through the financial system and could help the Iranian government spy on its own citizens. The defense said there was no evidence Huawei knew the dollar-clearing would violate US sanctions law.
In 2018, Huawei’s chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, was detained in Vancouver after being picked up on a US warrant as a part of the original indictment. articles.content_html:
A US prosecutor described China’s Huawei as a criminal enterprise that stole from US companies to build its telecommunications empire, as ⁠the trial against the tech company kicked off in Brooklyn federal court on Wednesday.

“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Taylor Stout, a trial attorney from the US Department of Justice, said in the government’s opening statement. “For 20 years, that’s how Huawei, a massive Chinese telecommunications company, victimized American companies ⁠and abused the American financial system, all ⁠in an effort to dominate the telecommunications ​industry around the world.”

Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from five US companies, including operating system source code for internet routers from Cisco Systems and a robotic arm to test phones from T-Mobile, to gain an unfair competitive advantage and grow its business, ⁠the prosecutor told jurors.

“We’ll hear from people who caught Huawei red-handed trying to steal American tech,” Stout said, adding there was video of an employee stealing the robotic arm.

The defense painted a very different picture of the company and its success in court.

“It’s about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, ⁠not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct,” Brian Heberlig, one of a team of lawyers representing Huawei, said in his opening. “Huawei earned its success ... There was no blueprint for crime.”

Huawei is known ​for its telecommunications equipment, mobile phones and, in recent years, AI chips. It does ‌business globally but its networking gear is restricted in ‌the US and suppliers are banned from exporting US goods and technology to the company without approval from the Department of Commerce.

On Thursday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said “the Chinese ‌government firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises,” when asked about the case and the US prosecutor’s “criminal enterprise” description.

China “firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests”, the spokesperson said at a regular press conference.

The case against Huawei began in 2018 with an indictment charging the company and its chief financial officer with bank fraud and sanctions violations for allegedly misrepresenting its business in Iran to get around US sanctions and move millions of dollars through the US financial system.

In the ensuing years, it grew into a sprawling indictment that includes racketeering, a pattern of illegal activity conducted by an enterprise to generate profit.

Heberlig, defending Huawei, told jurors that prosecutors will describe routine activities ‌by global tech companies “but will twist those ordinary activities to try to make them look criminal”.

after newsletter promotion

He said the incidents involving Cisco and T-mobile were “actions by individual employees” and that ​management worked to make things right after learning of them.

The prosecutor also accused the company of keeping the nature of its work in Iran secret so it could launder US dollars through the financial system and could help the Iranian government spy on its own citizens. The defense said there was no evidence Huawei knew the dollar-clearing would violate US sanctions law.

In 2018, Huawei’s chief financial officer, ​Meng Wanzhou, was detained in Vancouver after being picked up on ​a US warrant as a part of the original indictment. She fought extradition for nearly three years before being freed to return to China ​in a diplomatic agreement between the US, China ‌and Canada.

The charges against her ​were dismissed in 2022 as part ​of a deferred prosecution agreement but admissions she made are set to be introduced as evidence at the trial, which is expected to last three months.

articles.title: Physical AI Takes the Wheel: How the World’s Robotaxi Leaders Are Building With NVIDIA Technologies
articles.description: Physical AI Takes the Wheel: How the World’s Robotaxi Leaders Are Building With NVIDIA Technologies NVIDIA Blog
articles.description_html: Physical AI Takes the Wheel: How the World’s Robotaxi Leaders Are Building With NVIDIA Technologies  NVIDIA Blog
articles.article_title: Physical AI Takes the Wheel: How the World’s Robotaxi Leaders Are Building With NVIDIA Technologies
articles.heading: Physical AI Takes the Wheel: How the World’s Robotaxi Leaders Are Building With NVIDIA Technologies
articles.summary: NVIDIA’s modular, full-stack robotaxi pipeline — a three-computer solution spanning AI training, simulation and in-vehicle computing — is being adopted across the robotaxi ecosystem.
articles.content:
The global robotaxi market — physical AI’s first commercial breakthrough — is projected to reach $400 billion by 2035, with over 6 million commercial vehicles in operation as driverless fleets are already moving people through some of the world’s busiest and most complex streets.
Deploying a driverless vehicle is one challenge. Scaling a fleet is a next-level computing challenge; it means delivering the same safe, reliable performance across thousands of vehicles.
Meeting those demands requires enormous amounts of compute across the robotaxi development lifecycle, from preparing and training AI models to simulating and validating driving behavior, as well as real-time processing in the vehicle.
NVIDIA provides an open platform for AI training, simulation and safety validation, with libraries, software development kits, workflows and models that developers can use alongside their own technology stacks.
Every major robotaxi program operating at commercial scale today is running on NVIDIA’s modular stack, spanning AI training, simulation, in-vehicle computing — or a combination of the three — to develop and deploy fleets at scale.
What Is a Robotaxi Technology Stack?
A robotaxi technology stack is the end-to-end set of technologies used to develop, validate and deploy autonomous vehicles (AVs) — from data and AI model training to simulation, safety validation and real-time in-vehicle computing.
NVIDIA’s robotaxi and AV platform brings these capabilities together in a three-computer solution: the model training computer, simulation and validation computer, and in-vehicle computer.
1. Training Computer: NVIDIA DGX
Robotaxi intelligence advances as programs turn growing volumes of fleet data into increasingly capable models. Driving models can be trained on NVIDIA DGX systems.
The NVIDIA Alpamayo portfolio of open reasoning vision language action (VLA) models, simulation frameworks and physical AI datasets gives developers building blocks they can adapt to their own data, requirements and technology stacks. Its reasoning models help address long-tail AV challenges by breaking complex driving situations into smaller steps, reasoning through each one and selecting the safest trajectory.
NVIDIA also provides physical AI datasets, reinforcement learning blueprints and recipes for post-training and distillation, helping developers optimize models for their target vehicles.
2. Simulation and Validation Computer: NVIDIA Omniverse and Cosmos on NVIDIA RTX PRO
Robotaxi programs can’t rely on physical miles alone to capture rare, long-tail driving scenarios. NVIDIA Omniverse NuRec models reconstruct real-world driving scenarios from sensor data, while NVIDIA Cosmos world foundation models generate physically based variations of them, enabling developers to turn thousands of real-world corner cases into millions of combinations of driving behavior, traffic, weather, lighting and sensor conditions.
Running on NVIDIA RTX PRO Servers, NVIDIA Omniverse and Cosmos support closed-loop simulation and validation. The NVIDIA AlpaSim simulation framework extends the workflow for training and evaluating reasoning-based autonomous-driving models, helping developers identify weaknesses before deployment.
3. In-Vehicle Computer and Sensor Architecture: NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion With DRIVE AGX
NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion is NVIDIA’s modular in-vehicle compute and sensor reference architecture for level-4-ready robotaxis. DRIVE Hyperion 10 pairs dual NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor systems-on-a-chip, built on the NVIDIA Blackwell platform, with 14 high-definition cameras, nine radars, three lidars and 12 ultrasonics for real-time, 360-degree sensor fusion. Its redundant compute and sensing design supports fail-operational driving if a sensor or compute component fails.
The dual DRIVE AGX Thor is designed to run modern AI workloads — including VLA models — for perception, reasoning, path planning and driving actions.
NVIDIA Halos provides a production-ready safety foundation through Halos OS, and a broader validation and certification framework spanning independent inspection, system validation, large-scale simulation and continuous testing from cloud to car.
Robotaxi Leaders Adopting NVIDIA’s Robotaxi Technology Stack
NVIDIA’s robotaxi ecosystem spans every region where commercial robotaxi services are emerging today: Asia, Europe, the Middle East and North America. Across these markets, mobility providers, AV developers and automakers are adopting NVIDIA’s three-computer architecture to train AI models, simulate and validate driving behavior, and deploy autonomous vehicles at scale.
Scaling Robotaxi Services Globally
- Uber is scaling its fleet of NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion, with plans to reach 28 cities by 2028. Uber and NVIDIA are also building a robotaxi AI data factory on NVIDIA Cosmos to curate fleet driving data for rare scenarios. Together, Uber and NVIDIA are collaborating with Autobrains, Avride, Lucid, May Mobility, Mercedes-Benz, Momenta, Nissan, Nuro, Pony.ai, Stellantis, Waabi, Wayve, WeRide and Zoox to bring NVIDIA-powered robotaxi services to the Uber platform.
- May Mobility is planning to operate autonomous ride-hailing services through Uber’s network, while developing its software stack on the NVIDIA DRIVE platform.
- Bolt uses NVIDIA technologies to develop and scale AVs across Europe.
- Lyft plans to use NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion as a reference architecture for future autonomous fleets. May Mobility vehicles are also currently operating on Lyft’s network in Atlanta, powered by NVIDIA DRIVE.
- Through its partnership with Grab, WeRide plans to bring its DRIVE Hyperion- and DRIVE AGX Thor-based GXR to key markets across Southeast Asia.
- Waymo partners with NVIDIA to help build its autonomous computing system.
Building Robotaxi Intelligence
Behind these services, AV developers are using NVIDIA accelerated computing, simulation and in-vehicle platforms to build the intelligence that operators and automakers deploy.
- Wayve, Nissan and Uber are developing a global robotaxi program using a prototype vehicle that combines Nissan’s vehicle engineering, Wayve’s embodied AI and the NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion platform.
- Autobrains is developing robotaxi programs with Uber in Munich and VinFast in Southeast Asia, built on NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion and enabled by Autobrains’ Agentic AI technology.
- Zoox uses NVIDIA DRIVE for in-vehicle computing and cloud-based training and simulation.
- Momenta is developing its software stack based on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX running on DriveOS.
- Pony.ai developed its new-generation autonomous-driving domain controller with NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion and DRIVE AGX Thor.
- Tensor is developing its level 4 Robocar with eight NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor systems-on-a-chip in its in-vehicle supercomputer.
- Waabi expands into the robotaxi market through a deployment collaboration with Uber; its Waabi Driver platform is built on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor.
- TIER IV and Isuzu are deploying level 4 autonomous buses built on NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion and DRIVE AGX Thor.
- Lenovo is supplying its NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor-based AD1 level 4 domain controller for a next-generation robotaxi program with SWM.
- DeepRoute.ai is developing a new generation of robotaxis built on the NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion platform with DRIVE AGX Thor.
Bringing Robotaxis Into Production
As these systems move from development into production, automakers are integrating NVIDIA technology into autonomous and robotaxi-ready vehicle programs.
- Tesla trains its autonomous-driving neural networks on NVIDIA supercomputers.
- Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA are collaborating with Uber to develop a robotaxi ecosystem based on the new S-Class, built on the NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion architecture, full-stack NVIDIA DRIVE AV L4 software, and NVIDIA Alpamayo open AI models, simulation tools and datasets to support reasoning-based, safety-first autonomy.
- Stellantis, Wayve and Uber are collaborating to develop and deploy L4 driverless mobility services, leveraging NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion and AI computing technologies.
- Lucid, Nuro and Uber are developing a global robotaxi service using NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor, part of the DRIVE Hyperion platform.
- Hyundai Motor and Kia are expanding their collaboration with NVIDIA to develop data-driven autonomous-driving systems built on NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion. NVIDIA will also explore expanded collaboration with Hyundai Motor Group’s joint venture, Motional, to advance level 4 robotaxi services.
- Geely, alongside its ecosystem partners, plans to develop and commercialize robotaxis using DRIVE Hyperion.
- Zeekr, a Geely Auto Group brand, has adopted DRIVE AGX Thor for a centralized domain controller.
From cloud to car, nearly every layer of the robotaxi platform is being developed on NVIDIA accelerated computing.
Explore NVIDIA’s complete platform for robotaxi development.

articles.title: Hydrofoil could provide link to Scilly, says firm
articles.description: Hydrofoil could provide link to Scilly, says firm bbc.com
articles.description_html: Hydrofoil could provide link to Scilly, says firm  bbc.com
articles.article_title: Hydrofoil could provide link to Isles of Scilly, says firm
articles.heading: Hydrofoil could provide link to Scilly, says firm
articles.summary: A marine technology company is running demonstrations of a hydrofoil which could run in winter.
articles.content:
Hydrofoil could provide link to Scilly, says firm
A marine technology firm has been showcasing an all-weather electric hydrofoil vessel it says could travel between Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly.
Artemis Technologies said the hydrofoil, which uses underwater wings to lift the boat out of the water, could operate in winter when seas are choppy.
John Patterson, from the firm, said said four days of demonstrations in Newlyn and St Mary's were "really exciting" for the region.
They follow a feasibility study run with the Council of the Isles of Scilly to see if the technology "could help make life easier for the locals" with "quick, clean, efficient transit".
If it gets the go-ahead Patterson said a full-size ferry could take 150 passengers at a speed of 32 knots between Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly in just over an hour.
"The whole joy of the hydrofoil system is it lifts the vessel out," he said, adding it made for a "more comfortable ride".
The feasibility study run with the council and transport firm Connected Places Catapult was aimed at showing "modern technology can provide an alternate solution which may be able to overcome the issues which the Isles of Scilly have in the depths of winter", he added.
Patterson said the firm was looking for an operator and the earliest it could arrive at the islands was "probably 18 months to two years, with fair winds behind us".
"This is all about showing that [with] modern technology there is a solution which can be adopted for cheap, fast transfer between the mainland and the Scilly Isles," he said.
Robert Francis, lead member for transport, economy of tourism at the Council of the Isles of Scilly said: "We are backing the project because we believe it may well be a really good opportunity for us.
"Our community is struggling with unaffordable passenger fares and unaffordable freight costs and this really green 100% electric vessel is going to be the future we believe."
He said it would be "huge" if the boat could run through the winter as "we've got families marooned on the islands".
"We're hoping this is going to operate all year round and it's going to give us some affordable travel because connectivity is everything for us," he said.

articles.title: CiCLO® Technology Expands Across Home Textiles from Market Week to Climate Week
articles.description: CiCLO® Technology Expands Across Home Textiles from Market Week to Climate Week Yahoo Finance
articles.description_html: CiCLO® Technology Expands Across Home Textiles from Market Week to Climate Week  Yahoo Finance
articles.article_title: CiCLO® Technology Expands Across Home Textiles from Market Week to Climate Week
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Intrinsic Advanced Materials is expanding the commercial reach of CiCLO® technology across home and hospitality textiles this September with ADVANSA and HeiQ, followed by its partnership with Lonely Whale's Fashion the Future activation during NYC Climate Week.
articles.content:
ADVANSA and HeiQ collaborations create new opportunities for home and hospitality products as Intrinsic Advanced Materials brings the CiCLO ® technology story to NYC Climate Week

NEW YORK, Sept. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Intrinsic Advanced Materials is expanding the commercial reach of CiCLO® technology across home and hospitality textiles this September with ADVANSA and HeiQ, followed by its partnership with Lonely Whale's Fashion the Future activation during NYC Climate Week.

ADVANSA is introducing Suprelle® fiberfill made with CiCLO fibers, extending CiCLO technology into an established premium fiberfill portfolio designed around comfort and performance. At the same time, a collaboration with HeiQ Materials AG is creating opportunities to pair CiCLO fibers with functional technologies that address specific product needs, including cooling, moisture management, freshness and allergen reduction.

Together, the developments give manufacturers, brands and retailers more ways to create products around specific consumer needs while incorporating CiCLO technology designed to help reduce microplastic fiber persistence.

Microplastic fiber pollution caused by the shedding of synthetic textiles is one of the most prevalent forms of microplastic pollution. CiCLO® technology is a patented textile ingredient integrated into polyester and nylon fibers during manufacturing. It creates pathways designed to accelerate biodegradation when microplastic fibers enter end-of-life environments with moisture and microorganisms, reducing their persistence. Third-party laboratories independently test CiCLO fibers using recognized ASTM and ISO methods.

ADVANSA Adds CiCLO ® Technology to Suprelle ® Fiberfill Portfolio

ADVANSA is introducing Suprelle® fiberfill made with CiCLO® fibers for bedding, home and hospitality applications, bringing CiCLO technology into an established premium fiberfill portfolio built around comfort and performance.

The Suprelle portfolio gives product developers a range of fiberfill options designed around specific product needs, including cooling, down-like comfort, adaptable support, lasting loft and resilience, lightweight support, moisture management and recycled fiber options. This allows brands and retailers to select the comfort and performance attributes appropriate for pillows, comforters and other bedding products while incorporating CiCLO fibers.

"Our customers want fiberfill that delivers the comfort and performance consumers expect while helping support broader environmental priorities," said Jean-Christophe Rouyer, head of global business development at ADVANSA. "Adding CiCLO technology gives them another way to differentiate Suprelle products without changing the core benefits of the fiberfill."

HeiQ Collaboration Expands Functional Possibilities

Intrinsic Advanced Materials is also collaborating with Swiss materials innovator HeiQ to explore how CiCLO fibers can be paired with functional technologies across home, hospitality and apparel applications.

The collaboration gives manufacturers and brands access to a range of performance possibilities, including cooling and thermal comfort, allergen reduction, odor control and freshness, moisture management and faster drying.

Combined, the technologies create opportunities across bed linens, pillows, mattress protectors, mattress toppers, mattress ticking and apparel products. Product developers can select functionality based on application needs while incorporating CiCLO fibers designed to help reduce microplastic fiber persistence.

"Brands are looking for ways to build more functionality into products without adding complexity," said Mike Abbott, executive vice president of advanced materials and general manager, HeiQ USA. "Combining HeiQ technologies with CiCLO fibers gives developers more flexibility to create products around the performance benefits their customers value."

From Market Week to Climate Week

The conversation continues during NYC Climate Week, where Intrinsic Advanced Materials is partnering with Lonely Whale's Fashion the Future activation at PlanetHAUS, Sept. 21 and 22. The activation is open for drop-in visits from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. both days. Register here .

CiCLO technology will be featured within The Fashion Stream, an educational experience that follows textiles through upstream, production and downstream stages. Positioned within the production stage, CiCLO technology illustrates how innovation introduced when synthetic fibers are made can address microplastic fiber persistence if those fibers later enter the environment.

The Market Week collaborations demonstrate CiCLO technology moving into commercially relevant products, while Fashion the Future connects that adoption to the larger challenge of microplastic fiber pollution and the role material choices can play in reducing persistence.

"CiCLO sets a new industry paradigm," said Cheryl Smyre, vice president of Parkdale Advanced Materials. "Our collaboration with ADVANSA and HeiQ intersects highly functional chemistries and fiber performance with science to accelerate practical textile solutions. Our work with Lonely Whale's Fashion the Future amplifies awareness and represents a vital step forward in tackling the broader microplastic fiber crisis."

About Intrinsic Advanced Materials and CiCLO ® Technology

Intrinsic Advanced Materials, LLC (IAM), a joint venture between Intrinsic Textiles Group, LLC and Parkdale Advanced Materials, Inc., develops and commercializes advanced biodegradable technologies for the global textile industry, focusing on innovation and scalable solutions. articles.heading: 'We never recovered him': Quest to identify remains from Ground Zero continues
articles.summary: Since the attacks, New York officials are working with new, complex technology to find traces of more than 1,000 victims.
articles.content:
'We never recovered him': Quest to identify remains from Ground Zero continues
For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life is his mangled firefighter helmet.
Scauso's father, Dennis - part of a New York City Fire Department (FDNY) hazmat unit for 12 years - initially was not scheduled to work on 11 September, 2001, but switched shifts for the overtime pay.
The Long Island father of four was likely in the South Tower of the World Trade Center when it collapsed, the Scauso family was told. The helmet with his badge number was found months later.
"I've spent essentially my entire life knowing my father died, and learning to live with the fact that we never recovered him," said Scauso, who was four when he died.
Dennis Scauso is one of more than 1,000 people killed on September 11 in New York who have yet to be identified, according to New York City's Office of Chief Medical Examiner. Nearly 3,000 people died in the World Trade Center attacks that day.
Last month, the city announced the identity of a previously unknown victim of the terrorist attacks - the 1,654th person - using a new technology called forensic investigative genetic genealogy - or FIGG.
"There is real promise in using this approach," said Angela Soler, director of forensic anthropology in the city's medical examiner office. "There's hope for more families to receive answers, and hopefully we'll be able to test more remains in the future using this technology as well."
Since 9/11, Soler's office has sought to identify the remains of the 2,753 victims who died in the World Trade Center. So far, 60 percent of those killed have been identified.
"It's been one of the most complex identification efforts that I think anybody has ever really experienced," Soler said.
25 years later, DNA matches are still being made
Efforts to identify victims have been complicated by a number of factors.
Human remains were damaged in the plane crashes and fires caused by jet fuel, meaning the office had only portions of victims for DNA samples, Soler said.
Scauso added that because of the timing of the attacks, many firefighters were changing shifts, but some stayed to help, grabbing whatever extra gear they could find. This meant some first responders recovered were wearing uniforms with others' names, complicating identification.
The World Trade Center site also had many more victims than the other 9/11 terrorist attack sites.
The remains of five of the 184 people killed when American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon were never identified because of similar conditions. According to the National Park Service, enough remains were recovered to use DNA, dental records and fingerprints to identify all 40 victims aboard United Airlines flight 93, which crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
Remains from the World Trade Center have been packaged and sealed to help preserve DNA for testing in the years to come. Soon after the attacks, individuals were identified using fingerprints or dental records, but as time went on, when neither was available, the office turned to DNA. Officials were able to use new technology to extract DNA and retest the same remains.
"That's why all these years down the road, we're still getting new identifications, because we're just continuing to retest and retry with every new technology that becomes available," Soler said.
DNA technology has helped the office identify 1,495 victims since 9/11 - some solely with DNA and others with multiple methods - according to the medical examiner's office.
Last year, the city announced that with the help of DNA, 24 years later, it had identified three new victims - Ryan Fitzgerald, a 26-year-old currency trader, Babara Keating, a 72-year-old who was aboard American Airlines Flight 11 from Boston to Los Angeles, and a woman whose family kept her identity private.
Soler said the new FIGG technology uses whole genome sequencing - which provides a way to read someone's entire genetic code. It means investigators can make more potential matches to family members who are more distant relatives of the victim. Once those matches are made, the New York Police Department helps find relatives who are closer to the victims.
Reopening old wounds
The medical examiner's office in New York still gets weekly calls from loved ones asking about someone whose remains were never recovered.
Many have never been able to bury a loved one, but some families choose to leave the remains - once found - at a repository at the 9/11 memorial site in New York. The repository was built into the bedrock of the World Trade Center site and can only be accessed by medical examiner staff. A nearby private space, known as the reflection room, is available for families to mourn.
"That's where their loved one was in their last moments, and that's where they want them to stay", Soler said.
Some don't want to be notified, perhaps because the confirmation is too painful, said Soler, who helps inform families.
Scauso is one of those people. She knows people who, in recent years, got a call that a relative finally has been identified. The thought of being next on the list is scary for her family, who has worked hard to keep the memory of her father - a jack of all trades and a lover of jazz - alive.
"At this point, an identification wouldn't change the reality of his death. It wouldn't give me back my father, and I don't necessarily want to reopen something that has become part of the way I've learned to live and grieve," she said. "Especially 25 years later, it's going to open up the wounds again."
But, Scauso said, the technology is important.
Soler has seen the news provide a mix of both relief and sadness. "It's confirmation of something that they always knew to be true - they knew their loved one died on 9/11, but I think for many families, there's still that question in the back of their mind until the remains are formally identified," Soler said.
"Maybe they're reliving it a little bit more now, having this new identification. But at the same time, it closes one chapter of their journey after 9/11," she added.
To Soler - and some of her current colleagues who also were on the ground during 9/11 - the work is deeply personal. Workers from their office arrived at Ground Zero after the planes hit the towers, and were there when the buildings collapsed.
They are aware it is unlikely they will identify every victim of the New York attacks. In some instances, there may be no remains of a victim at all. Still, they have no plans to stop.
"As long as there's families looking for answers, we'll continue searching for them," she said.

New national survey finds 79% of Americans don't believe physical security has significantly improved in buildings since 9/11

CUPERTINO, Calif., Sept. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks reshaped aviation security in the United States, a new national survey finds most Americans do not believe physical security in the country's buildings has kept pace. According to the survey, 79% of U.S. adults do not believe physical security has significantly improved since 9/11, and 76% say office buildings never received investment comparable to what went into airports. The survey, conducted by YouGov, is the first national survey to measure public trust in badge- and credential-based physical security systems, 25 years after 9/11.

The survey was funded by Alcatraz after a summer of security breaches at four prominent U.S. buildings. In May, an intruder tailgated students through secured doors into UCLA dormitories, where he is accused of sexually assaulting four women in their rooms. That same week, a man followed a student through a card-secured gate and then a badge-secured door at Harvard University's Lowell House. He attempted to kidnap a female undergrad before she fought him off with the help of other students. In June, two people purchased tickets to the Empire State Building's 86th-floor observatory, hid inside after closing, and cut through two locks overnight to reach restricted floors. They went undetected until they livestreamed the breach from the building's spire to nearly two million followers that afternoon. Weeks later, a man followed an employee through a badge-secured door at 30 Rockefeller Center in New York and confronted TODAY show anchor Craig Melvin, before being detained by security.

Three of the four incidents involved tailgating, in which an unauthorized person follows someone with a valid credential through a secured door. It is the number one breach of secure spaces. Security industry researchers have identified tailgating as a persistent vulnerability in badge-based access control systems, which are designed to verify a credential but not the identity of the person using it.

"We have spent 25 years upgrading aviation security with the latest technologies but have not kept pace in the spaces where most of us live and work. Keycard and badge technology is 30 years old. It is completely unintelligent. These headline breaches this summer are a warning about the need to upgrade physical security in our buildings, and Americans are saying it is urgent, " said Tina D'Agostin, CEO of Alcatraz AI. D'Agostin is a security expert who helped shape physical security efforts for Chase Center and Salesforce Tower while at Johnson Controls.

Survey findings

- 79% of Americans do not believe physical security has significantly improved since 9/11.

79% of Americans do not believe physical security has significantly improved since 9/11.

- 76% say office buildings never received investment on par with aviation security.

76% say office buildings never received investment on par with aviation security.

- 73% call upgrading physical security technology at least somewhat urgent.

73% call upgrading physical security technology at least somewhat urgent.

- 53% say they feel less safe in public than they did 25 years ago.

53% say they feel less safe in public than they did 25 years ago.

- 64% say buildings with large numbers of occupants should be legally required to detect and report a security breach in real time — including 69% of Democrats and 72% of Republicans, one of the few security questions in the survey where both parties agree.

64% say buildings with large numbers of occupants should be legally required to detect and report a security breach in real time — including 69% of Democrats and 72% of Republicans, one of the few security questions in the survey where both parties agree.

- 60% say they do not trust the organizations responsible for their security to keep systems up to date.

60% say they do not trust the organizations responsible for their security to keep systems up to date.

- 58% are already aware that key cards and badges can be duplicated or shared as a security gap.

58% are already aware that key cards and badges can be duplicated or shared as a security gap.

- 43% incorrectly believe that standard badge and key-card systems already alert security in real time when an anomaly, such as tailgating, occurs. Most such systems only log that a valid credential was used.

43% incorrectly believe that standard badge and key-card systems already alert security in real time when an anomaly, such as tailgating, occurs. Most such systems only log that a valid credential was used.

- 68% believe a tailgater at their location would not be caught quickly — only 32% believe detection would be immediate or within a few minutes.

68% believe a tailgater at their location would not be caught quickly — only 32% believe detection would be immediate or within a few minutes.

"I spent a big part of my career securing airports. After 9/11, airports received investment, became more secure and learned to balance security with the passenger experience. We never did the same for the buildings people spend their days in. Nuclear and energy companies, data centers and critical infrastructure use state of the art technology. Updating technology to secure everyday spaces is long overdue, and the survey shows Americans understand that, " said Matthew Powell, Senior Director of Infrastructure Markets at Alcatraz AI.

About Alcatraz AI Alcatraz is known as the Face ID of physical spaces. Alcatraz is an AI-powered physical access control company headquartered in Cupertino, California. Its flagship product, the Rock, replaces badge-based and legacy biometric security with fully anonymized facial authentication and real-time tailgating detection. Alcatraz AI is trusted where security standards are highest and certifications hardest to earn: hyperscale data centers, financial institutions, airports, and nuclear and energy infrastructure. Its technology protects professional sports teams from the NBA to the NFL, Fortune 100 companies, universities, stadiums, and private individuals.

  • 60% say they do not trust the organizations responsible for their security to keep systems up to date.

  • 58% are already aware that key cards and badges can be duplicated or shared as a security gap.

  • 43% incorrectly believe that standard badge and key-card systems already alert security in real time when an anomaly, such as tailgating, occurs. Most such systems only log that a valid credential was used.

  • 68% believe a tailgater at their location would not be caught quickly — only 32% believe detection would be immediate or within a few minutes.

"I spent a big part of my career securing airports. After 9/11, airports received investment, became more secure and learned to balance security with the passenger experience. We never did the same for the buildings people spend their days in. Nuclear and energy companies, data centers and critical infrastructure use state of the art technology. Updating technology to secure everyday spaces is long overdue, and the survey shows Americans understand that," said Matthew Powell, Senior Director of Infrastructure Markets at Alcatraz AI.

About Alcatraz AI
Alcatraz is known as the Face ID of physical spaces. Alcatraz is an AI-powered physical access control company headquartered in Cupertino, California. Its flagship product, the Rock, replaces badge-based and legacy biometric security with fully anonymized facial authentication and real-time tailgating detection. Alcatraz AI is trusted where security standards are highest and certifications hardest to earn: hyperscale data centers, financial institutions, airports, and nuclear and energy infrastructure. Its technology protects professional sports teams from the NBA to the NFL, Fortune 100 companies, universities, stadiums, and private individuals.

articles.heading: High school students invited to Trades and Technology Day at Highlands College
articles.summary: High school students invited to Trades and Technology Day at Highlands College Montana Tech
articles.content:
Climb a utility pole. Change a tire. Build a wall. Take an X-ray. Trades and Technology Day at Highlands College of Montana Tech gives Montana high school students a chance to trade the classroom for hands-on career exploration on Wednesday, October 7, 2026.
“This is such an exciting opportunity for students, and one of our favorite events to host,” Director of Workforce and K-12 partnerships Kinsley Bennett said. “We love creating opportunities for students to step outside the classroom, explore possibilities they may have never considered, and discover new interests through hands-on experiences. It’s inspiring to see students engage, ask questions, and envision what their future could look like.”
Students will remain with their school throughout the day, with each school selecting their top three career programs for students to explore. Highlands College will organize each school’s experience around their selected programs, providing engaging, hands-on learning opportunities in areas such as automotive, broadband technology, civil engineering technology, healthcare, commercial equipment and driving operations, computer networks and cybersecurity, construction, mining technology, precision machining, web development, welding, and the pre-apprentice line program.
Students will also visit the Industry Room to explore local industries, learn about career opportunities, and discover the skills and training employers are looking for.
Trades and Technology Day will run from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Wednesday, October 7, at Highlands College, 25 Basin Creek Road in Butte. Lunch will be provided for students; dietary restrictions should be shared in advance. Space is limited, so students and schools are encouraged to register early. Chaperones are required to attend with schools, and students registering individually are required to bring a parent or guardian. Register at this link. Schools are encouraged to register students individually. To register a school as a group, contact Kinsley Bennett at krafish@mtech.edu or (406) 496-4684.
Trades and Technology Day is designed to help students explore the dynamic fields of trades and technology through hands-on learning. Students can discover programs that combine creativity, technical expertise and practical skills while learning more about potential career pathways.
