articles.article_title: Technology to debug code is hard, but people are harder
articles.heading: Technology to debug code is hard, but people are harder
articles.summary: Lauren Giroux, a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, said this during a leaders panel at an AWS event I attended in Arlington this summer. I laughed internally, recalling all
articles.content:
Lauren Giroux, a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, said this during a leaders panel at an AWS event I attended in Arlington this summer. I laughed internally, recalling all the hours I spent studying for my computer organization final and nights spent surviving on Red Bull and white Monster Energy, chasing bugs and staring at error messages destined to drive me insane.
But I wrote the line down.
As frustrating as technology can be, there is almost always a plan of action: an error to trace, documentation to read or another approach to try. People are different. There is no disclaimer or pop-up on our foreheads when you misunderstand someone, no rulebook for earning someone’s trust and no algorithm for figuring out what a person actually needs.
It has been a few weeks since I met Giroux and had the opportunity to talk to her about everything tech and people, and I’m still pondering this enough to write an article about it.
I think the line stuck with me because it perfectly encapsulates my journey as a computer science student. In class, we may learn about data structures, algorithms or system design. Even so, coming to terms with how to communicate, work in teams and comprehend people is something we can’t necessarily learn within the walls of the Classroom Building or Whittemore Hall.
Understanding what a stakeholder or client wants and truly needs, beyond what they explicitly tell you, means reading between the lines and thinking outside the box. However, doing those things is a different story. They can be harder to learn than data structures or system design. Then again, let’s be honest, people are a lot more fun. I would personally prefer my best friend listening to me yap about some annoying guy at work over a time complexity problem.
It does, however, make me wonder. We signed up to study fields built around solving technically hard problems, all the while forgetting the fact of the matter: that some of the hardest problems are human.
Ironically, we call many of the skills required to solve those problems “soft skills.” Maybe we call them “soft” not because they are easy, but because they are difficult to quantify.
You can put Python on a resume, earn an AWS certification and pass a technical interview. There is no certification for knowing when to shut up and listen, no LeetCode problem for resolving a disagreement and no grade for making somebody feel acknowledged and understood. Yet those skills might determine whether all the technical knowledge you’ve spent years acquiring actually becomes useful to anyone.
This feels increasingly relevant as artificial intelligence becomes better at doing more of the technical work itself. Technical systems can process information about a person. AI can identify patterns and suggest explanations. Nevertheless, there will always be a difference between recognizing a pattern and sitting across from someone and trying to understand why they’re frustrated, confused or simply not getting what they need.
Jennifer Murtell, writing for the American Marketing Association, makes a similar distinction: Technology may be getting better at predicting our behavior, but that does not necessarily make it capable of empathizing with how we feel.
You can get mad at Alexa for playing the wrong song or Siri for calling the wrong person, but they are not holding grudges against you; that girl who sat next to you in physics who you gave the wrong iClicker answer to in week eight might. ChatGPT will validate you more than any man ever will. Maybe that is also your cue to stop asking it for relationship advice and giving it lore drops. It is fine. Been there, done that.
I have no idea what the employment landscape will look like over the next few years. Regardless of whether we are writing code ourselves (which we already barely are), directing AI to write it or using tools that do not exist yet, technology will ultimately have human intervention.
As long as that is true, maybe the skills we call “soft” will be some of the hardest ones to replace.

articles.title: Humans need to 'surf the wave' of AI rather than get swallowed by it, Chesky says at Communacopia
articles.description: Humans need to 'surf the wave' of AI rather than get swallowed by it, Chesky says at Communacopia CNBC
articles.description_html: Humans need to 'surf the wave' of AI rather than get swallowed by it, Chesky says at Communacopia  CNBC
articles.article_title: Humans need to 'surf the wave' of AI rather than get swallowed by it, Chesky says at Communacopia
articles.heading: Humans need to 'surf the wave' of AI rather than get swallowed by it, Chesky says at Communacopia
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, and SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen are set to speak at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference.
articles.content:
The Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference continued on Thursday with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, and SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen among the notable names set to take the stage.
Artificial intelligence has been a big topic of discussion so far at the annual meeting of top executives, which started Tuesday.
AirBnb CEO Brian Chesky said the technology wasn't "inherently good or bad" in an interview with CNBC's David Faber that aired Thursday. He said the technology's potential is in human hands.
"I'm not confident I'm right. I'm not confident that it's going to be positive, but I think it can be. It's like nuclear power; it can either light up a city or destroy a city," Chesky said.
He added that his AI theory is of a "cognitive revolution" that helps humans get smarter along with the technology.
"We need to remind people of how valuable they will be to society, and that AI is a wave, and we can surf the wave rather than get swallowed underneath the water," he said.
Earlier this week, a former Anthropic researcher quit his job on Tuesday, warning that the rapidly-evolving tech "could kill us all by the end of the decade."
"Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing," researcher Jacob Coxon wrote in a post on X.
The post set off a wider debate around the technology and leading AI labs, which are already under scrutiny for recent rogue agent cyberattacks.
The cybersecurity threats that AI poses have become a political lightning rod ahead of the midterm elections, as lawmakers face more pressure about regulating the technology and public angst around AI's data center buildout grows.
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., formally launched an investigation on Wednesday into an OpenAI agent's hack into Hugging Face, according to The Information.

articles.content:
AVANTech delivers expert design, NQA-1 fabrication, and innovative solid and liquid waste treatment technologies, plus specialty packaging Solutions and precision glovebox systems – engineered to meet the most demanding nuclear and environmental requirements. Explore our new website at avantechllc.com.

Learn More

Mark Peters [email protected]

Perhaps at no point in recent years has an issue of Nuclear News devoted to new technology had more ground to cover. We are in the midst of a unique moment for nuclear energy. Outside the nuclear sector, emerging technologies are driving up electricity demand and creating new urgency around the need for clean, firm power. Within the industry, meanwhile, long-standing assumptions about reactor technologies, fuels, sizes, and applications are being reexamined at a scale not seen since the sector’s earliest days.

That reexamination is evident in the range of reactor concepts now attracting serious investment and commercial interest. Alongside the large, light water–cooled, low enriched uranium–fueled reactors that make up today’s operating fleet, developers are advancing designs ranging from single-digit to hundreds of megawatts and incorporating TRISO fuels, molten salts, gas coolants, liquid metals, and other technologies. Fusion developers are pursuing an equally diverse set of concepts, with dozens of companies exploring different fuels, confinement methods, materials, and pathways to commercialization.

Reactor design, however, is only one part of the innovation taking place across the nuclear enterprise.

The features in this month’s issue illustrate that breadth. They examine the history and continued development of TRISO fuel, Constellation’s digital modernization of its operating fleet, and PSEG’s work to establish commercial-scale cobalt-60 production in pressurized water reactors. These efforts differ greatly in their technologies and applications, but each demonstrates how innovation can improve performance, expand capabilities, and create new value from nuclear energy.

Many of these developments are also reaching audiences well beyond our industry. Major fundraising announcements, construction milestones, and reactor criticalities are drawing public attention. At the same time, support for nuclear energy appears to be growing as more people recognize its environmental and economic benefits.

What may be less apparent to the public—but is well understood within the nuclear community—is that the companies and technologies making headlines today stand on the shoulders of generations of researchers, engineers, operators, and institutions.

Today’s start-ups would not exist without yesterday’s research. The scientific knowledge, experimental facilities, materials data, operating experience, and regulatory understanding developed over many decades have created the foundation on which the current generation of innovators is building.

Consider the Experimental Breeder Reactor-II. The sodium-cooled, metal-fueled fast reactor operated from 1964 to 1994 and supported hundreds of fuel and materials experiments. Its work substantially advanced our understanding of liquid-metal reactor systems and continues to inform designs under development today, including TerraPower’s Natrium reactor and Oklo’s Aurora reactor.

EBR-II’s contribution did not end with its shutdown. Its containment structure is being repurposed as Idaho National Laboratory’s Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments (DOME) facility, where new reactor concepts will be tested safely for years to come. A facility built to advance one generation of nuclear technology will now help enable the next.

That continuity is important. New technologies are not simply tools for producing clean electricity, critical radioisotopes, industrial heat, or other valuable products. They are also platforms through which we expand our knowledge, improve our methods, and prepare the way for future advances.

Technology creates a powerful cycle at the core of our industry. Scientific knowledge enables practical applications, and those applications generate new knowledge. Each experiment, demonstration, and deployment adds to the foundation available to those who follow.

Like many across the nuclear community, I hope today’s momentum translates rapidly into operating facilities and electrons on the grid. Project execution and deployment matter, and the need for nuclear energy’s benefits is immediate.

But the significance of the work underway today extends beyond the projects now attracting attention. The knowledge we generate, the facilities we build, and the lessons we learn will be used by innovators for decades to come. That is how progress in nuclear energy has always been made—and how we will continue building its future.

articles.content:
WASHINGTON, Sept. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Riverside Research , a leading technology research and development nonprofit supporting U.S. national security, announces the appointment of Tom Lash as president and CEO. Lash is a recognized technology and business leader with nearly 30 years of experience supporting the federal market, bringing extensive expertise in national security, the U.S. intelligence community, strategic growth and emerging technology. Under his leadership, Riverside Research's nonprofit, mission-first identity and independent research model will continue to guide strategic priorities.

"Tom's proven ability to lead complex national security organizations, advance emerging technologies, and build trusted relationships across the intelligence community made him the clear choice to lead Riverside Research," said Jim Shields, chair of the Riverside Research Board of Trustees. "His strategic vision and mission-focused leadership will position the organization for continued growth while preserving the technical excellence and sponsor-focused culture that distinguishes Riverside Research."

Lash most recently served as CEO of Vibrint, a leading federal technology innovator. Lash led multiple acquisition strategies and expanded technology partnerships to build Vibrint into a highly competitive national security technology company with capabilities spanning AI, cyber, cloud, high-performance computing, mission resilience, quantum and next-generation communications.

Before joining Vibrint, he spent six years at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he created and led the Federal Delivery Organization responsible for contract execution across AWS's U.S. federal portfolio. He also led AWS's U.S. national security account team of more than 125 cleared technology professionals.

"Riverside Research has a distinguished legacy of technical innovation and trusted support to the national security community," Lash said. "I am honored to join the organization and look forward to working with its talented team to accelerate growth, deepen our sponsor partnerships, expand the impact of our research and mission solutions and advance next-generation research in AI/ML, sensing and secure architectures."

Before joining AWS, Lash held several leadership positions at SAIC and Leidos, including chief technology officer and chief strategy officer for the companies' intelligence systems and defense groups. He also led a series of progressively larger business portfolios focused predominantly on the U.S. intelligence community.

Lash's appointment comes as Riverside Research looks to build on its strong foundation, pursue strategic growth and advance its impact across the national security community.

Lash succeeds Steven Omick, Ph.D., who chose to step down after a decade of leadership that strengthened Riverside Research's sponsor relationships, research enterprise and position as a trusted national security partner.

Lash earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Virginia, a master's degree in electrical and computer engineering from George Mason University, and an MBA from Johns Hopkins University. He also serves as an adjunct lecturer at Georgetown University, where he teaches graduate cloud security.

About Riverside Research

Riverside Research is a national security nonprofit serving the Department of War and the U.S. intelligence community. Through its Open Innovation Center, Riverside Research invests in multidisciplinary research and development and encourages collaboration. WIU School of Engineering and Technology to Take Students to IMTS 2026

September 10, 2026

MACOMB/MOLINE, IL — Western Illinois University's School of Engineering and Technology is planning a student trip to the International Manufacturing Technology Show (IMTS) 2026 on Thursday, Sept. 17, at McCormick Place in Chicago, IL. Approximately 55 WIU students, faculty and staff are expected to participate in the trip, including students from the engineering programs at the WIU-Quad Cities campus and engineering technology programs at the Macomb campus. IMTS is the largest manufacturing technology trade show in the Western Hemisphere and provides students with an opportunity to experience some of the newest advancements in manufacturing and engineering technology firsthand. The event traces its history to 1927, when it began as the National Machine Tool Builders' Exposition. Over the decades, the show evolved into today's International Manufacturing Technology Show and has served as a showcase for technologies and approaches designed to make manufacturing faster, more precise and more efficient. Innovations in CNC, CAD, CAM, CAE and 3D printing are among the technologies introduced to the industry through IMTS during its nearly 100-year history. For WIU students, the trip provides an opportunity to see current technology in automation, design, manufacturing, robotics and related industrial equipment, including equipment and processes students may otherwise encounter only after entering the workforce. Beyond experiencing the technology on display, students will have the opportunity to interact with industry professionals and companies from across the manufacturing sector. The show provides a valuable networking environment for students to explore potential career, internship and professional development opportunities. IMTS 2026 will also feature a Student Summit designed specifically to connect students with manufacturing and engineering careers while building professional and leadership skills. Programming includes opportunities focused on communication, problem-solving and teamwork led by industry experts. By bringing together students from WIU's Macomb and Quad Cities campuses, the trip also provides an opportunity for students across the School of Engineering and Technology's programs to connect while experiencing one of the world's premier manufacturing technology events. For more information about the WIU School of Engineering and Technology, visit wiu.edu/SET .

articles.description: UNM expands academic commitment to quantum information science, engineering and technology UNM Newsroom
articles.description_html: UNM expands academic commitment to quantum information science, engineering and technology  UNM Newsroom
articles.article_title: UNM expands academic commitment to quantum information science, engineering and technology
articles.heading: UNM expands academic commitment to quantum information science, engineering and technology
articles.summary: As New Mexico makes significant investments to establish itself as a leader in quantum technology, The University of New Mexico is expanding its academic efforts to prepare students for the opportunities emerging alongside this growing industry and new...
articles.content:
As New Mexico makes significant investments to establish itself as a leader in quantum technology, The University of New Mexico is expanding its academic efforts to prepare students for the opportunities emerging alongside this growing industry and new era of discovery.
UNM will build on its existing programs in quantum information science and engineering (QISE), with a focus on strengthening academic pathways, aligning curriculum with emerging workforce needs, expanding faculty capacity, and connecting students with research and career opportunities.
“New Mexico is making a significant investment in its future, and UNM has an important responsibility in that work,” said Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs Barbara Rodríguez. “For us, this is about preparing our students for opportunities that are taking shape in our state and building on the tremendous expertise that already exists across our University.”
UNM already has a strong academic foundation in QISE. Undergraduate and graduate courses are offered across four departments; graduate students can pursue quantum concentrations within four degree programs; and UNM offers a graduate certificate in Quantum Science and Technology that is open to students from multiple graduate programs.
Building on this foundation, UNM will review existing curriculum, identify opportunities to integrate quantum concepts and skills across courses and programs, evaluate the need for new academic offerings, and strengthen pathways connecting students to coursework, research experiences and careers.
Faculty will be central to the effort. UNM already has significant expertise related to quantum science and technology across multiple disciplines, including 19 faculty fellows in the Quantum New Mexico Institute. The University will invest in additional faculty hiring to add teaching and research capacity, complement existing expertise, and support the continued development of quantum education and research at UNM.
Rodríguez emphasized that the opportunity extends well beyond traditional quantum disciplines.
“The strength of UNM is the breadth of our academic community,” Rodríguez said. “Quantum may begin with science and technology, but its impact reaches much further. There are important questions involving business, education, ethics, policy, communication, workforce development, health and society. A comprehensive research university like UNM brings those perspectives together.”
The expansion of UNM's academic offerings complements the University's growing quantum research and infrastructure and will help connect education, research, and workforce development as New Mexico's quantum ecosystem grows.
“Our goal is to build on what UNM already does well, create meaningful connections across disciplines and make sure our students are prepared for the opportunities ahead,” Rodríguez said.

Dollar General Literacy Foundation grants to fund books, technology at local schools
JONESBORO, Ark. (KAIT) - The Dollar General Literacy Foundation has awarded $90,000 in youth literacy grants to Arkansas schools, libraries and nonprofit organizations.
Several Northeast Arkansas schools are among those sharing in the donation.
Northeast Arkansas grant recipients
- Brookland: Brookland Elementary School—$2,500
- Jonesboro: Westside Consolidated School District—$2,500
- Melbourne: Melbourne School District—$4,000
- Pangburn: Pangburn School District—$3,500
- Searcy: Searcy School District—$1,500
- Trumann: Trumann Elementary School—$3,000
- Trumann: Trumann Middle School—$3,000
- West Memphis: Boys & Girls Club of Crittenden County—$4,000
- West Memphis: Hope Beyond Walls Foundation—$4,000
- Wilson: Rivercrest School District—$5,000
According to Thursday’s news release, the funds will be used for professional development opportunities and to purchase books, technology, equipment and materials.
“When students have access to books, technology and educational resources, they gain tools that can support their learning for years to come,” said Denine Torr, executive director of the Dollar General Literacy Foundation.
The funds are part of more than $4.1 million awarded across the country.
Applications for the 2027 grant cycle will be available at www.dgliteracy.org in January 2027.

articles.title: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member
articles.description: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member The Guardian
articles.description_html: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member  The Guardian
articles.article_title: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member
articles.heading: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member
articles.summary: US government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundation
articles.content:
OpenAI is not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level, a member of its non-profit board has said, amid spreading public and political concern that super-advanced AIs could one day wipe out humanity.
Paul Christiano, a US government technology adviser, said: “There is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.”
He added: “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.”
Christiano used to run model alignment at OpenAI and made the statement on Wednesday as he joined the board of the San Francisco company’s non-profit foundation.
He will also sit on the foundation’s committee that provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, which is developing some of the world’s most advanced models.
This summer, OpenAI admitted that hundreds of its AI agents went rogue during a training exercise, accessed the internet, conspired on message boards and hacked into a third-party website, Hugging Face.
Christiano said that “if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk”. His comments came after a senior employee at Anthropic, OpenAI’s major US rival in the race to AI supremacy, claimed on Tuesday there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade.
Evan Hubinger, the alignment science lead at Anthropic, warned that his company did not have a plan to ensure artificial superintelligence (ASI) was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. ASI is often defined as AI that far surpasses human intelligence across a large range of fields.
Fears of AI catastrophe were also ignited by the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic researcher who said he also previously worked at OpenAI, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly” and they were “gambling with our lives”.
Coxon said on Wednesday night in an interview with CNN: “Right now there’s no risk of extinction.
“The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages … in infrastructure.” He added they were “not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction”.
But he went on: “What’s just crazy is to look at the rate of progress. There is a very real possibility that in the immediate future … next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen and will enter the phase of Evan’s post, where he argues that there’s a chance we could all die.”
Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist known as one of the “godfathers of AI”, was asked on Wednesday for his view of Hubinger’s claim and told BBC Newsnight: “Nobody knows how to estimate it; a 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate.”
Christiano’s prognosis about the likelihood of the AI industry reducing risk came as concerns about the most extreme risks from super-powerful AIs, long discussed in Silicon Valley, broke out into the mainstream this week.
Politicians on both sides of the Atlantic, from Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders in the US to the MP Darren Jones in the UK, have called for government action and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Wednesday that “AI poses risks to our national security, but it also could be the source of solutions to keeping us safer”.
Meanwhile, Anthropic has admitted a new incident in which a version of its Claude model in training broke into third parties after its task could not be aborted. It said the incident happened in January and would be included in an independent investigation of a total of four incidents to be carried out by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisation METR.
Overall, it said the models were showing two forms of misalignment: biased reasoning, in which models selectively interpret evidence in ways that favour justifying their actions, and “recklessness, in which models have a propensity to keep trying to solve their task, even when this could lead to harm”.
Anthropic said it was especially concerned about misalignment it found in the behaviour of Claude Mythos 5, which it said “behaved recklessly” by going online and uploading malicious code to a public software repository, PyPI. This was a process that involved the AI agent trying to find cryptocurrency so it could pay for a phone number that would allow it to register an email address needed to access PyPI. When this failed, it found a free email provider and got in. Fifteen systems then downloaded the malicious code, which meant they leaked credentials that allowed Mythos to access a real security vendor’s database.
The company’s assessment of the incidents said: “This remains unsettled science – it is critical that alignment and security mature faster than capabilities advance, which is one reason we support a coordinated, verifiable approach to pacing frontier AI development.”
articles.content_html:
OpenAI is not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level, a member of its non-profit board has said, amid spreading public and political concern that super-advanced AIs could one day wipe out humanity.

Paul Christiano, a US government technology adviser, said: “There is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.”

He added: “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.”

Christiano used to run model alignment at OpenAI and made the statement on Wednesday as he joined the board of the San Francisco company’s non-profit foundation.

He will also sit on the foundation’s committee that provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, which is developing some of the world’s most advanced models.

This summer, OpenAI admitted that hundreds of its AI agents went rogue during a training exercise, accessed the internet, conspired on message boards and hacked into a third-party website, Hugging Face.

Christiano said that “if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk”. His comments came after a senior employee at Anthropic, OpenAI’s major US rival in the race to AI supremacy, claimed on Tuesday there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade.

Evan Hubinger, the alignment science lead at Anthropic, warned that his company did not have a plan to ensure artificial superintelligence (ASI) was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. ASI is often defined as AI that far surpasses human intelligence across a large range of fields.

Fears of AI catastrophe were also ignited by the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic researcher who said he also previously worked at OpenAI, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly” and they were “gambling with our lives”.

Coxon said on Wednesday night in an interview with CNN: “Right now there’s no risk of extinction.

“The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages … in infrastructure.” He added they were “not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction”.

But he went on: “What’s just crazy is to look at the rate of progress. There is a very real possibility that in the immediate future … next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen and will enter the phase of Evan’s post, where he argues that there’s a chance we could all die.”

after newsletter promotion

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist known as one of the “godfathers of AI”, was asked on Wednesday for his view of Hubinger’s claim and told BBC Newsnight: “Nobody knows how to estimate it; a 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate.”

Christiano’s prognosis about the likelihood of the AI industry reducing risk came as concerns about the most extreme risks from super-powerful AIs, long discussed in Silicon Valley, broke out into the mainstream this week.

Politicians on both sides of the Atlantic, from Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders in the US to the MP Darren Jones in the UK, have called for government action and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Wednesday that “AI poses risks to our national security, but it also could be the source of solutions to keeping us safer”.

Meanwhile, Anthropic has admitted a new incident in which a version of its Claude model in training broke into third parties after its task could not be aborted. It said the incident happened in January and would be included in an independent investigation of a total of four incidents to be carried out by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisation METR.

Overall, it said the models were showing two forms of misalignment: biased reasoning, in which models selectively interpret evidence in ways that favour justifying their actions, and “recklessness, in which models have a propensity to keep trying to solve their task, even when this could lead to harm”.

Anthropic said it was especially concerned about misalignment it found in the behaviour of Claude Mythos 5, which it said “behaved recklessly” by going online and uploading malicious code to a public software repository, PyPI. This was a process that involved the AI agent trying to find cryptocurrency so it could pay for a phone number that would allow it to register an email address needed to access PyPI. When this failed, it found a free email provider and got in. Fifteen systems then downloaded the malicious code, which meant they leaked credentials that allowed Mythos to access a real security vendor’s database.

The company’s assessment of the incidents said: “This remains unsettled science – it is critical that alignment and security mature faster than capabilities advance, which is one reason we support a coordinated, verifiable approach to pacing frontier AI development.”

articles.summary: For insurers struggling with Model Audit Rule “MAR” compliance, integrated Governance, Risk and Compliance systems can help in four distinct ways.
articles.content:
Four Ways Technology Can Ease the MAR Compliance Process
-
September 10, 2026
-

Most insurers struggle with Model Audit Rule (“MAR”) certification – not because of its complexity, but because they rely on traditional approaches that are no longer effective.
Crossing the $500 million premium threshold triggers MAR requirements that mandate stronger controls, formal accountability, and executive certification.1 Many organizations layer new requirements onto existing manual processes such as spreadsheets, emails, and disconnected control frameworks.
This approach leads to inefficiency, fragmented data, duplicated effort, and uncertainty about control effectiveness. MAR compliance becomes a resource-intensive process focused on tracking, validation and reconciliation, rather than reliable governance.
While MAR is a compliance hurdle, insurers quickly learn that it’s also an operational test, revealing an organization’s ability to administratively manage such a project across functions and at scale.
Technology can ease compliance burdens, but its value goes beyond increased efficiency. For organizations struggling with compliance structure and traceability, integrated Governance, Risk and Compliance (“GRC”) systems can be a game-changer.
The Accountability Test Behind MAR Certification
MAR certification requires management to answer four questions:
- Who owns the control?
- How do we know it was performed?
- What happened when it failed?
- What evidence supports management’s assertion?
Without visibility, ownership, evidence, and traceability, management cannot confidently answer these questions. While these questions center on accountability, technology is needed to answer them at scale.
How Technology Eases MAR Compliance
MAR compliance is more complex without the proper resources or technology the program truly requires. For many insurers, responsibility falls to internal audit or MAR compliance teams that are already stretched across multiple priorities. Even with the right expertise, managing the program and testing requirements can be difficult without dedicated technology.
The real value of a GRC platform is its ability to create a single source of truth across a platform that unites risks, controls, testing activities, deficiencies, and certifications. Many insurers already use GRC solutions to support existing programs, including Enterprise Risk Management and Cybersecurity Risk Management. By leveraging a shared data model across functions, organizations can improve visibility, reduce duplication of effort, and create stronger linkages between risk, controls, testing, and compliance activities.
Since MAR compliance involves finance, internal audit, compliance, IT, underwriting, claims, and executive leadership, organizations need a centralized platform to connect control ownership, testing, remediation, and certification activities across the enterprise.
Here are four key challenges with MAR readiness and how GRC platforms can help:
One: Accountability Begins With Evidence
Without a GRC platform, teams rely on email and manual follow-up to gather testing evidence from multiple stakeholders. As controls and stakeholders increase, these processes become more resource-intensive and harder to monitor, leading to delays, inconsistent documentation, and accountability gaps.
How GRC helps: MAR readiness evaluates an organization’s ability to consistently demonstrate control effectiveness. Technology supports this by centralizing evidence, strengthening accountability, and creating a defensible record of control performance. Additionally, finance departments could have their own controls that support both MAR and operational objectives. A GRC platform provides a consolidated view of controls, test results, and policies and procedures, enabling organizations to leverage existing compliance investments and minimize duplication.
Two: Accountability Requires a Single Source of Truth
When risks are maintained across spreadsheets and e-mails, no one has a complete picture of the organization’s risk profile or real-time visibility into MAR activities. This prevents the company from identifying interconnected risks, potentially creating compliance risk blind spots. Without ownership, accountability remains fragmented and compliance reactive. Teams spend more time gathering or reconciling information than managing risk.
How GRC helps: The platform centralizes risks, controls, processes, and systems into a single inventory, linking related documentation and evidence. More importantly, updates can be centralized to single point where updates are linked and automatically flow through to risk and control matrices, process narratives, flowcharts, and other documentation. This can reduce evidence duplication, inconsistency, and compliance resource efforts. MAR teams can focus on tasks that remain outstanding instead of chasing down control owners for updates on testing activities.
Three: Limited Risk Visibility Delays Remediation and Increases Risk
Control failures are inevitable, but the ability to respond effectively is what matters. Without a GRC system, organizations commonly rely on manual processes to log issues, assign accountability, manage remediation plans, monitor progress, and chase updates. This makes timely resolution difficult and onerous.
How GRC helps: Effective remediation requires visibility, accountability and timely escalation. A GRC platform can provide real-time insight into issue status, remediation progress, and ownership. By addressing deficiencies early, organizations can proactively manage risk.
Four: Executive Accountability Requires Defensible Evidence
MAR requires executive management, typically the CEO and CFO, to acknowledge their responsibility for establishing, maintaining, and designing effective internal controls over financial reporting (“ICFR”). This attestation must be supported by detailed documentation that is readily available upon a regulatory examination. Management must document how they evaluated ICFR effectiveness and disclose any unremediated weaknesses. CEOs and CFOs are held accountable when they sign the management reports. False or misleading statements could result in regulatory actions, civil actions, and penalties.
How GRC helps: Executive certifications are only as reliable as the evidence supporting them. A GRC platform creates structured certification workflows, captures sub-certifications from control and process owners, maintains supporting evidence, and provides executives with a defensible audit trail for management’s attestation.
The fundamental challenge of MAR extends beyond controls design, testing methodology, and documentation: it is accountability. Regulators expect organizations to demonstrate who was responsible, what was tested, what exceptions were identified, how those exceptions were resolved, and what evidence supports management’s conclusions. Organizations that rely on manual processes often struggle to answer these questions consistently. Integrated GRC platforms create the transparency and accountability needed to support executive certification.
Footnotes:
1: “NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines, and other Resources: Annual Financial Reporting Model Regulation” NAIC Accounting, MO-205-16 (Q3 2015).

articles.summary: Defense Department Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies said the Pentagon has to focus on “leveraging the fantastically skilled people that we have in a much more effective way.”
articles.content:
‘We have to throw technology at the cyber problem,’ Pentagon CIO says
Defense Department Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies said the Pentagon has to focus on “leveraging the fantastically skilled people that we have in a much more effective way.”
The Pentagon is shifting its cybersecurity posture to rely more on new capabilities to maintain its digital defenses rather than just bolstering its operational manpower, the department’s IT head said on Wednesday.
Speaking at the Billington Cybersecurity Summit in Washington, D.C., Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies said “we can't continue to throw people at the cyber problem; we have to throw technology at the cyber problem.”
Given DOD’s vast size, she said managing cybersecurity at scale means the department has to look at using “everything from automation to machine learning to actually AI,” since the threat environment and range of new and outdated IT systems across its operations presents “a complex Rubik's cube of problems.”
Davies noted that DOD maintains thousands of different networks and includes both civilian and military components, meaning that “this technology must be ready and available, and it must operate even when it's disconnected.”
When one small IT problem can have a ripple effect across the entire Pentagon, Davies said it’s also important to “think about leveraging the fantastically skilled people that we have in a much more effective way.”
“As we embrace AI and leverage massive, massive quantities of agentic AI, how do we do that in a way that's supportive of our workforce and provides innovation across that?” she said.
Davies noted that the department is working to onboard employees that know how to actually use new and emerging tech capabilities, with DOD prioritizing relevant job candidates’ abilities over their educational backgrounds. When it comes to using AI, she said, this means focusing more on applicants who are skilled at prompt engineering — developing instructions for the models to output accurate information.
“Why are we leveraging people for things that technology can do now? Like, let's really build skills and talent that know how to leverage technology very effectively,” Davies said. This mindset has already led to the department working to attract a new crop of cyber professionals.
DOD began accepting applications in July for a new Cyber Registered Apprenticeship Program to bring more cybersecurity talent into the agency, with a particular focus on prioritizing skills-based hiring. The department ultimately closed its first listing four days early after receiving more than 15,000 applications, although DOD has said it plans to open additional rounds of opportunities.
In a previous interview with Nextgov/FCW, Davies said her office was working to transition away from operating as a backend policy shop to taking more of an active role in DOD’s overall mission. She reiterated that mindset on Wednesday, saying that “reform is a big thing for us.”
Davies said this includes reforming the way DOD acquires new products, systems and weaponry. The first step in this process, she noted, was identifying policies and mandates that the department could whittle down or cut entirely — something that equated to more than 60% of relevant DOD guidance.
Now, the department is in the process of carrying out part two of the initiative, which entails looking at the actual process that companies have to go through when it comes to approving new capabilities.
Davies said this process could take anywhere from six to 18 months, but noted that the department just tested out a platform that took that standard timeline “and shortened it to 17 seconds.” She said, however, that the speed of the tested platform is just one component of what the Pentagon must evaluate when it comes to transforming its acquisition strategy.
“That doesn't address what some of the root things are that I still want to address, which is, ‘Are we asking the right questions? Are we demanding the right documentation from software companies?’ Is the output of a 17-second process actually reducing risk?’” she said.
One major step that Davies’ office has taken is its decision to suspend the second-phase requirements for third-party assessments under the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program. The mandatory security framework for defense contractors was stopped in July for a 60-day review by a CMMC Reform Task Force. That assessment period is set to end on Friday.
Davies said the task force has received more than 1,100 responses to a request for information about CMMC’s next steps.
“We wanted to hear more from the defense industrial base on what was important for meaningful, dynamic cybersecurity," she added.
Davies’ remarks came the same day that Washington Technology reported that DOD is moving beyond a suspension of CMMC’s phase two requirements and is effectively implementing a binding regulation that would codify the pause.

articles.heading: Meet the Master’s in Technology Management Class of 2027
articles.summary: Program on Entrepreneurship staff member Chelsea Spata introduces the incoming cohort.
articles.content:
Meet the Master’s in Technology Management Class of 2027
Program on Entrepreneurship staff member Chelsea Spata introduces the incoming cohort.
Each fall, Yale SOM opens its doors to a new cohort in the Master’s in Technology Management program—a one-year degree built exclusively for Yale College engineering graduates who want to augment their technical training with the leadership, entrepreneurial, and communication skills needed to run technology-driven organizations. The Class of 2027 arrived on campus this September.
This year’s students hold degrees in computer science, electrical engineering, environmental engineering, biomedical engineering, and cognitive science. They’ve gained experience at investment banks, global consulting firms, research labs, startups, and clean-energy companies. Collectively, the five students in the cohort have co-authored a NeurIPS submission on genomic data analysis, pursued a patent for a surgical device, scaled AI platforms to thousands of users, and pushed forward research in carbon capture and electrochemical energy storage. Outside their academic work, they’ve founded campus organizations, competed as Division I athletes, and run student conferences.
One student points to a senior-year stint at a computational biology lab startup as a turning point that led him to SOM. “I had a career trajectory experience that piqued my interest in working with consumer demands and technical researchers,” he says. “The Technology Management program was the perfect bridging of that gap to equip me for entrepreneurial leadership.”
Another, whose undergraduate research spanned carbon capture, desalination, and clean-energy systems, came to SOM to fill gaps in his engineering education. “I chose this program at SOM because I want to build on my background in engineering while developing the business and leadership skills needed to bring innovative ideas to life,” she says. “I’m looking forward to making the most of my year by building meaningful relationships, exploring new ideas, and finding ways to create lasting impact in water, energy, and sustainability.”
From here, the Class of 2027 will move through a curriculum that pairs core management coursework with entrepreneurship electives and advanced technical study. Alongside the classwork, they’ll spend the year learning from each other—trading expertise across disciplines as they sharpen their own thinking about how technology should be managed, deployed, and scaled responsibly.

Landmark project underscores market momentum and customer confidence in CATOFIN technology
HOUSTON, Sept. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Lummus Technology has been awarded a contract by Zhejiang Petroleum & Chemical Co., Ltd. (ZPC) to license its CATOFIN™ propane dehydrogenation (PDH) technology for a new unit in Zhejiang Province, China. articles.article_title: JETRO and Purdue University Sign MOU on Advanced Technology Collaboration
articles.heading: JETRO and Purdue University Sign MOU on Advanced Technology Collaboration
articles.summary: JETRO and Purdue University sign an MOU to expand U.S.-Japan collaboration in quantum technologies, semiconductors & advanced manufacturing.
articles.content:
- September 10, 2026

- AI , National , Quantum Business

Insider Brief

- JETRO and Purdue University signed an MOU to expand U.S.-Japan collaboration across advanced technology fields, including semiconductors, quantum technologies, AI and advanced manufacturing.

- The agreement will support connections among universities, research institutions, companies, startups, investors and public organizations through joint research, technology commercialization and industry-academia initiatives.

- The MOU was signed during the 10th Annual U.S. and Japan Digital Innovation Hub & Advanced Technology Workshop at Purdue University , held September 7–9, 2026.

PRESS RELEASE — The Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) and Purdue University today announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to strengthen innovation collaboration in advanced technology fields and further connect the innovation ecosystems of Japan and the United States.

The MOU was signed by Norihiko Ishiguro, Chairman and CEO of JETRO, and Mitchell E. Daniels, Jr., President of Purdue University .

Under the MOU, JETRO and Purdue University will leverage Purdue’s research capabilities and expertise in technology commercialization and JETRO’s extensive network in Japan and the United States to promote collaboration among universities, research institutions, companies, startups, investors, public organizations and other innovation stakeholders.

The collaboration will focus on advanced technology fields including semiconductors, quantum technologies, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and life sciences. The two organizations will also seek to promote exchanges among students, researchers and entrepreneurs and create opportunities for joint research, technology commercialization, startup engagement and industry-academia collaboration.

Purdue University is a leading U.S. research university with significant strengths in engineering and advanced technologies. In addition to research and education, Purdue has developed a strong ecosystem supporting technology commercialization, entrepreneurship, startups and industry collaboration.

JETRO and Purdue University have built a collaborative relationship through initiatives aimed at promoting innovation and strengthening connections between Japan and the United States. The new MOU provides a framework to further expand this relationship and create concrete opportunities connecting Japanese companies and other innovation stakeholders with Purdue researchers, startups and related organizations.

Through its global network, JETRO supports Japanese companies in accessing technologies, talent and research capabilities overseas and in developing partnerships with universities, research institutions, companies, startups and innovation organizations. Under the new MOU, JETRO will work with Purdue to expand connections between the Purdue ecosystem and Japanese companies and organizations and to facilitate concrete U.S.-Japan collaboration opportunities.

The MOU was celebrated during the 10th Annual U.S. and Japan Digital Innovation Hub & Advanced Technology Workshop, held at Purdue University from September 7–9, 2026. The workshop brought together leaders from academia, industry and government to discuss collaboration in areas including artificial intelligence, semiconductors, advanced materials and manufacturing, technology diplomacy, space and quantum technologies.

articles.title: Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub? Inside Ohio State’s work
articles.description: Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub? Inside Ohio State’s work The Columbus Dispatch
articles.description_html: Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub? Inside Ohio State’s work  The Columbus Dispatch
articles.article_title: Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub? Inside Ohio State’s work
articles.heading: Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub? Inside Ohio State’s work
articles.summary: Ohio State professor Ezekiel Johnston-Halperin explains quantum technology and why Columbus could become a hub for the emerging field.
articles.content:
Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub? Inside Ohio State’s work
- Ohio State University is developing a quantum sensing testbed with a $4 million planning grant from the National Science Foundation.
- Columbus and the Midwest are positioned to become major hubs for the emerging quantum technology industry.
A quantum computer powerful enough to break much of today’s digital encryption may still be years away, but the race to prepare for that future is already underway.
And some of that work is happening in Columbus.
"If we can get the quantum networking going, there’s a bit of an arms race," Ohio State University physics professor Ezekiel Johnston-Halperin said on the latest episode of Columbus in Color.
Johnston-Halperin is a co-director of Ohio State’s Center for Quantum Information Science and Engineering and leads an Ohio State team participating in the National Science Foundation’s National Quantum Virtual Laboratory program.
Backed by a $4 million planning grant, the team is developing a quantum sensing testbed designed to bring university researchers, national laboratories and industry partners together. The initial grant covers two years of planning for a potential five- to six-year project receiving up to $50 million.
“We want to serve the public good with the work that we’re doing,” Johnston-Halperin said.
What could quantum technology be used for?
Quantum physics describes the behavior of atoms and other particles that form the building blocks of nature. While the subject can sound abstract, Johnston-Halperin said it already underlies much of modern life, including medicine, smartphones, solar panels and other technologies.
Ohio State’s project focuses on quantum sensing, which uses the properties of atoms to measure the world with extreme precision. Researchers are exploring how the sensors could eventually detect radiation, support nuclear and fusion energy or help scientists study molecules and structures within cells.
The challenge now is determining where quantum sensors can solve problems that existing technology cannot.
“We know we can build a quantum sensor,” Johnston-Halperin said. “What’s it good for?”
Answering that question requires physicists and engineers to work alongside specialists in fields such as biology and medicine. Ohio State is also developing graduate programs that cross traditional academic boundaries, combining areas including physics, chemistry, mathematics, computer science and engineering.
Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub?
Johnston-Halperin believes Columbus and the Midwest have the ingredients to become major players in the emerging industry.
He pointed to the region’s research universities, manufacturing history and existing technology infrastructure. One of the earliest connections in ARPANET, a precursor to the modern internet, linked computing systems in Columbus and Chicago.
Ohio State is also supporting a second quantum testbed led by the University of Michigan and collaborating with researchers in Illinois.
"There really is sort of a Midwestern moment happening," Johnston-Halperin said.
For him, that work reflects Ohio State’s responsibility as a land-grant university to serve people across the state. It also offers Columbus another opportunity to build on the growth it has experienced over the past decade.
"I think Columbus has been having a moment," he said. "And I see a trajectory for that moment to continue."
Trending reporter Amani Bayo can be reached at abayo@dispatch.com.

articles.title: Colorado IT office rehires 15 of 173 laid-off state workers, says overhaul will save at least $6M
articles.description: Colorado IT office rehires 15 of 173 laid-off state workers, says overhaul will save at least $6M The Colorado Sun
articles.description_html: Colorado IT office rehires 15 of 173 laid-off state workers, says overhaul will save at least $6M  The Colorado Sun
articles.article_title: Colorado IT office rehires 15 of 173 laid-off state workers, says overhaul will save at least $6M
articles.heading: Colorado IT office rehires 15 of 173 laid-off state workers, says overhaul will save at least $6M
articles.summary: The state’s Office of Information Technology also created 98 new jobs, and have hired 88 people. Meanwhile, cyber threats have increased.
articles.content:
More than three months after a state-government agency reorganization left 173 workers unemployed, the Governor’s Office of Information Technology has hired 15 back.
That’s not great odds for the remaining public servants hoping to get rehired. The state agency had simultaneously announced 98 new jobs at the time of the layoffs.
Many former OIT workers are still looking for work in the current challenging economy, and continue to feel the sting of the abrupt layoff after years of working for the state, according to former OIT employees who shared their stories with The Colorado Sun.
But OIT has been in the hot seat for the past year, especially after failing to implement many of the cybersecurity resiliency recommendations offered by the Office of State Auditor. OIT has also struggled with low customer satisfaction ratings from clients, which are mostly other state agencies. A reorganization to focus on outcomes became a priority and the effort became very public May 27, when layoffs were announced.
Sarah Tuneberg, who replaced former OIT leader David Edinger on June 1, told the Colorado legislature’s Joint Technology Committee on Tuesday that progress has been made at the agency, which handles much of the state’s technology services.
She said OIT helped reduce the time low-income families spent to access a $120 benefit to buy healthy food for their children — down to 25 seconds, from two minutes. One of OIT’s core products, the state’s myColorado digital drivers license, is now accepted at airport security by the Transportation Security Administration.
“We’ve already achieved $6 million in platform savings via direct negotiations with our vendors,” Tuneberg told the Joint Technology Committee, which is tasked with oversight for OIT and the state’s technology projects.
Some savings came from using artificial intelligence at the Department of Corrections to reduce a system migration and “saving hundreds to thousands of manual coding labor hours,” according to an OIT report of the first 90 days since the layoffs. Another $1.2 million in savings came from “reducing hourly administrative bloat” at the Colorado Department of Public Safety.
Asked for details, DPS spokesperson Gianna De Fries said in an email, “The savings were from within their department, but these savings will be used to help OIT better support CDPS through enhanced technologies and increased capacity.”
OIT also negotiated a 10% reduction in Google Cloud costs after researching how much other jurisdictions paid for similar services, Tuneberg said. While some negotiations with vendors were in the works before the reorganization, there’s more to be done, she added.
“A large part of the overall savings also came from scaling back or canceling products we weren’t using or weren’t getting sufficient ROI from,” Tuneberg said in an email. “We’re currently in the midst of evaluating the (software) tools used internally at OIT, with an eye toward consolidating on enterprise solutions that create cost efficiency through scale and centralized management.”
Cybersecurity concerns
During the JTC meeting, Tuneberg also said OIT has seen “an uptick in external international actors attempting to attack our infrastructure,” including the possible Iranian water system attack that led her team to provide “crucial intelligence that supported that response.”
OIT also retooled its HR process, she said, after “seeing North Korean threat actors attempting to gain employment and access our systems.”
That led state Rep. Brianna Titone, the committee’s vice chair, to question OIT’s focus on nonsecurity projects.
“I’m wondering why you were prioritizing these kinds of more vanity projects than focusing on some of the other issues that seem to be more pressing … especially the cybersecurity threats,” said Titone, a Democrat from Arvada. “I have heard through the grapevine that there are many employees that are at their breaking point and are being overworked. Maybe that’s why you’re getting such great performance and cost reductions because you’re working people to the bone.”
Tuneberg didn’t address the cyber threats but said OIT’s staff is its greatest asset, but change is hard. Employee survey responses were positive, with 55% now on board with OIT’s direction, compared with 42% in March. However, according to data shared with The Colorado Sun, those who felt “stuck” had increased to 11%, from 4.5% in the same period.
“We are doing a lot of work to support employees through the change. That looks like significant amounts of training, more than we’ve ever offered. Very clear performance expectations so that people know what they’re expected to do and how they’re supposed to show up in this model,” she said. “I appreciate again that change is hard and I do not minimize that. We’re seeing people excited, and the feedback is strong.”

More than three months after a state-government agency reorganization left 173 workers unemployed, the Governor’s Office of Information Technology has hired 15 back.

That’s not great odds for the remaining public servants hoping to get rehired. The state agency had simultaneously announced 98 new jobs at the time of the layoffs.

Many former OIT workers are still looking for work in the current challenging economy, and continue to feel the sting of the abrupt layoff after years of working for the state, according to former OIT employees who shared their stories with The Colorado Sun.

But OIT has been in the hot seat for the past year, especially after failing to implement many of the cybersecurity resiliency recommendations offered by the Office of State Auditor. OIT has also struggled with low customer satisfaction ratings from clients, which are mostly other state agencies. A reorganization to focus on outcomes became a priority and the effort became very public May 27, when layoffs were announced.

Sarah Tuneberg, who replaced former OIT leader David Edinger on June 1, told the Colorado legislature’s Joint Technology Committee on Tuesday that progress has been made at the agency, which handles much of the state’s technology services.

She said OIT helped reduce the time low-income families spent to access a $120 benefit to buy healthy food for their children — down to 25 seconds, from two minutes. One of OIT’s core products, the state’s myColorado digital drivers license, is now accepted at airport security by the Transportation Security Administration.

“We’ve already achieved $6 million in platform savings via direct negotiations with our vendors,” Tuneberg told the Joint Technology Committee, which is tasked with oversight for OIT and the state’s technology projects.

Some savings came from using artificial intelligence at the Department of Corrections to reduce a system migration and “saving hundreds to thousands of manual coding labor hours,” according to an OIT report of the first 90 days since the layoffs. Another $1.2 million in savings came from “reducing hourly administrative bloat” at the Colorado Department of Public Safety.

Asked for details, DPS spokesperson Gianna De Fries said in an email, “The savings were from within their department, but these savings will be used to help OIT better support CDPS through enhanced technologies and increased capacity.”

OIT also negotiated a 10% reduction in Google Cloud costs after researching how much other jurisdictions paid for similar services, Tuneberg said. While some negotiations with vendors were in the works before the reorganization, there’s more to be done, she added.

“A large part of the overall savings also came from scaling back or canceling products we weren’t using or weren’t getting sufficient ROI from,” Tuneberg said in an email. “We’re currently in the midst of evaluating the (software) tools used internally at OIT, with an eye toward consolidating on enterprise solutions that create cost efficiency through scale and centralized management.”

Cybersecurity concerns

During the JTC meeting, Tuneberg also said OIT has seen “an uptick in external international actors attempting to attack our infrastructure,” including the possible Iranian water system attack that led her team to provide “crucial intelligence that supported that response.”

OIT also retooled its HR process, she said, after “seeing North Korean threat actors attempting to gain employment and access our systems.”

That led state Rep. Brianna Titone, the committee’s vice chair, to question OIT’s focus on nonsecurity projects.

“I’m wondering why you were prioritizing these kinds of more vanity projects than focusing on some of the other issues that seem to be more pressing … especially the cybersecurity threats,” said Titone, a Democrat from Arvada. “I have heard through the grapevine that there are many employees that are at their breaking point and are being overworked. Maybe that’s why you’re getting such great performance and cost reductions because you’re working people to the bone.”

Tuneberg didn’t address the cyber threats but said OIT’s staff is its greatest asset, but change is hard. Employee survey responses were positive, with 55% now on board with OIT’s direction, compared with 42% in March. However, according to data shared with The Colorado Sun, those who felt “stuck” had increased to 11%, from 4.5% in the same period.

“We are doing a lot of work to support employees through the change. That looks like significant amounts of training, more than we’ve ever offered. articles.title: Can the US battery market untangle from China?

articles.article_title: Can the US battery market untangle from China?
articles.heading: Can the US battery market untangle from China?
articles.summary: Energy storage is currently booming, largely thanks to cheap Chinese cells.
articles.content:
Can the US battery market untangle from China?
Energy storage is currently booming, largely thanks to cheap Chinese cells.
The US is hitting records for the rapid growth of its energy storage market. That’ll go a long way to shoring up the grid, increasing reliability and also cutting emissions, since batteries can help store energy from intermittent renewables like wind and solar.
Crucially, this is all happening with the help of cheap Chinese batteries, though there’s been a concerted effort to reduce the US’s reliance on them. Most recently, in an executive order in late August, the Trump administration declared a national emergency that essentially bans Chinese batteries from being used in grid-scale energy storage systems.
There’s an argument to be made about reducing reliance on any single source of a crucial energy technology. But all this tension raises a broader question for me: How much should countries take advantage of cheap, available tech, versus cutting off major sources to force development of their own factories even if that comes at a higher cost?
This is hardly America’s first push to move away from Chinese influence in the battery supply chain. One of the major policy tools used in recent years is restricting the tax credits designed to incentivize use of the new technologies. Limiting the types of projects that are eligible can help reduce the cost of local technologies so they’re more competitive with otherwise cheaper imported options.
Back in 2022, the US government designed the tax credits that were part of the Inflation Reduction Act to restrict where a battery’s minerals could be mined, processed, or recycled, as well as where a battery and its components were assembled.
Those tax credits underwent a makeover in 2025, but the Trump administration has taken a similar tack. New legislation requires that starting in 2026, 55% of the cost of materials used for new energy storage projects must come from outside China and other restricted countries or the projects won’t qualify for tax credits.
And we can’t forget about tariffs. Import taxes for batteries increased to 25% in January, up from 7.5%.
But the new executive order is a more drastic move. It bans the installation of “any foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment” that poses a national security risk. The order specifically calls out battery energy storage systems, as well as inverters and transformers.
“An outright ban was a bit of a surprise, and it does create a bit of concern for domestic players in the US,” says Shan Tomouk, energy storage and energy lead for Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, an energy industry analyst.
The move is likely to slow deployment of grid-connected energy storage projects in the near term, according to analysis from BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. Projects could face delays as developers wait for clarity on the rules.
Depending on the detailed guidance from the Department of Energy, which is expected by the end of the year, some projects may need to find alternative sources for their cells, whether they’re domestically produced or imported from other countries. These will likely be more expensive than Chinese imports, says Isshu Kikuma, an energy storage analyst at BloombergNEF. “Worst case, those projects could get canceled,” he says.
Technically, the order applies even to existing energy storage plants, though it’s unlikely that they’ll be taken offline because of their batteries’ origin. Since most of these plants currently use Chinese batteries, enforcing the order to the letter would essentially mean removing most installed battery energy storage from the US grid, Kikuma says.
In the longer term, the US will eventually be able to meet its own demand for batteries. The country could have enough capacity by about 2030, though some factories may not ramp up or run at their full capability, meaning domestic supply won’t actually meet demand until later in the 2030s.
New factories from LG Energy Solutions, Samsung SDI, Ford, and SK On are set to come online or ramp up by next year. In an ironic twist, a slowing EV market is helping, as some factories originally designed for vehicle batteries are retooling to build cells for grid storage instead.
But it will come at a cost. Today, batteries produced in the US are still significantly more expensive than those made in China. Even switching to imports from other countries like South Korea would likely be more expensive.
This is a crucial issue that goes beyond the US and even beyond batteries. China is miles ahead of much of the rest of the world on technologies like solar panels and batteries. Through years of government support and experience with research and manufacturing, the nation is an energy powerhouse.
There’s a delicate political balance to maintain as the world figures out how to navigate this situation. There’s cheap technology on offer, which can help drastically reduce emissions and energy costs. But there can be risks associated with relying too much on any one player for crucial technologies.

articles.title: Wisconsin using new tracking technology to better understand monarch butterfly migration
articles.description: Wisconsin using new tracking technology to better understand monarch butterfly migration wpr.org
articles.description_html: Wisconsin using new tracking technology to better understand monarch butterfly migration  wpr.org
articles.article_title: Wisconsin using new tracking technology to better understand monarch butterfly migration
articles.heading: Wisconsin using new tracking technology to better understand monarch butterfly migration
articles.summary: For the first time, researchers in Wisconsin are placing tiny solar-powered radio tags onto monarchs.
articles.content:
As the days are getting chillier, monarch butterflies in Wisconsin are getting ready to take flight to central Mexico. This year as they head south, some of the butterflies will be tracked in real time.
For the first time, researchers in Wisconsin are placing tiny solar-powered radio tags onto monarchs. The tags weigh less than a grain of rice and are glued onto the butterflies’ thorax. Similar technology has been used to track birds and other mammals, but in the past has been too heavy for insects.
“We’re really at the cusp of what we’re going to learn in terms of insect movement because the technology has gotten lightweight enough,” said Emma Pelton, a senior conservation biologist for the Xerces Society, a nonprofit that focuses on insect conservation.
Understanding Wisconsin, Together.
WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter.
Pelton said typically, butterflies have been tracked with sticker tags — small, lightweight stickers placed on butterfly wings. She said sticker tagged butterflies helped answer questions about where the butterflies that made it to Mexico came from, but offered no clues into their journey along the way.
“It’s really a mystery,” she said. “You just get that point A and point B. What’s really revolutionary about these new tags and this new technology is we’re getting almost real time, very detailed data during a lot of their flight paths.”
Monarch butterflies have been in dwindling, making efforts to understand their migration routes and protect habitat along the way more critical. The Xerces society estimates that monarchs that migrate to central Mexico have seen an 80 percent decline since the 1990s.
At a Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance event this month, staff and volunteers caught monarchs in nets and released 30 butterflies with the new radio tags at the Goose Pond Sanctuary. Brenna Marsicek is the director of outreach with the alliance.
“In order for us to better support this insect, we need to better understand what they’re up against along their migration and where the needs are for more habitat,” she said.
The tags stick to monarchs with the help of the same glue used for false eyelashes said Pelton. She said the glue is non-toxic and the most durable.
Marsicek said keeping the monarchs safe during tagging was a priority. She said research has shown that the tags don’t impact the butterflies’ mobility or behavior and the staff and volunteers doing the tagging are trained to handle the insects as little as possible to ensure their safety.
“We’re very conscious of anything that would do any harm to the butterfly,” she said. “So a lot of time is spent in training and ensuring that during the process the butterfly is as comfortable and as stress-free as possible.”
After the monarchs are tagged, Marsicek said they are observed for 10 minutes before being released to make sure they are acting normally.
“You release it and it just flies right out of your hand into the prairie and starts nectaring on a plant right away,” Marsicek said. “I think it’s just such a cool way to see that this science is now out there in the world and the butterfly is doing things as it normally would.”
The radio tags release a bluetooth frequency that can be received by smart phones. Community members can see the data on an app called Project Monarch. Pelton said it will allow for more comprehensive data to be collected about migration patterns.
“We essentially all have mini receivers in our pockets,” she said. “So we’re just getting so much more data, and again, on an animal that never could hold a traditional tag.”
Pelton said having the ability to track monarchs during their entire migration path could give researchers and the public more information on how to create suitable habitats for monarchs in areas along their flight paths.
“I think about it from a policy perspective,” Pelton said. “Not just this one protected area is important, but also this other area, and they’re traveling between them, makes me think about pesticides used in the landscape, makes me think about what nectar is out there.”
She said getting the community more aware of butterfly migration patterns could help focus conservation efforts.
“I do think of the power of storytelling and connection, and monarchs tend to be an animal people are naturally drawn to and culturally drawn to,” Pelton said. “Continuing to personify that and individual stories of what they went through and the storms, that’s really telling.”
