articles.title: How Stanford researchers are using 3D printing, advancing technology is improving football helmet safety and reduce concussions
articles.description: How Stanford researchers are using 3D printing, advancing technology is improving football helmet safety and reduce concussions ABC7 Bay Area
articles.description_html: How Stanford researchers are using 3D printing, advancing technology is improving football helmet safety and reduce concussions  ABC7 Bay Area
articles.article_title: How 3D printing, advancing technology is improving football helmet safety
articles.heading: How 3D printing, advancing technology is improving football helmet safety
articles.summary: Helmet manufacturers are using 3D printers to create special cushioning for football helmets as they work to reduce concussions among players.
articles.content:
KGO-TV
Wednesday, September 9, 2026 8:35PM
STANFORD, Calif. (KGO) -- Nothing excites NFL fans more than hard hits, but those collisions may be causing long-term brain damage in athletes.
A recent study found that at least 25% of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease.
David Camarillo, a former football player at Princeton University, researches the biomechanics of concussions in his lab at Stanford University.
Camarillo's team developed a mouthguard with sensors to measure the forces on impact.
"Concussions can happen in many ways. It can be a hit to the head. It can be a hit to the body where you have a whiplash injury," said David Camarillo, Ph.D., an associate professor of bioengineering at Stanford University.
Camarillo says that a blow to the head makes soft brain tissue slide and shake inside the skull. He especially points to slight twisting motions as a cause of brain injuries.
Helmet safety is much improved when Joe Montana was leading the 49ers to Super Bowl wins. Back then, helmets were just designed to prevent skull fractures.
"If you go back to those days, it was basically hard plastic and some version of a relatively generic foam that was on the inside of the helmet and that was about the extend of the design," explained Jeremy Erspamer, CEO of Certor Sports.
At the time, little attention was paid to brain injuries.
That started to change when former linebacker Junior Seau died by suicide. His family donated his brain for research, and it showed brain damage.
That ignited the conversation about the effects of repetitive head trauma.
"What happened to Junior Seau has evolved the way in which we design our products. It's evolved the way we test our products to make sure we are paying equal amount of attention to the high impact concussive type events but really paying equally amount of attention to lower impact repetitive testing," said Esparmer.
Certor Sports supplies helmets to about 40% of NFL players under the brands Schutt and VICIS.
The newest designs now have micro lattice cushioning that's 3D printed with different impact absorption points depending on the position of the player.
"We can put added impact absorption in the back of a quarterback's helmet because they're mostly taking the helmet to ground impact. Whereas an offensive or defensive lineman, we put more protective absorption material up in front of the helmet," said Ersparmer.
The NFL also requires additional head protection during practices when there will be contact.
Guardian Caps go over the hard helmet shell and provide additional padding. Wearing them during games is optional.
Camarillo was testing Guardian Caps when his team detected that the facemask area is another crucial impact point for brain trauma.
"In football in particular, a lot of the concussions and impacts are actually to the faceguard area," said Camarillo. "When you get hit low enough on the faceguard, the forces don't go through the helmet; they go through the strap."
Camarillo's team developed a wearable shock absorber for the chinstrap.
"During an impact, the liquid is squeezed from one chamber out into another chamber and then it returns and it's using that motion of the liquid in order to dampen the forces and protect the brain," explained Camarillo.
Marketed under the name SoftShox, the chinstrap reportedly reduces the intensity of head impacts by 35%.
Despite all the attention being paid to NFL head injuries, Camarillo said that cyclists make up the majority of head injuries.
If you are interested in checking the safety rating of consumer helmets, Virginia Tech developed a helmet safety rating system for all types of sports and construction work.

articles.title: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening
articles.description: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening TechCrunch
articles.description_html: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening  TechCrunch
articles.article_title: Apple Watch's new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening | TechCrunch
articles.heading: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening
articles.summary: Apple says its new watches won’t save raw audio, but features that can transcribe recent speech and summarize ambient conversations raise new questions about consent, privacy, and how people behave when they know they could always be recorded.
articles.content:
Apple is trying to get consumers to accept, and even welcome, a new reality: Your tech is always listening.
At Wednesday’s “Surprise and Shine” iPhone event, where the company introduced its new hardware lineup, the real surprise turned out not to be the foldable iPhone, but how the famously privacy-sensitive tech giant has decided its watches will now be able to process live audio and transcribe what was said.
Does this mean you’re always being recorded if the person you’re interacting with is wearing an Apple Watch? Not exactly — though it may make some people uncomfortable regardless.
It also raises the question of whether consumers actually want this technology, or if Apple forged ahead in this area because it was afraid that another company, such as OpenAI, would soon introduce a competitive AI device of its own.
Today, a number of startups are acting on the belief that AI-powered transcription is a key consumer use case for AI. So far, this more often involves transcribing meeting notes or recording lectures or interviews. Some companies, like the AI pendant Friend and Amazon’s Bee, ventured into other areas, too, with always-available AI companions that can help you remember your day by passively taking notes.
Apple decided to go a slightly different route. With its new watches’ “audio intelligence,” “Live Rewind,” and “Siri Recap” features, the company is straddling the line between accessibility and utility on one side, and what starts to feel like invasive technology on the other.
On its own, Audio Intelligence seems to be a useful feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, as it can alert Apple Watch owners to sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, babies crying, and more, using on-device AI. This can work even when the wearer’s iPhone is not with them and, in some cases, could provide life-saving assistance, such as when a fire alarm or carbon monoxide detector goes off. It’s doubtful anyone would take issue with this type of audio AI.
However, Live Rewind and Siri Recap move out of the assistive tech space and into a murkier area.
While Apple’s data protections may make these features more palatable to some, there’s still the possibility that normalizing listening technology may not be the best move for a privacy-conscious company. This is especially true given the broader consumer backlash against surveillance technology like Flock cameras, AI data centers, and AI apps in general.
For starters, the Live Rewind AI feature lets you go back in time 15 seconds and transcribe what was just said by double-pressing the watch’s digital crown. This transcription can then be saved to Apple’s new standalone Siri app so you can revisit the information later.
Apple suggests that this could be used to remember things like a “book recommendation, a colleague’s brilliant idea, or something you didn’t hear the first time,” but it also means that you can essentially catch anyone saying something they didn’t necessarily mean to have recorded and make a note of it.
This has implications around consent, not only from an ethical standpoint but from a legal one as well. AI device-maker Plaud, for instance, advises customers to obtain legally required consent before recording. Amazon’s Bee‘s terms of service remind users that they’re solely responsible for complying with the law around minors’ data privacy, not Amazon.
Since Apple isn’t saving audio, it’s unclear how the court system might handle these new, text-only transcripts. It’s possible the notes could be introduced as evidence in court, but their lack of audio could make them harder to authenticate or verify. Plus, the evidentiary rules around their use will also likely vary by state.
Beyond the legal issues, the idea that someone can always record from their watch has cultural implications.
Already, recording devices have impacted the way people behave in real life, studies have shown, as has social media and data surveillance culture. Knowing you could be recorded at any time has a dampening effect on how you interact with others and engage in self-expression.
However, recording a photo or video still requires a fairly obvious move on the recorder’s part: you have to hold up your phone and face it toward the action. Snapping up a bit of audio to turn into a transcript just by pressing the watch’s digital crown is arguably a much subtler gesture, even though it comes with an audible chime and full-screen animation of a microphone, as Apple says.
Another new Apple Watch feature, “Siri Recap,” uses ambient listening to “take high-level notes” of your conversations, which can be reviewed in the Siri iOS app. These notes will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points based on what was recorded and summarized by AI. They will not be exact transcripts.
Apple suggests this could make sense for recording meeting takeaways or key info from a parent-teacher conference, for instance.
The company also tried to assure users that it has approached these listening features with respect for user privacy.
Apple notes that Siri Recap doesn’t default to always being on like some other AI wearables are. Instead, you can choose when it’s enabled, like only at work or only during the day. Plus, you can turn the feature off and on at any time from Control Center.
Notably, Apple points out that it does not create or store audio recordings, and that the raw audio isn’t accessible, even to Apple. It also doesn’t identify or attribute the speakers, and it protects the generated transcripts and recaps with end-to-end encryption.
Whether that’s enough for consumers not to feel like the feature is creepy is another matter. Either Apple has found the right balance between utility and privacy, or it’s about to see some consumer backlash.

articles.content:
Former AI employee says insiders believe technology ‘could kill us all’ by decade’s end
(CNN) - AI safety concerns among workers in that field are becoming more commonplace.
Two days ago, the chief scientist for OpenAI warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers’ ability to reliably monitor and control them.
And now, another Anthropic employee has quit.
Former researcher Jacob Coxon posted to social media about his resignation.
“The people building AI earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” the 27-year-old said.
Coxon’s post gained attention after a more senior Anthropic employee, Evan Hubinger, commented that Coxon was correct.
He said that despite Anthropic’s good intentions, the company doesn’t have a plan to avoid so-called superintelligence.
That’s a state in which AI exceeds humans’ ability to control it.
Hubinger clarified his comments shortly afterward in a follow-up post.
He said Anthropic’s own risk report acknowledges the concern but also says present AI poses little chance of gaining such power.
In July, nearly 1,400 AI company employees signed an open letter urging the U.S. government to regulate the technology to rein in big tech and slow the pace of AI.

articles.summary: The response comes after three US agencies accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models.
articles.content:
China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft
The response comes after three US agencies accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models.
China has issued a forceful reply against claims by the United States that top Chinese artificial intelligence companies have engaged in “industrial scale” theft of their US counterparts’ AI models.
The response on Wednesday comes after three US federal agencies – the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), National Security Agency (NSA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) – accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models to benefit their own systems.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3OpenAI unveils latest AI model amid rising scrutiny and safety concerns
- list 2 of 3As the China-US AI race reaches Cairo, Egypt faces a strategic decision
- list 3 of 3AI researcher quits Anthropic saying AI race ‘could kill us all’
The joint advisory on Tuesday said Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot AI had distilled “billions of tokens” from US models since “at least late 2024”, likely with the Chinese government’s “awareness”.
Tokens are the smallest units of text that AI models read, or generate.
On Wednesday, China’s Commerce Ministry dismissed the allegations and accused the US of seeking a “monopoly of the AI industry”.
“If the U.S. suppresses Chinese AI companies under the pretext of targeting distillation, China will take resolute countermeasures,” the ministry said in a statement to the Associated Press.
Distillation is a method in which lesser AI models are trained on more advanced ones. The ministry said the practice is commonplace in the AI industry, including by US AI companies. But American firms say the volume in which it’s being done by Chinese AI models amounts to stealing.
“The sheer scale of these campaigns and their sophistication indicate that distillation is not a supplement to these companies’ AI model development, but the critical core of it,” the US advisory claimed.
The AP reported that China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called on the US to “refrain from making unfounded accusations or smears” against China.
“China’s AI development is the result of high-level technological self-reliance and strength,” ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters at a news conference. “We maintain that all parties should strengthen cooperation to promote AI development that is open, inclusive, universally beneficial and oriented toward the common good.”
Xi visit
The US advisory comes just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit the US, where President Donald Trump will host a summit on a range of topics, including AI.
In a rare move, Xi could be accompanied on his US visit by a large number Chinese executives, according to the Reuters news agency. It is not clear which executives would join the delegation, but past meetings between the two countries may indicate AI leaders could be in the mix.
Xi brought Alibaba founder Jack Ma during his 2015 visit to the US. When Trump visited Xi during a trip to Beijing in May, the US president was joined by more than a dozen American executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
Under Trump, the US government has taken a hardline against efforts to advance Chinese AI models. China is aggressively investing heavily in artificial intelligence and robotics, pouring nearly $300bn into what the government sees as the country’s next economic engine.
While speaking in Dallas on Tuesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an audience that China can “never get ahead” of the US in AI.
“The Chinese distill our models and they can never get ahead of us,” Bessent said.
The Chinese companies named in the US advisory did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

articles.heading: Trump drone tariffs target a technology still used unevenly across US farms
articles.summary: Drone use remains limited among most U.S. farms, but larger farms have adopted the technology at a higher rate than small farm operations, federal data show.  In 2023, 12% of large-scale family farms used drones, compared with 9% of midsize farms and 2% of small family farms, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Economic […]
articles.content:
Drone use remains limited among most U.S. farms, but larger farms have adopted the technology at a higher rate than small farm operations, federal data show.
In 2023, 12% of large-scale family farms used drones, compared with 9% of midsize farms and 2% of small family farms, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Economic Research Service report, America’s Farms and Ranches at a Glance: 2024 Edition.
Among farms that used drones, 40% cited increased yields as a reason for using the technology, and the same share cited saving labor time, according to the USDA’s report. Another 29% cited improving soil or reducing environmental impacts, a quarter said reducing purchased input costs was a reason, and more than one-fifth reported reducing operator fatigue.
The data provides a snapshot of agricultural drone use as the federal government changes the economics of buying the technology.
President Donald Trump announced new tariffs on imported drones and components Aug. 13, pointing out that reliance on foreign suppliers poses a national security risk. The main tariffs took effect Sept. 3.
The highest tariff — 100% — applies to drones weighing more than 25 kilograms, or about 55 pounds, and those equipped with thermal imaging capabilities. The tariff also applies to their docking stations and certain critical components.
The new policy imposes a 25% tariff on certain smaller drones that lack capabilities considered particularly relevant to national security.
Drones and components from the European Union, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan face a 15% tariff. Drones from the United Kingdom face a 10% tariff, provided that substantially all of their hardware, software and technology originate in those countries or the United States.
On farms, drones are used for a range of tasks. USDA has reported that farmers use aerial imagery provided by aircraft, drones, and satellites for crop mapping, livestock monitoring, land surveying, and spraying, among other uses.

<h1>Trump drone tariffs target a technology still used unevenly across US farms</h1> <p class="byline">by Mónica Cordero, Investigate Midwest, Investigate Midwest <br />September 9, 2026</p> <p>Drone use remains limited among most U.S. farms, but larger farms have adopted the technology at a higher rate than small farm operations, federal data show. </p> <p>In 2023, 12% of large-scale family farms used drones, compared with 9% of midsize farms and 2% of small family farms, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Economic Research Service report, <a href="https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/9120/eib-283.pdf?v=13732"><u>America’s Farms and Ranches at a Glance:</u></a> 2024 Edition.</p> </p> <p>Among farms that used drones, 40% cited increased yields as a reason for using the technology, and the same share cited saving labor time, according to the USDA's report. Another 29% cited improving soil or reducing environmental impacts, a quarter said reducing purchased input costs was a reason, and more than one-fifth reported reducing operator fatigue.</p> <p>The data provides a snapshot of agricultural drone use as the federal government changes the economics of buying the technology. </p> <p>President Donald Trump <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/08/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-bolsters-national-security-and-strengthens-u-s-supply-chains-by-imposing-tariffs-on-drones-and-their-parts-and-components/"><u>announced</u></a> new tariffs on imported drones and components Aug. 13, pointing out that reliance on foreign suppliers poses a national security risk. The main tariffs took effect Sept. 3.</p> <p>The highest tariff — 100% — applies to drones weighing more than 25 kilograms, or about 55 pounds, and those equipped with thermal imaging capabilities. The tariff also applies to their docking stations and certain critical components.</p> <p>The new policy imposes a 25% tariff on certain smaller drones that lack capabilities considered particularly relevant to national security.</p> <p>Drones and components from the European Union, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan face a 15% tariff. Drones from the United Kingdom face a 10% tariff, provided that substantially all of their hardware, software and technology originate in those countries or the United States.</p> <p>On farms, drones are used for a range of tasks. USDA has reported that farmers <a href="https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/charts-of-note/107207"><u>use aerial imagery</u></a> provided by aircraft, drones, and satellites for crop mapping, livestock monitoring, land surveying, and spraying, among other uses. </p> <p>This <a target="_blank" href="https://investigatemidwest.org/2026/09/09/trump-drone-tariffs-target-a-technology-still-used-unevenly-across-us-farms/">article</a> first appeared on <a target="_blank" href="https://investigatemidwest.org">Investigate Midwest</a> and is republished here under a <a target="_blank" href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nd/4.0/">Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License</a>.<img src="https://i0.wp.com/investigatemidwest.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/cropped-IM_RIT_logo_color-2.png?resize=150%2C150&amp;ssl=1" style="width:1em;height:1em;margin-left:10px;"></p> <img id="republication-tracker-tool-source" src="https://investigatemidwest.org/?republication-pixel=true&post=760282&amp;ga4=G-R9VE8P61LG" style="width:1px;height:1px;"><script> PARSELY = { autotrack: false, onload: function() { PARSELY.beacon.trackPageView({ url: "https://investigatemidwest.org/2026/09/09/trump-drone-tariffs-target-a-technology-still-used-unevenly-across-us-farms/", urlref: window.location.href }); } } </script> <script id="parsely-cfg" src="//cdn.parsely.com/keys/investigatemidwest.org/p.js"></script>

articles.article_title: New technology guides visitors through Fort Wayne airport, Grand Wayne Center
articles.heading: New technology guides visitors through Fort Wayne airport, Grand Wayne Center
articles.summary: The GoodMaps app is now available to offer directions through the inside of the Fort Wayne International Airport and the Grand Wayne Convention Center.
articles.content:
FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WANE) – Fort Wayne visitors don’t have to worry about losing track of their airport gate or missing a conference downtown thanks to newly implemented technology that maps out two of the Summit City’s largest facilities.
The GoodMaps app is now available to offer directions through the inside of the Fort Wayne International Airport and the Grand Wayne Convention Center. The platform uses precise indoor mapping technology and accessible wayfinding to provide users with real-time, turn-by-turn directions through their mobile device, as described in a press release shared Wednesday by the airport.
GoodMaps is a mobile app visitors can download on their phones. It’s also available on the airport’s website. The technology aims to guide users ranging from first-time visitors to longtime residents trying to navigate the two local facilities that are often crowded and have the potential to be overwhelming.
Kevin Kline, a community engagement representative for GoodMaps, said the platform can be particularly useful for those who have vision or hearing impairment, mobility challenges, or whose first language is not English.
In the video below, Kline demonstrates how GoodMaps can guide visitors through the Grand Wayne Center:
As one of the largest convention sites in the state, second only to a facility in Indianapolis, the Grand Wayne Center brings in thousands of visitors for more than 300 events annually, according to Visit Fort Wayne. Meanwhile, nearly one million passengers flew in and out of the Fort Wayne airport in 2025.
“We are thrilled to bring GoodMaps to the Fort Wayne community along with the Grand Wayne Convention Center,” said Scott Hinderman, Chief Executive Officer of the Fort Wayne-Allen County Airport Authority. “Fort Wayne International Airport is committed to providing an accessible travel experience for all passengers, as shown throughout our recently completed terminal expansion project. GoodMaps is another way we can give passengers confidence and independence throughout their journey, while continuing to make FWA an accessible and inclusive front door to northeast Indiana.”
GoodMaps was incorporated locally with the support of a grant from the WindSwell Foundation, an organization that supports children and adults with intellectual, developmental, and physical disabilities.
See other cities where GoodMaps is available and learn more about the platform on its website.

articles.title: DOD’s AI Push Faces Data, Technology, and Policy Barriers
articles.description: DOD’s AI Push Faces Data, Technology, and Policy Barriers meritalk.com
articles.description_html: DOD’s AI Push Faces Data, Technology, and Policy Barriers  meritalk.com
articles.article_title: DOD’s AI Push Faces Data, Technology, and Policy Barriers
articles.heading: DOD’s AI Push Faces Data, Technology, and Policy Barriers
articles.summary: The department must modernize data infrastructure, improve accessibility, and change how it approaches technology to get AI tools into the hands of warfighters faster, a senior DOD official said.
articles.content:
The department must modernize data infrastructure, improve accessibility, and change how it approaches technology to get AI tools into the hands of warfighters faster, a senior DOD official said.
Outdated data infrastructure, inadequate metadata standards, limited application programming interface (API) access, and policy challenges are among the barriers the Department of Defense (DOD) must overcome to operationalize artificial intelligence (AI) across the department, according to Cameron Stanley, DOD’s chief digital and AI officer.
Speaking Sept. 8 at the 17th Annual Billington Cybersecurity Summit in Washington, D.C., Stanley said organizations that have successfully adopted AI continuously refine how they use the technology, identify gaps in their data, and work to address them.
“This is something that you’ll see continuously throughout the department. It’s not just the systems themselves, the technology themselves, or even the data quality itself,” Stanley said.
Stanley said DOD needs to make data more accessible, develop digitally savvy operational personnel who can push vendors to demonstrate their capabilities, and integrate AI into decision-making workflows.
Getting there, he said, will require the department to change how it approaches technology.
“The ‘way we’ve always done [things],’ is the most risky course of action,” Stanley said, adding that the department needs to “think differently” if it wants to get AI tools into the hands of warfighters faster.
Modernizing data for AI
Much of DOD’s data remains locked in aging systems and repositories that were not designed for modern data processing, which creates hurdles for accessing and using that information in AI applications, Stanley said.
“You can’t just access that data using an API, where it’s not structured the right way for modern data processing systems to actually have access to it,” Stanley said.
Metadata standards present another challenge. Stanley said the department needs clear, high-quality metadata and tags for data objects so that classification requirements can be considered in advance and machines can process the information more effectively and quickly.
Stanley said that since 2018, DOD has pursued an approach to improving access to data sources by establishing standards for how department components hold and make data accessible.
“We can actually mandate that department elements have to adhere to certain data standards when it comes to their holding data and their accessibility of that data. So, we’re looking at a number of different ways to do that,” he said.
Helping allies advance AI
Stanley also discussed DOD’s efforts to help U.S. allies and partners adopt AI. “What we’re seeing from our allies and partners is they are behind,” Stanley said. “They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do. They don’t have the scale that we do.”
The United States is working with a number of partners to better understand their AI needs, Stanley said. Part of that effort involves helping allies avoid mistakes the United States made during its own AI development.
“There’s so many instances where you can point to and say we made a mistake and we should not have gone down that route,” Stanley said. “We wasted a lot of time and money learning that part of lesson. Do not learn that lesson. Go this way instead.”
Stanley said the approach is showing results with Five Eyes partners, several NATO partners and allies, and several Asian allies.

articles.content:
NJ TRANSIT UPGRADES REAL-TIME BUS TRACKING TECHNOLOGY AND INTRODUCES FREE ONBOARD WI-FI
New Onboard Technology Enhances Real-Time Bus Location Data, Supports More Accurate Arrival Predictions; System Also Provides Customers with Complimentary Wi-Fi Service
September 9, 2026
NEWARK, NJ — NJ TRANSIT today announced significant progress in its efforts to continue modernizing its bus fleet and improving the customer experience. President & CEO Kris Kolluri showcased a statewide initiative to upgrade computer equipment and antennas on buses to provide more accurate real-time location data. NJ TRANSIT is utilizing this improved data to provide more accurate bus arrival predictions, and the new hardware offers bus customers free Wi-Fi. The equipment and free Wi-Fi are currently available on more than 1,500 buses statewide and are scheduled to expand to nearly 2,000 buses by the end of 2026. The enhancements continue to advance Governor Mikie Sherrill’s Rapid Action Plan and her commitment to improving accessibility, safety, cleanliness, and technology across all NJ TRANSIT services.
"New Jerseyans rely on NJ TRANSIT to get to work, school, appointments, and everywhere else life takes them, and we should be doing everything we can to make those trips easier,” said Governor Mikie Sherrill. "By upgrading real-time bus tracking and providing free Wi-Fi for customers, we're making NJ TRANSIT work better for the people who rely on it every day."
“Offering free Wi-Fi, service updates, and real-time arrival information will make bus travel more convenient for our customers while modernizing the technology that supports our operations,” said NJDOT Commissioner and NJ TRANSIT Chair Priya Jain. “I appreciate Governor Sherrill’s leadership and the sense of urgency fostered by the Rapid Action Plan which is helping deliver lasting improvements for customers across New Jersey.”
"Customers want to know where their bus is and when it will arrive, and arrival predictions in our app have improved from 74 percent to 86 percent accuracy,” said NJ TRANSIT President & CEO Kris Kolluri. “With the introduction of free Wi-Fi on more than 1,500 buses today, and nearly 2,000 by the end of the year, we’re also delivering a ride that becomes more productive for our bus customers."
In total, more than 1,500 buses currently have the new technology. NJ TRANSIT retrofitted more than 1,300 buses with the hardware and free Wi-Fi, while new buses entering the fleet already have the upgraded components. Additional retrofits and more new buses joining the fleet will expand that number to more than 1,900 by the end of 2026, representing more than 80% of the 2,373 buses in the fleet. The remaining buses are marked for retirement and, as they are replaced, the new buses will be manufactured with the technology already installed.
Free Wi-Fi on Buses
The provision of free Wi-Fi on board NJ TRANSIT buses aims to address the inequity in broadband access by offering this critical feature in a setting which may be the only convenient and/or practical place for many bus customers to access the internet. This project is funded by a $15 million federal grant from the U.S. Department of Treasury as part of the Capital Projects Fund.
The NJ TRANSIT bus Wi-Fi network is structured to provide bandwidth for all customers on each bus, supporting general web browsing activities. Buses enabled with free Wi-Fi are marked with a sticker near the entrance of the bus. To connect to NJ TRANSIT’s Wi‑Fi, open your device’s wireless network list and select NJTRANSITWIFI. This will launch the Accept & Connect widget; press Accept & Continue to proceed. Your browser will then open the NJ TRANSIT Connected Bus landing page, which provides links to key New Jersey services related to employment, education, and health.
For more information and frequently asked questions on the NJ TRANSIT bus Wi-Fi network, click HERE.
Bus Arrival Predictions
NJ TRANSIT is advancing its real-time bus arrival information through an ongoing effort with Swiftly, a leading transit technology company. This work continues to improve the reliability of bus arrival predictions to some of the best in the country. Beginning in October, customers will see these enhanced predictions on the NJ TRANSIT website, the mobile app, station signage, and a wide range of third-party applications. NJ TRANSIT will continue strengthening these improvements through upgraded GPS hardware and antennas that provide more precise location data. The goal is to give customers clearer and more dependable information about where their bus is and when it will arrive.
Digital Bus Signs
NJ TRANSIT continues testing new high-tech bus stop signs with digital screens showing customers the real-time arrival information of the next bus. The pilot program showcases two companies’ technology at eight bus stops.
NJ TRANSIT has installed five signs from infrastructure provider BusPas at locations in Hudson County (two in Hoboken, two in Union City and one in Jersey City). The signs feature real-time customer information such as arrivals, detours, delays, service alerts and bus occupancy levels. As part of the pilot, the signs are solar powered and employ e-paper displays, like that of popular reading tablets, making them ADA-compliant. They also include text-to-speech announcement capability and automated safety lighting for improved nighttime visibility.
A similar pilot is underway in Manalapan Township and Howell Township in Monmouth County through a partnership with Urban Solar, a manufacturer of solar energy systems for bus stops and shelters.
The BusPas digital signs currently in service are located at:
• 15th Street and Willow Avenue, Hoboken
• 9th Street and Washington Street, Hoboken
• 31st Street and Bergenline Avenue, Union City
• 31st Street at JFK Boulevard, Union City
• Congress Street at Palisades Avenue, Jersey City
Urban Solar signs are located at:
Manalapan Township
- Route-9 North at Gordon’s Corner Rd. (two signs at this location)
Howell Township
- Aldrich Rd. Park and Ride (Route-9 North and Aldrich Rd.)
These efforts support NJ TRANSIT’s Bus Fleet Modernization initiative, which is improving customer experience through modern technology, enhanced connectivity, more reliable real‑time service information, and a fully modernized bus fleet by 2031. Together, these upgrades help make bus travel more convenient, productive, and dependable for customers.
About NJ TRANSIT
NJ TRANSIT is the nation's largest statewide public transportation system providing more than 925,000 weekday trips on 264 bus routes, three light rail lines, 12 commuter rail lines and through Access Link paratransit service. It is the third largest transit system in the country with 165 rail stations, 62 light rail stations and more than 19,000 bus stops linking major points in New Jersey, New York and Philadelphia.

Manalapan Township

Howell Township

articles.article_title: Creekstone Energy, University of Utah studying feasibility of novel water generation technology
articles.heading: Creekstone Energy, University of Utah studying feasibility of novel water generation technology
articles.summary: The developer behind the world's largest data center campus in Millard County on Wednesday announced a project that aims to capture water vapor from natural gas combustion and convert it into usable water.
articles.content:
- Creekstone Energy and the University of Utah are testing GIGAWATER technology for the Delta Gigasite data center campus.
- This technology aims to captures water vapor from natural gas combustion and converts it into usable water.
- Creekstone is funding the research and initial results are expected next summer.
SALT LAKE CITY — Data center discussions in the Beehive State start and stop with water.
Justifiably so, with the entire state sitting in either severe or extreme drought conditions, according to data from the U.S. Drought Monitor.
And despite a stretch of heavy rainfall and severe storms that began in late August, experts from the Division of Water Resources said the intense flooding from the storms won't be enough to end the drought.
With this reality in mind, Creekstone Energy — the developer behind the Delta Gigasite, the planned world's largest data center campus in Millard County — on Wednesday announced a project aimed at not just conserving water, but generating it.
'Change the way the data center industry thinks about water'
The patent-pending technology called GIGAWATER, Creekstone Energy CEO Ray Conley explained, aims to capture water vapor produced by the combustion of natural gas for electricity generation and convert it into water.
"We don't believe Utah should have to choose between economic growth and responsible water stewardship," Conley said. "Building the largest data center campus in the world, that comes to the forefront very immediately. And we think that the data centers have to be designed for the places where they're built."
Conley likened the technology to capturing water dripping from a vehicle's exhaust pipe, but at a much larger scale.
"We're taking an existing process of how those engines run and instead of running the exhaust up a pipe and letting it just float up into the air, we're instead running the pipe underground in a special way to capture the exhaust," Conley said.
At this stage, though, the GIGAWATER technology is conceptual only. To test if the system can truly perform as imagined and to scale, Creekstone has signed a formal research agreement with the University of Utah's Energy and Geoscience Institute to objectively and independently review the technology.
Conley noted that Creekstone is entirely funding the U.'s research.
"We have to pay that regardless of what their answer is. So I might end up paying them for the research and get a bad answer. That's the risk we take," Conley said.
Related:
The first phase of the U.'s review, Conley said, will test the "core assumptions" of the concept, including the chemistry, thermodynamics, heat transfer and expected water recovery from an operation of the Delta Gigasite's scale.
Milind Deo, principal investigator at the U.'s Energy and Geoscience Institute, called the science behind GIGAWATER "promising."
"(Energy and Geoscience Institute) is committed to rigorous, independent verification, moving from theory and math through computer modeling and, ultimately, to physical demonstration. If the results bear out, this could change the way the data center industry thinks about water," Deo said in a statement.
Phase two would include building a "working pilot" of the technology near the Delta site to actually test the system and confirm whether or not it works as intended.
"(Energy and Geoscience Institute's) work is really meant to just help us determine where the model is right, where it needs refinement and then what would be needed to take it to commercial-scale performance," Conley said, adding that he expects the research to be completed sometime next summer.
Potential water uses
Like the efficacy of the technology itself, there isn't a definite answer for how the collected water could be used.
Conley said he believes there's a good chance that with "at least a little bit of filtration" the water could be potable. He noted that it will likely have a higher degree of acidity, in which case it would have potential agricultural applications.
"We really have to do a little more chemistry ... and frankly, testing it to figure out, 'Is it agricultural? Is it potable?'" Conley said. "The goal doesn't have to be make it drinkable at the end of the day, because there's plenty of other uses."
Creekstone's internal engineering analysis projects a yield of approximately 4,000 acre-feet of water per year, according to a release from the company.
If the company's projections hold, Conley said he expects the site to create "vastly more" water than it would consume.
Who would technically own the water captured remains a question, Conley admitted, saying there's "no precedent" to go by when discussing water rights.
"It's not like we're doing something that's been done before and so it leaves an open question. Those are things that are really matters of law," Conley said.

articles.heading: NASA starts to craft engineering, tech services recompete
articles.summary: The space agency is aptly calling this new contract ORBIT and using industry feedback to structure the competition.
articles.content:
NASA starts to craft engineering, tech services recompete
The space agency is aptly calling this new contract ORBIT and using industry feedback to structure the competition.
NASA has started market research efforts to inform its work in creating a new small business set-aside contract supporting the agency’s Johnson Space Center, which houses spaceflight training and flight control operations.
The Operations, Research, and Broad Innovative Technology Services contract is being envisioned as a single vehicle that brings together mission engineering, specialized IT, mission support and other technology services.
Via this request for information posted Sept. 4, NASA is collecting capability statements to determine the level of competition and small business subcontracting goals for ORBIT.
ORBIT will be a multiple-award effort and succeed the current Mission Enabling Support Contract, which NASA awarded four spots on in 2020.
The agency has obligated $85 million in task order volume to-date against MESC ahead of its planned sunset in September 2027, according to Deltek data. Rothe Development has been the largest recipient at 43%, followed by Science Applications International Corp. at 29% and Mathematical Research at 21%. ASRC Federal represents the remaining 5%.
NASA has broken out ORBIT’s scope of work into four functional areas:
- Mission and systems engineering support
- Technical evaluation, analysis, and independent assessments
- Specialized IT and operations
- Advanced mission research-and-development
Work will support the Johnson Space Center’s Flight Operations Directorate and its affiliate organizations comprising approximately 2,500 individuals that include flight controllers, mission planners, trainers, astronauts flight directors, engineering support, and administrative staff supporting commercial, external, and international partners.
Responses to the RFI are due by 6 p.m. Eastern time on Oct. 6.

articles.title: Disgruntled AI researcher: This technology 'could kill us all by the end of the decade'
articles.description: Disgruntled AI researcher: This technology 'could kill us all by the end of the decade' Yahoo Finance
articles.description_html: Disgruntled AI researcher: This technology 'could kill us all by the end of the decade'  Yahoo Finance
articles.article_title: Disgruntled AI researcher: This technology 'could kill us all by the end of the decade'
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: A researcher who worked for both OpenAI and Anthropic says the companies are "gambling with our lives," prompting him to resign and leave the industry.
articles.content:
A researcher who worked for both OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) and Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) says the companies are "gambling with our lives," prompting him to resign and leave the industry.
"Do not underestimate the power of this technology," Jacob Coxon wrote in a widely shared thread on Tuesday evening. "These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing."
Coxon, who said he resigned from Anthropic this week, said the threat is coming from inside the house.
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger," he wrote.
Anthropic and OpenAI are arguably the two frontrunners in the furious race to develop and scale artificial intelligence. Both are set to go public at massive valuations as markets continue to bet heavily on the technology's potential, despite a historic debt run-up across the industry.
Claude Code AI parent Anthropic, which could file paperwork for its initial public offering as soon as this month, is expected to debut near $2 trillion, double what the company was worth four months ago. OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, is expected to go public later this year or early in 2027. Investors also expect its stock to debut above 13 figures.
Coxon, who was also interviewed by the Wall Street Journal, is a 27-year-old British researcher whose job was to train new AI models via vast data consumption. In his X thread, he described each firm's thinking about the stakes of AI.
"At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes," he wrote. "At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk."
He ended with a challenge for those continuing to work in the industry:
"Do you want to kick off a superintelligent (Reinforcement Learning) run without a rigorous understanding of its mind? Should you put your head down because 'it's happening anyway' — or take this moment to call for different conditions?"

articles.article_title: “Give People Proof They Can Hold”: Wildlife on Why Technology Needs Better Stories | LBBOnline
articles.heading: “Give People Proof They Can Hold”: Wildlife on Why Technology Needs Better Stories
articles.summary: Little Black Book, The LA-based creative company tells LBB’s April Summers about what it takes to translate highly technical ideas into experiences that consumers want to engage with – and actually care about
articles.content:
How do you tell stories about technology that people can actually understand, feel and remember? That is the question I posed to Scott Friedman, executive creative director and co-founder of Wildlife, whose work increasingly sits at the intersection of technology, creativity and experience.
It is a particularly pertinent query at a time when technological innovation is accelerating faster than most people can meaningfully keep up with. AI agents, cloud computing, developer tools and increasingly sophisticated infrastructure may be transforming how we work and live, but communicating what that actually means to a human being is another challenge altogether.

But, as the novelty of AI wears off and audiences become increasingly difficult to impress, the production company believes the technology itself is rarely the most compelling part of the story.
Instead, Scott tells me why Wildlife believes it's their job to find the one human moment hiding inside the technical spec, and how this approach has informed the studio’s work with technology brands including Amazon Web Services, for whom the team recently created ‘Rue Visionnaire’, which launched at Cannes.
For Scott, the thinking extends well beyond any one project. The bigger creative challenge is how to turn something abstract and often invisible into something people can see, touch, experience and ultimately remember. And increasingly, that means giving audiences something more powerful than an explanation. Instead, it gives them a reason to care.
LBB> Wildlife has become known for translating highly technical ideas into experiences people can actually engage with. What do you think makes telling technology stories such a unique creative challenge?

Scott> We lean into tactility and simplification. The further ahead the technology is, the more we try to ground it in something tangible that people can relate to or see a clear use case that might be less evident when they hear about a breakthrough feature. How can we give them something uniquely theirs to walk away with? A printed photo, a storefront, a game level, an object shaped by their hands.

Scott> It never starts with technology. It starts with the question, ‘What would make someone stop, lean in, and want to try this themselves?’. How can we simplify this and bring the core capability or value to life in a way the target audience can connect with? We work backward from that answer, and then figure out the execution needed to make it happen. Only once we know what's going to hook someone do we figure out what kind of experience and technologies are needed to deliver it.
Scott> No question, it’s to make them feel something, always. If someone walks away from one of our experiences able to recite a spec sheet, we've failed. If they walk away with a story to tell, something they made, or something that surprised them, we've done our job. Understanding can follow later through strategic channel strategy, which we also help our clients think through and improve. The reaction has to come first, and that excitement has a much longer half-life than a technical diagram.
‘Rue Visionnaire’ took something genuinely hard to picture – a team of AI agents reasoning through a business plan, a brand, a marketing campaign – and gave it a physical reveal: your unique vision made real, turned into an actual storefront in front of you with a sense of magic. It reaffirmed that audiences don't want a demo of the technology's intelligence. They want to watch their own idea become real in a way that would otherwise be impossible. The more sophisticated the system underneath, the more the experience on top needs to stay simple, human, and personal.
LBB> As AI, cloud computing and emerging technologies become increasingly central to people's lives, do you think the role of creativity in explaining innovation has become more important than ever?
Scott> More than ever. People are getting jaded, fast. The shiny new AI thing loses its allure in weeks, not years. We’re feeling that personally and professionally within our team at Wildlife. That raises the bar for creativity just to hold someone's attention, let alone earn their trust. We use ourselves as a benchmark, would we engage? Finding new ways to go beyond the usual demos or expected experiences. As these technologies get more powerful and less visible, creativity is what makes them legible and human again. Without it, innovation is just noise nobody has time to understand. The best innovations feel magical and set your imagination running wild, and the same is true with the best experiences.

articles.title: Gulf Blue, CNMOC Establish Partnership to Advance Technology Transfer and Innovation on the Gulf Coast

articles.description_html: Gulf Blue, CNMOC Establish Partnership to Advance Technology Transfer and Innovation on the Gulf Coast  The University of Southern Mississippi
articles.article_title: Gulf Blue, CNMOC Establish Partnership to Advance Technology Transfer and Innovation on the Gulf Coast
articles.heading:
Gulf Blue, CNMOC Establish Partnership to Advance Technology Transfer and Innovation
                     on the Gulf Coast
articles.summary: Gulf Blue, CNMOC Establish Partnership to Advance Technology Transfer and Innovation on the Gulf Coast The University of Southern Mississippi
articles.content:
Gulf Blue, CNMOC Establish Partnership to Advance Technology Transfer and Innovation on the Gulf Coast
Wed, 09/09/2026 - 10:34am
Gulf Blue, LLC, has entered into a five-year Partnership Intermediary Agreement (PIA) with Commander, Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command (CNMOC) to expand technology transfer, commercialization and collaborative research
opportunities between Naval Oceanography, small businesses and educational institutions
across the Gulf Coast.
The agreement establishes a formal framework through which Gulf Blue will help advance
U.S. warfighter capabilities by promoting cooperative activities between CNMOC and
industry, academia and entrepreneurs to rapidly identify dual-use technologies that
meet the mission-critical needs of the Department of War (DoW).
“This is an important step in strengthening the connections between CNMOC and innovators
in Mississippi,” said Brian J. Cuevas, Ph.D., associate vice president of research
and innovation at The University of Southern Mississippi. “Through Gulf Blue, Mississippi
has built an ecosystem focused on connecting innovation with opportunity. This PIA
gives us another powerful mechanism to help companies and researchers engage with
Naval Oceanography while supporting technology commercialization, economic development
and national security.”
CNMOC, headquartered at John C. Stennis Space Center in Mississippi, leads the Navy’s
meteorology and oceanography enterprise and supports naval and joint forces through
capabilities spanning meteorology and oceanography, hydrography, bathymetry, precise
time and related environmental intelligence.
Under the agreement, Gulf Blue will work with CNMOC to foster cooperative research,
technology transfer and economic development along the Gulf Coast Region by:
- Conducting technology showcases, market research and industry engagement activities;
- Highlighting technologies and capabilities from Gulf Coast companies and universities that may address Naval Oceanography research and operational needs;
- Supporting STEM outreach, mentorship, workforce development and connections between CNMOC subject-matter experts and educational institutions;
- Connecting small businesses and educational institutions with CNMOC technologies available for licensing;
- Identifying prospective partners for Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs);
- Connecting researchers and companies with CNMOC research priorities and Broad Agency Announcement opportunities;
- Supporting engagement around Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) opportunities; and
- Identifying CNMOC research capabilities that may support outside businesses and educational institutions.
“To meet the demands of the modern fleet, we have to move at the speed of innovation.
Gulf Blue acts as a direct extension of our Tech Transfer office,” said Sidney Dills,
N95 Office of Research and Technology Applications. “This PIA gives us the agile outreach
capability we need to continuously scout, evaluate and transition technologies that
address today’s immediate warfighting needs and tomorrow’s emerging threats.”
The partnership builds upon Gulf Blue’s broader effort to strengthen the Blue Economy
innovation ecosystem along the Mississippi Gulf Coast by connecting companies with
university research, federal assets, testing environments, industry expertise and
commercialization resources.
“This is exactly the type of connection Gulf Blue was created to facilitate,” said
Natalie Guess, assistant director of innovation and impact at The University of Southern
Mississippi. “The Mississippi Gulf Coast has an extraordinary concentration of federal
research, ocean science, defense, university and private-sector capabilities. By creating
stronger pathways between those assets, we can help innovative technologies move from
research to application while creating new opportunities for companies, researchers
and our regional economy.”
The agreement also provides opportunities for CNMOC and Gulf Blue to jointly showcase
technologies and research priorities, identify potential commercialization partners
and strengthen the regional pipeline of companies and talent supporting ocean science,
maritime technology and national security.
About Gulf Blue
Gulf Blue, LLC, is a wholly owned subsidiary of The University of Southern Mississippi
Research Foundation (USMRF), a nonprofit entity. By its Articles of Incorporation,
USMRF is administered and operated exclusively for the benefit of The University of
Southern Mississippi. Gulf Blue is considered a disregarded entity of USMRF for tax
purposes and thus is considered a 501(c)(3) not-for-profit organization. Gulf Blue
leads a collaborative, place-based innovation initiative supported by the university
and the USMFR to advance innovation, entrepreneurship and economic growth across the
Blue Economy. Through programs including Gulf Blue Navigator, Gulf Blue connects high-growth
companies with research expertise, coastal testing environments, federal and industry
partners, investment opportunities and other resources designed to accelerate commercialization
and growth along the Mississippi Gulf Coast.
About Commander, Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command
Commander, Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command leads the U.S. Navy’s meteorology
and oceanography enterprise from John C. Stennis Space Center, Mississippi. Naval
Oceanography provides environmental information and capabilities, including meteorology,
oceanography, hydrography, bathymetry and related scientific expertise that enable
naval and joint-force decision-making, safety and operational effectiveness.

articles.title: CoreWeave CEO chalks up public AI pushback to the speed of change: 'And that is frightening'
articles.description: CoreWeave CEO chalks up public AI pushback to the speed of change: 'And that is frightening' CNBC
articles.description_html: CoreWeave CEO chalks up public AI pushback to the speed of change: 'And that is frightening'  CNBC
articles.article_title: CoreWeave CEO chalks up public AI pushback to the speed of change: 'And that is frightening'
articles.heading: CoreWeave CEO chalks up public AI pushback to the speed of change: 'And that is frightening'
articles.summary: CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator spoke to CNBC at the Goldman Sachs' Communacopia + Technology Conference this week.
articles.content:
The public opposition to artificial intelligence and data centers is front and center at the Goldman Sachs Communcacopia + Technology Conference.
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator told CNBC's David Faber that companies haven't explained the technology's benefits well enough to the public.
"I don't think we have done a particularly good job of talking about the benefits of what the data centers allow the AI companies to be able to deliver to people, to governments, to decision making," Intrator said in comments that aired Wednesday.
The annual conference brings together leaders across the biggest tech and media companies, and AI adoption — along with the pushback many local communities are showing towards its buildout — is perhaps one of the biggest opportunities, and risks, facing businesses of every kind.
Intrator insisted that the fear around the transformation isn't about data centers, specifically, but is about how fast things are changing.
"It is really about: Hey, you know the world is changing, and it's changing very quickly, and that's going to have impacts on myself. It's going to have impacts on my children, and what is that going to look like? And that is frightening," he added.
As Goldman's conference got underway, another set of comments in the tech world caught attention as an AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic Tuesday, warning the rapidly-evolving technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade."
Jacob Coxon, who worked at both Anthropic and its chief competitor OpenAI, accused the companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race towards AI superintelligence.
"Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing," Coxon wrote in a post on X announcing his resignation.
Cable companies talk broadband pressure
Other disruptions were on the agenda Wednesday, as cable executives continued to forecast competitive pressure on the broadband business.
Both Comcast and Charter Communications have seen quarterly broadband customer losses in recent years due to the rise of alternatives, namely fixed wireless, or 5G, providers.
On Wednesday, Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong reiterated that those pressures still exist, particularly from fixed wireless.
"Satellite looms out there as a potential threat," Armstrong said Wednesday, in addition to competition from fixed wireless. He added that while competition from satellite providers like Starlink isn't necessarily happening yet, "there's no complacency around it."
"I think we'll see it over time … in particular in rural and maybe deep suburban markets," Armstrong said of potential satellite competition.
Comcast and Charter's stocks were each down more than 5% in midday trading.
Comcast and Charter have reworked pricing strategies and leaned on their growing mobile businesses as methods to retain, and potentially gain, more broadband customers in recent years.
Armstrong added that, as mentioned during Comcast's second-quarter earnings call, the company is starting to see "irrational competition" when it comes to pricing for fiber broadband and that's continuing into the third quarter.
For the period ended June 30, Comcast reported that it once again lost broadband customers, and revenue for the segment dropped due to lower pricing plans and promotions that began to take hold.
During an interview with CNBC's David Faber on Wednesday, Charter CEO Chris Winfrey said that while competition is affecting the cable broadband business in the short term, the executive is confident that long-term there will be improvements.

articles.article_title: AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?
articles.heading: AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?
articles.summary: Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligence
articles.content:
Does artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”. Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade?
These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine.
Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist.
Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.”
The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI).
On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade.
Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”.
Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race.
Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue. OpenAI pointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”
The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing.
Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.”
The Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”.
Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.”
On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action.
The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.”
ControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out.
Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity.
He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.”
Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI.
The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.”
Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”.
Other contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.”
David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”.
“AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable.
“What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.”
Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.
“These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.”
Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not.
“It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”

articles.title: Technology employment is growing despite tech sector layoffs
articles.description: Technology employment is growing despite tech sector layoffs HR Dive
articles.description_html: Technology employment is growing despite tech sector layoffs  HR Dive
articles.article_title: Technology employment is growing despite tech sector layoffs
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's HR industry news
articles.summary: As companies across industries prioritize artificial intelligence, tech job openings are coming from an increasing variety of organizations.
articles.content:
Dive Brief:
- Technology occupation employment grew by 86,000 workers in August, according to analysis by technology training and certification company CompTIA, based on data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
- On the other hand, tech companies cut approximately 14,700 positions, including technical and nontechnical roles, per CompTIA. The company said this data could be the result of recent layoffs from U.S.-headquartered tech firms.
- In addition, there were more than 320,000 active job postings requiring artificial intelligence-related skills in August, representing a 4.5% month-over-month increase, according to CompTIA's analysis of data from workforce analytics firm Lightcast.
Dive Insight:
The technology job market is changing rapidly as employers move past AI experimentation and toward AI implementation, CompTIA said. The company added that employers are now “increasingly incorporating AI into business operations, creating demand for workers who can apply AI tools, manage AI-enabled workflows, and support AI-driven initiatives.”
As a result, demand for technology talent remains strong despite what layoff numbers may suggest. CompTIA found “nearly 600,000 active technology occupation postings” in August, with 42% representing newly posted positions and the remaining percentage belonging to open roles still unfilled from previous months.
“Growth in tech support, infrastructure, project management and cybersecurity roles suggests employers remain focused on strengthening core technology functions while expanding emerging capabilities,” CompTIA said.
The analysis found that many of the available technology jobs came from outside traditional tech sectors, including manufacturing, administrative support services, and retail.
A July report from Indeed’s Hiring Lab found that the number of job postings with the words “artificial intelligence” in the title more than tripled in the U.S. since 2022, and “AI-touched job titles” increased across every tracked market. In five of the six countries the report examined, “more than half of all AI-touched job titles are now outside tech occupations,” while the U.S. led the nontech category at 63%. In addition, that report said that many roles with AI in the title were jobs that “have existed for decades” and been updated to include AI.
Another report, from tech career site Dice, found that job postings for roles with AI in the title jumped 173% year over year in Q1 2026, while software development jobs dipped 22% for the same period. Growth in tech hiring was uneven across sectors, the report noted, with tech listings in finance and banking up 47% year-over-year, compared to a 23% year-over-year increase in overall tech job postings.

articles.title: ‘Maxton Hall’ Uses Amazon AI Technology To Sync Actors’ Lips With Human-Dubbed Audio
articles.description: ‘Maxton Hall’ Uses Amazon AI Technology To Sync Actors’ Lips With Human-Dubbed Audio Deadline

articles.article_title: ‘Maxton Hall’ Uses Amazon AI Technology To Sync Actors’ Lips With Human-Dubbed Audio
articles.heading: ‘Maxton Hall’ Uses Amazon AI Technology To Sync Actors’ Lips With Human-Dubbed Audio
articles.summary: Amazon Prime Video series Maxton Hall is the streamer's first programming to feature AI technology synchronizing actors' lips with human-dubbed audio.
articles.content:
Amazon Prime Video series Maxton Hall is the first programming on the streaming platform to feature new AI technology synchronizing actors’ lip movements with human-dubbed audio.
The feature went live Wednesday on the first two seasons of the series, and will be used for its third season when it premieres later this year. The German YA series was quickly renewed for a second season in 2024 after it smashed viewership records for Prime Video. Season 3’s release date on December 9 was confirmed last week.
“Have you ever watched a dubbed movie only to notice the actors’ mouths continuing to move after the dialogue has ended, taking you completely out of the story?” Amazon asked in a blog post. “Prime Video is addressing this issue with a feature designed to create a more enjoyable and accessible viewing experience for our global customers.”
Watch on Deadline
Maxton Hall, a German series based on the 2018 novel Save Me by Mona Kasten, is Prime’s most-watched international original series ever.
The lip-syncing method will also be used on other series down the line, the company said. Raf Soltanovich, VP of technology at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said the goal is to create “a more seamless and immersive way for customers to enjoy global content” while also helping creators reach broader audiences. His statement went on to stress that “creative oversight” will help “ensure the integrity of their artistic vision is preserved.”
Netflix has led the charge among streamers in terms of cross-pollinating programming across global territories, establishing a template years ago with shows like Squid Game, Money Heist and many others. Amazon, Disney and other players have worked to ramp up their non-U.S. offerings in an effort to close the gap.
Amazon does have the advantage of its war-chest of tech resources. Last year, the company started testing new AI tools that dub movies into English and Latin American Spanish.
