articles.summary: Taking place September 29–October 1, 2026, on the MIT campus and online, EmTech Future is the reimagined flagship technology event from MIT Technology Review.
articles.content:
Leaders from enterprise and academia will gather at MIT to explore the convergence of AI, quantum, and energy.

CAMBRIDGE, Mass., Sept. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Taking place September 29–October 1, 2026 , on the MIT campus and online, EmTech Future is the reimagined flagship technology event from MIT Technology Review.

Curated by the editorial team of MIT Technology Review, this year's agenda explores the theme " Convergence," examining how the next wave of technological change may be shaped as much by the interaction between fields as by the advances within them.

Through keynotes, interviews, guided experiences, and conversations with industry-leading researchers and innovators, attendees will gain a clearer view of the systems, ideas, and breakthroughs that will define the coming decade.

Agenda highlights include:

- Convergence – Explore how AI, quantum technologies, and energy systems are beginning to intersect, creating new possibilities across business and society.

Convergence – Explore how AI, quantum technologies, and energy systems are beginning to intersect, creating new possibilities across business and society.

- At the Frontier of Intelligence – Examine the next advances in AI, from reasoning and autonomy to multimodal systems, and learn how they are expanding what machine intelligence can do.

At the Frontier of Intelligence – Examine the next advances in AI, from reasoning and autonomy to multimodal systems, and learn how they are expanding what machine intelligence can do.

- Powering the Future – Explore how rising demand, new technologies, and an increasingly electrified world are making energy a defining force in how technology scales.

Powering the Future – Explore how rising demand, new technologies, and an increasingly electrified world are making energy a defining force in how technology scales.

- At the Quantum Frontier – Examine the breakthroughs moving quantum technologies from laboratory experiments toward practical systems, with new possibilities emerging in computation, security, and beyond.

At the Quantum Frontier – Examine the breakthroughs moving quantum technologies from laboratory experiments toward practical systems, with new possibilities emerging in computation, security, and beyond.

- Into the Institute – Go beyond the conference stage through curated visits and conversations with researchers across MIT, offering behind-the-scenes access to active research environments in areas including quantum, robotics, advanced manufacturing, and nuclear science.

Into the Institute – Go beyond the conference stage through curated visits and conversations with researchers across MIT, offering behind-the-scenes access to active research environments in areas including quantum, robotics, advanced manufacturing, and nuclear science.

To access the full agenda, visit EmTechFuture.com .

Featured speakers include:

- Cory Doctorow , New York Times bestselling and award-winning author

Cory Doctorow , New York Times bestselling and award-winning author

- Mark Gorenberg , Chair, MIT Corporation

Mark Gorenberg , Chair, MIT Corporation

- Raia Hadsell , VP of Research, Google DeepMind

Raia Hadsell , VP of Research, Google DeepMind

- Krysta Svore , Vice President of Applied Research for Quantum Computing, Nvidia

Krysta Svore , Vice President of Applied Research for Quantum Computing, Nvidia

- Jaime Teevan , Chief Scientist and Technical Fellow, Microsoft

Jaime Teevan , Chief Scientist and Technical Fellow, Microsoft

- Evelyn Wang , Vice President for Energy & Climate, MIT

Evelyn Wang , Vice President for Energy & Climate, MIT

For all speakers visit EmTechFuture.com .

EmTech Future meets MIT Future Fest

Your exclusive access to the inaugural MIT Future Fest is included when you buy a hybrid ticket to EmTech Future 2026.

MIT Future Fest is a five-day festival that opens the Institute's doors to the world, bringing science, technology, creativity, and discovery to life across the MIT campus.

Tickets and last-call offer

In-person attendance is intentionally limited to 500 participants to preserve the quality of discussions, experiences, and networking opportunities. Livestream tickets are also available.

Secure your seat today at our last-call price, available until September 27, 2026.

Members of the media may obtain additional information and request press credentials by emailing press@technologyreview.com .

Leaders from enterprise and academia will gather at MIT to explore the convergence of AI, quantum, and energy.

Curated by the editorial team of MIT Technology Review, this year's agenda explores the theme "Convergence," examining how the next wave of technological change may be shaped as much by the interaction between fields as by the advances within them.

Through keynotes, interviews, guided experiences, and conversations with industry-leading researchers and innovators, attendees will gain a clearer view of the systems, ideas, and breakthroughs that will define the coming decade.

Agenda highlights include:

  • Convergence – Explore how AI, quantum technologies, and energy systems are beginning to intersect, creating new possibilities across business and society.

  • At the Frontier of Intelligence – Examine the next advances in AI, from reasoning and autonomy to multimodal systems, and learn how they are expanding what machine intelligence can do.

  • Powering the Future – Explore how rising demand, new technologies, and an increasingly electrified world are making energy a defining force in how technology scales.

  • At the Quantum Frontier – Examine the breakthroughs moving quantum technologies from laboratory experiments toward practical systems, with new possibilities emerging in computation, security, and beyond.

  • Into the Institute – Go beyond the conference stage through curated visits and conversations with researchers across MIT, offering behind-the-scenes access to active research environments in areas including quantum, robotics, advanced manufacturing, and nuclear science.

articles.content:
SandboxAQ unveils hardware-agnostic AQNav software platform for rapid integration across defense systems
PALO ALTO, Calif., Sept. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SandboxAQ announced it has successfully completed the world's first reported test of a magnetic navigation (MagNav) system on an attritable platform – Northrop Grumman's Lumberjack®, a Group 3 UAS attritable drone. It was also the world's first reported instance of a MagNav system being paired with a visual navigation system on an attritable, one-way attack platform. SandboxAQ has collaborated with Northrop Grumman (NYSE: NOC) to integrate and test its commercial, dual-use, AQNav MagNav technology on this unmanned aircraft system.
Conflicts in Ukraine and the Persian Gulf States prove small, expendable drones are now regularly operating in GPS-denied and spoofed environments. UAVs are a tool of war in these conflicts and militaries around the world are ramping up their stockpiles of drones. Northrop Grumman's Lumberjack, a one-way-attack drone, was designed and developed in under 14 months of its first flight. The versatility and modularity of this technology highlights Northrop Grumman's multi-use, loitering munition capabilities.
"Today's platforms need navigation systems they can trust as they operate in increasingly complex and contested environments. In collaboration with SandboxAQ, Northrop Grumman is aggressively enhancing our ecosystem of autonomous and unmanned systems with resilient and flight-hardened alternative navigation systems," said Max Schuster, program manager, Lumberjack, Northrop Grumman. "Pairing AQNav with Northrop Grumman's experience in unmanned aircraft and open mission systems will ensure our joint forces have an operationally validated navigation capability in even the most contested domains."
"AQNav's ability to provide unjammable navigation and positioning without GPS complements Northrop Grumman's efforts to fulfill the operational and mission-specific requirements for autonomous aircraft and shape the future of next generation unmanned platforms," said Luca Ferrara, General Manager of Navigation at SandboxAQ. "Leveraging our proven MagNav technologies and drone platform expertise, the flight test with Northrop Grumman further demonstrates the ease by which our AQNav software can be integrated into unmanned systems at the speed and scale required by leading defense organizations."
AQNav enables continuous positioning without reliance on satellite or other externally transmitted signals. Its passive, all-weather, and terrain-agnostic navigation can serve as a standalone capability or complement inertial, visual, and satellite navigation systems, advancing the future of alternative positioning, navigation and timing (Alt-PNT). In addition, AQNav's proven ability to operate over open water, feature-limited terrain, urban landscapes, and GPS-denied environments makes aircraft platforms more resilient and mission-capable.
AQNav's Software Expands Accessibility Across Platforms
Our AQNav software platform, demonstrated during the recent flight, extends the company's proven MagNav capabilities into a software-first architecture designed for rapid integration with current and future defense systems. This novel, hardware-agnostic offering processes sensor data in real-time, applies physics-based models to determine positioning and provides continuous navigation that can be easily incorporated into a broader PNT architecture.
The software is designed to run on existing onboard compute infrastructure with operationally relevant latency, reducing the need for additional processing hardware. It supports open architecture interfaces that simplify integration across platforms.
"AQNav now offers OEMs two distinct paths for deployment – a full-stack, performance-optimized solution that's built natively into your platform architecture, or a software-only solution developed specifically to deploy within existing architecture," said Ferrara. "With Northrop Grumman's Lumberjack, our engineers were able to install AQNav software into existing systems in less than an hour, giving the attritable platform MagNav capabilities for enhanced mission performance."
Proven Performance Across Defense and Commercial Applications
Since 2023, AQNav has been flight-tested by military, government, and commercial aerospace partners including Airbus and Boeing. SandboxAQ has worked closely with the United States Air Force to flight-test AQNav for more than three years, including testing aboard C-17 Globemaster III and C-130J Super Hercules transports and participating in three large-scale military exercises. AQNav was also selected to participate in the 2025 NATO DIANA cohort.
AQNav currently participates in the Defense Innovation Unit's (DIU) Transition of Quantum Sensing program (TQS), which tests MagNav technologies for military autonomous systems. Under that program, SandboxAQ integrated its AQNav software on a Group 3 unmanned aircraft platform and is evaluating its performance against defense-relevant use cases. The work with Northrop Grumman builds on those integration patterns and advances a shared objective of delivering scalable, resilient navigation for unmanned operations in GPS-contested environments.
About Lumberjack®
Northrop Grumman is the mission systems integrator, munitions and systems provider of many of the technologies that enable the aircraft to sense, detect and deter threats in the battlespace. ESAero Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of AV Inc., provides the Lumberjack air vehicle and its systems integration.
About Northrop Grumman
Northrop Grumman (NYSE: NOC) is a leading global aerospace and defense technology company. Our pioneering solutions equip our customers with the capabilities they need to connect and protect the world, and push the boundaries of human exploration across the universe. Driven by a shared purpose to solve our customers' toughest problems, our employees define possible every day.
About SandboxAQ
SandboxAQ is a B2B company delivering solutions at the intersection of AI and quantum techniques. The company's Large Quantitative Models (LQMs) deliver critical advances in life sciences, financial services, navigation, and other sectors. SandboxAQ is an independent, growth-backed company funded by leading investors and strategic partners including funds and accounts advised by T. Rowe Price Associates, Inc., Google, Alger, IQT, US Innovative Technology Fund, S32, Paladin Capital, BNP Paribas, Eric Schmidt, Breyer Capital, Ray Dalio, Marc Benioff, Thomas Tull, and others. For more information, visit www.sandboxaq.com.
SOURCE SandboxAQ

articles.title: 5 manufacturing professionals talk AI and technology trends
articles.description: 5 manufacturing professionals talk AI and technology trends Manufacturing Dive
articles.description_html: 5 manufacturing professionals talk AI and technology trends  Manufacturing Dive
articles.article_title: 5 manufacturing professionals talk AI and technology trends
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's Manufacturing industry news
articles.summary: Leaders from Google Cloud, Powerus, Furnace Record Pressing and more recently weighed in on the quickly evolving technology landscape.
articles.content:
Throughout the summer, Manufacturing Dive has done Q&A interviews with a host of industry leaders and experts to learn more about changing technology trends. Artificial intelligence, automation, data and labor remain top of mind.
You can catch up on their views of these trends, as well as read the broader interviews, below.
Do you have thoughts on how these trends are affecting your business? Contact us at [email protected].
Praveen Rao, global head of manufacturing at Google Cloud
MANUFACTURING DIVE: If you could change one thing about manufacturing, what would it be and why?
RAO: I would probably make it more multimodal. The manufacturing industry traditionally has been dealing with structured data, and then some unstructured data with manuals and other things. But we live in a live world.
If you walk into a shop floor, the machines are buzzing, screaming. They have the noise, they have vibration, they have harmonics. Why are we not taking advantage of all that? And without a doubt you absolutely can, because the stronger the context you have, the better your actions are going to be.
Just like how Industry 4.0 makes OT and IT, I truly believe the future is multimodal and that's where you would see some of our products.
They can understand things in their native modality, whether it's processing the videos or processing the noise vibrations. We don't convert that to text and analyze like the way some people are doing. We can look at a CAD drawing and really understand what you're trying to do. We can create different variations to make sure it's manufacturable. We can even tell you what's the likelihood of this getting damaged when you transport it. And we can tell you how sustainable this is when you ship a product. There are so many capabilities out there.
Brett Velicovich, cofounder of Powerus
MANUFACTURING DIVE: How is your company investing in advanced technology and automation?
VELICOVICH: Powerus is investing in advanced manufacturing technologies, including automation, digital production workflows, and robotics where they improve throughput, quality, and repeatability. The goal is not replacing people — it’s enabling faster scaling, more consistent production, and reducing bottlenecks in critical manufacturing steps.
Ignacio Basualdo, connected services digital product manager at Watson-Marlow Fluid Technology Solutions
MANUFACTURING DIVE: How is your company using AI, and how are you adapting to workforce trends?
BASUALDO: We're leveraging AI to enhance our institutional knowledge and manage it across our sales and support service teams. We’re also helping customers be more proactive in their operations, rather than reactive, by using AI-enabled intelligent monitoring.
As organizations adopt more automation and connected technologies, there is an increased demand for workers and expertise in areas such as systems integration, data analytics and industrial automation. In the pump industry, we're also seeing a need for skilled technicians and engineers who understand not only the pump technology itself and the fluid handling systems that we are experts in, but also how those systems integrate with increasingly automated and connected manufacturing environments.
Kathie Mahoney, president of MassMEP
MANUFACTURING DIVE: We hear a lot of talk about robotics and AI. At the same time, we hear plenty of small and medium companies don’t want to do it yet. What are you seeing in Massachusetts on that front?
MAHONEY: Anecdotally, it’s the same. It’s a lot of they don’t know what they don’t know. It’s how do we implement the technologies in the most efficient way for each facility, and it may not be the same for every facility. You may need sensors on your machine for one, whereas another you may want to measure the weight of a product.
That’s where the MEP centers are so valuable and so unique versus a traditional consultant.
All of our employees that go and do the training and the work within the manufacturing facility have a manufacturing background. So they have all been there. They understand it, they’ve done the work.
Ali Miller, CEO of Furnace Record Pressing
MANUFACTURING DIVE: Does Furnace plan to invest in robotics or automation?
MILLER: No, I don’t think so. I think final record pressing is one of those trades that you’re not too worried about [artificial intelligence] is going to come and take your job, which is a lucky place to be in the modern world.
I know that there are some plants that certainly use robotics or automation, in terms of [sleeving] a record on press, so it presses and it goes into a sleeve via metal arm. For us, it’s really important to look at every record. It’s part of our quality standard. We really stand strongly behind the idea that great records are made by great people, not great robots.
It’s an art, it’s a craft, and that requires people.

articles.article_title: Prime Video introduces new lip-sync technology on ‘Maxton Hall’
articles.heading: Prime Video introduces new lip-sync technology on ‘Maxton Hall’
articles.summary: Visual dubbing using AI and VFX technologies enhances the viewing experience for global customers.
articles.content:
Key takeaways
- Prime Video’s lip-sync technology delivers a more accessible viewing experience.
- Syncing mouth movements to audio, it eliminates the disconnect that can occur with traditional dubbing.
- The feature debuts on Maxton Hall S1-2 and will be available when Season 3 premieres on December 9.
Have you ever watched a dubbed movie only to notice the actors' mouths continuing to move after the dialogue has ended, taking you completely out of the story?

Prime Video is addressing this issue with a feature designed to create a more enjoyable and accessible viewing experience for our global customers.
Prime Video is addressing this issue with a feature designed to create a more enjoyable and accessible viewing experience for our global customers.
The technology synchronizes actors' lip movements with human-dubbed audio, creating a seamless viewing experience that allows audiences to remain fully immersed in the story. AI and VFX technologies power the process behind the scenes, responsibly applied to deliver a better customer experience.

The feature will be available on Prime Video’s most-watched International Original series ever, Maxton Hall. Lip-sync dubs are available from today on Maxton Hall Seasons 1 and 2 globally in English and will also be included when the third and final season releases exclusively on Prime Video on December 9. The upcoming Season 3 is based on the 2018 novel Save Me by Mona Kasten.

Lip-sync dubs are available from today on Maxton Hall Seasons 1 and 2 globally in English and will also be included when the third and final season releases exclusively on Prime Video on December 9. The upcoming Season 3 is based on the 2018 novel Save Me by Mona Kasten.
Looking ahead, Prime Video plans to expand the technology to additional titles, bringing this enhanced viewing experience to even more customers and content.
"At Prime Video, we're constantly innovating with new tools that enhance the viewing experience for our customers," said Raf Soltanovich, vice president of technology at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios. "With lip-syncing, we're creating a more seamless and immersive way for customers to enjoy global content. And for creators, we're making it easier for their stories to reach an even broader and global audience, all done under creative oversight to ensure the integrity of their artistic vision is preserved."
Prime Video continues to explore practical and useful applications of AI that help enhance the viewing experience, always with the customer at the center and creators in the driver's seat.

The Download: OpenAI’s turning point for math and a battery record
Plus: The US has accused six Chinese AI firms of “industrial-scale” theft.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
What OpenAI’s latest controversy tells us about the future of math
OpenAI says its agents have solved one of the most important open problems in mathematics. Under normal circumstances, that would be a huge milestone. But the announcement has been overshadowed by accusations that OpenAI failed to credit researchers whose AI-assisted work influenced its solution.
Whether those accusations are true or not, the episode may mark a turning point in the history of mathematics. AI models now seem essential for making progress on the field’s most important problems, but solving them may demand resources available only to a couple of frontier AI companies.
If that’s the future we are headed for, it is unclear how human mathematicians will fit into it.
Read on to see how AI could reshape mathematics.
—Grace Huckins
Batteries just broke another record in the US
Battery installations hit a new record in the US in the second quarter of 2026, with 20.2 gigawatt-hours of new capacity coming online. That’s enough to supply the daily electricity needs of 600,000 homes.
The surge puts the country on track for another record year, driven by cheaper batteries and an urgent need for more energy storage as renewables are added to the grid. But the boom looks different for grid-scale and residential batteries.
Take a closer look at the forces reshaping the US battery market.
—Casey Crownhart
This entrepreneur is developing agents that can plan ahead
Danijar Hafner’s office in San Francisco’s SoMa district sits mostly empty, but what it lacks in decor, it makes up for in robots. Humanoids of various shapes and sizes hang like marionettes from racks that run down the center of the wide-open space.
Hafner won’t say too much about his new venture just yet, but describes it as a continuation of his longtime work to enable AI to navigate environments it has not encountered in training.
Over the years, the 31-year-old has honed his approach by pitting agents trained within his world models against popular video games. More recently, he’s begun migrating his agents out of the virtual world and into physical reality.
Learn more about Hafner’s work teaching AI about our world.
—Mat Honan
Danijar Hafner is one of the artificial intelligence honorees on our 35 Innovators Under 35 list for 2026. Meet the rest of them here, or explore the full list across the biotechnology, AI, computing and robotics, and climate and energy categories.
MIT Technology Review Narrated: data from drones in Ukraine is fueling a new Wild West marketplace
Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones. But behind all that wreckage, there’s a new gold mine for the defense sector: the data those drones generate.
Ukraine has begun making millions of data points gathered during tens of thousands of drone flights available to military contractors and commercial companies. It’s a quick way to attract funding and partnerships, but it turns the front line into a model training site, using the chaos of war to create conditions that AI companies struggle to reproduce.
As this new industry takes shape, we need a regulatory system that ensures battlefield data isn’t treated like ordinary commercial material.
This is our latest article to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 OpenAI says it cracked a 90-year-old maths problem in 88 hours
It used 10,000 AI agents to tackle the Navier-Stokes equations. (CNBC)
+ OpenAI claims it’s the first major math problem solved by AI. (Nature)
+ But the breakthrough has been overshadowed by a credit controversy. (Axios)
+ OpenAI spent millions to win the $1 million math contest. (Quanta)
2 The US has accused six Chinese AI firms of “industrial-scale” theft
They include DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, and Z.AI. (CNN)
+ Officials accuse them of stealing America’s AI trade secrets. (Reuters $)
+ They allegedly used model distillation to train their systems. (WSJ $)
+ Targeting Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok, among others. (NBC News)
3 The Pentagon asked OpenAI for an AI model that rarely says no
The military wanted it to have “minimal refusal rates.” (Intercept)
+ The Pentagon says US allies can’t keep pace on AI. (Guardian)
+ AI firms may soon train on classified military data. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Apple is expected to unveil a $2,000 folding smartphone today
It would be the iPhone’s biggest design change since its 2007 launch. (Guardian)
+ And the first big test for new CEO John Ternus. (NYT $)
+ Xiaomi and Huawei launched their own new foldables before the event. (CNBC)
5 Meta’s new AI agent can access apps to send emails and make payments
Muse autonomously uses apps and websites on people’s behalf. (CNBC)
+ Internal tests found it could expose sensitive personal data. (Reuters $)
+ AI agents are not your “coworkers.” (MIT Technology Review)
6 Google says it’s “degrading” search in Europe to comply with EU rules
New results will give more prominence to comparison sites. (Reuters $)
+ The changes follow a €460 million EU antitrust fine. (Quartz)
7 Meta ads pushed AI apps that nudified real teens
Researchers found 332 ads containing CSAM this year. (BBC)
+ They identified several AI-manipulated photos of real children (Ars Technica)
+ Apple and Google have missed the UK’s deadline to block child nudity. (Wired $)
8 Border Patrol is using financial data to target Americans for stops
The predictive-policing program feeds intelligence to local police. (404 Media)
9 New paints could cool buildings on the cheap without electricity
They reflect sunlight and radiate heat back into space. (Economist $)
10 The creepy first trailer for the Sam Altman biopic just dropped
Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial will be released in the US on December 25. (Variety)
+ Amazon had dropped the film after investing in OpenAI. (Guardian)
Quote of the day
“This is a Deep Blue–Kasparov moment. The community needs to have serious and unhurried discussion about where to go from here.”
—NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster issues a statement comparing OpenAI’s math breakthrough to an IBM supercomputer defeating chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, a landmark moment for machine intelligence.
One more thing
The shock of seeing your body used in deepfake porn
When Jennifer got a research job in 2023, she ran her new professional headshot through a facial recognition program. She wanted to see whether it would pull up the porn videos she’d made more than a decade earlier. It did, but it also surfaced something she’d never seen before: one of her old videos, now featuring someone else’s face on her body.
Conversations about sexualized deepfakes usually focus on the people whose faces are inserted into explicit content without consent. But another group often gets ignored: the people whose bodies those faces are attached to.
Adult content creators say AI systems are training on their work, cloning their likenesses, and generating explicit content they never agreed to make, all with little legal protection or control. Read the full story on the threat to their rights, livelihoods, and ownership of their own bodies.
—Jessica Klein
We can still have nice things

+ Artist Ali Hill stitches extraordinarily intricate buildings and cityscapes into fabric.

+ Check out the breathtaking winning images from the 2026 International Aerial Photographer of the Year competition.

articles.title: Making Adjustments: Students React To Technology Changes
articles.description: Making Adjustments: Students React To Technology Changes The Villanovan
articles.description_html: Making Adjustments: Students React To Technology Changes  The Villanovan
articles.article_title: Making Adjustments: Students React To Technology Changes
articles.heading: The Villanovan
articles.summary: A new school year brings changes. This includes a new Cabrini Campus, Falvey Library at Vic Maggitti Hall opening soon and changes to technology services. Starting this past summer, Villanova transitioned to D2L Brightspace, a modernized Learning Management System. Provost Patrick Maggitti chose the platform after receiving feedback from an LMS Steering Committee, which includes...
articles.content:
A new school year brings changes. This includes a new Cabrini Campus, Falvey Library at Vic Maggitti Hall opening soon and changes to technology services.
Starting this past summer, Villanova transitioned to D2L Brightspace, a modernized Learning Management System.
Provost Patrick Maggitti chose the platform after receiving feedback from an LMS Steering Committee, which includes members of the faculty, the offices of the Provost and Online Programs, Technology Services and other administrators.
The LMS Steering Committee was selected to provide feedback for the three LMS finalists: Anthology Ultra, D2L Brightspace and Instructure Canvas. While Canvas was favored by the majority of the committee, D2L Brightspace was selected for its modern and innovative features.
“I can navigate Brightspace fine, and I think the software is more modern than Blackboard was,” sophomore Hattie Philips said.
Villanova was previously using Blackboard Learn, an older version of the vendor’s LMS.
The platform was not popular among students and professors, and many thought it was not user-friendly and difficult to navigate.
“Brightspace feels cleaner and more organized, and I especially like having easy access through the mobile app,” junior Elizabeth Howard said.
The positive reactions to Brightspace have their limits, though. It has taken professors some time to get used to, which can make it difficult for students to use it effectively.
“The only trouble I have is that some of my professors still don’t know how to use it, which makes it more difficult for me,” Philips added.
Along with Brightspace, the implementation of Microsoft Authenticator in place of Duo Mobile has been a change students are getting used to.
When signing into a Villanova account, the Authenticator sends a notification to a user’s phone, which then opens the app. From there, the user is asked to enter a number, an extra step, when compared to Duo Mobile.
“I find it to be faster than Duo, but more annoying when I need to type the number in,” Philips said.
Although the new authenticator may be redundant, the decision to implement it was made with the students’ and university’s interests in mind.
The transition is part of the University’s “Rooted. Restless.” 10-year strategic plan, Tech Nova 2026, an initiative carried out by the University Technology Services.
With the changes, the university has made a noticeable commitment to helping students and professors understand how to use the new platforms.
“I think Brightspace will be easier in the long term, even if there is a slight learning curve in the short term, as there is with any major transition,” Howard said. “It has been great to see how intentionally the rollout was planned with students in mind, including pilot users, training, student guides and workshops.”
Luckily, the 2026-2027 academic year is young, giving students and faculty plenty of time to iron out any issues that may pop up. University Technology Services will be hosting faculty office hours over Zoom to offer staff personalized support.
With support from students and Technology Services, Brightspace and Microsoft Authenticator will be positive changes that make learning and accessing materials easier for all.

articles.title: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'
articles.description: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans' BBC
articles.description_html: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'  BBC
articles.article_title: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'
articles.heading: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'
articles.summary: It is the latest in a series of increasing warnings about the safety threat posed by artificial intelligence.
articles.content:
Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'
A top safety researcher at Anthropic has warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
Evan Hubinger said in a post on X the risk from the models which currently exist was "low" but he was "worried" the technology might develop and improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.
He did not spell out how he thought AI systems could in future result in humans being wiped out.
But his comments are the latest in a series of increasingly stark warnings about AI, with the debate shifting from whether it truly poses a risk to how big that risk is.
Hubinger's intervention was in response to another post on X from Jacob Coxon, who described himself as an AI researcher who had just quit Anthropic and who previously worked at OpenAI.
"Neither company is acting responsibly," he wrote.
"These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources."
OpenAI has been approached for comment.
Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who advises the UN on AI, told the BBC she was "shocked" by Hubinger and Coxon's social media posts.
She told the World at One on BBC Radio Four some of it could be "PR and marketing" however, as Anthropic and OpenAI raced towards highly anticipated stock market debuts.
But she added: "Why would someone want to say that? I would plead with investors not to invest in this company if that is their value system."
Separately, the Financial Times reported Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Safety Institute (AISI), one of the leading bodies in the world for assessing AI risk.
The BBC has approached Anthropic for comment.
A Cabinet Office spokesperson did not comment on whether the latest model had been withheld from the AISI - instead saying it "continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer".
No plan for superintelligence
In his post, which has been viewed more than 10 million times, Hubinger said "we really do earnestly believe" AI poses a species-ending risk to humans.
"I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to," he added.
Hubinger works in AI alignment, which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'

Getty Images

A top safety researcher at Anthropic has warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Evan Hubinger said in a post on X the risk from the models which currently exist was "low" but he was "worried" the technology might develop and improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.

He did not spell out how he thought AI systems could in future result in humans being wiped out.

But his comments are the latest in a series of increasingly stark warnings about AI, with the debate shifting from whether it truly poses a risk to how big that risk is.

Hubinger's intervention was in response to another post on X from Jacob Coxon, who described himself as an AI researcher who had just quit Anthropic and who previously worked at OpenAI.

"Neither company is acting responsibly," he wrote.

"These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources."

OpenAI has been approached for comment.

Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who advises the UN on AI, told the BBC she was "shocked" by Hubinger and Coxon's social media posts.

She told the World at One on BBC Radio Four some of it could be "PR and marketing" however, as Anthropic and OpenAI raced towards highly anticipated stock market debuts.

But she added: "Why would someone want to say that? I would plead with investors not to invest in this company if that is their value system."

Separately, the Financial Times reported Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Safety Institute (AISI), one of the leading bodies in the world for assessing AI risk.

The BBC has approached Anthropic for comment.

articles.content:
How Technology Stocks Have Influenced Broad Value Indexes
The more things change, the more they stay the same.
Large tech stocks have started to find their way into broad value indexes. Index construction is part of the reason, but the fundamentals of some technology companies have changed a lot over the past year, along with their prices and valuations.
Keeping Score
Russell Indexes rebalanced its popular benchmarks in late June. In any given year, the rebalance gets a lot of attention because many large index funds track Russell indexes, and a lot of active managers benchmark themselves to the same bogies. Said another way, there’s a lot of money tied to the trades that occur when these indexes turn over, making the Russell rebalance among the busiest trading days of the year.
This year, the rebalance received more attention than normal because three large tech stocks claimed the largest positions in the Russell 1000 Value. Amazon.com AMZN became the largest constituent after its weight jumped to 5.80% from 1.72%. It’s a consumer stock but close enough to technology that it’s worth mentioning. Apple AAPL and Microsoft MSFT were added as well, and the stakes weren’t small. Apple’s 5.27% position made it the second largest in the index, followed by Microsoft’s 3.88%.
Holding large tech stocks isn’t unique to the Russell 1000 Value. The S&P 500 Value index tracked by iShares S&P 500 Value ETF IVE and the S&P 900 Value index tracked by iShares Core S&P Value ETF IUSV had similar large stakes in Apple and Amazon.com.
Furthermore, technology stocks have always been a part of the Russell 1000 Value and other broad value benchmarks. On average, they occupied about 10% of these indexes over the past 15 years, but that has changed over the past 12 months. The information technology sector grew to almost 20% of the Russell 1000 Value, and that happened before the June rebalance.
In other words, the recent additions of Amazon.com, Apple, or Microsoft didn’t cause the increase. Smaller tech stocks already in the Russell 1000 Value went on a tear over the 12 months leading up to the rebalance. Their revenue and earnings grew with demand for the semiconductors and memory chips they develop and manufacture, and their market caps and valuations increased accordingly.
The table below shows the rate of return of the largest technology stocks in the Russell 1000 Value over the 12 months leading up to the June rebalance. Alphabet’s GOOGL 102% return was the smallest of the bunch.
Meanwhile, Amazon.com returned about 7% and Apple 37%, while Microsoft lost almost 28% over the same period. Their fundamentals and prices looked a lot less growthy than the eight stocks in the previous table.
Cheap(ish) Tech
The extreme growth of the former eight combined with the tepid growth of the latter three helps explain why Amazon.com, Apple, and Microsoft sit atop the Russell 1000 Value. Those three are no longer the growth leaders of the broader market, and all sit in the middle of the
Index construction also plays a role. Index providers, including Russell, split the market into value and growth buckets, and they typically use several growth and value indicators to determine where a stock lands. The value and growth metrics used to classify stocks, along with the approaches to cutting the market in half, vary from one index provider to the next, but the basic idea applies to all mainstream value and growth indexes.
There is always a group of stocks that land in the middle. They aren’t quite value stocks, and they don’t quite fit in with pricier growth names. Amazon.com, Apple, and Microsoft were straddling the line between value and growth during the June rebalance, so the rules underpinning the Russell 1000 Value split their market caps between the two indexes. Furthermore, Apple and Microsoft had larger weights in the Russell 1000 Growth than the Russell 1000 Value.
Micron Technology MU, Applied Materials AMAT, Advanced Micro Devices AMD, Sandisk SNDK, Western Digital WDC, and Marvell Technologies MRVL graduated out of the Russell 1000 Value and became members of the Russell 1000 Growth. Intel INTC stayed put. All benefited from the demand for memory chips and have grown immensely over the past year. Alphabet gets partial consideration. It jumped out of value and into growth as well, but it sits in the communication services sector.
While the individual names changed, technology did not take over Russell 1000 Value at the rebalance. The sector’s weight remained largely the same, while others saw modest changes. Industrials declined by a few percentage points because heavy equipment manufacturer Caterpillar CAT became a growth stock. Likewise, communication services lost 3.8 percentage points because Alphabet was pushed into the Russell 1000 Growth. Consumer cyclicals increased by 4 percentage points because Amazon.com’s weight increased by a similar amount.
Forests & Trees
The Russell 1000 Value, and other broad value indexes like it, did exactly what it is supposed to do. It shed expensive stocks that have grown and added those that were relatively cheaper. Much of the trading at Russell’s June rebalance happened to take place around the technology sector.
Broad value indexes still possess many of the characteristics that have defined the cheaper side of the market for decades. Their average valuation is lower than their growth counterparts, and they still place more weight on cyclical sectors of the economy. The financial, consumer cyclical, and industrial sectors still hold prominent positions.
Tech stocks have always been a part of the value index. Their weight has increased, but that’s because they’ve done well across the board and not because a few big names entered at the last rebalance. The companies that sit within those sectors have changed, but the indexes are just capturing that dynamism as they always have.
Large stakes in Amazon.com, Apple, and Microsoft are likely more relevant to active managers in the large-value

articles.content:
Stitching the Future: Technology as a Sacred Trust
By grounding our digital strategy in the same values as our ancestors, we can ensure technology serves our school community rather than consuming it.
September 9, 2026
Paul McKinnon / Shutterstock
In an era where artificial intelligence promises to archive human culture at the touch of a button, Indigenous communities face a vital question: Who has the right to own, shape and digitize sacred knowledge?
Long before AI became a headline in education, this question fundamentally reshaped my work as the instructional technology coordinator at Indian Community School. But understanding how to protect our community’s digital future didn’t start in a computer lab; it began in a quiet valley in Wisconsin, with my grandmother’s unfinished quilt and a ribbon skirt workshop that changed everything I knew about knowledge itself.
I grew up in a small rural village tucked into Wisconsin’s Driftless Area, where winding roads disappear between steep bluffs and deep valleys, and every hill seems to reveal another breathtaking view. It was a place shaped not by glaciers, but by time. A landscape as rugged as it was beautiful.
It was also home to my grandmother — a strong cheesemaker’s wife who was, in some ways, the quintessential grandmother figure. She hosted Sunday family dinners, baked fresh bread, volunteered at the local food pantry and quilted with the other ladies from church twice a week. She also cursed like a sailor and wasn’t stingy with her love or hugs.
In my teen years, she became my shelter — a quiet refuge from a chaotic home and a reminder that love exists even in the hardest seasons. When I went away to college, she sent me away with a quilt made just for me, a special gift we all only receive once. As an adult, she became the reason we visited the Driftless Area and was the glue that kept our families together. During that time, she showed that love to my children, who adored her.
After a long stay in a nursing home and years of declining health, my grandmother passed away last year. After her passing, my twin sister and I discovered her last unfinished quilt tucked away in a forgotten storage bin. Her hands hadn’t been able to hold the material or work the sewing machine for a long time, and we thought all the quilts had been claimed. Finding one more, even unfinished, felt like a blessing.
Around the same time, my twin sister and I both signed up for a staff ribbon skirt class where members of the Indigenous community would teach us not only how to make ribbon skirts, but also share teachings about how to wear them respectfully and as true allies. Carrying pieces of our grandmother’s unfinished quilt with us, we set out to create ribbon skirts in her honor.
Before that class, I knew very little about ribbon skirts beyond seeing them worn at school celebrations and community events. I quickly learned they are not tied to a single tribe, but are worn by Indigenous women across many Nations, each with their own traditions, teachings and stories. I also learned that a ribbon skirt is much more than a beautiful piece of clothing. It represents identity, resilience, and the enduring strength of Indigenous women.
Today, communities across North America celebrate Ribbon Skirt Day each January, recognizing not only the skirts themselves, but the right of Indigenous people to wear them with pride after generations of policies that sought to erase their cultures.
What surprised me most was that our class wasn’t really about making skirts. It was about learning the responsibility that comes with them. We learned when it was appropriate to wear a ribbon skirt, what it meant to wear one as an ally, and why those teachings mattered as much as the sewing itself. Anyone can buy a ribbon skirt online, but creating one alongside community members who generously shared their knowledge transformed it into something entirely different. Every stitch became part of a relationship built on trust, respect and a willingness to learn.
That experience changed the way I thought about knowledge itself. I realized that some things are valuable not because they can be owned, bought, or preserved, but because they carry stories, relationships and responsibilities that extend far beyond any one individual. They belong to the communities that shaped them and to the generations who will inherit them.
The tension between owning knowledge and stewarding it sits at the very heart of my work as the instructional technology coordinator at Indian Community School. If knowledge is built on trust and community relationships, then technology cannot simply be an instrument to extract, scale, or monetize data. That conviction was tested in 2021, well before generative AI became a household conversation, when a company approached our language and culture department with an extraordinary proposal.
They offered innovation. A way to immortalize language and culture through “virtual ancestors” — artificial intelligence trained on the stories, voices, and wisdom of living tribal elders. As the instructional technology coordinator, I was initially excited about what an extraordinary opportunity it would be to place our school at the forefront of modern technology!
However, the more my colleagues and I analyzed the pitch, the more our excitement gave way to deep alarm. The offer was riddled with deep red flags: vague promises around intellectual property, zero accountability for data privacy and a predatory push to extract sacred community knowledge. But recognizing those red flags was only half the battle.
Facing a tool this complex also exposed the gaps in my own understanding of artificial intelligence at the time. I realized that properly vetting this proposal and ensuring our school’s technology program moved forward in a good, grounded way required more than just caution. It demanded that I build my own AI literacy so I could stand as an informed guardian for our community’s data.
That 2021 proposal became the catalyst for a journey that has defined my work ever since. Recognizing gaps in my own understanding, I immersed myself in AI literacy, digital ethics and Indigenous data sovereignty frameworks. As we start the 2026-27 school year, AI is no longer a distant possibility; it is actively shaping how stories are told, how knowledge is created and how data is harvested.
In response, my role has evolved from simply managing technology infrastructure to helping our school build an ethical digital sanctuary. We began facilitating professional development sessions that empower our teachers to critically evaluate AI tools through a lens of cultural safety and data privacy. In the classroom, we reaffirmed our dedication to active digital stewardship over passive consumption.
Rather than allowing third-party algorithms to dictate or summarize Native experiences, our students now engage in hands-on digital storytelling, learning how to protect their personal and cultural data while using modern tools to amplify their authentic voices on their own terms.
The core lesson I learned in that ribbon skirt class remains my guiding principle: technology, like knowledge, is only as valuable as the relationships and trust behind it. For educators, leaders, and communities navigating this fast-shifting landscape, maintaining agency over our stories requires asking hard questions before we ever sign a contract or adopt a tool:
- Who owns the data being used to train this system? In my school, we actively reject software platforms that do not explicitly provide full intellectual property rights to the school.
- Does this tool respect the sovereignty and living culture of the community it serves? I work with stakeholders to ensure that software and platforms do not train on student or staff data, and I prioritize tools with the least environmental impact.
- Are we adopting technology to enhance human relationships, or replace them? We prioritize tools that bring elders, teachers and students together in real-world dialogue, using technology as a bridge for connection rather than a substitute for human presence.
When my sister and I stitched pieces of our grandmother’s unfinished quilt into our ribbon skirts, we weren’t just preserving her memory; we were continuing a relationship rooted in love, honor and continuity. That is the true essence of stewardship. When we approach technological innovation not as a rush to extract the future, but as a solemn duty to protect what was handed down to us, we ensure that modern tools honor where we came from. In the age of AI, our responsibility remains unchanged: to stitch technology into the living fabric of our communities in a good way, ensuring our stories remain whole, authentic and undeniably our own.

When we approach technological innovation not as a rush to extract the future, but as a solemn duty to protect what was handed down to us, we ensure that modern tools honor where we came from. In the age of AI, our responsibility remains unchanged: to stitch technology into the living fabric of our communities in a good way, ensuring our stories remain whole, authentic and undeniably our own.

articles.article_title: Local cranberry farm uses technology to navigate drought conditions
articles.heading: Local cranberry farm uses technology to navigate drought conditions
articles.summary: A local cranberry farm is working with a company to better manage their water usage.
articles.content:
Wisconsin faces drought and dry conditions in most of the state. Farmers may see impacts when it comes to their crops. Severe drought conditions can cause crop yields to decline, and can affect water quality and availability.
Traditionally, a job set in the hands of mother nature, cranberry farmers are using technology that can help them better manage their irrigation and water management on their land.
Understanding Wisconsin, Together.
WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter.
A local cranberry farm is working with a company to better manage their water usage.
While looking across the bogs at Lake Nokomis Cranberries you can see a post stick out of the carpet of vines and berries.
That equipment comes from a company named Hortau. It helps a variety of farmers and crops keep track of their water usage.
It has a large cylinder mounted on a pole, with a wind mill and another small post holding a solar panel with cords running on the ground and a short metal probe.
The device helps farmers, like Dave Zawistowki and his son Michael who run Lake Nokomis Cranberry Farm in Eagle River, better manage their water irrigation to help prevent plant stress and over usage during dry times.
“It keeps us on our toes. We got to watch this more frequent and water. You got to wake up earlier and water more,” said the younger Zawistowski. “That’s a little more work on our end, but that’s what this is for.”
Hortau measures the push and pull of water molecules from soil molecules and reports that information to farmers to better understand the amount of water needed for maximum fruit and plant quality. Cody Jones is the Midwest and Northeast territory manager for Hortau.
“Each crop that we work with has a blue band, or a comfort zone, where the soil tension likes to live, and that blue band is also measured by the plant health and also the health of the crop it spits out,” said Jones. “Especially in drought years, growers can really hone into that blue band.”
Cranberries are hearty plants but they can still face damage to quality and overall plant health without the proper regulation of water usage.
Hortau assists Lake Nokomis beyond just watering their bogs. Dave Zawistowski says it also helps with frost protection.
“Because the ground is lower here, it’s usually 10-15 degrees cooler here than where they take the temperatures in town at the airport,” said Dave.
Devices like Hortau are helping farmers stay within the “sweet-spot” of moisture in the ground.
For cranberries that is around 4 to 7 kPa, or the force necessary for its roots to pull up moisture.
“As it dries out, we’ll take in other data and we’ll forecast exactly when the cranberry fields or beds will actually reach that dry irrigation threshold,” Jones said. “We can know exactly when to plan an irrigation event. If we do need to refill a reservoir, we can plan ahead for that as well.”
Hortau collects and updates data in real time that can be viewed via an app and allows farmers to take a look at all of their Hortau equipment spread across land. The Zawistowki’s also own two other cranberry farms, Stone Lake and another in Three Lakes.
“So like right there. You know, if you go like this is our other farm Stone Lake, so it’s wet, perfect, and it’s a little dry there,” said Michael showing how it looks on his phone. “Then if we scroll over to ours, it’s a little wet, little wet, good, and a little dry, but that one’s dry because it’s in a more sandy spot.”
Water is extremely important this time of year for cranberry farmers. Harvest is about a month away and the famous flooded bogs rely on smart decisions on water irrigation and management. Dave was quick to comment how it has changed their system.
“We use less now. No question about it,” said Dave. “We were always overwatering to be on the safe side.”
As conditions in northern Wisconsin continue to remain dry, farm technology is helping farmers navigate the changing landscape to ensure quality crops.
Maria Peralta-Arellano is a reporter covering water quality and the environment for WXPR and a Report for America corps member. Originally published by WXPR as part of the Wisconsin News Collaborative.

articles.title: Minnesota State prepares to pilot new technology to combat financial aid fraud. Is it enough?
articles.description: Minnesota State prepares to pilot new technology to combat financial aid fraud. Is it enough? MinnPost
articles.description_html: Minnesota State prepares to pilot new technology to combat financial aid fraud. Is it enough?  MinnPost
articles.article_title: Minnesota State prepares to pilot new technology to combat financial aid fraud. Is it enough?
articles.heading: Minnesota State prepares to pilot new technology to combat financial aid fraud. Is it enough?
articles.summary: 'Ghost students' are a growing national financial aid fraud problem largely targeting public two-year institutions like Century College.
articles.content:
WHITE BEAR LAKE, Minn. — A two-year school in the Twin Cities suburbs, Century College educates about 8,700 students. And its employees spend roughly 60 hours a week fending off financial aid fraud attempts by criminals.
Those hours are largely spent scouting out so-called “ghost students,” criminals who enroll in classes using stolen or fake identities just long enough to receive financial aid — and then disappear.
History professor Joe Haker first noticed the problem three years ago, when he wondered why one student in his gender studies class had submitted the same assignment as a student in his history course.
“I thought, ‘Well, that’s weird. That probably could only happen if they were the same person,’” Haker said.
Nine students turned out to be the same person. This summer, Haker suspects as many as a third of his 90 online students could have been fake.
“It’s so maddening,” he said. “You can’t help but feel very, very strange when you realize that this student that you’re devoting even some time to is just scamming.”
The Minnesota State system of 26 colleges and seven universities is preparing to pilot a new automated identity verification system that it says will help combat the ever-evolving problem of ghost students. The Legislature this spring allocated $3 million toward the effort, which Craig Munson, who oversees information security for the system, said should provide guardrails for a couple of years.
While faculty and financial aid officers applaud the move, some question whether the new technology will do enough, quickly enough, to curb a problem that largely has been left to individual schools and their staffs to confront.
“This is not a Century College problem,” said Pam Engebretson, Century’s financial aid director. “It’s a system office problem, and we need a system office solution to be able to support all of the work that we do.”
Century uses its own software to help filter out fake students from real ones and devotes at least 1.5 full-time staff to the problem, Engebretson said.
While those steps have reduced fraud, Engebretson believes a handful of fake students obtained financial aid this summer — and even more enrolled in classes before faculty or other staff noticed.
“We’re doing everything we can to correct it,” Engebretson said. “We’re as much of a victim as anyone else.”
In California, a potential bellwether for Minnesota in its approach to fighting ghost students, lawmakers have spent at least $150 million since 2022 on technology to help verify the 2.2 million students within its community college system.
This spring, the system reported losing $1.5 million in federal aid to fraudulent students. However, that’s a decrease from $5.6 million in spring 2025 and a fraction of all financial aid paid out, according to the news outlet CalMatters.
One problem in Minnesota, critics note, is that the true scope of financial aid fraud isn’t clear.
Related: As college graduates fret over finding jobs, a record shortage of workers is projected
The Minnesota State system, which serves over 290,000 students each year, says it flagged 2,696 financial aid applications as fraudulent or potentially fraudulent in the 2025-26 school year, down from 7,715 the year before.
However, citing security concerns, system officials declined to disclose how much federal or state aid has been lost to ghost students, even after questions from state lawmakers this spring.
U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon claimed in a 2025 letter to Gov. Tim Walz that 1,834 fake students in Minnesota had received $12.5 million in taxpayer-funded grants and loans. But McMahon provided no additional details, and the agency did not respond to clarifying questions from MinnPost.
In an interview, Munson said he had no idea where the $12.5 million figure came from. Nearly 100 higher education institutions in the state participate in federal financial aid programs. Munson said the system’s 33 schools “certainly are probably a portion of that. I would suspect a small portion.”
“If they do have information about where it came from, we’d love to see it,” he added, “because we want to do our due diligence and make sure that we’re finding what we should be finding and stopping what we should be stopping.”
At Century College alone, some $500,000 was paid out to suspected fraudulent actors within one academic year, according to several people who requested anonymity to avoid Century getting singled out for a far more widespread situation.
In a statement, the college declined to confirm or deny that figure, referring questions to the system office.
Haker said it’s important to know the full extent of the problem so Minnesota State can develop a comprehensive response.
“Because you don’t have anything coming from the system, it’s all based on your own experience,” he said. “And if I’m going off of my own personal experience this summer, it’s an enormous problem still.”
A patchwork of responses
Ghost student fraud is big and getting bigger all across the country.
It usually works like this: Thieves use stolen or fake IDs, or pay kickbacks to “straw students” to use their personal information, to apply for federal financial aid via the FAFSA form. Then they enroll in classes. The U.S. Department of Education distributes financial aid to individual colleges, which take what’s needed to cover tuition and fees and distribute the rest directly to the “students.”
The Department of Education estimates it has lost nearly $90 million to ghost students. In just two examples of recent cases, a Detroit man pleaded guilty to submitting fraudulent FAFSA claims for nearly 1,300 people in a scheme involving 100 schools in 24 states; over $10 million was disbursed. And a North Carolina woman was sentenced to five years in prison for stealing over $3.5 million in aid.
Community colleges are most at risk because of open admissions policies that aim to welcome all and reduce the complexity of the application process. The expansion of online classes during COVID-19 made it even easier to game the system.
The scope of the problem in California — where the state system of 116 public community colleges paid over $17.5 million in federal aid to fake students between 2022 and 2025 — drew national attention to the issue. But no state is immune. In Utah, a June audit estimated seven public institutions had devoted over 15,000 staff hours and lost over $830,000 to fake students in just one year, despite existing fraud detection systems.
At the national level, the Department of Education earlier this year launched a verification system that flags suspicious FAFSA applicants. Anyone deemed high-risk must confirm who they are by presenting a government-issued identification and going on camera for a photograph.
But the federal government has also made clear that schools are expected to have their security, and they are on the hook to repay money distributed to fraudulent students.
Minnesota’s largest system of two-year colleges, Minnesota State, has spent years relying on its individual schools to contend with ghost students while looking for systemwide solutions.
In 2023, the system created a work group on enrollment fraud, which the Legislature formalized two years later. The group issued a report in January, recommending the new systemwide verification system, along with more training for staff and students and annual reporting about enrollment fraud trends and mitigation.
The work group also published a user guide with protocols to deter enrollment fraud and for how to respond. The system tracks and logs fraud attempts, Munson said, and staff are expected to manually verify students’ IDs as needed.
“It’s a lot of labor,” he said. “We want to rightsize that and then get the automation where we can, and that’s where we asked for the help from the Legislature.”
Without that help, Munson said, Minnesota State eventually would have been able to invest in software, but it would have been “more homegrown, a little bit later, and we didn’t want to get past the tipping point where it became out of control.”
Related: Charging up: As more electric vehicles hit the road in Minnesota, more schools are training the mechanics needed to work on them
It’s difficult to grasp what prevention efforts look like internally across the system’s community colleges. MinnPost contacted all 26 with questions about protocols. Most did not answer, and several deferred to the system office while citing concerns about revealing information that could be useful to crime rings.
Mark Grant, a communication studies professor at Dakota County Technical College and representative for the Minnesota State College Faculty union, said the response varies from place to place.
“We have campuses that are doing an enormous amount because they have the resources,” he said. “We have campuses that are less equipped because they have less resources.”
Minneapolis College hired an outside company to review student IDs, said Dean of Enrollment Management Heidi Aldes, but scrapped it after determining their internal process was more effective.
“It takes significant human resource time,” Aldes said. “I would say the benefit is, as the attempts become more sophisticated, we sort of have a real-time understanding of what those changes are.”
Normandale Community College purchased software to aid its fraud team, which spans admissions, student services, records and registrar staff, among others. Since 2023, the school of about 11,000 students has flagged 29,000 applications for review, a college spokesperson told MinnPost.
The college estimates 31% of all incoming applications since 2025 have required additional review for any number of reasons — including because they are potentially fraudulent.
“Even if it’s just a few minutes, it’s wasted time,” said Susan Ant, director of financial aid and scholarships at Normandale. “We’re taking time that is meant for real students to get an education, graduate, do all those things, and there’s somebody who’s kind of working against that.”
Munson said the system is still deciding whether ID verification should be required of all students or just those whose applications are flagged. That’s part of a broader concern the system is dealing with, to ensure new security measures don’t prevent its diverse range of students from enrolling.
Technology to prevent stolen financial aid is a now-booming business.
Among the companies responding is AMSimpkins & Associates, which has grown its client base from six schools in 2023 to over 500 this year, according to founder Maurice Simpkins. Another 12 to 15 schools contact the company each week, he said.
Simpkins said colleges and universities are almost guaranteed to have some internal mechanisms in place to fight ghost students. And dealing with the issue poses recurring budget costs for schools, he said, given how quickly perpetrators adapt their tactics to security upgrades.
“Fraud trends change weekly, sometimes daily, sometimes hourly,” he said, meaning it doesn’t take long for a security system to become antiquated and “for the fraudsters to either find a way around it or to just circumvent it as a whole.”
‘Testing our system’
Among the piles of papers on Engebretson’s desk at Century College are emails from victims of identity fraud. They often contact her after applying for a student loan or a mortgage, only to learn their information has been stolen and used to apply for financial aid.
It’s one of the many ways she deals with attempts to steal public money in her day-to-day job. Although that’s always been an issue during her 15-year tenure at Century, she said it worsened significantly beginning around 2021 or 2022 with the boom in online classes during the pandemic.
“We believe that they were testing our system to see how easy it was to be able to get financial aid,” Engebretson said. “And the answer was, it was easy.”
Since then, she’s done everything in her power to make it anything but easy.
The goal is to freeze fake students’ accounts before money goes out the door at the beginning of each semester. But that requires finding them.
The software Century uses looks for indicators of financial aid fraud in student accounts. If an account raises red flags, the student is asked to take a selfie, which the software cross-references with an ID.
While Engebretson instructs faculty to alert her if they notice suspicious student behavior, there’s no systemwide guidance for faculty.
Grant, the union faculty representative, told lawmakers in February that faculty struggle knowing what to do when ghost students “slip through” and enroll in classes. If faculty are expected to go beyond just flagging potential ghost students, he said, “somebody needs to tell us that.”
“Absent that direction, we have faculty who are still employing a number of strategies to combat this,” he said in a February committee hearing, like meeting with dozens of students at the beginning of a semester just to make sure they are real.
Related: Demuth will run on fraud to beat Klobuchar, but their anti-fraud proposals are similar
As of August, nothing has changed, he said in an interview.
In his own online classes, Grant sometimes asks students to turn on their cameras and wave at the screen so he knows they are real.
Haker has other strategies — like compiling IP addresses on a spreadsheet to spot when the same address is attached to more than one student.
“Have we ever been told, here are some techniques to identify those students? Not really, and certainly not at the system level,” Haker said. “Anything that we have gotten has been from Century College specifically.”
Sen. Heather Gustafson, DFL-Vandais Heights, represents Century College and sponsored the legislation to create the work group that oversees enrollment fraud.
Advocating to create that group, Gustafson told lawmakers during a committee meeting the issue “places a significant strain on institutions,” and despite colleges’ efforts to respond, “many lack the resources for dedicated fraud prevention.”
Gustafson draws a connection between the ghost student issue and other attempts to steal public dollars. This session, lawmakers devoted $90 million to replace antiquated technology that has been linked with fraud in the state’s social services programs.
But she said it’s important that the ghost student problem, a national issue, not be turned into “another Minnesota fraud story.” Minnesota was able to take action earlier than other states because of “some really vigilant employees at our community colleges,” she said.
“Even if we don’t get it perfect, the more we do the more it sends the signal that we are not open for fraud business here,” Gustafson said in an interview. “We are not an easy target anymore, and people should know that.”
Munson, of Minnesota State, has repeatedly said the system will never be able to stop every attempt to steal financial aid. He notes the $3 million in legislative funding is less than the amount of money lost to fraud and to staff time spent fighting it.
Nevertheless, he said, the system has a “high success rate” in preventing criminals from slipping through.
“That doesn’t mean we stop everyone,” he said. “But we aren’t satisfied until we get that as close to zero as humanly possible.”
Minnesota State has selected a vendor for its new software, he said, and will pilot it with a few schools before rolling the technology out systemwide.
Among those waiting for that launch is Aldes, who said she doesn’t know exactly what’s coming, but, “Boy am I anxious to know.”
“We’re doing everything we can on a local level, and any systemic changes that maybe alleviate some of the manual work that we’re doing would be awesome,” Aldes said. “In the meantime, we’re going to protect our students, we’re going to protect our institution, we’re going to try and mitigate the harm as much as possible.”
Cleo Krejci is an investigative reporter covering community colleges as part of a collaboration between MinnPost and Open Campus. If you think you’ve been a victim of identity theft related to financial aid fraud – or are a college employee dealing with this issue – we want to hear from you. Reach out at ckrejci@minnpost.com.
