Shayne Longpre, Ayush Chopra, and Ariel Ekblaw are recognized for work spanning AI accountability, population-scale simulation, and self-assembling space architecture.

Creative Commons

Attribution 4.0 International

MIT Technology Review today unveiled its 2026 Innovators Under 35 — and three MIT Media Lab researchers are among this year's honorees. As one of the most prestigious recognitions in science and technology, the annual list identifies engineers, researchers, and entrepreneurs under the age of 35 who are tackling important problems in creative ways and making real, measurable progress. This year's class was selected from more than 550 nominations spanning nine countries, evaluated with the help of dozens of expert judges, and organized across four categories: artificial intelligence, biotechnology, climate and energy, and computing and robotics. MIT Media Lab claimed two of those categories.

- Shayne Longpre , a recent PhD graduate from the Human Dynamics group , is named in the Artificial Intelligence category. Now at Anthropic, his Data Provenance Initiative built global infrastructure to audit AI training data, expose hidden harms, and advocate for independent researcher access. His work helped shape the EU AI Act's red-teaming protections.

- Ayush Chopra , a researcher in the Camera Culture group , is also recognized in the Artificial Intelligence category. He developed Large Population Models (LPMs): hundreds of millions of AI agents that simulate complex, population-level events. For example, an LPM-based model correctly identified 87 of 100 predicted bird flu hot spots. He is now modeling how AI may reshape the working lives of 151 million Americans.

- Ariel Ekblaw , founder and director of the Space Exploration Initiative , is named in the Computing and Robotics category. She invented self-assembling magnetic tiles that autonomously construct large-scale infrastructure in orbit, thus eliminating the need for suited astronauts to perform dangerous manual assembly. Through the Aurelia Institute and Rendezvous Robotics, she is bringing this technology to commercial scale.

Their work reflects the Media Lab ethos at its core: transformative, human-centered, and built for a better world.

We still don’t know how people are really using AI

"No single company report tells the whole story,” says Shayne Longpre, a recent PhD graduate from the MIT Media Lab.

articles.article_title: Unit 5 superintendent talks technology use expectations, SNAP eligibility
articles.heading: Unit 5 superintendent talks technology use expectations, SNAP eligibility
articles.summary: Kristen Weikle said students may be having an easier time following phone expectations in year two of the district's policy limiting classroom use.
articles.content:
The superintendent of Unit 5 said students are having a “much easier” time following responsible phone use expectations in year two of the district’s electronics usage policy.
Kristen Weikle discussed that and a number of other key topics in McLean County’s largest school district during the first month of the 2026-27 school year on WGLT’s Sound Ideas.
Phones
Unit 5 implemented a new phone use policy for students before the 2025-26 school year. While it brought more restrictions, it did not place an outright ban — something a number of teachers requested as the school district evaluated the results of a study on phone use in classrooms.
Weikle said the teachers she has talked to this year have noticed a change now that students have a year of experience with the expectations.
“They've already seen the impact this year because kids came in knowing what the rules are, and so it was much easier to start the year and review those expectations with them than maybe what it was a year ago,” said Weikle.
At the high school level, phones need to be silent and away during class periods, but rules are not as strict during passing periods. They can be used during class if they are granted permission from a teacher, provided that it is being used for educational purposes. Up until high school, devices must be silent and away without these exceptions: from the beginning of the school day until the final bell.
New state regulations on cell phones coming for the start of the 2027-28 school year will not change things at Unit 5. The current policy falls underneath what the state law requires, which is the prohibition of use of “wireless communication devices” during school hours. Like Unit 5’s rule, it does not require strict enforcement during passing periods.
At District 87’s Bloomington High School, the new policy implemented for the 2025-26 school year was an outright ban throughout the school day.
AI policy
Artificial intelligence policy at Unit 5 is “ahead of the game,” said Weikle.
“We very much view it as a tool, and it can be used as a tool to help students, you know, learn,” said Weikle.
“Unit 5 is committed to providing a high-quality education that leverages AI as a tool, not a replacement, for human interaction and expertise,” notes Unit 5’s position statement on AI technology.
The Illinois State Board of Education offered similar guidance in July — that teaching and learning comes from human experiences first and that AI is not meant to be a substitute for it.
Unit 5 also provides a list of AI tools that are approved for certain uses within the district, denoting what each resource can be useful for and in what contexts they are allowed to be used. Certain options are for teacher use only.
Food stamps
Unit 5 families affected by federal cuts to SNAP [Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program] benefits still have options for recourse.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that over a million children have lost food benefits since the signing of the federal budget in July 2025, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That affects school cafeterias across the country, including at Unit 5, where SNAP benefits secure free and reduced-price breakfast and lunch for eligible kids.
Families that have experienced a cut or a loss to SNAP benefits become eligible through an application process with the state of Illinois. Weikle said Unit 5 families can receive help from people at their child’s school.
“We frequently help families complete the paperwork or gather anything that might be needed to see if they're eligible,” said Weikle.
“If they think they might be eligible, or if they're curious, reach out to your child's school,” said Weikle. “That's the best way to find out, how do you apply?”
Unit 5 families who are not SNAP eligible can apply for meal benefits on the Unit 5 website. According to the state's school report card, roughly 40% of the district's student population is considered low-income, characterized as eligible to receive free or reduced lunches or recipients of public aid.
That's well below the state average of 49.7%. In District 87, 62.3% of the student population is considered low-income.

Up until high school, devices must be silent and away without these exceptions: from the beginning of the school day until the final bell.

New state regulations on cell phones coming for the start of the 2027-28 school year will not change things at Unit 5. The current policy falls underneath what the state law requires, which is the prohibition of use of “wireless communication devices” during school hours. Like Unit 5’s rule, it does not require strict enforcement during passing periods.

At District 87’s Bloomington High School, the new policy implemented for the 2025-26 school year was an outright ban throughout the school day.

AI policy

Artificial intelligence policy at Unit 5 is “ahead of the game,” said Weikle.

“We very much view it as a tool, and it can be used as a tool to help students, you know, learn,” said Weikle.

“Unit 5 is committed to providing a high-quality education that leverages AI as a tool, not a replacement, for human interaction and expertise,” notes Unit 5’s position statement on AI technology.

The Illinois State Board of Education offered similar guidance in July — that teaching and learning comes from human experiences first and that AI is not meant to be a substitute for it.

Unit 5 also provides a list of AI tools that are approved for certain uses within the district, denoting what each resource can be useful for and in what contexts they are allowed to be used. Certain options are for teacher use only.

Food stamps

Unit 5 families affected by federal cuts to SNAP [Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program] benefits still have options for recourse.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that over a million children have lost food benefits since the signing of the federal budget in July 2025, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That affects school cafeterias across the country, including at Unit 5, where SNAP benefits secure free and reduced-price breakfast and lunch for eligible kids.

Families that have experienced a cut or a loss to SNAP benefits become eligible through an application process with the state of Illinois. Weikle said Unit 5 families can receive help from people at their child’s school.

“We frequently help families complete the paperwork or gather anything that might be needed to see if they're eligible,” said Weikle.

“If they think they might be eligible, or if they're curious, reach out to your child's school,” said Weikle. “That's the best way to find out, how do you apply?”

Unit 5 families who are not SNAP eligible can apply for meal benefits on the Unit 5 website. According to the state's school report card, roughly 40% of the district's student population is considered low-income, characterized as eligible to receive free or reduced lunches or recipients of public aid.

That's well below the state average of 49.7%. In District 87, 62.3% of the student population is considered low-income.

articles.summary: Penn State’s Teaching and Learning with Technology has announced the recipients of the New Faculty Recognition Award for the 2025-26 academic year.
articles.content:
UNIVERSITY PARK. Pa. — Penn State’s Teaching and Learning with Technology (TLT) has announced the recipients of the New Faculty Recognition Award for the 2025-26 academic year. This award, established in 2025, recognizes new faculty at Penn State who have demonstrated a clear and ongoing commitment to enhancing student learning by actively engaging with TLT’s resources, events, consultations and programs.
By taking part in a variety of opportunities, including instructional consultations, faculty development sessions and initiatives focused on the use of technology in teaching, these new faculty members worked to develop their digital fluency skills with the goal of advancing teaching methods and student learning outcomes. TLT collaborated with IT Learning and Development and the Schreyer Institute for Teaching Excellence to deliver content for some sessions.
“By investing in professional growth and embracing new educational technology tools during their first year, these faculty will explore new approaches, build confidence with instructional technology and connect with a community focused on student success,” said Angela Dick, acting senior director of Teaching and Learning with Technology. “Their commitment reflects the thoughtful and innovative teaching taking place across Penn State, and we’re pleased to celebrate their accomplishments.”

Madison Allen Kuyenga
Assistant Professor of Learning, Design and Technology
Penn State University Park
Eyal Ben-Yehuda
Physical Sciences Librarian, Physical and Mathematical Sciences Library
Penn State University Park
Melissa Correll
Research and Instruction Librarian
Penn State Abington
Pamela Dixon
Teaching Professor of Human Resources Management and Organizational Leadership
Penn State University Park
Azharul Islam
Assistant Teaching Professor of Economics
Penn State Harrisburg
Gina Mejia-Madrid
Assistant Teaching Professor of Computer Science
Penn State Abington
Laura Rice
Assistant Professor of Agricultural and Extension Education
Penn State University Park
Penn State identifies new faculty recipients each year based on their first-year engagement with TLT. More information on each recipient can be found on the New Faculty Recognition Award webpage.

articles.content:
Stop Wasting Money on Smart Garden Technology You Don’t Need
The more money you pour into smart garden technology, the more likely it is that your garden is actually getting worse.
That sounds backwards, but it is the pattern showing up across gardening communities, expert recommendations, and product reviews in 2026. Gardeners are spending $200 - $500 on app-connected sensors, automated garden kits, and subscription-based grow systems, only to end up with overwatered plants, dead Bluetooth connections, and monthly fees they didn't see coming. Meanwhile, the gardeners with the healthiest beds and the lowest bills are using tools that cost less than a bag of potting soil. When AeroGarden's cloud platform went down in 2024, locking users out of their own systems for months, it was a $200 lesson many are still paying for, writes Slashdot.
This matters right now because fall is when smart spending compounds. Every dollar wasted on a gadget that will collect dust by November is a dollar that could have gone toward spring bulbs, a quality soil amendment, or the one piece of garden tech that actually earns its keep. According to Gardening Know How, the average all-in-one smart garden kit costs over $200, while the single most recommended tool by gardening professionals costs $12.
Here is what experienced gardeners and horticultural experts say you should stop buying, what actually works, and where your money will go furthest before the first frost arrives.
1. The $200 Smart Garden Kit That Does Less Than a Stick in the Dirt
The smart garden industry has a pricing problem, and it is not in the direction you would expect. The most expensive kits, like those with Bluetooth soil sensors, LED panels, and companion apps, routinely underperform the simplest tools on the market. Andrea, the gardener behind Andreasgarden.com, put it plainly to Gardening Know How: "A $12 soil moisture probe. Not even a smart one; just the basic stick-in-the-dirt kind. Most people kill plants by watering on a schedule instead of watering when the plant actually needs it. One probe fixes that habit faster than anything else I've seen."
The accuracy gap between cheap and expensive is smaller than the marketing suggests. Independent testing reported by VerdeNook found that capacitive soil sensors, the kind built into pricey smart systems, achieve approximately ±3% accuracy but require soil-specific calibration. In clay-heavy soils, they can give wildly misleading readings without recalibration that most home gardeners never perform. A $12 analog probe, by contrast, gives you a reliable moisture reading every single time, no app required.
2. Smart Irrigation Timers That Actually Overwater Your Plants
Smart irrigation is the one category where technology genuinely delivers, but only when installed and configured correctly, which most homeowners do not do. The EPA's WaterSense program certifies that properly installed smart irrigation controllers save the average American home approximately 7,600 gallons of water per year. That is real money; in many regions, it translates to $50 to $100 off an annual water bill.
The problem is the gap between "properly installed" and "bought it at a hardware store and followed the quick-start guide." Elin Harryson, a plant expert at the gardening app Planta, told Gardening Know How that smart irrigation systems "are prone to app bugs, Wi-Fi disconnections, and, if not configured correctly, can actually overwater."
The villain here is the "set it and forget it" promise. Smart irrigation works when a professional calibrates it for your specific soil type, sun exposure, and plant selection. Without that setup, you are essentially paying $150 for an automated way to drown your tomatoes.
3. Per-Plant Sensors That Cost More Than the Plants Themselves
Individual Bluetooth plant sensors are among the most appealing products on the smart garden shelf and among the most returned. At $25 to $50 per sensor, costs multiply quickly; a modest herb garden with six plants could run you $300 in sensors alone, more than the plants will produce in a lifetime.
Elin Harryson at Planta offered a measured take in Gardening Know How: "Soil moisture sensors can be helpful, but their impact depends on how they're used. For beginners, they can prevent overwatering and help build awareness of how quickly soil dries out. However, they're not always perfectly accurate, and they shouldn't replace observation. The biggest benefit is as a learning tool, not a decision-maker."
The practical problems compound quickly. Gardeners report Bluetooth sensors losing connection beyond 15 to 20 feet, making them useless for anything beyond a windowsill or patio. In clay soils, capacitive readings fluctuate without recalibration. And for gardeners over 50 who aren't as familiar with technology devices, the learning curve of pairing devices, calibrating apps, and interpreting dashboards can be steep.
4. The Subscription Trap Nobody Warns You About
The sticker price on smart garden technology is rarely the full cost. Gardyn's AI gardening assistant, marketed as a key selling point of their indoor growing systems, requires a subscription of approximately $30 per month after purchase, according to VerdeNook's 2026 analysis. That is $360 a year, enough to buy a season's worth of organic seedlings, premium compost, and still have change for dinner.
Replacement pods, proprietary nutrient solutions, and premium app features add up across nearly every smart garden brand. One community analysis found that ongoing subscription costs often exceed the initial hardware purchase within the first year.
The deeper risk is obsolescence. When AeroGarden's cloud platform experienced an extended outage in 2024, users were locked out of core functionality for months. The hardware still sat on their countertops, but the brains behind it were gone. Every cloud-dependent garden system carries this risk; when the company folds or pivots, your $200 investment becomes a very expensive planter.
What a $12 Probe and a Free App Can Actually Do
The most effective smart garden setup in 2026 costs under $15 and fits in your back pocket. Andrea's recommendation to Gardening Know How was direct: "PlantNet for plant ID; it stops you from guessing wrong and caring for a plant the wrong way. And honestly, your phone's weather app. Checking a 10-day forecast before you plant or fertilize saves more crops than any gadget I could recommend."
The formula is simple: one soil moisture probe, one free plant ID app, and whatever weather app is already on your phone. Use the probe before every watering. Use the app when you are unsure what something is or whether it belongs where you planted it. Check the 10-day forecast before you fertilize or transplant. That is a smarter garden than any $500 kit will give you.
Between a $12 probe and free apps, you are replacing $200 or more in gadgets with more accurate tools that require no charging, never lose Wi-Fi, and will never lock you out because a company's servers went down. The best technology in your garden is the one you will actually use every morning.
The Smart Garden Trick Your Grandmother Already Knew
Before moisture probes existed, before apps, before Bluetooth anything, gardeners tested their soil the same way: they pressed a thumb three centimeters into the dirt. If the impression held sharp edges, the plant needed water. If the soil felt cool and held together, it was fine. This method, as VerdeNook noted in their 2026 smart gardening analysis, "remains the foundational gardening tool" regardless of what sensors say.
Your grandmother did not need a dashboard. She needed her hands, her eyes, and the patience to walk the garden every morning. That practice- 10 minutes with a cup of coffee, noticing which leaves are yellowing, which stems are leaning, where the soil is cracking- will always outperform a notification on your phone.
For gardeners who have been at this for 20+ years, this is not a step backwards. It is a reminder that the instincts you have already built are worth more than any sensor on the market. As Andrea told Gardening Know How: "Good tools make you more observant. A moisture probe trains your fingers. A plant ID app trains your eyes. If a tool is just sending you notifications and you're not actually learning anything, ditch it."
The Only Smart Garden Investment Worth Making This September
Not all smart garden technology is a waste. A few categories consistently prove their value, and September is the right time to invest before the first frost closes the window.
Smart drip irrigation, not timers, is worth the money. A basic drip system with a manual timer delivers water directly to roots, reduces evaporation, and costs a fraction of Wi-Fi-connected controllers. For gardeners putting in fall crops or winterizing perennial beds, a $30 to $50 drip kit will pay for itself in water savings and healthier root systems by spring.
Motion-activated sprinkler deterrents are one of the best-reviewed smart garden tools on the market. At $25 to $40, they reliably keep deer, raccoons, and rabbits out of fall vegetable gardens without chemicals or fencing. Gardening.org reports they "get good results" across a range of wildlife pressure.
Seedling heat mats, at $15 to $25, are the unsung hero of fall gardening. For anyone starting cool-season seeds indoors this month, a heat mat accelerates germination dramatically. Gardening.org calls them "a must if you have a cold house," and for gardeners in their 50s and 60s who have shifted to indoor seed-starting, they are one of the highest-ROI purchases available.
Skip the $200 kits. Invest $50 to $75 in tools that solve specific problems, and put the savings toward what your garden actually needs this fall.

articles.title: Catholic cardinal highlights technology’s role in transforming Africa’s resources
articles.description: Catholic cardinal highlights technology’s role in transforming Africa’s resources EWTN News
articles.description_html: Catholic cardinal highlights technology’s role in transforming Africa’s resources  EWTN News
articles.article_title: Catholic cardinal highlights technology’s role in transforming Africa’s resources
articles.heading: Catholic cardinal highlights technology’s role in transforming Africa’s resources
articles.summary: Cardinal Peter Turkson, the chancellor of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences in Rome, said the Church should recognize the natural resources available in creation as gifts from God.
articles.content:
ABUJA, Nigeria — Technology can help humanity transform the resources provided by God into practical benefits for people and communities across the African continent, the chancellor of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences in Rome said.
In an interview with ACI Africa, the sister service of EWTN News in Africa, on Sept. 3 during the launch of a 1.5-megawatt solar project that Earth Our Common Home (ECHo) is providing for Veritas University, Abuja, Cardinal Peter Turkson said ECHo’s mission is to provide clean energy for Catholic Churches and their institutions across Africa because of the importance of energy to man.
“There’s hardly anything that happens in this world without energy. Hardly anything. The solar energy initiative at the Catholic university demonstrates how human ingenuity can harness God’s creation to meet concrete needs while promoting integral human development,” Turkson said.
The Ghanaian-born cardinal said the Church should recognize the natural resources available in creation as gifts from God and use appropriate technology to transform them for the benefit of humanity.
“We need energy for everything that we do. So far, we’ve tried to produce that energy using generators, diesel fuel, and all of that,” he said.
Turkson continued: “It is, however, good to also notice that God, who created this, also provided the wherewithal to carry out everything that we do, providing this great source of energy. All it takes is that technology to transform this into our concrete use.”
The cardinal explained that God provides the raw materials while human creativity and technology transform them into useful products.
“God created cotton; God did not create a vest. Business transformed cotton into a vest that you wear. God created trees; he didn’t create furniture. Business people convert trees into furniture,” he said.
He added: “So we have solar light and a technology that is going to convert this into specific, concrete needs of this community. So that’s what we gathered here to do.”
Beyond providing electricity for teaching, learning, and other activities, Turkson said the project could significantly reduce the financial burden associated with diesel-powered electricity.
“It’s going to save this university not only by providing energy for people to study and learn, but save this university a lot of money,” he said.
He described the implementation of the project at a significantly reduced cost as an important opportunity for the Church, particularly as Catholic institutions seek sustainable ways of funding their educational and pastoral missions.
Turkson said the initiative should not be seen as benefiting Veritas University alone, noting that the experience could open the way for similar interventions in other Catholic institutions across Africa.
“From our small office, we’ve just tried to put together this small group to help our continent. So the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Nigeria is beginning with this, but from here it’s going to go on,” he said.
He explained that the vision was to make the benefits of the initiative available to Catholic bishops’ conferences and local churches across Africa.
“The benefits of ECHo and what it can facilitate and fund is something that is meant for all the bishops’ conferences of Africa, all the local churches in Africa, to support what the Church does for the promotion of integral human development,” Turkson said.
The Vatican official linked the project to the ecological vision of Pope Francis, particularly the late pope’s encyclical Laudato Si’, which calls Christians and the wider human family to care for creation.
He said the encyclical invites people to reflect on the impact of human activity on the natural environment.
“Everything that God created was good, very good. It comes into the hands of human beings, and we make it very good or very bad,” Turkson said.
He said the transition to renewable energy could help reduce the negative impact of human activities on creation.
“In terms of promoting the well-being of human beings or people, this project over here will go a long way toward determining how we reduce our negative impact on creation,” he said.
The cardinal emphasized that the environmental benefits of renewable energy are closely connected to human well-being.
“As Pope Francis would say, we turn the pain of the earth into our own personal pains. And we want to reduce that. Reduce that by producing less carbon dioxide, producing less greenhouse gas, whatever type of thing, and so polluting less,” he said.
He noted that reducing pollution would benefit both the environment and human health.
“When we pollute less, then we promote the environment more. Not only do we promote the environment, but we also promote the health of human beings, who also need this for their own existence,” he said.
For Turkson, the Veritas University project therefore represents more than an alternative source of electricity; it is an example of how faith, technology, and responsible stewardship can work together to support education, reduce costs, and advance human well-being.
“Everything that is happening here not only helps the advancement of the educational process but ultimately also enhances the well-being of creation and the human beings,” he said.
Meanwhile, the vice chancellor of Veritas University, Abuja, Father Hyacinth Ichoku, who spoke to ACI Africa during the same event, said the initiative was driven by the need to respond to the environmental damage caused by continued dependence on fossil fuels.
“We are part of the global consciousness about the Earth, our common home, and thatʼs why the project is actually about our Earth, our common home, about consciousness about the Earth and consciousness about the environment,” he said.
He noted that the continued release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere contributes to environmental degradation and poses risks to human life and ecosystems.
“The continuous transmission of carbon dioxide into the air is damaging our Earth, killing us, killing things, killing our environment. So we decided to move away from fossil fuels to solar energy, which they regard as clean energy,” Ichoku said.
This story was first published by ACI Africa, the sister service of EWTN News in Africa, and has been adapted by EWTN News.

ABUJA, Nigeria — Technology can help humanity transform the resources provided by God into practical benefits for people and communities across the African continent, the chancellor of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences in Rome said.

In an interview with ACI Africa, the sister service of EWTN News in Africa, on Sept. 3 during the launch of a 1.5-megawatt solar project that Earth Our Common Home (ECHo) is providing for Veritas University, Abuja, Cardinal Peter Turkson said ECHo’s mission is to provide clean energy for Catholic Churches and their institutions across Africa because of the importance of energy to man.

“There’s hardly anything that happens in this world without energy. Hardly anything. The solar energy initiative at the Catholic university demonstrates how human ingenuity can harness God’s creation to meet concrete needs while promoting integral human development,” Turkson said.

The Ghanaian-born cardinal said the Church should recognize the natural resources available in creation as gifts from God and use appropriate technology to transform them for the benefit of humanity.

“We need energy for everything that we do. So far, we’ve tried to produce that energy using generators, diesel fuel, and all of that,” he said.

Turkson continued: “It is, however, good to also notice that God, who created this, also provided the wherewithal to carry out everything that we do, providing this great source of energy. All it takes is that technology to transform this into our concrete use.”

The cardinal explained that God provides the raw materials while human creativity and technology transform them into useful products.

“God created cotton; God did not create a vest. Business transformed cotton into a vest that you wear. God created trees; he didn’t create furniture. Business people convert trees into furniture,” he said.

He added: “So we have solar light and a technology that is going to convert this into specific, concrete needs of this community. So that’s what we gathered here to do.”

Beyond providing electricity for teaching, learning, and other activities, Turkson said the project could significantly reduce the financial burden associated with diesel-powered electricity.

“It’s going to save this university not only by providing energy for people to study and learn, but save this university a lot of money,” he said.

He described the implementation of the project at a significantly reduced cost as an important opportunity for the Church, particularly as Catholic institutions seek sustainable ways of funding their educational and pastoral missions.

Turkson said the initiative should not be seen as benefiting Veritas University alone, noting that the experience could open the way for similar interventions in other Catholic institutions across Africa.

“From our small office, we’ve just tried to put together this small group to help our continent. So the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Nigeria is beginning with this, but from here it’s going to go on,” he said.

He explained that the vision was to make the benefits of the initiative available to Catholic bishops’ conferences and local churches across Africa.

“The benefits of ECHo and what it can facilitate and fund is something that is meant for all the bishops’ conferences of Africa, all the local churches in Africa, to support what the Church does for the promotion of integral human development,” Turkson said.

The Vatican official linked the project to the ecological vision of Pope Francis, particularly the late pope’s encyclical Laudato Si’, which calls Christians and the wider human family to care for creation.

He said the encyclical invites people to reflect on the impact of human activity on the natural environment.

“Everything that God created was good, very good. It comes into the hands of human beings, and we make it very good or very bad,” Turkson said.

He said the transition to renewable energy could help reduce the negative impact of human activities on creation.

“In terms of promoting the well-being of human beings or people, this project over here will go a long way toward determining how we reduce our negative impact on creation,” he said.

The cardinal emphasized that the environmental benefits of renewable energy are closely connected to human well-being.

“As Pope Francis would say, we turn the pain of the earth into our own personal pains. And we want to reduce that. Reduce that by producing less carbon dioxide, producing less greenhouse gas, whatever type of thing, and so polluting less,” he said.

He noted that reducing pollution would benefit both the environment and human health.

“When we pollute less, then we promote the environment more. Not only do we promote the environment, but we also promote the health of human beings, who also need this for their own existence,” he said.

For Turkson, the Veritas University project therefore represents more than an alternative source of electricity; it is an example of how faith, technology, and responsible stewardship can work together to support education, reduce costs, and advance human well-being.

“Everything that is happening here not only helps the advancement of the educational process but ultimately also enhances the well-being of creation and the human beings,” he said.

Meanwhile, the vice chancellor of Veritas University, Abuja, Father Hyacinth Ichoku, who spoke to ACI Africa during the same event, said the initiative was driven by the need to respond to the environmental damage caused by continued dependence on fossil fuels.

“We are part of the global consciousness about the Earth, our common home, and thatʼs why the project is actually about our Earth, our common home, about consciousness about the Earth and consciousness about the environment,” he said.

He noted that the continued release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere contributes to environmental degradation and poses risks to human life and ecosystems.

“The continuous transmission of carbon dioxide into the air is damaging our Earth, killing us, killing things, killing our environment. So we decided to move away from fossil fuels to solar energy, which they regard as clean energy,” Ichoku said.

This story was first published by ACI Africa, the sister service of EWTN News in Africa, and has been adapted by EWTN News.

articles.summary: KINGSTON, R.I. – Sep. 8, 2026 – The University of Rhode Island will host its second annual Tech Showcase, Tuesday, Sept. 22, from 4 to 7 p.m. at Toray Commons in the Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering on the Kingston campus. The showcase will allow emerging research, technologies, and ventures from across the University to […]
articles.content:
KINGSTON, R.I. – Sep. 8, 2026 – The University of Rhode Island will host its second annual Tech Showcase, Tuesday, Sept. 22, from 4 to 7 p.m. at Toray Commons in the Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering on the Kingston campus. The showcase will allow emerging research, technologies, and ventures from across the University to collaborate with investors, industry leaders, alumni, and community partners.
Presented by URI Innovations, the showcase is designed to strengthen the path from university research to commercial application by creating direct connections around licensing, venture development, investment, and industry collaboration.
This year’s event comes amid growing momentum across URI’s innovation community. Multiple URI-affiliated startups have seen commercialization milestones within the past year.
Juice Robotics, a URI ocean technology spinout, secured venture investments from Rhode Island-based Rogue Island Ventures after developing a connection during last year’s showcase. The company has also licensed four URI-developed technologies, advancing its transition from university research to commercial venture. The company also recently received the BlueTide Catalyst Award, recognizing its potential operational transition and impact on the blue economy.
Another URI spinout, Trace Sensing Technologies, has reached a major funding milestone having recently closed a series seed round of more than $2 million to advance TRACE-E, its non-invasive breath-based diagnostic platform.
Additionally, FastFlowLM has joined AMD, bringing technology with roots in university research into one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies. Founded by URI professor of computer engineering Ken Qing Yang with Tao Wei and Alfred Xu, the startup develops software designed to make large language models and other AI workloads run more efficiently on neural processing units.
The 2026 Tech Showcase will bring these developments into a broader presentation of work currently moving through URI’s innovation pipeline. Featured participants include FinSight Intelligence, CHAMP, Looey, and URI-developed technologies focused on smart wound monitoring, PFAS detection, and more.
Keynote speaker Jon Soderstrom, founder of Yale Ventures, brings more than four decades of experience in intellectual property and university technology commercialization. During more than 25 years at Yale, his work contributed to the formation of more than 75 ventures and more than $1 billion in venture investment.
The showcase reflects URI Innovations’ larger role in helping research move beyond the University through commercialization. By bringing researchers and founders into direct contact with investors and industry, the event creates opportunities for technologies to advance through licensing, company formation, private investment, and market adoption.
The event is part of Rhode Island Startup Week, powered by RIHub. Registration is open and for more information on how to register head to: https://urishowcase.my.canva.site/.

URI Innovations

articles.heading: Andrea Fletcher tapped to lead Virginia’s government technology overhaul
articles.summary: Virginia is creating a team of technology specialists to improve state websites and computer systems while guarding against costly technology contracts and wasted taxpayer dollars. Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday named Andrea Fletcher director of the new Virginia Digital Service, which will bring together engineers, designers and other technical experts to modernize state government operations and make public services easier to use.
articles.content:
Andrea Fletcher tapped to lead Virginia’s government technology overhaul
New Digital Service agency will focus on modernizing state systems, simplifying access to public services and scrutinizing technology programs.
Andrea Fletcher will lead the new Virginia Digital Service, a team charged with modernizing state websites and computer systems and improving how the state purchases technology. (Courtesy of Virginia Governor’s Office)
Virginia is creating a team of technology specialists to improve state websites and computer systems while guarding against costly technology contracts and wasted taxpayer dollars.
Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday named Andrea Fletcher director of the new Virginia Digital Service, which will bring together engineers, designers and other technical experts to modernize state government operations and make public services easier to use.
The team will also review how Virginia buys and uses technology, with an eye toward identifying problems before the state commits taxpayer money to poorly designed systems or contracts.
“State government should work for the people it serves — and that means making sure Virginians can access the services they need quickly, easily, and reliably,” Spanberger said in a statement.
Spanberger proposed establishing the Digital Service through an amendment to Virginia’s biennial budget after her administration said it discovered the state had lost $52 million on a failed IT project under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration.
The project involved a two-year effort by the Virginia Department of Social Services to modernize APECS, the state’s decades-old child support enforcement computer system. The department had hired CGI Technologies and Solutions for the project, known as vCHAMPS, but abandoned the overhaul after what an internal report described as “significant issues.”
Under Fletcher’s leadership, the team will work with agencies across state government computer systems, improve websites and speed up delivery of programs used by Virginia families, according to the governor’s office.
“We also have a responsibility to make sure every taxpayer dollar is used as effectively and efficiently as possible,” Spanberger said. “At a time of unprecedented uncertainty and disruption out of Washington, Virginia can — and should — be a model of how we make smart, sound investments in technology.”
Fletcher previously served as the first chief digital officer at the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, where she led the agency’s Digital Service team. She also established what the governor’s office called the federal government’s first Open Source Program Office.
She began her tenure with the federal government through the U.S. Digital Service in 2021 after working in federal healthcare information technology policy, artificial intelligence governance and global health systems. Her work included projects in more than 20 countries and support for digital health systems responding to COVID-19, Ebola and HIV.
Fletcher received a Service to the Citizen Award in 2025 and was nominated in 2024 for the Samuel J. Heyman award for emerging government leaders.
“Virginians should have an expectation that government services be intuitive and easy to use,” Fletcher said in a statement. “I’m excited to help deliver on that goal for the people of the commonwealth and demonstrate that government can build great technology.”
David Wilkinson, Virginia’s chief transformation officer, said residents should be able to navigate state systems easily whether they are applying for a driver’s license, opening a business or seeking essential services.
“In launching the Virginia Digital Service, the governor is bringing a proven approach to Virginia,” Wilkinson said. “Andrea Fletcher is a nationally respected digital leader with a track record of delivering results that save time and money.”
Originally from western Pennsylvania’s Appalachian region, Fletcher earned a bachelor’s degree from Washington & Jefferson College and a master’s degree in public health from Emory University. She lives in Alexandria with her husband and daughter.
One of the new team’s early assignments will be helping state agencies respond to federal funding and eligibility changes under H.R. 1, the tax and spending reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer at the behest of President Donald Trump.
The administration said the Digital Service will support efforts to maintain access to healthcare coverage and Supplemental Nutrition Access Program.
The move follows a separate legislative effort to modernize Virginia’s benefits system. House Bill 66, sponsored by Del. Michael Feggans, D-Virginia Beach, would have directed the departments of Social Services and Medical Assistance Services to develop a plan for updating technology used to administer federal medical and other benefit programs. The measure was continued to the 2027 session.
Last month, Spanberger launched the “Keep Virginia Covered” policy directing executive agencies as they implement the federal law and seek to limit its effect on Virginians.
Virginia is not the first state to create a government-run technology team. Similar programs elsewhere have been used to review contracts, simply applications for public benefits and rebuild government websites.
In Colorado, the state’s digital team helped negotiate a grant-management system covering 17 programs and more than $60 million in annual grants before money was committed to the system.
Pennsylvania used its team to haul over the process for appealing denied insurance claims, replacing what Spanberger’s administration described as a confusing form with a simpler system.
Meanwhile, Maryland consolidated applications for Medicaid, SNAP, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, the Special Supplemental Assistance Program for Women, Infants and Children, and energy assistance into a single process. More than 220,000 applications were completed through the new system in six months, according to the state’s Gov. Wes Moore.
Maryland also redesigned its unemployment insurance website around a five-step process for claimants. The changes reduced the number of pages on the site by 40% and increased its completion rate by 15%.

articles.summary: Intermountain Health St. Mary’s Regional Hospital has invested more than $2 million for new equipment and technology to improve quality of care and comfort of their patients receiving cancer care in the Grand Junction area.St. Mary’s Cancer Centers of Colorado purchased a new a new computed tomography (CT) scanner that offers several enhance...
articles.content:
New Cancer Care Technology at Intermountain Health St. Mary’s Improves Precision and Comfort for Western Colorado Patients
Intermountain Health St. Mary’s Regional Hospital has invested more than $2 million for new equipment and technology to improve quality of care and comfort of their patients receiving cancer care in the Grand Junction area.
St. Mary’s Cancer Centers of Colorado purchased a new a new computed tomography (CT) scanner that offers several enhancements over the center’s existing scanner. The new model, a Siemens SOMATOM go.SIM CT Simulator, has access to the latest tools.
Physicians rely on having clear images of a patient’s cancerous tumor, so the dosimetrist can create plans of how radiation can target that tumor. Intermountain Health manager of oncology services and radiation oncology April Grumley said that it is important to be as precise as possible when delivering radiation so only the tumor is impacted and surrounding tissue and organs are protected.
One of the new tools provides the ability to do a CT scan with contrast. This is a standard imaging procedure in which a dye is injected into the body, and it allows the dosimetrist to better see critical anatomy and certain tumors. This helps the dosimetrist be more precise and develop better treatment plans for patients.
The new CT machine also removes metal artifacts such as a pacemaker, dental implants, or the hardware in a shoulder, hip or knee replacement from the images it produces. When those artifacts are removed from the scan, the physicians and dosimetrists can see structures more clearly and create more accurate treatment plans. Previously, patients went to the hospital to have a CT scan with contrast.
The cancer center has also expanded the technology that improves how radiation treatments are delivered. Vision RT Surface Guided Radiation Therapy allows the radiation therapist to continually monitor the position of patients throughout treatment. The technology detects even the slightest movement of the patient in real time and can stop the treatment until the patient is positioned correctly. The cancer center has used this type of technology since 2015. Now, with the latest version added to the linear accelerator, they can serve more patients who have a wider range of cancer diagnoses.
“Perhaps most important for patients is the ability to now wear an open-face mask during treatment,” Grumley said. Previously, patients wore a full-face mask that attaches to the patient's board and keeps them from moving throughout the treatment, which often lasts as long as 15 minutes.
The final piece of equipment the cancer center acquired literally makes a small degree of change with the patient but has a big impact on the precision of their treatment, Grumley said. The 6 Degrees of Freedom Treatment Couch can tilt in six directions enabling greater precision in placing the patient, improved treatment accuracy for difficult treatment sites, and better alignment between the daily imaging and treatment delivery.
“This new equipment and technology is a major advancement for our patients in Western Colorado and shows our commitment to bringing the most advanced capabilities to the Grand Valley,” Grumley said.
The new technology will benefit patients diagnosed with several types of cancer including head and neck, brain, and lung.
Cancer Centers of Colorado, St. Mary’s Regional Hospital at 750 Wellington Ave., in Grand Junction offers medical and radiation oncology, genetic counseling, palliative care, clinical trials, support groups and survivorship care. St. Mary’s is accredited by American Society for Radiation Oncology’s Accreditation Program for Excellence, the Commission on Cancer, and the National Accreditation Program for Breast Centers. For more information, visit Intermountain Health St. Mary’s Regional Hospital Cancer.

articles.content:
Trinity Health plans to lay off 500 information technology-related roles
Trinity Health Corp. expects to permanently lay off 557 workers in Wayne County, Michigan, as part of a restructuring effort.
The details of the layoffs were related in a WARN Act notice filed with the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity.
The Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, also known as the WARN Act, requires companies undergoing mass layoffs and/or site closures to issue advance public notice to the state's labor department if certain size or employment thresholds are met.
The layoffs from its site on Victor Parkway in Livonia will take effect between October 25 and November 19, the notice said. The affected positions include service desk support, systems administrators, data engineers and information technology roles.
Trinity Health, which is based in Livonia, is one of the country's largest faith-based health care systems. Its network includes hospitals, surgery centers and senior care facilities. The corporation had about 133,000 employees during its June 2025 year-end report.
A quarterly report issued for the time frame ending on March 31, 2026, said "to address ongoing industry pressure and evolving legislative impacts," the corporation would "redesign and reposition" some of its services.
The company also announced in June that it would move some of its in-house technology and information services roles to an outside partner. "This change affects TIS roles that involve internal technology support services, including the service desk and applications support. It does not affect clinical, patient-facing roles," the announcement said.

articles.title: Spanberger is creating a new state technology team
articles.description: Spanberger is creating a new state technology team Virginia Scope
articles.description_html: Spanberger is creating a new state technology team  Virginia Scope
articles.article_title: Spanberger is creating a new state technology team
articles.heading: Spanberger is creating a new state technology team
articles.summary: Gov. Abigail Spanberger is creating a new state technology team after her administration says it uncovered $52 million that was lost on a failed effort to replace Virginia’s child support enforcement system under the previous administration.
articles.content:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger is creating a new state technology team after her administration says it uncovered $52 million that was lost on a failed effort to replace Virginia’s child support enforcement system under the previous administration.
Spanberger on Tuesday announced that Andrea Fletcher, a former federal digital services official, will lead the Virginia Digital Service, which is intended to bring engineers, designers and other technology experts into state government to improve websites, modernize outdated systems and scrutinize technology contracts.
Virginia’s recently approved two-year budget included the new office after Spanberger proposed startup funding. The administration says the goal is not simply to make state websites easier to use, but to prevent the kind of costly technology failures that have plagued government agencies.
Spanberger has criticized her predecessor, Republican Gov. Glenn Youngkin, over the $52 million loss, saying the state paid millions for technology that did not work as intended.
“My predecessor might have thought it was okay to just write off losses like this one, but I don’t,” Spanberger said last month.
The state budget now requires the Department of Social Services to provide quarterly reports on spending and implementation of a new child support technology system.
“State government should work for the people it serves — and that means making sure Virginians can access the services they need quickly, easily, and reliably,” Spanberger said in a statement announcing Fletcher’s appointment.
Fletcher comes to Virginia after working in the federal government, where she served as the first chief digital strategy officer at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. She previously led the CMS Digital Service team and established an open-source program office.
She entered government through the U.S. Digital Service in 2021. Her career has also included work on federal health IT policy, artificial intelligence governance and digital health systems in more than 20 countries.
“Virginians should have an expectation that government services be intuitive and easy to use,” Fletcher said.
The new team is also expected to work on issues created by changes in federal policy. Spanberger’s administration says the Digital Service will help agencies respond to federal cuts affecting programs such as health care coverage and SNAP.
Spanberger’s announcement pointed to digital service teams in other states as examples of what Virginia hopes to accomplish.
Colorado’s team helped the state evaluate a proposed grant management system covering 17 programs and more than $60 million in annual grants before the state committed to the system, according to Spanberger’s office.
In Maryland, a digital services team created a single application for Medicaid, SNAP, TANF, WIC and energy assistance. The state says more than 220,000 applications were completed in less than six months.
Maryland also redesigned its unemployment insurance website, reducing the number of pages by 40% and increasing the completion rate by 15%, according to Spanberger.
The Virginia Digital Service will operate alongside the Virginia Information Technologies Agency, the state’s existing central technology agency, which oversees information technology infrastructure and major technology investments.

articles.title: SiriusXM Names Sean Gibbons Chief Product and Technology Officer
articles.description: SiriusXM Names Sean Gibbons Chief Product and Technology Officer PR Newswire
articles.description_html: SiriusXM Names Sean Gibbons Chief Product and Technology Officer  PR Newswire
articles.article_title: SiriusXM Names Sean Gibbons Chief Product and Technology Officer
articles.heading: SiriusXM Names Sean Gibbons Chief Product and Technology Officer
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- SiriusXM (NASDAQ: SIRI) today announced that Sean Gibbons has been promoted to Senior Vice President, Chief Product and Technology Officer,...
articles.content:
Longtime SiriusXM leader will advance the Company's product experiences and technology strategy
NEW YORK, Sept. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SiriusXM (NASDAQ: SIRI) today announced that Sean Gibbons has been promoted to Senior Vice President, Chief Product and Technology Officer, reporting to Chief Executive Officer Jennifer Witz and joining the Company's Executive Leadership Team. In this role, Gibbons will lead product and technology across SiriusXM and Pandora, with responsibility for product strategy and development, technology platforms and engineering, automotive and streaming distribution partnerships, and advertising technology.
"Sean has helped shape SiriusXM through some of our most important product and technology transformations, including the development and successful rollout of SiriusXM with 360L," said Jennifer Witz, Chief Executive Officer, SiriusXM. "He brings more than two decades of experience, deep knowledge of our business and a strong track record of bringing together teams, technology and partnerships to deliver for consumers. Sean is a highly respected leader and the right person to help us accelerate innovation, improve the customer experience and advance the products, platforms and partnerships that will support our growth."
Gibbons' key priorities will include advancing SiriusXM with 360L and the Company's next generation of in-car experiences; shaping the long-term technology roadmap supporting SiriusXM's satellite, broadcast and streaming platforms; applying AI to improve personalization, discovery and customer service; and creating more dynamic, connected and participatory experiences across SiriusXM's in-vehicle and streaming platforms.
"SiriusXM has a unique set of assets and a tremendous opportunity to make them work together even more powerfully for listeners," said Gibbons. "We can pair the reach and reliability of satellite with the flexibility of streaming and the intelligence of AI to make it easier for people to discover what they love, stay connected wherever they listen and participate more deeply in the content and moments that matter to them. I'm excited to take on this role and help shape the next generation of the SiriusXM experience."
Gibbons joined Sirius in 2000, before the company's first satellite launch, and has held leadership roles spanning product management, engineering, automotive, streaming, content technology and strategic partnerships. During his tenure, he established SiriusXM's first formal Product Management organization and later founded and led its first Streaming organization, expanding the SiriusXM experience across mobile, web and connected-home platforms.
Most recently, Gibbons led SiriusXM's Automotive organization, bringing together product, user experience, engineering and automotive partnerships to advance the company's in-vehicle experiences and relationships with leading automakers. Across more than two decades at SiriusXM, he has played a central role in many of the Company's most significant product and technology transformations, including its evolution toward connected, software-defined vehicle experiences and hybrid satellite-and-IP services.
About Sirius XM Holdings Inc.
SiriusXM is the leading audio entertainment company in North America, with a portfolio of audio businesses including its flagship subscription entertainment service SiriusXM; the ad-supported and premium music streaming services of Pandora; an expansive podcast network; and a complete ecosystem of advertising solutions through SiriusXM Media and AdsWizz. SiriusXM offers live, on-demand, and human-curated programming across music, talk, news, sports, and podcasts, and the company reaches approximately 255 million monthly listeners across its platforms. With deep automotive manufacturer relationships and unique spectrum assets, SiriusXM is built to reach listeners wherever they are. The company connects fans to the voices, creators, and moments they love - creating communities where listeners engage, participate, and belong. For more about SiriusXM, please go to: https://www.siriusxm.com/

articles.title: First-year RIT students study the relationships between AI, technology, and society
articles.description: First-year RIT students study the relationships between AI, technology, and society Rochester Institute of Technology
articles.description_html: First-year RIT students study the relationships between AI, technology, and society  Rochester Institute of Technology
articles.article_title: First-year RIT students study the relationships between AI, technology, and society
articles.heading: First-year RIT students study the relationships between AI, technology, and society
articles.summary: RIT introduces new courses to equip first-year students with the tools to think critically about artificial intelligence and its impact on human life.
articles.content:
First-year RIT students study the relationships between AI, technology, and society
The two new pilot courses, offered by the College of Liberal Arts, focus on how AI and emerging technologies impact human society
The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and tools has undeniably altered human life and the workforce, but Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) is making sure students are confidently prepared to navigate these changes.
Two recently introduced pilot courses with a focus on AI and emerging technologies aim to arm students with the knowledge to think critically about technology’s impact on human life. The interrelated pilot courses, offered by RIT’s College of Liberal Arts, were developed with a goal of enhancing first-year students’ understanding of the complex relationships between technology, society, and their college experience.
These pilot courses, Interdisciplinary Explorations of Human Problems and Science, Technology, and Values, are based in the Department of Criminal Justice and the Department of Science, Technology, and Society, respectively. Though the two courses share an overall curricular goal, each version of the pilot course is tailored to the individual department’s field of study.
These are the first of several planned courses that will introduce first-year students to the intersection of technology and society and encourage them to investigate the potential societal impacts of emerging technologies.
Irshad Altheimer, the Ellen M. Granberg Endowed Professor, is teaching the Criminal Justice-based pilot course, and Associate Professor Kaitlin Stack Whitney is teaching the Science, Technology, and Society-based pilot course.
Stack Whitney explained that the Department of Science, Technology, and Society was perfectly poised to test out a course of this nature.
“Science and technology studies is all about how people shape technology, and how technology effects change. That bi-directional understanding and approach is key, it’s not one or the other,” she explained.
The department recently launched a new immersion, minor, and dedicated course in Artificial Intelligence in Society. Stack Whitney was involved in these developments and has taught the course three times since it was introduced, so she was intrigued by the opportunity to teach this new pilot course.
In her version of the course, Science, Technology, and Values, students will explore how tools like social media, AI, surveillance systems, and medical innovations reshape communities, power, identity, and opportunity. Students will also investigate how human values, culture, politics, and economics shape what gets built, who benefits, and who gets left out.
“Technologies aren’t neutral. They reflect the goals and visions that folks have for both the present and the world they want to make,” she said. “We can help students understand how automation has changed life in the past and help them think critically about claims being made with certainty about the future.”
After witnessing the impact of AI tools on the justice system firsthand, Altheimer was similarly intrigued by the opportunity to craft the criminal justice-oriented version of the pilot course, Interdisciplinary Explorations of Human Problems. He will co-teach the course with Ashique KhudaBukhsh, assistant professor in RIT’s Golisano College of Computing and Information Sciences.
“Justice is a bedrock of a democratic society. How we use AI in the criminal justice system reflects our own ethics and values,” he said.
Students enrolled in Altheimer and KhudaBukhsh’s course will study the use of AI tools at different stages of the criminal justice system, and the impact that it has on key criminal justice outcomes such as arrect, conviction, and incarceration.
“Particular attention will be paid to whether AI tools actually make our system better, or if they just provide the illusion of justice,” said Altheimer. “Our students need to be equipped with the analytical tools that can help them evaluate this technology and its impact on society.”
Going forward in future semesters, any College of Liberal Arts faculty member will be able to craft and offer their own discipline-specific course on emerging technologies. The courses are also helping to inform planning for revisions to RIT’s General Education framework, which is currently in the vetting and approval stages.
These pilot courses add to a healthy variety of AI-related curricular offerings across the university. RIT recently introduced a new bachelor’s degree in AI and, in 2023, RIT began offering a master’s degree in AI. The university also aims to launch an AI institute in 2027, which will advance AI education, research, and responsible application across disciplines while helping develop the talent needed to guide, apply, and improve emerging technologies.
Go to RIT's Artificial Intelligence webpage to learn more about how AI is being studied across the university.

articles.title: NLM Photonics Adds New Investors to Scale Organic Photonics Technology
articles.description: NLM Photonics Adds New Investors to Scale Organic Photonics Technology The Quantum Insider
articles.description_html: NLM Photonics Adds New Investors to Scale Organic Photonics Technology  The Quantum Insider
articles.article_title: NLM Photonics Adds New Investors to Scale Organic Photonics Technology
articles.heading: NLM Photonics Adds New Investors to Scale Organic Photonics Technology
articles.summary: NLM Photonics has added Pangaea Ventures and Diamond Edge Ventures as investors to support commercialization of its photonics technology.
articles.content:
Insider Brief
- NLM Photonics has added Pangaea Ventures and Diamond Edge Ventures to its investor base, alongside increased investments from several existing backers, to support commercialization of its organic photonics technology.
- The funding will support development of organic hybrid photonic integrated circuits for optical transceivers, data-center interconnects and potential quantum computing applications.
- NLM has reported demonstrations of 1.6-terabit and 3.2-terabit silicon-organic hybrid PICs and began customer sampling of those products in 2026.
PRESS RELEASE — NLM Photonics, the leader in the development of organic electro-optic (OEO) technology based upon its Selerion™ family of materials, has added new financial and strategic investors to its cap table to accelerate commercialization of its organic photonic ecosystem.
Pangaea Ventures, widely regarded as the world’s leading hard tech venture capital firm, and Diamond Edge Ventures, the venture investment arm of Mitsubishi Chemical Corporation, have joined NLM Photonics to commercialize its technology. Existing investors Emerald Technology Ventures, Oregon Venture Fund, Idemitsu, Tokyo Ohka Kogyo Co., Ltd. (TOK), and StoryHouse Ventures strengthened their investment, alongside private investors and company employees.
As part of the round, David Weekes, from Pangaea Ventures, will join NLM’s Board of Directors. NLM is the first company to secure investment from both Pangaea Ventures and Emerald Technology Ventures, two influential investors across advanced materials and hard tech landscapes.
“We’ve assembled an investor base that mirrors the ecosystem we’re building, bringing together firms with decades of experience scaling deep technology companies alongside global leaders in semiconductor materials and manufacturing,” said Brad Booth, CEO of NLM Photonics. “Pangaea is the firm where material incumbents and semiconductor giants turn to when validating breakthroughs. Emerald is one of the most established names in industrial and cleantech investing. Having both invest in NLM while rounding out with strong investors in the material space – TOK, Idemitsu and Mitsubishi Chemical Corporation – is a powerful signal to the photonics market that NLM has secured the material supply chain while on a path to scale for manufacturing.”
The investment reflects growing market confidence in NLM’s organic materials as a path to faster, more energy-efficient photonics, driven by surging AI workloads and demand for higher-bandwidth, lower-power optical interconnects. The capital infusion will accelerate NLM’s ecosystem development for commercial-scale, multi-foundry production of organic hybrid photonic integrated circuits (PICs) for high-speed optical transceivers, next-generation data center interconnects, and quantum computing based upon NLM’s OEO material families.
With expertise in foundational science, Pangaea has backed hard tech breakthroughs in chemistry, novel semiconductor substrates, and advanced hardware components. Emerald brings decades of experience scaling hard-tech companies from demonstration to deployment. Diamond Edge Ventures provides access to deep materials and manufacturing expertise through its parent company, Mitsubishi Chemical Corporation. Returning investors Idemitsu, a major player in advanced materials, and Tokyo Ohka Kogyo Co., Ltd., a major player in semiconductor materials, further strengthen a cap table optimized for both scientific innovation and volume manufacturing.
“We invest in technologies that materially transform the systems that the world increasingly depends on. NLM‘s organic photonics platform is a clear example of technology that not only improves the rate at which data is moved, but does so with substantially lower energy requirements,” said David Weekes of Pangaea Ventures, who joins the NLM board. “NLM has already brought in partners who understand what it takes to move a materials breakthrough into high-volume manufacturing. That combination of strong science and a credible path to scale is rare, and it’s why we wanted to partner with NLM Photonics.”
NLM has rapidly advanced its technology development and commercial engagements. In 2025, the company demonstrated the industry’s first 1.6-terabit and 3.2-terabit multi-channel silicon-organic hybrid photonic integrated circuits, and in 2026, began customer sampling of its 1.6T and 3.2T PICs. With the expansion of its investors and customers backing that trajectory, NLM is positioned to scale its organic photonics platform toward volume manufacturing.
Investor Quotes
“Bringing a new material into volume production requires years of customer qualification, consistent quality, and reliable supply. Mitsubishi Chemical Corporation has supported the semiconductor industry through that process for decades and understands what NLM will need to demonstrate as its technology advances. Through this investment, we intend to support NLM as its organic electro-optic materials progress toward commercial production,” said Curtis Schickner, President of Diamond Edge Ventures.
“Our increased investment reflects the strong progress NLM has made since our initial investment. The team has repeatedly met important technical milestones while forging the strategic partnerships needed to bring its technology to market. The combination of technical execution and ecosystem development gives us confidence in NLM’s path to commercial success,” said Frank Balas, Investment Director, Emerald Technology Ventures.
“Since our initial investment, we have been encouraged by NLM Photonics’ progress in advancing its organic electro-optic technology and by its growing engagement with customers across the photonics industry. We believe this technology has the potential to contribute to the next generation of high-speed, energy-efficient optical communications. Through this follow-on investment, we look forward to supporting NLM Photonics as it builds on this momentum,” said Hidenori Tanaka, Executive Officer, General Manager of Business Investment Office, Idemitsu Kosan Co., Ltd.
“NLM has evolved from a promising technology into a business with real commercial momentum and world-class strategic partners. We’re proud to have backed NLM from an early stage, and to be deepening our commitment as it moves from breakthrough demonstrations toward commercializing its materials,” said Deepthi Madhava, Partner, Oregon Venture Fund.
“NLM has continued to validate its vision over the past couple of years through disciplined execution, technical leadership, and the ability to attract exceptional talent and partners. We are proud to continue investing in and supporting the company’s growth, and are grateful to have the company in our portfolio and in the Claremont Colleges startup ecosystem,” said Josh Tatum, GP, StoryHouse Ventures.
“Commercial success in photonics depends on technologies that can move beyond the laboratory into scalable semiconductor manufacturing. NLM has made impressive progress in building an ecosystem that supports that transition, and we are excited to continue supporting its commercialization efforts,” said Naoki Watanabe, Division Manager, New Business Development Div., Tokyo Ohka Kogyo Co., Ltd.
