- Taiwan eyes silicon photonics as next big tech leap By Liao Chia-ning and William Hetherington / Staff reporter, with staff writer Add TT as Preferred Source Taiwan, which accounts for more than half of the global outsourced semiconductor assembly and testing market, is well-positioned to develop copackaged optics (CPO) and manufacture precision silicon photonics chips, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday. Silicon photonics are emerging as a mainstream optical communications technology and is seen as key to overcoming bottlenecks in AI computing power. The technology is a key project under the government’s New 10 Major AI Infrastructure Projects, with industry, government, academia and research institutions working to overcome critical technological hurdles and build a self-reliant silicon photonics supply chain, the ministry said. A silicon wafer is displayed during Semicon Taiwan in Taipei on Sept. 11 last year. Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA Nvidia Corp in March invested US$4 billion in silicon photonics technology, the ministry added. The technology was a major topic at Semicon Taiwan, which concluded on Friday last week. Silicon photonics replaces traditional copper wire transmission of electronic signals between chips with optical signals. As light generates almost no heat during transmission, the technology can reduce power consumption by 30 to 50 percent, allowing devices to stream high-definition content and generate artificial intelligence content more quickly, the ministry said. Taiwan has key advantages in the transition, including a comprehensive semiconductor ecosystem and more than 90 percent of global advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity for 7 nanometer chips or below, the ministry said. Taiwan accounts for more than half of the global semiconductor assembly and testing market, which gives it a key role in developing CPO, a technology aimed at overcoming the 1.6-terabit-per-second bandwidth limit of traditional electronic transmission. The government launched a silicon photonics research and development (R&D) initiative under its A+ Enterprise Innovation R&D Program earlier this year to support the development of key technologies. The ministry and the SEMI have helped more than 30 leading companies, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控), MediaTek Inc (聯發科) and Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密), establish the Silicon Photonics Industry Alliance in 2024, it said. The alliance aims to overcome key technological hurdles, particularly in CPO, and ensure that Taiwan retains control of the silicon photonics supply chain, it said.

Taiwan, which accounts for more than half of the global outsourced semiconductor assembly and testing market, is well-positioned to develop copackaged optics (CPO) and manufacture precision silicon photonics chips, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.

Silicon photonics are emerging as a mainstream optical communications technology and is seen as key to overcoming bottlenecks in AI computing power.

The technology is a key project under the government’s New 10 Major AI Infrastructure Projects, with industry, government, academia and research institutions working to overcome critical technological hurdles and build a self-reliant silicon photonics supply chain, the ministry said.

Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA

Nvidia Corp in March invested US$4 billion in silicon photonics technology, the ministry added.

The technology was a major topic at Semicon Taiwan, which concluded on Friday last week.

Silicon photonics replaces traditional copper wire transmission of electronic signals between chips with optical signals.

As light generates almost no heat during transmission, the technology can reduce power consumption by 30 to 50 percent, allowing devices to stream high-definition content and generate artificial intelligence content more quickly, the ministry said.

Taiwan has key advantages in the transition, including a comprehensive semiconductor ecosystem and more than 90 percent of global advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity for 7 nanometer chips or below, the ministry said.

Taiwan accounts for more than half of the global semiconductor assembly and testing market, which gives it a key role in developing CPO, a technology aimed at overcoming the 1.6-terabit-per-second bandwidth limit of traditional electronic transmission.

The government launched a silicon photonics research and development (R&D) initiative under its A+ Enterprise Innovation R&D Program earlier this year to support the development of key technologies.

The ministry and the SEMI have helped more than 30 leading companies, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控), MediaTek Inc (聯發科) and Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密), establish the Silicon Photonics Industry Alliance in 2024, it said.

The alliance aims to overcome key technological hurdles, particularly in CPO, and ensure that Taiwan retains control of the silicon photonics supply chain, it said.

articles.description: AI Symposium Asks: Will Technology Bring an Apocalypse or a Renaissance? Benedictine College
articles.description_html: AI Symposium Asks: Will Technology Bring an Apocalypse or a Renaissance?  Benedictine College
articles.article_title: AI Symposium Asks: Will Technology Bring an Apocalypse or a Renaissance?
articles.heading: AI Symposium Asks: Will Technology Bring an Apocalypse or a Renaissance?
articles.summary: We have to get AI right in order to Transform Culture in America, said keynote speakers.
articles.content:
AI Symposium Asks: Will Technology Bring an Apocalypse or a Renaissance?
“Be very afraid,” or “Be not afraid”?
In the face of the artificial intelligence revolution, those were the options posed at the Symposium on Transforming Culture at Benedictine College in Atchison, Kansas, on September 4-5.
The Symposium, an annual conference at the college, gathers scholars, field professionals, religious, clergy, and students for fellowship and conversation. The Symposium took place partially in the new classically designed Moritz Library in D’Aniello Hall. Architect Eric Bootsma, who played a role in its design, was one of the Symposium speakers and provided explanations of the structure. The topic of AI was explored by more than 65 presenters, including both critics of its dehumanizing effects and those advocating ways to use it responsibly.
The words of the recently deceased Christian poet Wendell Berry put it best:
“It is easy for me to imagine that the next great division of the world will be between people who wish to live as creatures and people who wish to live as machines.”
Kristen Collier: Human Medicine
Kristen M. Collier M.D. (above), one of three keynote speakers at the conference, quoted Berry as part of her presentation, “AI and the Future of Medicine.”
“My patients are very worried by our increasing technological paradigm. They already feel dehumanized by it,” said Collier, a family practitioner and associate professor at the University of Michigan Medical School.
The Symposium was cosponsored by Benedictine College’s Center for Technology and Human Dignity promoting Catholic digital and biomedical ethics.
“I went into medicine to take care of people. Not diseases, not pathologies, but human beings who are someone’s mother, friend, or lover,” said Collier. “These things are taking place inside someone who has inviolable dignity and inherent worth.”
She added, “This is the time for Benedictine College and others to build the medical system that respects the human person.”
Marla Golden, the founding dean of Benedictine College’s proposed School of Osteopathic Medicine was in attendance.
Golden told the Symposium attendees, “We are building the school [Dr. Collier] is calling for. And we intentionally decided that a portion of our first-year curriculum would leave machines and electronics out so that students can encounter others fully.”
Paul Scherz: Mentors, Not Chatbots
A second keynote speaker, Notre Dame theologian Paul Scherz, spoke about the need for personal, human mentorship and argued that AI chatbots can’t do what human beings do.
“Stoics connected virtue with an art of living,” he said, explaining how mentorship once meant a deep immersion. Mentees “spent time with an illustrious citizen, saw when he woke, ate, bathed, etc. This would teach them how to live well and wisely. These aspects of embodied life all emerge out of the details of living.”
He said that AI can imitate technique, but it cannot offer the embodied expression of important truths — and it can’t do one other thing.
“One difficult skill ancients in Rome and Greece had to learn was parrhesia — bold and risky truth telling,” he said. The willingness to speak truth to power led to the deaths of several great philosophers.
But in the case of chatbots, “AI is not a person, thus it cannot be a bearer of responsibility.” Worse, he said, AI is designed by corporations that know that risky truth telling would make their products unpopular.
Matthew Sanders: Two Futures
The final speaker was Matthew Sanders of Longbeard, who has been digitizing magisterial teachings to make them part of the data sets AI uses to answer questions. His products include Magisterium AI, Vulgate AI, and Ephrem.
He said this calendar year has been significant for AI because this was the year “the machines stopped being a consultant and became a ‘colleague.’” He said the rapid rise of AI will continue and that “what is coming will be 10 times bigger than the Industrial Revolution and arrive maybe 10 times faster.”
He worried that, since in its bare essentials, “AI is electricity turned into ‘intelligence’” in the United States, our ambitions exceed our energy supply, while “China generates twice the energy it needs.”
He painted a portrait of two possible futures. One is a “dark path” that keeps to the status quo, in which, as Pope Leo XIV pointed out in Magnifica Humanitas, “computational resources and regulatory influence remain in the hands of a few.” At the end of that path is a world where human beings are subservient to the technocratic paradigm.
The other is a “golden future” in which households have their own AI technology and its proper use allows Catholics to take the lead in building community, pursue craftsmanship, and lead more human lives.
He summed up:
“We are the generation posted at the fork, before the defaults harden into destiny. The machines won’t decide what we do. Do not let the algorithm write your story. Use technology wisely … don’t let technology use you.”
A Needed Conversation
Kansas City, Kansas, Archbishop Emeritus Joseph Naumann ended the Symposium by praying for the fully human future to prevail.
Benedictine College theologian Matthew Muller organized the event around the theme “The Church in an Algorithmic Age” in hopes of fostering the kind of robust dialogue the speakers brought.
“We expect these conversations to include a fair share of debate and discussion,” he said. “Our presenters come from a variety of disciplines and professional fields. Algorithms and artificial intelligence impact all of these.”
Benedictine College President Stephen D. Minnis said the Symposium puts Benedictine College in step with Pope Leo XIV’s efforts to address the challenges posed by artificial intelligence.
“This Symposium is great example of our mission of educating within a community of faith and scholarship,” he said. “It is only through mastering these new technologies, rather than being mastered by them, that our students will help Transform Culture in America.”

“Be very afraid,” or “Be not afraid”?

In the face of the artificial intelligence revolution, those were the options posed at the Symposium on Transforming Culture at Benedictine College in Atchison, Kansas, on September 4-5.

The Symposium, an annual conference at the college, gathers scholars, field professionals, religious, clergy, and students for fellowship and conversation. The Symposium took place partially in the new classically designed Moritz Library in D’Aniello Hall. Architect Eric Bootsma, who played a role in its design, was one of the Symposium speakers and provided explanations of the structure. The topic of AI was explored by more than 65 presenters, including both critics of its dehumanizing effects and those advocating ways to use it responsibly.

The words of the recently deceased Christian poet Wendell Berry put it best:

“It is easy for me to imagine that the next great division of the world will be between people who wish to live as creatures and people who wish to live as machines.”

Kristen Collier: Human Medicine

Kristen M. Collier M.D. (above), one of three keynote speakers at the conference, quoted Berry as part of her presentation, “AI and the Future of Medicine.”

“My patients are very worried by our increasing technological paradigm. They already feel dehumanized by it,” said Collier, a family practitioner and associate professor at the University of Michigan Medical School.

The Symposium was cosponsored by Benedictine College’s Center for Technology and Human Dignity promoting Catholic digital and biomedical ethics.

“I went into medicine to take care of people. Not diseases, not pathologies, but human beings who are someone’s mother, friend, or lover,” said Collier. “These things are taking place inside someone who has inviolable dignity and inherent worth.”

She added, “This is the time for Benedictine College and others to build the medical system that respects the human person.”

Marla Golden, the founding dean of Benedictine College’s proposed School of Osteopathic Medicine was in attendance.

Golden told the Symposium attendees, “We are building the school [Dr. Collier] is calling for. And we intentionally decided that a portion of our first-year curriculum would leave machines and electronics out so that students can encounter others fully.”

Paul Scherz: Mentors, Not Chatbots

A second keynote speaker, Notre Dame theologian Paul Scherz, spoke about the need for personal, human mentorship and argued that AI chatbots can’t do what human beings do.

“Stoics connected virtue with an art of living,” he said, explaining how mentorship once meant a deep immersion. Mentees “spent time with an illustrious citizen, saw when he woke, ate, bathed, etc. This would teach them how to live well and wisely. These aspects of embodied life all emerge out of the details of living.”

He said that AI can imitate technique, but it cannot offer the embodied expression of important truths — and it can’t do one other thing.

“One difficult skill ancients in Rome and Greece had to learn was parrhesia — bold and risky truth telling,” he said. The willingness to speak truth to power led to the deaths of several great philosophers.

But in the case of chatbots, “AI is not a person, thus it cannot be a bearer of responsibility.” Worse, he said, AI is designed by corporations that know that risky truth telling would make their products unpopular.

Matthew Sanders: Two Futures

The final speaker was Matthew Sanders of Longbeard, who has been digitizing magisterial teachings to make them part of the data sets AI uses to answer questions. His products include Magisterium AI, Vulgate AI, and Ephrem.

He said this calendar year has been significant for AI because this was the year “the machines stopped being a consultant and became a ‘colleague.’” He said the rapid rise of AI will continue and that “what is coming will be 10 times bigger than the Industrial Revolution and arrive maybe 10 times faster.”

He worried that, since in its bare essentials, “AI is electricity turned into ‘intelligence’” in the United States, our ambitions exceed our energy supply, while “China generates twice the energy it needs.”

He painted a portrait of two possible futures. One is a “dark path” that keeps to the status quo, in which, as Pope Leo XIV pointed out in Magnifica Humanitas, “computational resources and regulatory influence remain in the hands of a few.” At the end of that path is a world where human beings are subservient to the technocratic paradigm.

The other is a “golden future” in which households have their own AI technology and its proper use allows Catholics to take the lead in building community, pursue craftsmanship, and lead more human lives.

He summed up:

“We are the generation posted at the fork, before the defaults harden into destiny. The machines won’t decide what we do. Do not let the algorithm write your story. Use technology wisely … don’t let technology use you.”

A Needed Conversation

Kansas City, Kansas, Archbishop Emeritus Joseph Naumann ended the Symposium by praying for the fully human future to prevail.

Benedictine College theologian Matthew Muller organized the event around the theme “The Church in an Algorithmic Age” in hopes of fostering the kind of robust dialogue the speakers brought.

“We expect these conversations to include a fair share of debate and discussion,” he said. “Our presenters come from a variety of disciplines and professional fields. Algorithms and artificial intelligence impact all of these.”

Benedictine College President Stephen D. Minnis said the Symposium puts Benedictine College in step with Pope Leo XIV’s efforts to address the challenges posed by artificial intelligence.

“This Symposium is great example of our mission of educating within a community of faith and scholarship,” he said. “It is only through mastering these new technologies, rather than being mastered by them, that our students will help Transform Culture in America.”

articles.content:
SPS Technologies in Abington reaches settlement following class-action lawsuit over 2025 fire
If approved by a court, affected parties within a 1-mile radius of the former facility at 301 Highland Ave. could be eligible to receive cash payments.
From Delco to Chesco and Montco to Bucks, what about life in Philly’s suburbs do you want WHYY News to cover? Let us know!
SPS Technologies and its parent company Precision Castparts Corp. reached a settlement in a class-action lawsuit filed after a 2025 four-alarm fire at their plant in Abington Township, according to a Friday release.
If approved by a court, affected business owners, employees of impacted businesses and residents within a 1-mile radius of the former facility at 301 Highland Ave. could be eligible to receive cash payments.
The payments could cover unreimbursed business losses of up to $5,000, unreimbursed property damage losses of up to $300 and unreimbursed hourly wage losses of up to $200.
To be eligible for a cash payment, settlement class members must fill out a claim form by Dec. 3. The court will hold a hearing on May 25, 2027, to decide whether to approve the settlement.
What happened to the SPS Technologies facility — and when could it return?
The Standard Press Steel Company was first incorporated in 1903 and bought the parcel of land from Wharton Switch Works in 1920. In 1978, the company changed its name to SPS Technologies. Precision Castparts Corp. acquired SPS Technologies in 2003.
Over the years, the aerospace manufacturing plant in Abington became one of the nation’s key producers of high-tolerance fasteners and parts used in U.S. military vehicles.
A fire broke out inside the facility on the evening of Feb. 17, 2025. According to the company, the sprinklers were inoperable due to maintenance, but “alternative fire prevention protocols” were in place. Fire crews rushed to the scene, but the inferno raged beyond control.
By morning, officials ordered evacuations and school closures. No one was injured — but the fire burned for days. It took 68 fire crews from Abington, Cheltenham, Jenkintown and beyond to finally extinguish the blaze on Feb. 22, 2025.
More than 80% of the 600,000-square-foot building was left either charred or compromised. SPS Technologies began demolishing the facility in May 2025. The plant, which was a major source of local jobs, laid off 250 employees.
In September 2025, SPS Technologies unveiled plans to construct a smaller, two-story, 350,000-square-foot facility on the same property.

During a recent lunch break, Jill Sennett saw something so unappetizing she had to share it with her 26,000 X followers: Artificial intelligence-generated menu images from a Jamaican barbecue pop-up restaurant in which the meats looked like leather belts crawling with tiny beetles.
The images were reshared by more than 500 people who similarly expressed their disgust. Eating is “such an essential human experience”, said Sennett, a 37-year-old nurse in Denver. “I think it’s a bad cultural thing that restaurants are converting to these horrific, uncanny food images that are unappetizing.”
Still, Sennett ordered chicken and macaroni and cheese. It was one of her only lunch options, and she had eaten there before.
Increasingly, consumers are encountering AI-generated images of food on restaurant menus or marketing material. Diners like Sennett say the images are unappealing and misleading, while restaurants say they’re trying to cut costs at a time when food and labor prices are high, so profit margins are slim.
A 2026 report from the National Restaurant Association found 26% of restaurant operators use AI to help with marketing, inventory management, employee scheduling, optimizing menus and taking orders.
But consumer backlash to the technology can be swift and fierce, especially in the Bay Area, a hotbed for AI development. When San Francisco cafe Grind & Unwind put up a sign depicting menu options that locals quickly identified as AI-generated, vandals graffitied the storefront with a word cafe owner Lyndsey Lozano deciphered as “seriously”. In a Reddit post titled “Yum, slop”, commenters compared the images of bread to textures like reptile skin and a loofah.
Lozano told SFGate in July that the response was “not what we were expecting”, and that the signage was only meant to be temporary. Lozano and her husband took down the AI signage, and spent an estimated $700 to paint over the graffiti, according to SFGate. Lozano did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
Sennett takes some pleasure in AI fumbling food pictures so badly. “It can do uncanny videos of celebrities, but it can’t depict a hamburger,” Sennett said. “I hope it stays that way, honestly, and we can shame [restaurants] into stopping.”
The manager of Jamaican Jerk and Barbecue Restaurant, the Denver restaurant that hosted a pop-up at Sennett’s hospital, confirmed that he had used ChatGPT for the menu images instead of paying a graphic designer as he does for his bricks-and-mortar location.
“We decided we would design something that was eye-catching,” he said, declining to give his name for publication. “Restaurant people are trying to be cost-effective.”
As norms for AI in advertising are still being established, some restaurant industry professionals are thinking critically about when AI might be advantageous or detrimental to their businesses. Hunter Lewis, editor in chief of Food and Wine magazine, said he’s seeing restaurants grow as they begin to automate parts of their back-end operations. But use of the technology should be invisible to diners, as AI images can be “a real turnoff”, Lewis noted
“The American dining public is smart,” he said. “They know what they want, and they know what is real.”
Some restaurants are going viral for proclaiming they will never use AI and instead posting hand-drawn images of their burgers on social media. When Wyoming restaurant Chugwater Soda Fountain shared its pledge, written on a piece of cardboard, the Instagram post got over 200,000 likes. Some commenters celebrated the homespun authenticity, while others pointed out the irony of posting the message on an AI-powered platform.
Often the thing AI gets wrong is the food’s texture, said Jamie Soja, a professional photographer in the Bay Area who’s shot images for restaurant marketing and for food-delivery services.
“The color and texture and the ingredients look kind of off in the way that they’re arranged,” Soja said, adding that the lighting can also look unnatural.
Tech companies, including food-delivery app DoorDash, are infusing AI into their platforms, intensifying the debate of AI-made menus. DoorDash offers AI photo tools “to improve the presentation of an existing image of a dish,” by adjusting the lighting, color or background, the company said in an emailed statement. The company’s policies prohibit eateries from creating or altering misleading images of menu items. DoorDash says it reviews menu images to ensure compliance.
A cursory search showed some images marked with DoorDash’s “AI-enhanced” label, which is automatically applied when a restaurant uses its AI editing tool. Still, it can be hard to determine whether images are AI-generated or simply overedited, even for a professional photographer like Soja.
Researchers are starting to study how seeing AI images of food affects consumers’ opinions and appetites. In a 2024 study Charles Spence, a University of Oxford professor of experimental psychology, found consumers generally preferred AI-generated food images when they didn’t know they were made by a machine. After that disclosure, however, diners found the images less appealing.
He found bots alter food in predictable ways: AI often adds fat, like butter on mashed potatoes, when prompted to make food images look more appealing. Spence worries that such AI images might subconsciously nudge diners and chefs toward larger portions with higher fat content.
AI images can leave a bad taste in consumers’ mouths, particularly those who work with the technology day in and day out. When Brandon Hill, CEO of a design and marketing agency in San Francisco, walked by Bella Cafe downtown recently, he was so put off by its AI images that he snapped a photo and shared it with his over 86,000 X followers with a Japanese caption. “Even in San Francisco … places are starting to use generative AI for menu images. But they don’t look all that appetizing, you know,” reads X’s English translation of the post.
AI images also make him “skeptical of what the actual meals will look like,” he said.
Despite Hill’s post, Nila Norero Salvatore, the owner of Bella Cafe, said she personally hasn’t received any complaints about the ChatGPT-designed signs on the street or those advertising the breakfast menu inside her restaurant, both of which include images of the food. The 65-year-old said she and her husband are “old-fashioned,” adding that experimenting with AI is “fun” and “new for us.” She also uses ChatGPT to help write reference letters for workers and craft the cafe’s employee handbook.
In addition to saving money on graphic design, Norero Salvatore likes how the AI images look.
“I think it’s a great way of advertising our products, even though sometimes [people] say AI isn’t effective or it’s not natural,” she said.

articles.title: This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years
articles.description: This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years The Atlantic
articles.description_html: This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years  The Atlantic
articles.article_title: This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years
articles.heading: This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years
articles.summary: The $70 Xteink X3 puts Silicon Valley to shame.
articles.content:
This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years
The $70 Xteink X3 puts Silicon Valley to shame.
No matter how you read it, The Power Broker is a serious undertaking. The paperback weighs as much as a brick; to avoid lugging around all 1,344 pages, people have cut it apart at the spine and chunked it into sections. Others have organized in-person Power Broker marathon readings that run continuously for three full days. I decided to try something else.
Over the past several weeks, I’ve spent 10 hours paging through Robert Caro’s masterpiece on an e-reader the size of a credit card. It’s magnetic, and small enough to attach to the back of my iPhone without adding any real bulk to my pocket. (Yes, this does mean that I have a screen on the back of another screen.) It’s called the Xteink X3, and at a glance, it looks like a cheap gimmick: more electronic junk made by unknown brands and sold on Temu and TikTok Shop—the kind of thing influencers are always hawking. (Can I interest you in a programmable LED hat for $11.60? Or how about $20 AirPod look-alikes made by “Fhumsh”?)
In a sense, it is that. Xteink sounds less like a real brand name than the kind of garbled text you’ll find in AI-slop memes. (Speaking of which, the official website of the China-based company is full of AI-generated photos of people posing with the device.) And indeed, since the X3’s release on Amazon in May, TikTokers and YouTubers have raved about how the device is a steal and you should buy it right now—just click the link in bio.
And so I did. On Amazon, the X3 is $69 and tops the “hot new releases” list for e-readers, beating out a slew of Kindles. In person, the Xteink is many things: plasticky. Flawed. Finicky. Nevertheless, it is the single best piece of technology that I have purchased in years. In the two months before getting this cartoonishly tiny e-reader, I finished only one book. In one month with the X3, I read three books without even really trying—and my iPhone’s average daily screen time dipped by 25 minutes.
The X3 is great because of its size, not in spite of it. (For once, “fun-size” actually lives up to the billing.) Because this is such a runt of a device, you can stick it to your phone and have an e-reader in your pocket at all times. As a result, I’ve found myself reading on my morning commute, in line at a museum, even while waiting through Netflix ads. The display on my Xteink may be roughly half the size of the smallest Kindle, but the text is big enough to easily read. Even after three straight hours of inching through The Power Broker, my eyes weren’t strained.
The device’s size actually helped me develop a different relationship to reading altogether: Because each “page” on the Xteink amounts to just a paragraph or two—and sometimes less—I’m compelled to finish it. And now that I’m onto the next page, I might as well finish that one too. A YouTuber who recently reviewed the Xteink had the same experience—she referred to the uniquely addictive experience of using the device as the “TikTokification of reading.” I know how terrifying that sounds, but consider the outcome: Whenever there’s even a couple of minutes of free time, I now have a healthy alternative to doomscrolling on Instagram. I don’t even have to put my phone down. Flip over the Bad Screen and fire up the Good Screen.
For all of its charm, the Xteink is a pretty basic piece of hardware. For $70, you get what you pay for. Other popular e-readers now come with AI-powered recaps, high-definition displays, and Android operating systems. Meanwhile, the Xteink has no touch screen, color display, or backlight for reading in the dark. (Xteink recently launched the X4 Pro, a slightly larger and more expensive model that has a reading light and a touch screen.) Just reading a book on the device isn’t necessarily seamless: The preloaded software is horrific and can’t even display book covers or properly format some text. Unlike with a Kindle, you can’t port over books from Amazon with one click.
In spite of itself, the Xteink X3, in all of its 3.7 inches of glory, has become a viral hit. Online, people have posted photos of their Xteink on trips to the Austrian mountains or the Aegean Sea; one anesthesiologist says he tucks it into his scrubs. People are mounting the Xteink X3 to their kitchen hood to display recipes and are making all sorts of bespoke accessories, including 3-D-printed reading lights and a case that looks like a gun (I’m serious). Fans have built their own open-source firmware, Crosspoint, that considerably upgrades the device. The version I downloaded displays reading stats and an array of fonts, and it lets me screenshot pages as I read. Late last month, Crosspoint added the ability to access books on Libby, the popular library ebook app.
The best thing about the Xteink is not any one feature. It’s that this tiny e-reader is fun in a way so few gadgets are anymore. Despite all our advances, the consumer-electronics landscape of 2026 is predictable and banal. Our laptops, smartphones, and tablets are thinner and more powerful than ever, but that feels like a weak substitute for innovation. Next week, Apple is poised to launch one of its most hyped products in years: a folding iPhone. But even folding smartphones are old news; Samsung released its version in 2019. After shelling out hundreds or thousands of dollars for a new gadget, you might still have to pay for subscriptions and endure annoying ads. Sometimes, your purchases aren’t even really yours. Amazon recently removed the ability to download ebooks you already own and transfer them to non-Kindle devices.
In other words, we need more gadgets like the Xteink: cheap, simple, and customizable. With few exceptions, these products are now coming out of China. Neck fans from brands such as JisuLife and Civpower have become sensations for helping people endure the summer heat. Anker’s portable projectors and earbuds are both Wirecutter-recommended. Silicon Valley has left a gaping hole in the gadgets markets, and Americans are more than willing to look elsewhere.

articles.title: I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI
articles.description: I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI The Guardian
articles.description_html: I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI  The Guardian
articles.article_title: I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI
articles.heading: I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI
articles.summary: A Dr Seuss-style story written in seconds alerted me to the power – and perils – of the technology. But how can children embrace it without forgetting core skills?
articles.content:
When I was growing up, my dad and I often talked about a story we wanted to write together. It was called “The Day Nobody Went to Disneyland”. One day, the story goes, the weather is so perfect that everyone in the world decides to stay away from Disneyland because they expect it to be far too busy. But my dad, who has the same thought as them, sees the disappointment on my face that morning – and decides to risk it. We set off. And when we arrive, the park is completely empty. Nobody else was brave enough to visit. We have everything – the rides, shows, food – to ourselves.
I loved the idea of writing that story. But, as so often happens, we were too busy to do anything about it. Life ran away from us. I grew up, and we both forgot about it.
Thirty years later, I was at my parents’ for dinner with my own children (eight, five and two). For some reason, the idea popped into my mind again. I told my oldest about it – and she wanted to hear the full thing. We turned to ChatGPT, gave it the vague outline and asked it to have a go at writing the story in the style of Dr Seuss (one of our favourites). Within a few seconds, we had it. She read it out – and we laughed.
Of course, what this AI generated wasn’t perfect. A few lines didn’t quite make sense; a few Americanisms had slipped in (“sneakers”, “cinnamon buns”). But that night on the sofa we had great fun together tweaking the prompts, refining the story, adding more scenes, working with this strange new creative partner to do something that had escaped my grasp for decades.
For the last 15 years, I have been exploring the impact of AI on work and society. But becoming a dad of three small people has made these disruptions far more personal: it is clear that their future is going to look wildly different from my past.
For my wife, that realisation really sunk in a few weeks ago, on a journey to her parents’ in Suffolk. Three children, confined in a car, stuttering along the A12, is a combustible setup. So we were thrilled to find a rare podcast that everyone miraculously enjoyed: History’s Not Boring, a series of 15-minute bursts of conversation, on a kaleidoscope of subjects, narrated by two children.
As we listened, we started to speculate in the car about who these whiz-kids might be. Where were they from? How were they selected? How did they juggle this job with school? Eventually, I went to the website to find out. All our answers were wrong. The kids did not, in fact, exist. The entire podcast seemed to be generated by AI. None of us had realised.
It was a strange moment, learning that people we had grown fond of were not actually people at all. It was also remarkable that AI could create such high-quality educational content. But for my wife, a podcast and documentary maker, it was an unsettling moment as well: here was something that would have taken her and a talented team several days to make, and now it was being done without people.
My work on AI has taken me to boardrooms and conference halls, classrooms and government buildings. But wherever I go, one question is now asked more than any other: what should my children do?
Today, we are floundering. Teachers worry that the way they teach no longer seems to work. Parents, watching their children use AI to solve problems and answer questions, wonder what they really know. Employers doubt whether traditional educational achievements, awarded in time-honoured ways – coursework, exams, assessments – are still a useful guide to what young people can do.
Yet reacting to these new technologies by putting barriers up, as many instinctively want to do – banning, admonishing, punishing – just cannot be right. To begin with, this is the water in which the next generation will swim: we are letting them down if we prepare them for the world that we grew up in, not the one they will actually inhabit.
How often, for instance, have you heard people accuse students of cheating if they use AI to help them with their work? But at what point are we cheating them by failing to overhaul the way we are educating them? If AI is making education “too easy” for young people, at what point does the burden shift on to us, the adults, to make their education more testing, to push them on, to stretch them?
More importantly, this dismissiveness of AI is also unimaginative. It stops us appreciating the astounding possibilities AI could create for the next generation as well. Of course there are risks. But at the same time, if we use this technology wisely, what difficult ideas might the next generation now grasp, ones that were beyond us when we were in their shoes? What hard problems might they now solve, ones that once required years of training and experience – if they were solvable at all?
Forget future-proofing skills
A big part of the challenge of AI is that our traditional response to technological disruption in the working world – the idea of “future-proofing” people – no longer works. In 2013, the then prime minister David Cameron announced that England would become the first place in the world where all children in primary and secondary schools would learn to code. This, in the words of education secretary Michael Gove, would “equip every child with the computing skills they need to succeed in the 21st century”.
The idea seemed bold and clever: in the years that followed, it was hard to find an advanced country that did not follow our example.
Fast-forward to today. What does it turn out that the latest AI systems, such as ChatGPT and Claude, are best at doing? Writing code. In January 2026, Anthropic reported that 90% of the code for Claude Code – their AI-powered coding assistant – was itself written by AI. Skills that were meant to protect kids from technological disruption for their entire lives were largely redundant before they had even left school.
For politicians and policymakers, it is tempting to dismiss the coding saga as an unfortunate blip. But this is a mistake. The reason they slipped up was because they had believed in the idea of “future-proof” skills, the thought that there exists some valuable set of skills that AI will not be able to do for some time – and that by thinking deeply enough about the future, we can accurately identify them.
The truth is that we know only two things about what lies ahead. One is that it will be full of technologies that are far more capable than today. And the other is that we know little else. But rather than attempting to resolve this uncertainty, we have to accept it and instead ask a different question: how do we prepare the next generation to flourish in a future that we actually know surprisingly little about?
Get back to basics
The first step is to get back to basics. Since 2009, literacy and numeracy have been falling among young people around the world, according to the OECD’s programme for international student assessment (Pisa); the same holds true for adults. In itself, this is worrying. But given the uncertainty that we face about the future, these trends are a disaster.
Why such a calamity? To begin with, while it might be hard to say precisely which more advanced skills will turn out to be most valuable in the future – creativity, judgment, something else – they will rely in some way on these basic skills. They are the foundations for everything else.
What’s more, AI systems are far from flawless. They make mistakes, often on simple problems; they hallucinate, providing confident and plausible answers that are completely made up. They are, as the computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton put it, “idiot savants”. So, with both those reasons in mind, we should be focusing intensely on teaching literacy and numeracy, even if AI does them better, as it increasingly seems to do. Getting back to basics is what an economist would call a “no-regrets” strategy – we will never regret improving these basic skills, however the future turns out to be.

It was enormous, forensic – and is now largely forgotten. But it may turn out to be the most important document written for thinking about the future of education, because of its response to the electronic calculator.
It is fascinating to read Cockcroft’s report and discover how the challenges of the calculator back then were so similar to the ones we face with AI today – from the fear that it would undermine “basic skills” to the intimidation many felt at the complexity of this strange new technology (“Some … had been discouraged by the large number of figures which had appeared after the decimal point”).
Cockcroft was realistic: “all candidates”, he expected, “will have access to a calculator by 1985”. Thirty years later, I was at my parents’ for dinner with my own children (eight, five and two). For some reason, the idea popped into my mind again. She read it out – and we laughed.

articles.title: Labor movement gaining ground in tech
articles.description: Labor movement gaining ground in tech sfexaminer.com
articles.description_html: Labor movement gaining ground in tech  sfexaminer.com
articles.article_title: Labor movement gaining ground in tech
articles.heading: Tech workers start to see promise in unions
articles.summary: The industry has resisted organizing for decades, but activists see new opportunity.
articles.content:
Lucas said he’s been in the Bay Area working in the tech industry for 10 years — primarily at startups, but also at one of the big tech companies. He’s worked as a software engineer and managed small teams. Currently, he works for a 500-person company that makes software for biologists.
So far, so normal in Silicon Valley.
But Lucas’ present ambition is a bit different from many of his tech-industry peers, past and present. He isn’t aiming to found his own unicorn or invent some new, mega-popular product or service.
Instead, he’s working to form a union at his company and trying to help other tech workers who have similar ideas.
Lucas, who asked not to use his real name for fear of putting his job at risk, said he sees the organizing efforts as a way for workers like himself to build power, form a community, have more say over their jobs and working conditions — and counter the influence of billionaire tech CEOs and venture capitalists.
“I want the tech industry to serve the community around me,” Lucas said.
“There’s a lot of folks that feel that way,” he said.
California is one of the most union-friendly states in the nation, and the San Francisco region is one of the most unionized metro areas in the state. Despite that, labor organizers have never made many inroads in the tech industry; exceedingly few tech workers are represented by unions or have even been involved in organizing efforts.
Labor activists such as Lucas say they believe the tide is turning. Support for unions among the American public is at its highest level in about 60 years, according to Gallup. Younger workers, which make up much of the tech industry’s ranks, are particularly pro-union.
Meanwhile, the massive layoffs of recent years, the wholesale moves by companies to push artificial-intelligence tools into the workplace and their products, and a growing sense of precarity and powerlessness have spurred some tech workers to look into organizing in their industry, Lucas and other activists say. So, too, have the increasingly close ties between certain companies and the military.
“Most of the people that we get in touch with find us right now, rather than us finding them,” said Joshua Carroll, one of the leaders of the Bay Area chapter of the Tech Workers Coalition, a grassroots group trying to raise awareness of unions among industry workers and help with organizing efforts.
“People are very happy to find out they’re not alone,” said Carroll, a product manager at Google Cloud.
Union efforts and labor activism in the tech industry date back to at least the mid-1970s, when workers at IBM started organizing themselves. Such activity has ebbed and flowed over the years, typically rising amid economic downturns or uncertainty such as the dot-com bust or the Great Recession, said Ron Hira, a political-science professor at Howard University who focuses on labor issues and policies.
But outside of the digital publishing industry, which has seen a slew of unions, few of those efforts succeeded in forming unions that were able to collectively bargain on behalf of workers.
The IBM effort, for example, existed for decades as a member organization that represented workers and pressured management, but it never sought or formed a bargaining unit that was recognized by the company or the National Labor Relations Board. It shut down in 2016 in the wake of job cuts at the company.
Generally speaking, it’s hard to form a recognized union in this country, labor experts say. Companies often fight organizing efforts and frequently retaliate against organizers. Even without that opposition, it can take years to build enough support to win a majority vote within a discrete group of workers.
As union membership has dwindled in the country— compared with its peak in the middle of the last century — fewer people are growing up in union households or know people who are in unions, Hira said. Labor representatives are rarely on TV, he said.
“If you’re not exposed to them, you’re not even thinking that way,” Hira said.
The tech industry has been particularly tough for the labor movement to crack. Even within antiunion corporate America, the tech industry has fought particularly hard against organizing efforts.
But there are plenty of other reasons for the industry’s dearth of unions, labor experts say. Tech jobs have tended to be high paying, with lots of benefits and stock-based compensation offering a chance for even bigger paydays.

That said, things have started to change over the past 10 years.

articles.title: Opinion | The one thing parents agree on about technology in schools: Limit AI.

articles.article_title: Opinion | The one thing parents agree on about technology in schools: Limit AI.
articles.heading: The one thing parents agree on about technology in schools: Limit AI.
articles.summary: Silicon Valley wanted to 'move fast and break things.' Families have a problem with that.
articles.content:
On Wednesday, New York City banned the use of artificial intelligence in its public elementary and middle schools, which count 600,000 children as students. But millions of American children this fall will open school-issued laptops with an artificial intelligence assistant already installed, ready to draft essays, solve math homework problems and polish slide presentations. In most places, no parent was consulted. No classroom teacher asked for it. The decision was made in Silicon Valley — by people who will never meet these kids or anyone else in the communities raising them.
Technology is transforming our nation’s classrooms at an unprecedented pace. A study published by the Rand Corporation last year found that more than half of middle and high schoolers now use AI for school — an increase of 15 percentage points in just the past two years. Yet less than half of school principals say their school or district has any policy on the use of AI at all.
Families are not happy. On behalf of my organization, the Century Foundation, Morning Consult conducted a survey of 2,000 voters. The poll asked about six developments in classroom technology, ranging from students using AI tools to complete assignments without learning, to private companies collecting and profiting from students’ data. In all six cases, at least 80% of Americans said they are concerned.
Growing evidence backs the public’s instincts. Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found students who rely heavily on large language models like ChatGPT accumulate “cognitive debt,” outsourcing thinking before they have developed the underlying capacity for it. A separate analysis of AI use across 1,300 school districts revealed that roughly 1 in 5 student interactions with these tools involved cheating, self-harm, bullying or other troubling behavior.
Big Tech talks publicly about AI as an opportunity to enhance learning and support educators. But behind closed doors, many executives view schools as a trove of personal data just waiting to be mined. This year, one of the country’s largest ed-tech companies paid $17 million to settle claims that its college planning software — which many students were required to use — secretly tracked their data, including private messages to school counselors, and shared it with third-party advertising firms.
In Washington, President Donald Trump has dismissed these risks and made AI adoption a centerpiece of his education agenda. He signed an executive order directing the Education Department to prioritize AI funding in its grant programs; the White House gathered more than 60 tech companies to pledge AI tools for classrooms (in addition to welcoming teacher-robots into the East Wing); and the administration shuttered the Office of Educational Technology, the only federal office whose job was helping schools use AI tools responsibly.
Congress has done little better. In June, the House of Representatives passed a children’s online safety bill only after gutting the the Senate-passed version’s “duty of care” provision, which would require platforms to be designed safely by default so their engagement-maximizing features don’t foreseeably harm kids. Meanwhile, neither major political party has offered a comprehensive national plan for governing AI in K-12 education.

The one thing parents agree on about technology in schools: Limit AI.
On Wednesday, New York City banned the use of artificial intelligence in its public elementary and middle schools, which count 600,000 children as students. Families are not happy. On behalf of my organization, the Century Foundation, Morning Consult conducted a survey of 2,000 voters. The poll asked about six developments in classroom technology, ranging from students using AI tools to complete assignments without learning, to private companies collecting and profiting from students' data. In all six cases, at least 80% of Americans said they are concerned.
Growing evidence backs the public's instincts. Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found students who rely heavily on large language models like ChatGPT accumulate "cognitive debt," outsourcing thinking before they have developed the underlying capacity for it. A separate analysis of AI use across 1,300 school districts revealed that roughly 1 in 5 student interactions with these tools involved cheating, self-harm, bullying or other troubling behavior.
Big Tech talks publicly about AI as an opportunity to enhance learning and support educators. But behind closed doors, many executives view schools as a trove of personal data just waiting to be mined. This year, one of the country's largest ed-tech companies paid $17 million to settle claims that its college planning software — which many students were required to use — secretly tracked their data, including private messages to school counselors, and shared it with third-party advertising firms.
In Washington, President Donald Trump has dismissed these risks and made AI adoption a centerpiece of his education agenda. He signed an executive order directing the Education Department to prioritize AI funding in its grant programs; the White House gathered more than 60 tech companies to pledge AI tools for classrooms (in addition to welcoming teacher-robots into the East Wing); and the administration shuttered the Office of Educational Technology, the only federal office whose job was helping schools use AI tools responsibly.

Congress has done little better. In June, the House of Representatives passed a children's online safety bill only after gutting the the Senate-passed version's "duty of care" provision, which would require platforms to be designed safely by default so their engagement-maximizing features don't foreseeably harm kids. Meanwhile, neither major political party has offered a comprehensive national plan for governing AI in K-12 education.
While too many lawmakers race to embrace AI in schools, families are increasingly asking a more basic question: Shouldn't we figure out the rules before we hand our kids over to unregulated technology?
The Century Foundation's polling shows a resounding yes. Almost 4 in 5 Americans want clear government standards governing AI in schools. Nearly half (49%) go further and say AI in classrooms should be kept to a minimum. Remarkably, Republicans are more likely to support both new government rules and keeping AI use to a minimum (at 54%, compared with 47% of Democrats). Less than a quarter of voters (23%) favor the current hands-off approach.
None of this means schools should reject new technologies. For example, the American Federation of Teachers recently built a national academy — alongside some of the very companies making these tools — to train teachers to use AI wisely, because educators should master this technology rather than be mastered by it. Enact a kids' online safety bill with a "duty of care" provision so the burden of proof sits with billion-dollar companies, not 10-year-olds. Keep screens and AI chatbots out of the earliest grades, where the developmental risks are the greatest, and give educators and parents a genuine seat at the table before districts adopt new technologies. Finally, invest in what families actually want: smaller classes, safe schools and well-paid educators. It is still true that children learn best from humans — not because we're nostalgic for some pre-AI era, but because decades of learning science says so.
For years, the tech industry's motto was "move fast and break things." These companies have now moved into the nation's classrooms at record speed. The question is no longer whether AI will be part of our children's education — it is who decides how, on what evidence and in whose interest. Americans have given their answer: Public schools belong to us, not Silicon Valley.

It is still true that children learn best from humans — not because we're nostalgic for some pre-AI era, but because decades of learning science says so.

For years, the tech industry's motto was "move fast and break things." These companies have now moved into the nation's classrooms at record speed. The question is no longer whether AI will be part of our children's education — it is who decides how, on what evidence and in whose interest. Americans have given their answer: Public schools belong to us, not Silicon Valley.

The post The one thing parents agree on about technology in schools: Limit AI. appeared first on MS NOW.

Zendure Wins Double Honors at the Global Product Technology Innovation Awards 2026, with SolarFlow 4000 Mix Pro Taking Gold
At IFA 2026 in Berlin, Zendure's flagship SolarFlow 4000 Mix Pro earns the Sustainable Home Energy Storage System Gold Award, while Zendure receives the Smart Energy Solutions Brand Award.
BERLIN, Sept. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zendure, a global pioneer of plug-in home energy management systems (HEMS), announced that it has received two honors at the Global Product Technology Innovation Awards 2026. Its flagship home storage system, the SolarFlow 4000 Mix Pro, won the Sustainable Home Energy Storage System Gold Award, while Zendure was named a winner of the Smart Energy Solutions Brand Award. Presented during the opening days of IFA 2026 in Berlin, the two awards recognize Zendure's focus on the clean-energy storage sector and its lightweight, intelligent, and low-carbon approach to powering the home.
Sustainable Home Energy Storage System Gold Award — SolarFlow 4000 Mix Pro
The SolarFlow 4000 Mix Pro is a 4 kW bidirectional AC, AI-driven, all-in-one plug-in home energy storage system that brings home-storage-grade capacity and power to a plug-in form factor. A single unit scales from 8 kWh to 50 kWh, and up to 150 kWh when paired with Zendure's PowerHub accepts up to 13 kW of total solar input, making it well-suited to larger homes, heat pumps, and EV charging. Combined with rooftop solar, it can reduce household electricity costs by up to 91%, equivalent to around €2,560 a year in a typical German scenario.
Smart Energy Solutions Brand Award — Zendure
The Smart Energy Solutions Brand Award recognizes Zendure's broader leadership in intelligent home energy. Zendure's SolarFlow ecosystem scales seamlessly from plug-and-play storage to whole-home energy management. At its core is Agentic HEMS, which draws on consumption, solar, weather, and dynamic-pricing data to automate energy decisions, shift usage to lower-cost periods, and cut household electricity costs, a clear step toward the company's vision of becoming the home energy hub of the AI era.
Zendure is showcasing the SolarFlow 4000 Mix Pro and its full ZEN + Home ecosystem at IFA 2026, Hall 2.2, Stand 124, from September 4 to 8 in Berlin.
About Zendure
Driven by our purpose to accelerate a sustainable future, Zendure is a global pioneer of plug-in HEMS. With R&D and operations centers spanning major tech hubs like Silicon Valley and the Greater Bay Area, alongside Japan and Germany, our vision is to become The Home Energy Hub of the AI Era. Zendure's mission is to empower every household worldwide with the ultimate freedom of energy control. We deliver this through the SolarFlow ecosystem—combining modular storage, intelligent power management, and flexible solar input. Scaling seamlessly from plug-and-play and retrofit storage to whole-home energy management, SolarFlow maximizes self-consumption, reduces grid dependence, and ensures reliable backup.

articles.article_title: Philips Appoints Technology Chief and First Chief AI Officer
articles.heading: Philips Appoints Technology Chief and First Chief AI Officer
articles.summary: CEO Roy Jakobs confirms that Laura Matz will join Philips as Chief Innovation and Technology Officer, while Shez Partovi becomes its first Chief AI Officer
articles.content:
Philips Appoints Technology Chief and First Chief AI Officer
Philips has announced two major changes to its executive committee and technology leadership, signalling AI’s increasingly integral role in company strategy.
Marking a first at Philips, Shez Partovi will take on the role of Chief AI Officer and will, according to CEO Roy Jakobs, “guide our transformation into a people-led, AI-powered company.”
Announced at the same time, Laura Matz joins Philips from Merck KGaA as its latest Chief Innovation and Technology Officer.
“These appointments strengthen our Executive Committee as we accelerate our plan to drive profitable growth to deliver sustainable value,” writes Roy on LinkedIn.
“They sharpen our focus on creating more value through innovation and AI so we can deliver better care for more people,” he continues.
Philips is a global health technology company focused on improving patient outcomes through connected care, diagnostic imaging, monitoring and precision diagnosis.
Its healthcare portfolio spans MRI, CT, ultrasound, patient monitoring and informatics, helping hospitals streamline workflows, support clinicians and deliver more personalised, data-driven care across the patient journey.
Uncharted territory
For the first time, Philips will have a Chief AI Officer in its ranks.
Philips has embedded AI across several areas of its healthcare portfolio, particularly diagnostic imaging, clinical workflow and patient monitoring. A core focus lies in embedding AI directly into the healthcare infrastructure clinicians already use.
Shez’s focus will be on both how AI is embedded in the company’s products to benefit clinicians and how it can support the company’s efforts to improve internal efficiency and performance.
- €17.8bn (US$20.7bn) — Philips’ global sales in 2025.
- ~64,800 — employees worldwide at the end of 2025.
- 100+ countries — Philips provides sales and services across more than 100 countries.
- 2 billion lives — the number of people Philips says it improved through its products and solutions in 2025.
- 700 patents — new patents filed by Philips in 2025, with a strong focus on health technology services and solutions.
On LinkedIn, Shez writes: “The mandate of this new position is enterprise-wide: how AI shows up in what we build for clinicians and patients, and how it reinvents the way we work inside Philips.
“AI is not the goal. Impact is. The opportunity is a people-led, AI-powered Philips — technology that gives clinicians back time, helps us move faster, and lets us focus on what matters most: listening to our customers, solving the clinical problems that improve lives, and delivering better care for more people,” he continues.
“AI is not the goal. Impact is. The opportunity is a people-led, AI-powered Philips. ”
Alongside his new chief AI role, Shez will continue to lead Philips’ Enterprise Informatics business.
Prior to joining Philips in 2021, Shez held senior positions at Amazon Web Services and Dignity Health.
Innovation and technology
Laura Matz joins Philips from Merck KGaA, where she served as the company’s Chief Science and Technology Officer.
It follows 19 years spent at the German firm, including at its affiliated companies Air Products, Versum Materials and Athinia.
“Philips’ purpose - to improve people’s health and well-being through meaningful innovation - has never felt more relevant,” writes Laura on LinkedIn.
“I look forward to working with new colleagues, customers and partners to connect science, technology, data and digital capabilities in ways that create real value for patients, healthcare professionals and consumers,” she continues.
Philipp Harbach will take over as Chief Science and Technology Officer at Merck KGaA on an interim basis following Laura’s departure.
Merck KGaA is a global science and technology company spanning healthcare, life sciences and electronics. Its healthcare business develops innovative medicines and technologies across oncology, immunology, neurology and fertility, while its Life Science division supplies tools and solutions supporting pharmaceutical research, bioprocessing and healthcare innovation worldwide.
Philips - key partners
WellSpan Health
CEO: Roxanna Gapstur | HQ: York, Pennsylvania
In June 2026, WellSpan Health partnered with Philips on a seven-year strategic alliance spanning advanced imaging, diagnostics, AI and research. The collaboration will see the organisations co-develop and validate new technologies across WellSpan’s 12 hospitals and wider network. The partnership aims to improve clinical workflows, efficiency and patient care.
Edwards Lifesciences
CEO: Bernard Zovighian | HQ: Irvine, California
Philips and Edwards Lifesciences collaborated to develop DeviceGuide, an AI-powered solution providing real-time guidance during minimally invasive mitral valve repair. The technology combines Philips’ imaging expertise with Edwards’ structural heart technology to track and visualise its PASCAL Ace repair device. FDA clearance was secured in March 2026.

Is Align Technology a Bargain on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow model looks at the cash Align Technology is expected to generate for shareholders and discounts it back to today. Align Technology currently produces last twelve month free cash flow of about $639 million, and analysts expect this to keep growing from this base rather than shrinking. On those assumptions, the model points to an intrinsic value of about $311 per share.

That compares with a current share price that implies roughly a 49.0% discount to the cash flow based estimate. The projections beyond 2030 fade to more modest growth, which presents this as a maturing business rather than a blue sky story. If Align Technology can sustain free cash flow around or above recent levels, the current market price appears cautious relative to the discounted cash flows implied by this model.

On these Discounted Cash Flow assumptions, Align Technology stock currently screens as undervalued.

Our Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) analysis suggests Align Technology is undervalued by 49.0%. Track this in your watchlist or portfolio , or discover 47 more high quality undervalued stocks .

Head to the Valuation section of our Company Report for more details on how we arrive at this Fair Value for Align Technology.

Is Align Technology Fairly Priced on Earnings?

P/E works well for Align Technology because it highlights what investors are paying for each dollar of current earnings. The stock trades on a P/E of about 27.2x, which is very close to the broader medical equipment industry average of roughly 27.2x and sits below the peer group average of about 35.3x.

The fair P/E ratio, which reflects Align Technology's specific growth profile, margins, size and risk, is estimated at around 30.2x. That is only modestly above the current multiple and suggests the stock is not pricing in a large premium or discount based on earnings alone. For investors comparing Align Technology with other medical equipment stocks, the P/E signal points to a valuation that is broadly in line with what would typically be expected for this type of business.

articles.content:
Luzerne County Community College Surgical Technology program celebrated the graduation of its Class of 2026 on Aug. 7 at the Educational Conference Center on the college’s main campus in Nanticoke.
The graduates completed rigorous training designed to prepare them for the fast-paced and critical role of a surgical technologist in the operating room.
“Our surgical technology students are trained to be calm, focused and precise, ready to take on a critical role in the operating room,” said Sondra Ferraro, director of surgical technology at LCCC. “The students embody discipline, teamwork and attention to detail, qualities that directly impact patient care.”
Throughout the program, students mastered sterile technique and surgical instrumentation while developing critical decision-making skills. They also learned not only the science of surgery, but the art of anticipating the surgeon’s next move.

By Ayana Birbayeva in Nation on 6 September 2026

ALMATY – Kazakh scientists have developed a drone-based technology to automatically distribute beneficial insects across agricultural fields, potentially making biological crop protection faster and more effective, the Ministry of Agriculture reported on Sept. 2.

Photo credit: The Ministry of Agriculture of Kazakhstan

Researchers at the Zhiembayev Kazakh Research Institute of Plant Protection and Quarantine developed the BioDrop technology. The system combines biodegradable spherical BioDrop capsules, a specialized distribution device and an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV).

The capsules contain entomophages – natural enemies of agricultural pests. Loaded onto a drone, the capsules are automatically distributed across a field according to a pre-set flight route. Once they reach the ground, the capsules gradually release the beneficial insects, which then seek out and destroy agricultural pests.

The spherical capsule design accommodates the dosing mechanism while preserving the viability of the biological material.

Field trials show higher efficiency

Field trials showed higher biological effectiveness than traditional manual distribution of entomophages.

On the 14th day after distribution, biological effectiveness under the conventional method averaged 70–73%. With BioDrop, the figure reached 81–83%. This represents an average increase of 10–11% compared with manual distribution.

The technology also reduces the time required to treat fields. Manual distribution in the test area took about 1–1.5 hours, while the same work with a drone took 10–15 minutes, including equipment preparation.

According to the researchers, the time savings could make biological crop protection more practical on large agricultural areas and in hard-to-reach locations.

Technology already used by farms

BioDrop has already been introduced and is being used by four agricultural enterprises, demonstrating its potential for practical application in crop protection. The technology could subsequently be integrated into precision agriculture systems and used alongside phytosanitary monitoring technologies.

Using entomophages is part of an environmentally oriented approach to plant protection, reducing reliance on conventional pest-control methods. Automating their distribution could further expand biological crop protection by making it faster and more efficient.

The researchers also see potential in combining BioDrop with digital agricultural technologies to improve the timing and precision of pest-control measures.

articles.summary: A fast-moving wildfire scorched over 200 acres in Texas County this week, pushing volunteer crews to their physical limits.
articles.content:
How drone technology helped Texas County crews battle 220-acre wildfire
LICKING, Mo. (KY3) -A fast-moving wildfire scorched over 200 acres in Texas County this week, pushing volunteer crews to their physical limits.
But emergency officials say a critical piece of technology, a drone, is the main reason they were able to get ahead of the flames and protect nearby homes.
The wildfire broke out around 1:15 p.m. on Thursday off Slaughter Road near BB Highway in Licking due to a property owner burning trash in a grassy area during high heat and dry conditions.
For Licking resident Sandy Freeman, the afternoon quickly turned chaotic.
“I was a nervous wreck,” Freeman said. “It started over in here on my property. And it was burning pretty good when I came home from town. But if it had headed that direction farther, especially out in this grass, I would have probably left.”
Texas County Emergency Response Team Director Travis Maddox described how quickly the fire began shifting across the rugged Missouri landscape.
“There are areas further back in the woods that you can’t hardly walk through. And there’s ravines all over the place,” Maddox said. “So the terrain here makes everything more complicated. So I kind of already thought that if this ends up being a larger fire, this is going to be a bad one.”
Maddox said the combination of steep terrain, extreme heat, and drought conditions made it one of the most punishing firefights they have seen in years.
“For several years, this one had to be one of the worst to fight,” Maddox said. “Not because of the size or even the dryness, because we have certainly experienced that, but it was all because of combined with the heat. Usually this level of drought and fire happens in this area in late winter, early spring.”
With smoke thick in the air and visibility low, firefighters faced a grueling battle on the ground. Maddox said finding the active edge and “head” of a wildfire manually drains critical time and physical energy from volunteer responders.
“You see smoke, but we don’t know exactly where the fire is,” Maddox explained. “So we send teams out, and they have to spend all this time and energy just finding the fire. Then they have to figure out where the head of the fire is.”
That is where their drone technology changed the game.
“Whereas with the drone, we were able to put it up in the sky and figure out very quickly where the fire line was,” Maddox said. “Where the head of that fire was, where it was moving, and direct firefighters right there. So it made a really big impact.”
By using the drone to scout the path of the flames from above, commanders were able to guide crews directly to hot spots, minimizing their exposure to the extreme outdoor conditions.
The heat took a heavy toll on responders during the nine-hour battle. Four firefighters suffered from heat exhaustion, and three others dealt with dangerously high blood pressure.
Crews ordered nearby neighbors to evacuate their homes as a precaution. Fortunately, no bystanders were injured, and only one vehicle was lost to the flames.
Maddox credited the local volunteer forces for their dedication under such harsh conditions.
“We really had to stay on top of it. The guys out there, they’re amazing,” Maddox said. “These volunteers in this county are the best.”
Following the successful deployment during Thursday’s fire, Maddox says the department plans on purchasing more drones in the near future to expand their aerial firefighting capabilities.

articles.content:
Technology City Hub Building
POA Architects released the design of ‘Technology City Hub Building’.
Wenzhou, a bright pearl on the southeast coast of China, is one of the three central cities of Zhejiang Province, and the economic, cultural, scientific and technological, financial and transportation centre of southern Zhejiang. 2012 August, Wenzhou High-tech Zone was upgraded to a national high-tech zone with the approval of the State Council. 2015 Early 2015, Wenzhou Municipal Party Committee and Municipal Government decided to build the Wenzhou National High-tech Zone based on the principles of ‘industry concentration, element concentration, function integration and production-city integration’, and to promote the comprehensive transformation and upgrading of the industries in Wenzhou and southern Zhejiang. In early 2015, Wenzhou municipal party committee and municipal government decided, based on Wenzhou national hi-tech zone, with the principle of ‘industry concentration, element concentration, function integration, industry-city integration’, to build Wenzhou Zhennan Science and Technology City, to comprehensively transform and upgrade the industries in Wenzhou and Zhennan area, and to promote the construction of the eastern city centre of Wenzhou.
The total land area of the project is 11,090 square metres. The total building area is 37,507 square metres, of which 25,507 square metres are above ground and 12,000 square metres are underground. The project is located in Wenzhou Zhennan Science and Technology City, which has a good location advantage. The project aims to be a gateway to the city, enhance the overall urban style and contribute to the quality of the office environment in the new area.
The development of Tech City inspired the design team to incorporate four key values: foresight, science, efficiency and harmony in order to properly reflect the value of a mixed-use project in an urban area and as a place for people to gather. The space is digitally activated to create a dialogue between the traditional and the future. Our design embraces ancient Eastern philosophies that look to science and humanity, and presents them in a modern way.
Eco-sustainability continues to be a topic of emphasis, utilising green and clean energy to create a passive office building with ultra-low energy consumption. Upon completion, the Digital Hub Building in Zhennan Science and Technology City will be on the regional eco-friendly list along with the surrounding park belt.

articles.content:
- Align Technology (NasdaqGS:ALGN) appoints Quentin Blackford of iRhythm Technologies to its board of directors.
- Andrea L. Saia plans to resign from Align Technology's board after serving for more than a decade.
- The board change introduces new operating and strategy experience as Align Technology marks the end of Saia's long tenure during its growth as a digital dentistry leader.
For investors tracking how leadership shifts can influence long term direction, it can be useful to compare Align Technology with other founder influenced businesses highlighted in 19 top founder-led companies.
Align Technology operates in medical equipment with a focus on digital orthodontics, combining its Invisalign clear aligners, Vivera retainers, and iTero intraoral scanners for dentists and orthodontists in the US and internationally. As a result, board changes affect both its hardware and software driven workflows.
What Align Technology's board reshuffle signals for the Narrative
For investors, this board move at Align Technology speaks directly to the execution side of the existing Narrative. Quentin Blackford brings current CEO experience from iRhythm and prior operating leadership at Dexcom, which is a medical device business with data heavy workflows. That aligns with the Narrative's focus on digital workflow investments, automation and manufacturing expansion as key drivers for margins and earnings quality. Andrea L. Saia's planned departure is framed as unrelated to disagreements, which supports governance continuity rather than raising new risk flags.
If we take a look at the community Narrative for Align Technology, we can see how this news fits into the bigger investment story.
The practical test for whether this refresh is helping will be how Align Technology communicates and executes on its digital and manufacturing programs in results through 2027. Watch for whether Blackford's influence shows up in clearer operating milestones, such as progress updates on regionalized production, scanner and AI treatment planning uptake, and any commentary on cost efficiency in quarterly calls and filings.
