articles.article_title: In 2020, Cincinnati mixed 4,290 pounds of recycled plastic, equal to 71,000 retail bags, into a 2,885-square-yard parking lot at its technology center
articles.heading: In 2020, Cincinnati mixed 4,290 pounds of recycled plastic, equal to 71,000 retail bags, into a 2,885-square-yard parking lot at its technology center
articles.summary: One of the most difficult recycling issues facing the business is plastic film trash since, once collected, thin bags and wraps never find a profitable second life and frequently block sorting equipment. Instead of dumping this stuff in landfills, manufacturers and recyclers have spent years looking for businesses that could consume it at scale.
articles.content:
One of the most difficult recycling issues facing the business is plastic film trash since, once collected, thin bags and wraps never find a profitable second life and frequently block sorting equipment. Instead of dumping this stuff in landfills, manufacturers and recyclers have spent years looking for businesses that could consume it at scale. One such effort moved from laboratory research to a real parking lot in Cincinnati in 2020.
The project brought together the Plastics Industry Association and LyondellBasell, a chemical business whose Cincinnati Technology Centre served as a test site for a novel application of recycled plastic film. Rather than melting bags down into pellets for new products, the team mixed shredded polyethylene film directly into hot asphalt using what is known as a dry process, where the recycled material acts as a solid additive during mixing rather than a separate binder. According to
LyondellBasell
, the collaboration used the equivalent of 71,000 plastic retail bags to pave 2,885 square yards of the Cincinnati Technology Center parking lot in Ohio using recycled polyethylene.
That single installation added more than 4,000 pounds of recycled film into the asphalt mix, a modest amount by industrial standards but a meaningful proof of concept for an approach that had mostly existed on paper before this. The work formed part of a wider effort called the New End Market Opportunities project for film asphalt, which researchers had been developing since 2017 to find practical uses for the huge volumes of polyethylene film that pile up from packaging and retail bags each year. Getting a real parking lot built with the material, rather than just a test batch in a lab, mattered because it let engineers see how the mix behaved under actual weather, traffic and time.
Why a parking lot became the test case
Selecting a parking lot at a technology facility made sense for several reasons beyond convenience. Through the site, LyondellBasell was able to monitor how recycled asphalt performed on a real-world surface at a location under its control in contrast to a normal mix. According to a project profile kept up to date by the Index Project, this installation was the first use of the New End Market Opportunities project for film asphalt, integrating plastic waste and urban infrastructure into a unified sustainability goal. If the material worked well under typical vehicle traffic and seasonal temperature variations, its use on public highways and larger commercial venues would be strengthened in the future. The project also pointed toward larger applications. Project planners estimated that a future installation could use about 20,000 pounds of recycled film, equivalent to roughly 1.5 million plastic bags, if the approach proved successful. That kind of volume would represent a genuine dent in the film waste stream rather than a symbolic gesture, since most recycling programmes still struggle to find buyers for used plastic bags and wrap at any meaningful scale.
An AI-generated image showing workers used a dry-process method to incorporate shredded polyethylene film directly into hot asphalt, giving discarded plastic bags and wraps another use. Credits - Google Gemini
Plastic film has long posed a difficult recycling problem because thin bags and wraps can be difficult to process through conventional recycling systems. The Cincinnati project showed that recovered polyethylene film could instead be incorporated directly into asphalt. According to
National Academies
, The installation used 4,290 pounds of recycled polyethylene, equivalent to about 71,000 retail bags, across 2,885 square yards of the LyondellBasell Cincinnati Technology Center parking lot.
Asphalt must withstand heavy loads, temperature changes and repeated traffic, so the Cincinnati installation served as a real-world demonstration of whether recycled polyethylene could function in a demanding pavement application. Later research has continued to examine recycled plastic in asphalt mixtures, but the 2020 Cincinnati project itself remained a demonstration installation rather than proof that the approach had become standard practice.Asphalt has to withstand heavy loads, temperature extremes and constant wear for decades without failing. Even so, the Cincinnati trial offered something recycling programmes badly needed at the time, a working example rather than a theoretical one, showing that discarded shopping bags could end up supporting the weight of cars and lorries rather than drifting through waterways or piling up in landfill.

Plastic film has long posed a difficult recycling problem because thin bags and wraps can be difficult to process through conventional recycling systems. The Cincinnati project showed that recovered polyethylene film could instead be incorporated directly into asphalt. According to

National Academies

, The installation used 4,290 pounds of recycled polyethylene, equivalent to about 71,000 retail bags, across 2,885 square yards of the LyondellBasell Cincinnati Technology Center parking lot.

Asphalt must withstand heavy loads, temperature changes and repeated traffic, so the Cincinnati installation served as a real-world demonstration of whether recycled polyethylene could function in a demanding pavement application. Later research has continued to examine recycled plastic in asphalt mixtures, but the 2020 Cincinnati project itself remained a demonstration installation rather than proof that the approach had become standard practice.Asphalt has to withstand heavy loads, temperature extremes and constant wear for decades without failing. Even so, the Cincinnati trial offered something recycling programmes badly needed at the time, a working example rather than a theoretical one, showing that discarded shopping bags could end up supporting the weight of cars and lorries rather than drifting through waterways or piling up in landfill.

articles.article_title: Horizon Technology Finance Provides $15 Million Loan Facility To Bioness Medical
articles.heading: Horizon Technology Finance Provides $15 Million Loan Facility To Bioness Medical
articles.summary: Horizon Technology Finance has provided Bioness Medical with a $15 million senior credit facility, including $10 million funded at closing and up to an additional $5 million available to support continued growth.
articles.content:
Horizon Technology Finance has provided Bioness Medical with a $15 million senior credit facility, including $10 million funded at closing and up to an additional $5 million available to support continued growth.
Horizon Technology Finance is an affiliate of Monroe Capital.
Bioness develops and commercializes FDA-approved neurorehabilitation technologies intended to improve mobility and function for people recovering from stroke, spinal cord injury and other neurological conditions.
Backed by Accelmed Partners, Bioness provides clinically validated technologies used across hospital, outpatient and home-based care environments.
Its portfolio spans functional electrical stimulation, robotic gait training and neuromodulation products for clinicians, patients and healthcare systems.
Bioness plans to use the additional capital and financial flexibility to continue investing in innovation, expand its product portfolio and support further growth.
KEY QUOTES:
“Providing flexible growth capital to innovative companies with proven business models and strong market positions is a core focus of Horizon’s venture lending platform. Our team has extensive experience partnering with healthcare and life sciences companies and delivering tailored financing solutions that help management teams execute on their growth objectives. Bioness is representative of the high-quality businesses we seek to support, and we are pleased to add another leading healthcare technology company to Horizon’s portfolio. We look forward to continuing to deploy capital in support of innovative companies across our target markets.”
Paul Seitz, Chief Investment Officer of Horizon Technology Finance
“Horizon’s deep understanding of the life sciences sector and ability to structure a financing solution tailored to our needs made them an attractive partner. This facility provides additional capital and flexibility as we continue investing in innovation, expanding our product portfolio and serving patients and healthcare providers around the world.”
Todd Cushman, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Bioness Medical

articles.title: Flock Cameras Are Coming Down Around The Country Only To Be Replaced By The Same Technology With A Different Name
articles.description: Flock Cameras Are Coming Down Around The Country Only To Be Replaced By The Same Technology With A Different Name Yahoo
articles.description_html: Flock Cameras Are Coming Down Around The Country Only To Be Replaced By The Same Technology With A Different Name  Yahoo
articles.article_title: Flock Cameras Are Coming Down Around The Country Only To Be Replaced By The Same Technology With A Different Name
articles.heading: Flock Cameras Are Coming Down Around The Country Only To Be Replaced By The Same Technology With A Different Name
articles.summary: Replacing one system of surveillance with another isn't a win. And the system some cities are replacing their Flock cameras with could be even more intrusive.
articles.content:
- Many law enforcement agencies are switching from Flock cameras to other ALPR companies like Axon, continuing the use of surveillance technology despite backlash.

- Flock has made changes to its data retention policies and does not offer live video feeds, while Axon retains data for longer periods and offers live video capabilities through its ALPR cameras.

- Critics argue that while Flock has faced criticism for its ALPR technology, other companies like Axon also contribute to the issue of mass surveillance and potential privacy violations.

There's been a great deal of backlash against Flock cameras, with constant vandalism and numerous reports of crooked cops misusing them , leading to more and more communities to cancel their contracts . While Flock has received the most backlash, there are other ALPR companies out there. Rather than ending their use of technology that spies on you , and in a move that doesn't really solve the problems associated with mass surveillance, some departments that have dropped Flock have simply switched to other companies that do the same thing, reports NPR .

One of those competitors is Axon. If that name sounds familiar, it's probably because you've seen it displayed on body cam videos, since Axon is the leading supplier of body cams to law enforcement, according to The Intercept . After a bit of rebranding in 2017 (the same year Flock was founded), many people don't know that Axon is the company formerly known as Taser , the electrical stun gun — another technology that police never, ever misuse .

While Flock had to develop not only its technology, but also its law enforcement contacts and clients, Axon already had the clients in its Rolodex thanks to its other products. Law enforcement agencies may be fleeing from Flock contracts like rats from a sinking ship, but they still want ALPR technology. In places like Denver, Colorado , for example, switching ALPR providers is easy when you're getting your new camera tracking access through a supplier you likely already do business with.

Read more: These Are The Cars That Let You Down The Hardest

Potentially more invasive than Flock

David Mcnew/Getty Images

Flock recently announced a number of band-aids measures, claimed as solutions to remedy the widespread abuse that's hit the news lately. One of these changes to Flock processes was reducing its default data retention period from 30 to seven days, with a maximum retention period of one year. Axon's default period remains 30 days, and there is no limit on how long data can be stored, though some states limit this duration by law .

After a brief pilot program, Flock decided not to offer live video feeds from its ALPR cameras. In Flock's YouTube video about its security changes, CEO Garrett Langley explained why:

Many of our competitors do offer live video on their ALPR devices. We decided we will not. Every device we sell should do exactly what a community expects it to do. Our ALPR cameras capture still images, our live video cameras capture video.

Many of our competitors do offer live video on their ALPR devices. We decided we will not. Every device we sell should do exactly what a community expects it to do. Our ALPR cameras capture still images, our live video cameras capture video.

Axon's attitude is the exact opposite. Axon Outpost cameras not only scan license plates and other vehicle recognition attributes like Flock, but also livestream video, all from one device. Axon Lightpost transforms existing streetlights into combined live video and ALPR cameras with no additional wiring, making it easy and affordable to install even more cameras.

Integration is one of Axon's main selling points, particularly its AI-based Fusus system that saves and searches all data from all devices in one all-seeing database. (Axon has also pushed AI-generated police reports in its Draft One product.) As Axon describes a hypothetical search for a missing child:

Within seconds, Axon Outpost , a compact, solar-powered ALPR camera perched quietly on a nearby pole, flags a match: silver SUV, roof rack, visible bumper sticker. It sends the alert to AxonFusus , which instantly cross-references the livestream with a dozen other nearby feeds, pulls the path of travel, and pushes it straight to officers in the field. Within minutes, the child is found safe.

Within seconds, Axon Outpost , a compact, solar-powered ALPR camera perched quietly on a nearby pole, flags a match: silver SUV, roof rack, visible bumper sticker. It sends the alert to AxonFusus , which instantly cross-references the livestream with a dozen other nearby feeds, pulls the path of travel, and pushes it straight to officers in the field. Within minutes, the child is found safe.

No one would argue against saving an abducted child as quickly as possible. But the same technology can be used for other purposes. Unlike Flock, Axon does contract with the federal government, and supplied $3.5 million worth of tasers and taser supplies to ICE last year. We don't know whether or not ICE uses Axon ALPRs or has access to Fusus, but it's a short, slippery slope to get there.

It's the same thing, only different

Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

The Electronic Frontier Foundation is quite clear about its position regarding ALPRs:

EFF's position is that ALPR mass surveillance—the indiscriminate, continuous collection and retention of location data on every driver, regardless of suspicion—should not exist. Because it nonetheless does, EFF also urges courts and state legislatures to impose strict, enforceable restrictions, such as warrant requirements and deletion deadlines.

EFF's position is that ALPR mass surveillance—the indiscriminate, continuous collection and retention of location data on every driver, regardless of suspicion—should not exist. Because it nonetheless does, EFF also urges courts and state legislatures to impose strict, enforceable restrictions, such as warrant requirements and deletion deadlines.

EFF does not single out Flock, Axon, or any other ALPR manufacturer. It recognizes that the technology enables mass surveillance, regardless of whose name is on it. While Flock has caught a great deal of criticism lately, that does not absolve Axon and other ALPR manufacturers of being part of the problem as well. The American Civil Liberties Union agrees:

...with Flock rightly receiving most of the heat, it's important to realize that its competitors aren't so great either, and that simply replacing Flock surveillance with another company's surveillance won't necessarily solve any of the privacy and other civil liberties problems posed by this mass surveillance technology.

...with Flock rightly receiving most of the heat, it's important to realize that its competitors aren't so great either, and that simply replacing Flock surveillance with another company's surveillance won't necessarily solve any of the privacy and other civil liberties problems posed by this mass surveillance technology.

The main issues with Flock cameras, like that they are going to get drivers killed , are just as true with these other systems — Axon included. The technology isn't perfect, and in many cases, it's got such a terrible track record that using the cameras creates entirely new problems rather than solving the intended ones.

articles.title: US soldiers stormed a desert city in preparation for a high-tech war against a top foe. Here's how it went.
articles.description: US soldiers stormed a desert city in preparation for a high-tech war against a top foe. Here's how it went. Business Insider
articles.description_html: US soldiers stormed a desert city in preparation for a high-tech war against a top foe. Here's how it went.  Business Insider
articles.article_title: US soldiers stormed a desert city in preparation for a high-tech war against a top foe. Here's how it went.
articles.heading: US soldiers stormed a desert city in preparation for a high-tech war against a top foe. Here's how it went.
articles.summary: Out in the Mojave Desert, soldiers working with some new technologies attacked simulated enemy forces holed up in an urban setting.
articles.content:
The US Bradley Fighting Vehicles were visible on the horizon as they raced toward the city. Smoke, deployed to conceal movement, formed wisps around the outskirts. Assault forces, preparing to storm the enemy stronghold, gathered on the northern edge, navigating barbed wire, cars, and concrete blocks — enemy obstacles meant to slow the assault down.
The urban assault, part of a simulated conflict against a formidable peer adversary, followed days of combat.
The US Army exercise tested soldiers on moving through a city caught in conflict, pushing them to clear streets and buildings while fighting. The fight also had another layer. Though not at scale the way combatants in Ukraine are, soldiers were integrating new technologies, including drones and software, to determine whether these systems made a difference in how they saw, sensed, and engaged the enemy.
Traditional warfighting skills remain central to combat operations though.
At the Army's Project Convergence Capstone exercise at Fort Irwin in California this summer, close to 10,000 soldiers gathered to experiment with new weapons and technology while fighting a mock war. Enemy forces consisted of troops from Irwin's 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment, known as "Blackhorse."
Across the hot, dusty Mojave Desert, soldiers grappled with the heat's effects on themselves and their equipment.
A little over an hour before assault forces breached the training city, Blackhorse drones were flying above, scouting the area.
Inside a building, a unit commander asked a drone operator flying a Black Widow quadcopter to use it to assess vehicles pushing into the city. The drone could fly up to four kilometers away, extending the unit's view beyond what soldiers could see from the ground.
"I'm able to find with my UAS [uncrewed aerial system], I'm able to fix with fires, and then I finish with my AT [anti-tank] weapons systems," Capt. Mohamed Elmaola with the 4th Infantry Division told Business Insider.
While remotely piloted uncrewed aircraft proved advantageous for early surveillance operations, they were used only sparingly once the fighting moved into the city, occasionally flying above to scout positions, terrain, and movement. Soldiers said that the use cases for the drones had changed as the exercise went on, with the focus shifting toward the on-the-ground fight.
One ground robot, an uncrewed ground vehicle called the NOMAD, had been put to use outside the city limits earlier that morning, but it didn't see use in the assault.
"What we really want to be able to do is not just saturate the environment with a bunch of technology" because "that becomes so distracting" that soldiers can't train efficiently and effectively, Brig. Gen. Daniel Hibner, head of the Army Joint Modernization Command, told Business Insider.
The simulated city, which the Army calls Razish, was sprawling, with winding streets, buildings of different heights, underground tunnels, and hidden positions. During the training exercise, two key objectives for the assault forces were the jail and a large palace at the center of the city.
As the two opposing forces clashed inside the training city, troops dismounted from their fighting vehicles and began checking buildings for enemies. Dismounted infantry and Bradley crews work together in combat, with each protecting the other as they advance.
Bradleys equipped with heavier weaponry engage threats farther away while soldiers on foot armed for close-in combat clear buildings and eliminate threats to the vehicles nearby.
"You don't want your Bradleys to outpace your dismounted infantry," one soldier told Business Insider, explaining that dismounted enemy troops armed with anti-vehicle weaponry will "just shoot your Bradley."
Enemy forces hid in alleys and on the top floors of buildings, occasionally taking a shot at a gunner exposed atop a Bradley vehicle or a dismounted soldier running across the street. At one point, enemy forces successfully hit a Bradley. The turret shot up, signaling that the vehicle had been destroyed. In many respects, this kind of fighting wouldn't have been unfamiliar to veterans of the Global War on Terror.
The sounds of the fighting came in waves, loudest when assault forces raided the jail and palace. Even in quieter moments, bursts of gunfire could be heard in the distance.
Soldiers positioned on rooftops or in windows would peek up, aim, and fire their weapons before ducking back down. If "killed," soldiers would stop fighting and sit or stand where they were.
Hours into the fight for the city, some of the assault forces gathered inside and alongside a low building just across the street from the gates surrounding the palace. They were assessing whether they had enough ammunition to keep fighting.
One asked where they were located and whether any friendly forces were around them. Another opened his End User Device, a smartphone mounted to his chest, and checked out a map, reading off the building number aloud.
The soldier was using the Army's prototype Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, a software- and artificial intelligence-enabled battlefield network.
At Project Convergence Capstone, troops were examining how NGC2 performed in a large-scale combat scenario, marking the latest iteration of a series of tests. Prior tests had taken place at Fort Carson in Colorado, where the Army's 4th Infantry Division developed NGC2 with industry partners.
One soldier said he was using NGC2 to see where friendly forces were located within the city and where enemy forces might be hiding. Another soldier said that connection issues, either problems with the NGC2 system or the result of electronic warfare and jamming, had left it mostly unusable.
That mix of success and failure was exactly what Army leaders said they wanted to see at the exercise, characterizing it as a chance to gather feedback on what worked and what didn't.
"We're gonna have some failures out here in the desert, and that's good," Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army vice chief of staff, said on a call days after the exercise concluded. "If there is something out here that's not living up to what has been advertised, we're going to walk away from that."
The urban assault showed both the advantages and the challenges of training while experimenting with new technology.
Soldiers had to answer big questions about whether experimental systems were actually useful while still being judged on basics such as whether they properly cleared or marked buildings.
The training environment gave the Army a demanding place to test new technology, but the experimentation also gave soldiers one more thing to manage while trying to win a fight.

One asked where they were located and whether any friendly forces were around them. Another opened his End User Device, a smartphone mounted to his chest, and checked out a map, reading off the building number aloud.

The soldier was using the Army's prototype Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, a software- and artificial intelligence-enabled battlefield network.

At Project Convergence Capstone, troops were examining how NGC2 performed in a large-scale combat scenario, marking the latest iteration of a series of tests. Prior tests had taken place at Fort Carson in Colorado, where the Army's 4th Infantry Division developed NGC2 with industry partners.

One soldier said he was using NGC2 to see where friendly forces were located within the city and where enemy forces might be hiding. Another soldier said that connection issues, either problems with the NGC2 system or the result of electronic warfare and jamming, had left it mostly unusable.

That mix of success and failure was exactly what Army leaders said they wanted to see at the exercise, characterizing it as a chance to gather feedback on what worked and what didn't.

"We're gonna have some failures out here in the desert, and that's good," Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army vice chief of staff, said on a call days after the exercise concluded. "If there is something out here that's not living up to what has been advertised, we're going to walk away from that."

The urban assault showed both the advantages and the challenges of training while experimenting with new technology.

Soldiers had to answer big questions about whether experimental systems were actually useful while still being judged on basics such as whether they properly cleared or marked buildings.

The training environment gave the Army a demanding place to test new technology, but the experimentation also gave soldiers one more thing to manage while trying to win a fight.

articles.content:
- By

- September 5, 2026

After cancerous tumors and surgery on her spine, a Kentucky mom is using a new rehabilitation machine to relearn how to walk.

Kaycie Jackson, a mother of three, was told she had two tumors on her spine in 2024. She had surgery to remove them, but it left her wheelchair-bound. While Jackson is cancer-free, she’s still fighting an uphill battle.

“I couldn’t even bathe my twins or anything like that in the beginning, because I couldn’t even walk. I was in a wheelchair, had to use a Hoyer lift at home,” Jackson said. “I learned to never take anything for granted because it could be snatched from me in a blink of an eye.”

When she began her rehabilitation journey at the University of Louisville Health’s Frazier Rehab in Kentucky, she initially struggled to move her legs without assistance. Now, she is walking, side-stepping, and even throwing a ball while walking, thanks to UofL Health’s Zero-G 3D Body Weight Support System.

Want more content like this? Subscribe to our News We Love newsletter here .

UofL Health physical therapist Lindsay Nalley said the benefits of the machine, which is the only one of its kind in Kentucky, are that it protects patients’ balance while providing varying levels of support to help them gradually regain strength.

“With Kaycie, we’ve done lots of challenges outside of the Zero-G environment. But I’m really able to get creative and find difficult ways to challenge her in that safe environment,” said Nalley.

Jackson said she’s slowly getting her life back. She was recently able to drive her kids for the first time since surgery. Small wins like that, she said, are what push her to keep going.

“I’ve learned to never take anything for granted because it could be snatched from me in a blink of an eye,” said Jackson.

The Zero-G 3D equipment at UofL Health is now available for all patients at Frazier Rehab.

articles.title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
articles.description: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true? The Guardian
articles.description_html: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?  The Guardian
articles.article_title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
articles.heading: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
articles.summary: A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models
articles.content:
Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.
These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.
Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.
That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.
The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.
Yet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots.
“We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” said Trager. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.”
The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German website as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks, according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterise it as a hack.
There is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, the US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents which hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence”.
He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control”.
Concerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware.
Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”.
Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology. “AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned. And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labour MP Alex Sobel to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK.
The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen, according to one count.
With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which is targeting a $2tn stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defences is even higher than we previously believed”.
AI’s double edge – opportunity and risk – was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Its marketing video focused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts.
Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra, said it was “more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover”.
Astra also has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability – the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder”.
The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient – and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words – as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers.
OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging”.
The company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning”. Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better”.
OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure”.
“We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.”
His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.”
And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”.
He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”

articles.title: Opinion - Mark Policinski: Arrival of Waymo’s driverless technology is a transportation win for the region
articles.description: Opinion - Mark Policinski: Arrival of Waymo’s driverless technology is a transportation win for the region nkytribune.com
articles.description_html: Opinion - Mark Policinski: Arrival of Waymo’s driverless technology is a transportation win for the region  nkytribune.com
articles.article_title: Opinion - Mark Policinski: Arrival of Waymo’s driverless technology is a transportation win for the region
articles.heading: Opinion – Mark Policinski: Arrival of Waymo’s driverless technology is a transportation win for the region
articles.summary: The announcement that Waymo is coming to our region is an advancement that will greatly benefit the OKI region and our 2.2 million citizens. More than 10 years ago, I said this incredible driverless…
articles.content:
The announcement that Waymo is coming to our region is an advancement that will greatly benefit the OKI region and our 2.2 million citizens. More than 10 years ago, I said this incredible driverless technology was going to happen far sooner than most industry experts expected. Today it has done just that for our region.
Waymo’s remarkable record of safety, security and efficiency is to be both applauded and viewed with amazement. For too long, its technology has been ridiculed as more Jetson than genuine. To society’s benefit, Waymo persisted and kept their minds and talents aimed at the ultimate goal of producing marketable driverless cars. That goal is simple: For the first time in history, everyone will have mobility when and where they want it. The advantages to commerce and economic growth from exponential increases in freight efficiencies are sky-is-the-limit in nature.
More importantly, autonomous technology will provide mobility to those who thirst for it the most. Consider the elderly, persons with disabilities, the poor, households with zero vehicles, and every person whose life is limited because they cannot get to their doctor, school, the grocery store, a job, or visit their families. These populations will now have options to do so.
What the future brings and when, we cannot know. But, I do remember a decade ago, I was told by the experts of the day that driverless cars would not serve Americans to any degree until 2040 or after. I thought differently and shared that with many audiences over the years. OKI has been consistently at the forefront of pushing the possibilities of remarkable autonomous technology. So, Waymo’s recent announcement it was coming to our region has special meaning to OKI.
We should admire the power of this technology in many regards, and chief among them is the speed with which it can be brought to serve our neighborhoods. The women and men of Waymo who have invested their time, talents, and fortunes have given us a remarkable opportunity to change not just our commutes, but our culture.
200 years ago, Cincinnati was a transportation powerhouse on the banks of the mighty Ohio River. Today, Cincinnati stands ready to advance again the power of a cutting-edge transportation technology that will make our lives infinitely safer, more mobile, more prosperous and better in many other ways.
See you soon and let’s catch a ride with no one behind the wheel.
Mark Policinski CEO of the OKI Regional Council of Governments, a council of local governments, business organizations and community groups committed to developing collaborative strategies, plans and programs to improve the quality of life and economic development potential of Tri-State region.

articles.title: 5 Big Precision Technology Takeaways from 2026 Farm Progress Show
articles.description: 5 Big Precision Technology Takeaways from 2026 Farm Progress Show Precision Farming Dealer
articles.description_html: 5 Big Precision Technology Takeaways from 2026 Farm Progress Show  Precision Farming Dealer
articles.article_title: 5 Big Precision Technology Takeaways from 2026 Farm Progress Show
articles.heading: Channels
articles.summary: I just got back from the 2026 Farm Progress Show in Boone, Iowa, where precision technology was hotter than the 100-degree heat indexes during the 3-day event.
articles.content:
I just got back from the 2026 Farm Progress Show in Boone, Iowa, where precision technology was hotter than the 100-degree heat indexes during the rain-shortened, 3-day event.
As I begin to sift through my notes, interviews and videos, here are a few big tech takeaways from my 26,000-step journey across the nation’s largest outdoor farm show.
Autonomous Implements
When I learned that Carbon Robotics was going to be at the show, I assumed its well-known LaserWeeder would be front and center. But instead, I was surprised to see a Carbon Autonomy-equipped John Deere tractor and a Great Plains Manufacturing implement on display when I approached the booth.
The Seattle, Wash.-based company announced the launch of its Carbon Autonomy Ready program, enabling implement manufacturers to make their equipment optimized for autonomous tractor operation using the Carbon Autonomy kit.
Great Plains Manufacturing was announced as the first company to join the program.
“We believe the Carbon Autonomy platform can transform the ways that modern farmers work their fields, and Great Plains is the perfect first partner to launch this program,” says Carbon Robotics founder and CEO Paul Mikesell. “Our belief is that autonomous farming implements will help farmers be more efficient and lower costs by extending working hours, solving skilled operator shortages, and increasing tractor utilization.”
“At Great Plains, we see producers continually fine-tuning their operations to capture small, incremental gains in yield and efficiency. Real-time adjustments will be critical to maximizing those efforts,” says Doug Jennings, senior product manager at Great Plains. “We look forward to expanding sensing, communication, and control channels through this agreement with Carbon Robotics to provide producers with the most efficient, timely field adjustments possible.”
The Carbon Autonomy kit is compatible with 2019 or newer John Deere 6 or 8 series tractors and is currently available for pre-order in the U.S.
Dealers Invest in Precision Spraying
I got an up-close look at Ag Zen’s AI-powered precision spraying technology (see how it works in the demo in the video below), which has been picked up by over 260 dealers this year, including AgRevolution, AgriVision, Greenway, KanEquip, PrairieLand Partners and Sloan Implement, to name just a few.
“You can talk to your local dealer and they probably support it,” says Vishnu Jayaprakash, AgZen CEO and founder. “That growth all happened basically in one quarter. Dealers have seen the value that we can bring to growers. That’s the only way you get pretty much every color dealer signing up to support and sell this.
“We can now measure coverage on the soil, so every residual pass we can optimize,” he adds. “We’re also measuring and controlling how quickly the droplets evaporate and die. With dicamba coming back, that’s going to be important to make sure there’s no off-target movement.
“This year was great for us. Farmers as small as 2,000 acres paid the system off in 1 year. Farmers as large as 400,000 acres have been paying it off since 2024. We’re excited about expanding those use cases.”
Real-Time Kernel Processing
The major OEMs always have some type of new technology on display, and this year was no different.
New Holland debuted ForageCam, which allows producers and operators to view real-time kernel processing scores and make adjustments to meet desired forage quality.
As New Holland precision director Paul Welbig explains in the video below, the system features a spout-mounted camera with AI-powered vision to constantly analyze the chopped corn flow.
For dairy and beef producers, feed quality is the most important indicator of forage harvester performance,” says Patrick Weitzel, forage harvester marketing manager for New Holland North America. “With ForageCam, producers and custom operators are getting a real-time KPS and can assess right away if the quality is high enough the moment their forage is running through the harvester. In the past, we had to guess from the cab what the score was or send samples to the lab to determine the KPS. Now, we instantly know the forage score and quality.”
JD, the New AI Assistant
John Deere introduced JD, the AI assistant built into the Operations Center that gives farmers a new way to put their data to work, simply by asking a question.
Jackson Baca, product marketing manager with John Deere, gives us the scoop in the video below.
“Farmers have more data available to them than ever before, but the value comes from their ability to use it in the moments that matter,” said Jahmy Hindman, chief tchnology officer at John Deere. “JD changes the experience from navigating through a sea of data to simply asking it a question. It puts advanced data analysis within reach by enabling farmers to receive answers tailored to their farm and their needs in a matter of seconds.”
Ag Leader’s New API Interface
Before thunderstorms brought our day at the show to an abrupt end, Ag Leader introduced us to its new application programming interface (API) that enables third-party camera sensor providers to integrate with RightSpot, Ag Leader’s pulse width modulation (PWM) rate control system.
In the video below, Logan Handsaker explains how the new API gives farmers and dealers greater flexibility in addressing challenging weed control issues by allowing them freedom to choose from a select group of camera sensors that will interface with Ag Leader’s application system.
“Farmers are looking for solutions that help maximize every spray pass while reducing input costs and improving herbicide effectiveness,” says John Howard, crop care product manager at Ag Leader. “By opening the RightSpot platform to compatible camera sensor technologies, Ag Leader is making it easier for customers to adopt the technology that best fits their operation without sacrificing the precision, accuracy, and reliability of their application system.”
Stay tuned for more Precision Farming Dealer coverage from 2026 Farm Progress Show in the coming days!

articles.summary: Two members of the Joliet Police Department have been placed on paid administrative leave for alleged misuse of Flock Safety Technology.
articles.content:
JOLIET, Ill. (WGN) – Two members of the Joliet Police Department have been placed on paid administrative leave for alleged misuse of Flock Safety Technology.
The police department said the two members involved are a sworn officer and a dispatcher.
Police officials said once the discovery was made, the police department took administrative action and referred the incident to the Joliet Inspector General for investigation, as well as the Illinois State Police for an independent review.
“The Joliet Police Department recognizes the seriousness of these allegations, and we continue to review and strengthen policies governing the use of this technology and will enact department-wide audits to reinforce appropriate use and accountability. These efforts reflect our continued commitment to responsible policing, transparency, and maintaining the trust of the community we serve,” the police department said.
No other information on the alleged misuse was made available and the police department said the investigation remains ongoing.

articles.title: RISD expands technology, safety initiatives on school buses
articles.description: RISD expands technology, safety initiatives on school buses communityimpact.com
articles.description_html: RISD expands technology, safety initiatives on school buses  communityimpact.com
articles.article_title: RISD expands technology, safety initiatives on school buses
articles.heading: RISD expands technology, safety initiatives on school buses
articles.summary: Richardson ISD continues to expand its technology systems that support its school bus fleet and other vehicles, while also increasing safety initiatives and professional development for drivers and staff members.
articles.content:
Richardson ISD continues to expand its technology systems that support its school bus fleet and other vehicles, while also increasing safety initiatives and professional development for drivers and staff members.
The overview
Mike Jasso, assistant superintendent of district operations, said RISD runs one of the largest transportation operations in the area, transporting between 5,000 and 6,000 students daily.
RISD’s fleet of 189 school buses covers 1.1 million miles every year, said Thomas Gipson, executive director of transportation. In addition to the yellow school buses, the district’s fleet includes 85 trucks, 48 vans and 25 SUVs that are used for operations, maintenance and alternative student transportation.
Richardson ISD uses several technology systems to support their transportation fleet, including Samsara AI technology and a new app that parents can use to track their student’s bus.
Safety on the buses is a priority for the district, Jasso said, as well as aligning disciplinary measures between the transportation departments and campuses.
“We consider ourselves an extension of the classroom,” Jasso said.
The details
Richardson ISD recently introduced the Stopfinder app to district families, which parents can use to track their student’s bus and receive notifications from the district’s transportation department. Families can use the app to set up alerts to know when their student’s bus is approaching their stop or when a bus is delayed.
RISD uses Samsara AI technology, a cloud-based fleet management platform, to monitor fleet vehicles and support safety efforts. The technology setup includes real-time GPS, AI dashcams and vehicle diagnostics that can tell district officials where a bus is, how many miles it has driven and who rode on it.
“You hear AI is good in some ways and bad in some ways,” Gipson said. “With the bus system, it’s a good thing because we can protect the kids, we can protect the drivers.”
Gipson said while the district does not actively monitor the camera feed, they can access them when needed to address safety or conduct violations. The Samsara system also monitors driver safety, tracking things like taking their eyes off the road or coming to a rolling stop.
Each bus has six cameras on it, with RISD operating a total of 1,134 integrated AI and HD cameras.
Gipson said the technology improves operational efficiency and helps to reduce fuel and maintenance costs by keeping district officials up to date on vehicle needs.
Last year, RISD also introduced a student ID badging system, requiring students to scan a customized ID when they board and exit the bus, which Jasso said helps the district know when students are on the bus.
A closer look
The Samsara system supports a new joint initiative between RISD’s transportation and risk management departments, Jasso said, which uses the data to recognize drivers who consistently demonstrate safe driving behaviors.
“We want to not only spend time on our staff [to say], ‘Hey, don’t roll that stop sign’ [or] ‘Don’t look down at your phone,’ but we also want to recognize the folks that do a great job daily,” Jasso said.
Jasso said the transportation department also ramped up staff training and professional development for drivers and other transportation staff members last year, especially related to student safety. The district saw a “double-digit” decrease in preventable accidents last year.
Staff retention has also been a priority for RISD, and since improving recognition and professional development efforts, the district has seen reduced turnover, Jasso said.
Diving in deeper
State funding for transportation has remained fairly constant, while RISD has seen its cost increase over the last several years. The majority of the transportation budget goes toward payroll, which has increased due to growing ridership in the district.
There is a “significant gap” between the funding RISD receives from the state and the transportation needs in the district, Branum said. Transportation funding could be a legislative priority for RISD to advocate for during the upcoming 2027 Texas Legislature session.
“We know advocating for increased funding for public [education] is going to be one of those line items, but specifically these underfunded areas in transportation would be high on that list,” Branum said.
Looking ahead
RISD’s 2025 bond will fund transportation updates for all four of the district’s band programs. Most peer districts use big rigs to transport band equipment, but RISD currently rents vans for that, Branum said.
Branum said the new band vehicles will save money in the long run and will be an investment in a “more permanent solution that would be part of our infrastructure.” She said she expects the new vehicles to come in 2028, after the district completes the middle school transformation, also funded by the 2025 bond.

articles.title: Sacramento company develops clean energy technology for AI data centers
articles.description: Sacramento company develops clean energy technology for AI data centers KCRA
articles.description_html: Sacramento company develops clean energy technology for AI data centers  KCRA
articles.article_title: Sacramento company develops clean energy technology for AI data centers
articles.heading: Sacramento company develops clean energy technology for AI data centers
articles.summary: Sacramento company develops clean energy technology for AI data centers
articles.content:
Sacramento company develops clean energy technology for AI data centers
LiCAP Technologies, a Sacramento-based clean energy technology company, is developing advanced ultracapacitors that charge and release energy faster than batteries, with a patented process that reduces environmental impact.
"We believe that Sacramento is a hub for clean technology in the region," said Richard Qiu, president of LiCAP Technologies.
Richard Qiu said the company recently announced its new rack level ultracapacitor energy storage system which is engineered for the high-power and fast-response demands of AI data centers.
LiCAP’s patented a process called "activated dry electrode technology" to create ultracapacitors while most of the industry uses a wet coating process that's more harmful to the environment according to the company.
"It's a major environmental impact to remove that chemical from the process," said Eric Fodge.
Fodge added, "Doing something that can literally impact everyone on the planet is very rewarding."
The company, which employs nearly 50 people, plans to triple the size of its facility and hire more workers in the Sacramento region.
"Our belief is not only are we making interesting technology, but also we want to make sure we're building resources that help the local community...to do this all together," Qiu said.
In June, the California Energy Commission awarded LiCAP an $11.3 million grant to expand its manufacturing capabilities.

articles.title: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
articles.description: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged? BBC
articles.description_html: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?  BBC
articles.article_title: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
articles.heading: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
articles.summary: The AI-powered cameras have been vandalised across the US, as citizens object to the growing surveillance network.
articles.content:
Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined.
These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see coordinated vandalism. Yet here four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.
The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording".
These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California, and Georgia.
Proponents say they have made communities safer, and helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have led some to worry. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.
They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.
A new age of surveillance
Founded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.
But little is known about the extent that Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide, and estimates there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.
Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.
Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.
For example, Houston's METRO Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show METRO has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.
And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year on year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.
By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.
Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship. And that's very problematic".
There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.
He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.
Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.
CCTV cameras, licence plate readers, and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice, and tune in to the capabilities of the technology around them.
With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.
One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that doesn't mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.
The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI. The tool includes a database of over 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a License Agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.
Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.
Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. The office did not respond to requests for comment.
Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime.
"It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer." Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.
Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had got lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."
Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable.
"But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."
'I feel like I'm being stalked'
Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".
The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching a licence plate.
Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card.
"It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.
In response, she's changed her commute to work: "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."
But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.
In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.
Hundreds of contracts cancelled
Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle, and Austin, Texas.
In total, over 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in the month of August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy.
Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.
The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits, and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to 7 days, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.
Flock Safety's CEO and founder, Garrett Langley, told the BBC it's up to individual cities to decide how long to store data, and what information to share with whom.
"I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says.
"As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."
Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.
He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find over 10,000 missing people.
"The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".
But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."

They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.

A new age of surveillance

Founded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.

But little is known about the extent that Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide, and estimates there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.

Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.

Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.

For example, Houston's METRO Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show METRO has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.

And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year on year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.

By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.

Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship. And that's very problematic".

Reuters

There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.

He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.

Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.

CCTV cameras, licence plate readers, and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice, and tune in to the capabilities of the technology around them.

With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.

One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that doesn't mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.

The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI. The tool includes a database of over 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a License Agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.

Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.

Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. The office did not respond to requests for comment.

Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime.

"It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer." Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.

Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had got lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."

Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable.

"But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."

'I feel like I'm being stalked'

Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".

The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching a licence plate.

Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card.

"It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.

In response, she's changed her commute to work: "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."

But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.

In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.

Hundreds of contracts cancelled

Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle, and Austin, Texas.

In total, over 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in the month of August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy.

Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.

The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits, and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to 7 days, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.

Flock Safety's CEO and founder, Garrett Langley, told the BBC it's up to individual cities to decide how long to store data, and what information to share with whom.

"I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says.

"As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."

Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.

He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find over 10,000 missing people.

"The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".

But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."
