articles.article_title: New Columbus police directive sets limits on surveillance technology
articles.heading: New Columbus police directive sets limits on surveillance technology
articles.summary: Columbus police are establishing new rules for how officers can use automated license plate readers, neighborhood cameras, gunshot detection systems and other s
articles.content:
New Columbus police directive sets limits on surveillance technology
Columbus police are establishing new rules for how officers can use automated license plate readers, neighborhood cameras, gunshot detection systems and other surveillance technology, including limits on how long certain data can be retained and how officers can use the information.
The revised Columbus Division of Police Directive 11.08, titled “Sensor Technologies,” sets requirements for accessing, using, storing and auditing data collected through the technology.
The directive is scheduled to take effect Sept. 30.
Under the policy, officers cannot stop or detain someone solely because an automated license plate reader, or ALPR, generates an alert. Officers must verify that the vehicle matches the alert and determine that there is an independent, lawful reason for the stop.
The policy also limits how the technology can be used. Officers are prohibited from using sensor technology to gather information solely about First Amendment-protected activity, to target people based solely on characteristics such as race, religion, political affiliation, nationality or sexual orientation, or to harass or intimidate individuals or groups.
The directive also restricts the use of the technology to detect or apprehend people based on suspected immigration status, unless a judicial warrant exists, a criminal violation has been reported or an arrest has been made.
The policy says officers generally may monitor only areas where people do not have an expectation of privacy unless exigent circumstances exist or a warrant has been obtained. It also requires privacy blocks in the neighborhood camera system to prevent officers from viewing inside private residences.
The directive establishes different retention periods for different types of sensor data.
Footage from neighborhood safety cameras will generally be retained for 14 days. Automated license plate reader data will be retained for seven days. Data from the Division's gunshot detection system will be retained indefinitely, while retention periods for third-party camera feeds vary by the owner and system.
Data identified as evidence in an investigation can be retained beyond those standard periods.
Officers also will be required to use Division-owned devices to access sensor technology systems and complete specific training before receiving access. Access is limited to authorized personnel, including sworn officers and certain analysts and civilian employees.
The policy requires sensor technology systems to document the date, time, user and reason for every query. The Technical Services Section lieutenant is required to audit ALPR use every other month and conduct an annual review of the audit findings.
The directive also establishes requirements for adding license plates to police hotlists. Officers must have reasonable suspicion that a vehicle is associated with a criminal offense or an exigent public safety circumstance, and supervisor approval is required. Plates must be removed once the vehicle is no longer being sought for a law enforcement purpose.
The policy comes as the use of automated license plate readers and other surveillance technology has faced increased scrutiny in Columbus and elsewhere. Columbus officials announced Sept. 3 that the city was suspending its use of Flock cameras after a suspected misuse of the technology by a Columbus police officer.
The new directive, however, covers a broader range of sensor technologies, including city-owned neighborhood cameras, mobile trailer cameras, gunshot detection systems and third-party camera feeds.
The directive says the Division's goal is to use sensor technology to improve public safety, officer productivity and investigative capabilities while protecting civil liberties, personal privacy and data integrity.

articles.heading: Franklin County Sheriff’s Office installs new jail inmate medical monitoring technology
articles.summary: The Franklin County Sheriff’s Office has recently installed a new state-of-the-art health monitoring system for inmates.
articles.content:
Franklin County Sheriff’s Office installs new jail inmate medical monitoring technology
FRANKLIN COUNTY, Ill. (Heartland News) - The Franklin County Sheriff’s Office has recently installed a new state-of-the-art health monitoring system for inmates.
The Franklin County Jail installed the new device in a medical holding cell.
The system utilizes ultra-wideband radar technology to continuously monitor an inmate’s heart rate, respiratory rate, and motion without requiring wearable devices or direct physical contact by staff.
Sheriff Kyle Bacon said this adds an extra layer of protection for both inmates and jail staff.
“If we have a detainee who has a heart condition or maybe a sleep disorder, implementing this technology into their care is a big plus for everyone involved. Part of our job is to manage risk and to provide the best care that we can within the jail setting,” said Bacon.
The sheriff added that county jails are increasingly being called upon to provide a higher level of medical care due to the long-term and chronic health conditions of many incarcerated individuals.
Sheriff Bacon said this technology will provide jail staff with an additional tool to assist in the early detection of a potential medical emergency and allow for a more timely response when an individual’s health condition may be changing.
The device cost $7,500 and was made possible by state-issued grant funding.

articles.summary: The Board discussed chronic absenteeism, technology policies and grants, updates on matters related to special education, and the financial situation in the Winston-Salem / Forsyth County school system. Read the full article here.
articles.content:
State Board discusses chronic absenteeism, technology, special education, and more
The State Board of Education convened for its monthly meeting this week, where the Board heard a presentation on 2025-26 school accountability data, which showed, among other things, that the statewide graduation rate increased a full percentage point to 88.8% — the highest graduation rate in North Carolina history.
“This graduation rate moves North Carolina’s public schools closer to reaching a ‘Best in Nation Measure’ as identified in the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction’s (NCDPI) strategic plan, Achieving Educational Excellence,” a DPI press release says. You can read more about the new report in the EdNC article below.
The Board also discussed chronic absenteeism, technology policies and grants, updates on matters related to special education, a financial update from Winston-Salem/Forsyth County Schools, and more.
Sign up for the EdDaily to start each weekday with the top education news.
School attendance bright spots
Gov. Josh Stein recently declared September 2026 as “Attendance Awareness Month.” In North Carolina, chronic absenteeism is defined as missing 10% or more days of school. Chronic absenteeism peaked in the state during the pandemic at 31% and was around 24% in the 2024-25 school year.
Nonprofit AttendanceWorks put forward a national challenge to reduce chronic absenteeism by 50% by 2030, and in North Carolina, DPI took up that goal by launching the statewide initiative, AttendNC Counts.
Dr. Sean Kellogg, senior director of the DPI Office of Research and Promising Practices, explained to the Board this week that DPI has conducted research on best practices across the state, providing “research-based planning guides, resources, reports for schools and districts.”
On Thursday, the Board also heard a presentation from Kellogg and a panel of principals from schools that have reduced chronic absenteeism significantly, recognized as “Bright Spot Schools” by DPI.
Overall, researchers identified 310 bright spot schools statewide, and you can explore those schools here. Seven of those schools, in northeastern North Carolina, were interviewed by DPI to develop an understanding of effective strategies in practice currently.
“Our next agenda items really highlights one of the conditions that makes stronger outcomes possible, that is student attendance,” said Board member Catty Moore, welcoming the panel to the meeting. “Students cannot fully benefit from strong instruction, effective teachers, and academic supports when they are regularly missing instructional time.”
The principals spoke about the importance of strong relationships, flexibility, creative attendance incentives, and working to understand individual student situations.
Elenia Riddick, principal of Hertford County Middle School, described how her school has utilized daily check-ins for chronically absent students and students trending toward being chronically absent, which encouraged students to be at school.
“We have to create the environment for them where they want to come, feel connected, and they have their voice when they come in the building,” said Riddick. “And they’re excited to come to school when they know that someone is there looking for them.”
Washington County High School Principal Torrey Hines said his school believes in “leading with love” when it comes to encouraging attendance, making sure that they directly check-in with students and parents when a student is absent.
Kellogg said that across all interviewed bright spot schools, relationships between the school and students and the school and parents emerged as a critically important part of reducing absences.
For instance, Northwest Elementary School Principal Taimak Willis said that when he has relationships with students, he’s “able to respond with love and care and try to figure out the next steps to keep them at school consistently.”
Overall, each school took a different approach to ensuring that their students and families understood that attendance was a priority.
“There’s really no single attendance intervention represented here or at the seven schools,” said Kellogg. “… Each school’s been responding uniquely to their unique circumstances.”
However, he said several strategies were successful at multiple schools, including noticing an attendance problem early, understanding why a student is absent, acting together as a school to respond, creating connections with families and students, and following through on responsibilities. Some reasons why students might be missing school include transportation, family circumstances, a lack of connection to school, or basic needs — and different barriers may require different school responses.
The Board asked the panelists several questions regarding the effect of attendance policies on students, the results seen at their schools.
The first question came from the newest student adviser to the Board, Keely Deal.
“How can we make sure students… have a voice in developing attendance solutions rather than attendance policies being created solely by adults?” asked Deal.
Willis said his school’s student leadership council helps students have a voice while also helping the administrative team understand what would incentivize students to come to school. Riddick added that her school allows students to have a part in crafting attendance incentives, like coming up with ideas for field trips.
Board Chair Eric Davis thanked the panelists for sharing their expertise and better helping the Board understand “the why” behind chronic absenteeism. You can watch the full panel discussion here.
Technology in schools
Last year, North Carolina lawmakers passed a bill that requires school districts to develop policies prohibiting students from using personal devices during instruction. Stein signed House Bill 959 into law on July 1, 2025, and the law took effect on Jan. 1, 2026.
According to DPI’s mandated report to the General Assembly, most public school units adopted the North Carolina School Boards Association Policy 4318, which established policy consistency across the state.
Currently, five public school units have not submitted compliance plans to DPI, but Dr. Matthew Mayo, DPI’s director of Digital Teaching & Learning and School Connectivity, noted that DPI is in continuous communication with those schools. (In December, the Governor’s Advisory Council for Student Safety and Well-Being reported that every North Carolina school district had a plan in place for cellphone-free classrooms.)
The report found uniformity across three main areas for schools that have complied thus far:
- Standardized class-time storage expectations, although there is some difference in if a school requires that devices be placed in pouches or simply powered off
- Consistent integration of statutory exemptions
- Tiered administrative consequences for violations of the schools’ policy
“One of the things that our legislature has supported, that we have supported, and that is being implemented around the state are these pouches,” said Board Vice Chair Alan Duncan. “There are some districts that cannot afford to purchase the pouches. It strikes me that — with the recent settlement with Meta — some of the money from that would be appropriate to support the social emotional welfare of our students with the use of those pouches, coming into compliance with best practices as they’ve been described.”
The Board also received recommendations for the 2026-27 Digital Learning Initiative (DLI) grants, established under the North Carolina Digital Learning Plan.
The DLI Grant aims to “expand effective digital learning practices across all North Carolina K-12 public schools.” Since its launch in 2017, the program has awarded over $12.5 million to public schools across the state.
Consultant Lindsey Sipe presented the 2026-27 recommended grantees to the Board, explaining the evaluation process for grant applications and the two pathways that schools can apply for funding through. One pathway focuses on professional learning, and the other on integrating innovative technologies.
In total, 76 schools applied, and five are being recommended to receive the grants, which totals about $1.2 million in funding, including continued funds for prior grantees. You can read about the schools recommended for funding and their proposals here.
Grant applications are also now open for the newest cohort of the 21st Century Community Learning Centers Grant Program, which is supported by funds from the U.S. Department of Education. The department sets certain priority requirements that states must abide by when considering grant applications, including giving priority to Title I, Part A schoolwide programs.
You can explore the other priorities here. More information on how to apply will be available in October, and applications will be due by 12:00 p.m. on Nov. 18.
Report on accountability for alternative schools
The Board also heard an update on accountability for alternative schools last week, defined by DPI as “safe orderly, caring and inviting learning environments that assist students with overcoming challenges that may place them ‘at-risk’ of academic failure.”
Alternative schools must select one of three options for accountability models.
- Alternative schools can report a School Performance Grade.
- Alternative schools can report data on student achievement and growth and receive a status of “Progressing,” “Maintaining,” or “Declining” based on the comparison of year-to-year performance.
- Alternative schools can propose their own alternative accountability models to the State Board of Education for approval. The proposed alternative accountability model must include criteria for achievement and growth.
Curtis Sonneman, director of the DPI Office of Accountability, explained that only one school has opted for the first option, 82 have opted for the second, and 23 schools have opted to design their own model. The report he presented to the Board included each of the school’s individual accountability plans, which you can explore here.
Reports on special education
Senior Director of the DPI Office of Exceptional Children Dr. Carol Ann Hudgens also presented the results of the Special Education Census and the Child Find Census.
The results of the Special Education Census, required by state statute, are listed below, and they identify 220,730 students with disabilities in North Carolina from Dec. 2, 2024, to Dec. 1, 2025. This reflects an increase of about 2,500 identified students with disabilities from 2024.
The Board is also required to perform an annual census of all students aged 3-21 in North Carolina who might need special education and related services, which is known as the Child Find Census. You can see the results of that census below, from the reporting period July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025.
According to the report: “The data provided distinguishes between students navigating the initial referral process through placement during the reporting period of July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025 (Child Find census) and students with active Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) during the reporting period of December 2, 2024 through December 1, 2025 (Special Education census).”
Hudgens also presented the annual federal performance plan and annual performance report on the state formula grant program under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). “The U.S. Department of Education uses four determination levels to assess states and U.S. territories in their implementation of the IDEA. Those levels are: meets requirements, needs assistance, needs intervention, and needs substantial intervention,” said Hudgens. “In July, North Carolina received its determination. For data collected in the 24-25 school year, 21 states met requirements. North Carolina was one of 33 states that was determined to need assistance.”
More about special education in NC
Because of this determination, the state is required to access federal technical assistance centers and report actions taken as a results of that support in a February 2027 report.
Currently, educational performance for students with disabilities has remained relatively consistent across the last four years, according to a DPI report. However, in the 2024-25 school year, vacancies for Exceptional Children (EC) teachers were “a recurring theme of concerns across grades,” said Hudgens. There were 1,535 EC teacher vacancies in 2024-25, which is nine fewer than the 2023-24 school year.
Hudgens highlighted the office’s EC tuition assistance program, that “supports the completion of coursework for licensure.” In total, the office invested $142,525 in tuition reimbursements, which was about $60,000 more than last year. Furthermore, the office provided support for professional learning, grants, and technical assistance across the state. You can read more about their efforts to support EC teachers here.
“We recognize that there is much work to be done to improve outcomes for our students, and we are thankful to our dedicated Exceptional Children personnel in the field for helping students with disabilities achieve the gains highlighted earlier in the aggregate accountability data for the 25-26 school year,” said Hudgens.
Additionally, the Board helped to establish the Exceptional Children Competitive Grant for State-Level Targeted Assistance last year. Hudgens presented a brief update on the first award, which was granted in February. However, she explained that she hoped to establish a “fall cadence” for the award, so the presentation also included a recommendation for recipients of the award to be approved in October.
Of the roughly 230 applications received, the office is recommending funding be awarded to 132 groups, or about 57% of applicants. Across all recipients, the funding totals more than $8.3 million. Both K-12 and pre-K groups were eligible for funding, and the regional breakdown of those awards is mapped below.
Winston-Salem/Forsyth County Schools gives budget update

Deanna Kaplan, chair of the Winston-Salem/Forsyth County Schools Board of Education, gave an update to the Board this week, saying the district’s budget is now balanced, and its debt eliminated. She said the eventual solution was one based in the power of community, specifically recognizing the work of her fellow board members. The main aspects of their plan involved relying on their community and fundraising.
“Through the extraordinary generosity of individuals, businesses, foundations, and community leaders, more than $11 million was raised to support our school district,” said Kaplan.
In addition to fundraising, Kaplan explained there were furloughs and other reductions in services. She acknowledged that those cuts caused pain that affected “real people, real families, and individuals who had devoted themselves to our school system.”
However, district leaders focused on a positive outlook for the new school year ahead.
“The community support and collaboration and what is yielded from that couldn’t be more evident than what we’ve seen in the Winston-Salem Forsyth County schools,” said Dr. Don Phipps, superintendent of Winston Salem/Forsyth County Schools, who came into the role in December 2025, and is retiring effective Sept. 30. “… We lived under a deep dark cloud last year, but there were great things happening underneath. I could see that when I came in in December.”
Read more
Other updates
- The Board unanimously approved a timeline for considering a proposal from the Catawba County Board of Commissioners to merge Catawba County Schools, Hickory City Schools, and Newton-Conover City Schools into a single countywide school district. If approved, the proposed merger would take effect July 1, 2028. The Board’s vote approves the process for reviewing the proposal, not the merger itself.
- The Board heard recommendations for the 2026-27 Career and Technical Education Grade Expansion Grant Program, which helps expand CTE for sixth- and seventh-grade students. This year, 57 applications were submitted, and 25 returning grantees for awards of up to $65,000 each were recommended to receive this year’s grants.
- Dr. Charles Aiken, section chief of Math, Science, and STEM at the DPI Office of Teaching and Learning, presented the final draft of the K-12 mathematics standards. If the Board approves the standards, DPI plans a two-year installation period during the 2026-27 and 2027-28 school years, with implementation and state assessments aligned to the new standards tentatively beginning in 2028-29.
- The Board also heard a draft of the report on teacher bonuses, which attempts to understand the program’s affect on teacher bonus and retention. Teachers who received a bonus in 2024 and 2025 were most likely to receive a bonus in 2026. Read the full report here.
- Alexis Schauss, DPI’s chief financial officer, reviewed the year-end budget closeout, highlighting the unprecedented nature of the last financial year because of the lack of a comprehensive budget. Overall, less than 1.5% of the total authorized budget was reverted to the state, per the presentation.
- Eric Davis and Alan Duncan were also both reelected to their positions of chair and vice chair, respectively.
The Board will convene for it next meeting Sept. 29-Oct. 1 for the Board’s planning and work session. You can watch the livestream here.

articles.summary: After introducing a new technology in schools across Calhoun County, local dispatch gave a demonstration of how it all works.
articles.content:
Calhoun County 911 Dispatch demonstrates new technology in schools for emergencies
MARSHALL, Mich. — After introducing a new technology in schools across Calhoun County, local dispatch gave a demonstration of how it all works.
52 schools throughout the area, including all public schools and a few charter schools, are now connected to Calhoun County Consolidated Dispatch through a system known as Command Central Aware, allowing 911 dispatchers to access live security cameras during an emergency.
Dispatchers will then have access to real-time information during instances ranging from active threats, to fires, to medical emergencies, relaying it directly to first responders.
“In an emergency, it can be very chaotic. Callers may give different descriptions on their perspective or report different things,” Michael Armitage, executive director of Calhoun County 911, said. “Having the ability for the communicator now to have eyes on the scene, be able to actually see what's going on, where it's happening and then provide accurate information to the first responders, I think it's a game changer.”
The team ran through a demo from Harper Creek Schools.
In this case, a 911 call was placed from inside the school, prompting the system to automatically pull up nearby cameras and display them on every dispatcher's screen.
“This is done automatically so the telecommunicators don't have to fumble through and try to find cameras in an emergency,” Armitage said. “If they want to focus in on one camera or another, they can [also] do that.”
Before this system, dispatchers relied on a VPN to access school cameras, which was a much clunkier and slower process.
This system brings over 1,000 cameras from participating schools and puts them all into one place, and the benefits can already be seen.
“We had a school resource officer in a school dealing with an unruly student that turned aggressive and assaultive,” said Lieutenant Chris Young, Emergency Manager, Calhoun County Sheriff's Office. “When dispatch was trying to check their status, they couldn't raise her on the radio. But then they could get on the camera system and say, okay, she's all set.”
The system has been years in the making, supported by a $1.7 million grant from the U.S. Department of Justice. The project included camera installations and upgrades at schools needing additional infrastructure, along with the technology to connect school camera systems to dispatch.
The original project specifically sought to ensure smaller and rural schools could benefit from enhanced safety technology alongside larger districts.
A connection like this between schools and dispatch doesn’t exist anywhere else in the nation, said Young, and he hopes it’s something legislators and committee members look into spreading further across the county.
“It's an excellent toolkit for virtually all hazards,” Young said. “It gives the officers and responders confidence because, with the coupled system, they can take a breath. They can slow down for just a second, be able to get a picture of where the area is they need to respond to, instead of trying to go in blind with your adrenaline pumping.”
Since its launch, Armitage said other entities have already reached out expressing interest in joining the program. He said the door is open for others to do the same.

“In an emergency, it can be very chaotic. Callers may give different descriptions on their perspective or report different things,” Michael Armitage, executive director of Calhoun County 911, said. “Having the ability for the communicator now to have eyes on the scene, be able to actually see what's going on, where it's happening and then provide accurate information to the first responders, I think it's a game changer.”

The team ran through a demo from Harper Creek Schools.

In this case, a 911 call was placed from inside the school, prompting the system to automatically pull up nearby cameras and display them on every dispatcher's screen.

“This is done automatically so the telecommunicators don't have to fumble through and try to find cameras in an emergency,” Armitage said. “If they want to focus in on one camera or another, they can [also] do that.”

Before this system, dispatchers relied on a VPN to access school cameras, which was a much clunkier and slower process.

This system brings over 1,000 cameras from participating schools and puts them all into one place, and the benefits can already be seen.

“We had a school resource officer in a school dealing with an unruly student that turned aggressive and assaultive,” said Lieutenant Chris Young, Emergency Manager, Calhoun County Sheriff's Office. “When dispatch was trying to check their status, they couldn't raise her on the radio. But then they could get on the camera system and say, okay, she's all set.”

The system has been years in the making, supported by a $1.7 million grant from the U.S. Department of Justice. The project included camera installations and upgrades at schools needing additional infrastructure, along with the technology to connect school camera systems to dispatch.

The original project specifically sought to ensure smaller and rural schools could benefit from enhanced safety technology alongside larger districts.

A connection like this between schools and dispatch doesn’t exist anywhere else in the nation, said Young, and he hopes it’s something legislators and committee members look into spreading further across the county.

“It's an excellent toolkit for virtually all hazards,” Young said. “It gives the officers and responders confidence because, with the coupled system, they can take a breath. They can slow down for just a second, be able to get a picture of where the area is they need to respond to, instead of trying to go in blind with your adrenaline pumping.”

Since its launch, Armitage said other entities have already reached out expressing interest in joining the program. He said the door is open for others to do the same.

articles.description_html: Beach safety sergeant saves choking infant using Live 911 technology  WKMG
articles.article_title: Beach safety sergeant saves choking infant using Live 911 technology
articles.heading: Beach safety sergeant saves choking infant using Live 911 technology
articles.summary: A 9-month-old baby is recovering after choking on a piece of gummy candy Wednesday afternoon in Daytona Beach Shores — and a quick-thinking beach safety sergeant got there just in time.
articles.content:
VOLUSIA COUNTY, Fla. – A 9-month-old baby is recovering after choking on a piece of gummy candy Wednesday afternoon in Daytona Beach Shores — and a quick-thinking beach safety sergeant got there just in time.
Beach Safety Sgt. Derek Taylor was nearby when he heard a mother’s 911 call come in through the department’s new Live 911 system, which allows crews to hear emergency calls in real time and track their location. Even though the call was coming from a condo — not the beach — Taylor made the call to respond.
“It was a judgment call. If we have rip currents all day, I’m not necessarily going to head off the beach for a non-emergency call but when I hear it’s a choking infant I know time is of the essence and a matter of seconds can make a difference,” Taylor said.
When Taylor arrived, the mother was standing outside the condo downstairs, holding her unresponsive infant. He immediately began back slaps — a technique used to dislodge objects from an infant’s airway.
“I flipped the baby over and gave him five back slaps and when I flipped him back over, I was definitely in a nervous state as far as I know I’m about to have to do chest thrusts on this little infant but when I flipped him back over I noticed the object sitting right there in his teeth,” Taylor said.
The baby was taken to the hospital to be checked out and is expected to be okay. Beach Safety is using the incident as a reminder for parents and caregivers to take a CPR class, noting that choking response is a major part of that training.
“Everyone should take a CPR class. One of the statistics they show is that people who take a CPR class you’re going to end up doing CPR on one of your relatives more likely than you’re going to do it on somebody in the public so if you’re the only person that’s available to give CPR or some other type of life saving efforts to one of your family members, it’s good to be educated,” Taylor said.
The Live 911 system was adopted by Volusia County Beach Safety four months ago.

articles.content:
Precision Hermetic Technology cuts ribbon on Ogden operation
Rob Nielsen, Standard-Examiner
OGDEN — A company that makes small components with a big impact is getting underway with its mission in Ogden.
On Thursday, officials and employees cut the ribbon on Precision Hermetic Technology’s Ogden manufacturing plant in the Business Depot Ogden.
Precision Hermetic Technology founder, President and CEO Daniel Schachtel told the Standard-Examiner that the company started in California in 1989 but is making its way into Utah on a full-time basis.
“We manufacture electrical connectors for very high reliability applications,” he said. “We make parts that go into spacecraft, submarines and everything in between. Most of our customers use us in areas where they need a completely foolproof kind of connector that has really, really bizarre requirements.”
He said that some of these components have extremely demanding standards to live up to.
Rob Nielsen, Standard-Examiner
“We do a lot of stuff for high pressure requirements,” he said. “In fact, the highest pressure connector that we make has to withstand 115,000 pounds per square inch pressure. Which is a lot. It’s about four times the yield strength of stainless steel.”
From the defense industry to medicine, Schachtel said the company has clients in a wide range of fields.
“We started making parts of this type of support primarily military applications, a lot of space applications, oil and gas, medical — made parts for implantable medical devices,” he said. “A lot of stuff that goes in the nuclear industries.”
He said that components built by Precision Hermetic Technology have been used in Martian rovers, Blue Origin spacecraft and SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rockets.
Schachtel said that Utah is a natural fit for the company.
Rob Nielsen, Standard-Examiner
“The reason that we moved to Utah was that there’s such a pool of talented people who are all working in very similarly related businesses — businesses which, in fact, are our customers,” he said. “And that’s kind of what precipitated our move up here.”
He said that the Utah operation just received its International Organization for Standardization, or ISO, certification and that operations just got underway in the last couple of weeks — though there’s still work to be done at their new Ogden facility.
“There’s 40% of the building that’s still under construction,” he said. “So it’s going to take us another year to get all of that stuff up and running. But, again, the plan is to exit California as an entity and just have everything under the same roof over here. … This is an 80,000-square-foot building. We have hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of tons of equipment that are being moved up here. Initially, the last time I moved was 25 years ago, and I moved seven miles, and that took me a month. So, if anything, I underestimated the amount of time it was going to take to get this up and running. And also, when we first occupied this building, it was a call center for Home Depot, so turning it into a production facility was a non-obvious choice.”
Schachtel said despite the deviation from the facility’s last purpose, it still works well for their needs, even if it has created a challenge or two.
“Some of the building created some advantage for us, but it also, at the same time, kind of created some challenges because it was so different than what a regular warehouse would look like,” he said. “But what our plan here is we want to have the tightest possible controls over our environment and our processes, so the fact that it’s a 100% air-conditioned building is perfect for our needs. Because our customers are among the most demanding in the world, and we don’t like to fail them.”
Rob Nielsen, Standard-Examiner
While the new facility is starting off still under construction, he said he’s happy to get operations going in Ogden.
“I’m so excited about it,” he said. “It’s been climbing up Mount Everest.”
Other local officials are also enthusiastic about Precision Hermetic Technology’s move to Ogden.
During the ribbon cutting ceremony, Ogden City Chief Administrative Officer Taylor Nielsen said the company is a great fit for the city.
“When you have stuff that’s involved in what seems like a myriad of things from spacecraft to military stuff to medical equipment, it matched in my mind something that kept coming back, where good enough isn’t good enough,” he said. “Your guys’ failure is not an option, and that’s a great mindset that matches, especially with what we’re trying to do here at the city, where we expect and always want to see great things as they come through.”

articles.summary: The Turlock Fire Department has implemented new digital alerting technology designed to improve roadway safety and provide motorists with earlier warning when emergency vehicles are approaching or operating on scene. HAAS Alert’s Safety Cloud® works
articles.content:
The Turlock Fire Department has implemented new digital alerting technology designed to improve roadway safety and provide motorists with earlier warning when emergency vehicles are approaching or operating on scene.
HAAS Alert’s Safety Cloud® works alongside traditional emergency lights and sirens by sending real-time digital alerts through participating navigation applications and compatible vehicle systems. The added notification provides motorists with more time to recognize an approaching emergency vehicle, safely react, and make way for first responders.
Two Turlock Fire engines are currently equipped with the technology. Two additional engines currently being built for the Department will also be equipped with Safety Cloud when they are placed into service, expanding the system across more of the Department’s frontline apparatus.
“This technology gives motorists critical extra time to recognize that we’re approaching and safely react,” said Division Chief David Mallory. “With just two engines equipped, we’re already seeing how frequently these alerts are reaching drivers. Adding the technology to two more engines will expand that reach, but the message we want motorists to remember is the same: if you see lights and hear sirens, pull to the right.”
“Public safety means making sure our first responders have the tools they need to do their jobs safely and effectively,” said City Manager Dr. John J. Murphy. “This technology is another example of Turlock investing in practical solutions that strengthen emergency response and help protect both our employees and the community they serve.”
When an equipped Turlock Fire engine activates its emergency lights, Safety Cloud can automatically send an alert through participating navigation applications and compatible in-vehicle systems. According to HAAS Alert, notifications are currently available through Waze and Apple Maps, as well as compatible systems in select vehicles.
The technology can also provide advance warning when Turlock Fire crews are operating at an emergency scene along an active roadway, helping alert approaching motorists to emergency personnel and apparatus ahead.
“California law requires motorists to yield the right-of-way to approaching emergency vehicles displaying emergency lights and sounding a siren. Digital alerts provide an additional safety tool, but do not replace a driver’s responsibility to remain alert and respond appropriately to emergency vehicles. Combining new technology with greater public awareness has the potential to make our roads safer and save lives,” said Deputy Fire Chief Jeffrey Serpa.
For Turlock Fire, the public safety message remains simple: If you see lights and hear sirens, pull to the right.
The Turlock Fire Department will continue expanding the use of Safety Cloud as its two new engines are completed and placed into service.

articles.summary: NVIDIA, Amazon, Palantir, Dell and Fortinet stand out as founder-run companies with strong vision, innovation and long-term growth drivers.
articles.content:

An updated edition of the July 20, 2026, article. Founders often leave a lasting imprint on the companies they create, influencing strategy, culture and long-term priorities. Their conviction and personal commitment can make them more willing to take calculated risks, operate through uncertainty and pursue opportunities that professional managers might dismiss. As these businesses frequently reflect the founder's values and vision, they can develop an identity that supports sustained growth. Today, roughly 11% of large-cap U.S. companies are founder-led. Although founder-led businesses represent less than 5% of the S&P 500, their economic influence is far greater. Entrepreneurs such as Elon Musk, Warren Buffett, Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates have transformed industries and created some of the world's most valuable companies. NVIDIA NVDA, Amazon AMZN, Meta Platforms, Tesla, Berkshire Hathaway, Alphabet and Netflix highlight the perseverance of founder-driven leadership. Collectively, these companies make up nearly 15% of the S&P 500's market capitalization, with technology businesses forming the largest share. Many founder-led enterprises begin with innovative ideas tied to technological advancement and market demand. In their early years, founders often face skepticism from investors and rely on personal savings or bootstrapping before attracting outside capital. Even as their companies grow, many maintain meaningful ownership positions, helping align their interests and strategic decisions closely with those of long-term shareholders. Founder-led companies are not without risks. Founders may resist delegating authority and assume several roles to retain control over their original vision. Although such involvement can maintain strategic focus, it may hinder expansion and prevent companies from fully benefiting from specialized talent. Even so, founder-led businesses have often delivered stronger returns than their peers. According to a Motley Fool report, publicly traded companies still run by their founders generated average annual returns of 25% over the past decade versus 14% for the S&P 500. Our Founder-Run Companies Screen makes it easy to identify high-potential stocks. Currently, stocks like NVIDIA, Amazon, Palantir Technologies PLTR, Dell Technologies DELL and Fortinet, Inc . FTNT look appealing. Ready to uncover more transformative thematic investment ideas? Explore 37 cutting-edge investment themes with Zacks Thematic Screens and discover your next big opportunity.

5 Founder-Run Companies to Add to Your Portfolio

NVIDIA , with a market capitalization of approximately $5.5 trillion, is a global leader in visual computing and the pioneer of the graphics processing unit (GPU). NVIDIA, once best known for its dominance in PC graphics, has successfully expanded into artificial intelligence-driven technologies powering high-performance computing, gaming, and immersive virtual environments. CEO Jensen Huang emphasizes that accelerated computing and generative AI are reshaping not only the tech sector but industries across the globe. The company has leveraged this transformation to build multiple billion-dollar businesses in areas such as gaming, healthcare, automotive and robotics. NVIDIA continues to benefit from broad demand for accelerated computing as customers build AI factories across hyperscalers, AI clouds, enterprises and sovereign buyers. Blackwell Ultra is supporting growth while Vera Rubin broadens the platform across GPUs, CPUs, networking and software. A key driver of NVIDIA's growth is its data center segment. As enterprises increasingly adopt cloud-based infrastructure, demand for data centers continues to surge worldwide. Major cloud providers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet are rapidly expanding their capacity, fueling strong and sustained demand for NVIDIA's cutting-edge GPU technologies. NVDA currently carries a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank stocks here. Amazon , with a market capitalization of approximately $2.8 trillion, is one of the largest e-commerce providers, with sprawling operations in North America, now spreading across the globe. Its online retail business revolves around the Prime program, well-supported by the company's massive distribution network. Jeff Bezos, the founder, serves as the executive chairman. Continued investments in AI, logistics automation and cloud infrastructure position Amazon to capitalize on secular growth across industries. Its vast ecosystem strengthens customer retention and network effects, creating significant competitive barriers. Expansion into emerging international markets offers additional e-commerce growth opportunities, while diversification across AWS, advertising and streaming broadens revenue sources and reduces dependence on retail. For the third quarter of 2026, Amazon expects net sales between $197 billion and $202 billion, indicating growth of 9% to 12% compared with the third quarter of 2025. Improving operating efficiency and a growing contribution from higher-margin businesses should support margin expansion, earnings growth and attractive long-term shareholder returns. It carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). Palantir Technologies , currently valued at roughly $438.6 billion, develops advanced software platforms for intelligence, defense, and enterprise operations. Founded in 2003 by Alex Karp, Peter Thiel, Stephen Cohen and Joe Lonsdale, the company has become a key technology partner for the U.S. intelligence and defense communities. Karp currently serves as executive chairman. Palantir's AI strategy is built around its core platforms, Foundry and Gotham, which support mission-critical operations and advanced analytics. Unlike many AI competitors still operating in pilot phases, Palantir has focused on delivering scalable, production-ready solutions. Its emphasis on practical AI deployment—including autonomous agents and integrated operational systems—has helped establish a strong competitive edge in both government and commercial markets. The company has also strengthened its standing through close alignment with U.S. defense priorities, reinforcing its reputation as a trusted national security partner. Its modular sales model allows customers to adopt individual platform components before committing fully, reducing implementation barriers and supporting growth in the U.S. commercial sector. Additionally, this Zacks Rank #2 company promotes enterprise AI adoption through AIP boot camps that provide hands-on demonstrations and training for prospective clients. For 2026, Palantir projects revenues between $8.15 billion and $8.158 billion. Dell Technologies , with a market capitalization of approximately $333.7 billion, is a global leader in servers, storage systems, and personal computers. Founded by Michael Dell, the company is well-positioned to benefit from renewed demand tied to the ongoing PC refresh cycle. Dell serves enterprise customers across on-premise, cloud, and edge environments with a broad portfolio of infrastructure solutions. Its advanced storage offerings, including PowerProtect Data Domain and PowerScale, incorporate AI-driven ransomware detection capabilities that enhance cybersecurity and operational resilience. The company has also emerged as a major supplier of AI-optimized servers and data center infrastructure, supported by rising enterprise demand for AI training and inference workloads. This Zacks Rank #1 company continues to benefit from sustained AI infrastructure demand as customers secure capacity and modernize data centers. Its broad portfolio across AI servers, traditional compute, storage and commercial PCs supports share gains and gives Dell several avenues for growth. Its expanding lineup of AI-focused servers, combined with strategic partnerships with NVIDIA and AMD, further strengthens its position in the AI infrastructure market. Strong cash generation and disciplined capital allocation also reflect the company's healthy financial profile. Management raised fiscal 2027 revenue outlook by $25 billion to $192 billion, plus or minus $2 billion, and lifted non-GAAP earnings guidance to $25.50 per share, plus or minus 25 cents. Fortinet , with a market capitalization of approximately $114.7 billion, is a leader in cybersecurity, driving the convergence of networking and security. Ken Xie is the co-founder, chairman, and chief executive officer of Fortinet, which he established alongside Michael Xie. Fortinet's strong product roadmap, built on FortiOS 8.0, AI-driven security, next-generation SASE, quantum-safe capabilities and new FortiGate 3500G/400G firewalls, positions the company to capitalize on escalating cybersecurity demands throughout 2026. The network security market is experiencing structural expansion as enterprises prioritize AI, OT, edge security, SASE, cloud protection and vendor consolidation, creating substantial growth runway for Fortinet in 2026. Organizations replacing point solutions with consolidated security frameworks generate larger deal sizes and recurring revenue opportunities. The shift toward subscription-based security consumption models aligns with Fortinet's business transformation. Fortinet's ongoing investments in sales capacity, cloud infrastructure, and proprietary ASIC development are translating into meaningful operating leverage. It sports a Zacks Rank #1. Fortinet raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $8.02-$8.18 billion, implying about 19% growth, and its non-GAAP EPS outlook to $3.41-$3.47. This Zacks Rank #1 company is well-poised for long-term balanced growth with strong cash generation, recurring revenues and a shareholder-focused long-term growth capital allocation strategy, banking on the combination of AI-driven security demand, an integrated and accelerated SASE Firewall platform solution and a strong operating model position.

articles.article_title: CLAAS expands harvesting portfolio with new technology | An official publication of Michigan Farm Bureau
articles.heading: CLAAS expands harvesting portfolio with new technology
articles.summary: A leading manufacturer an agricultural machinery is expanding its harvesting portfolio to include new headers, tedders, intelligent automation systems and precision technologies.
articles.content:
A global manufacturer of agricultural machinery is expanding its harvesting portfolio to include new headers, tedders, intelligent automation systems and precision technologies.
CLAAS of America’s new offering ranges from forage and grain harvesting to hay tools, designed to help producers maximize throughput, improve crop quality and make more informed decisions about their entire operation.
"Innovation starts with listening to our customers," said Dennis Ogle, head of sales for self-propelled harvesters.
"Every product we're introducing reflects our commitment to North American producers and the way they farm, bringing together advanced technology, proven performance and practical solutions that help them operate more efficiently every day."
Expanding forage harvesting efficiency
CLAAS continues to expand its JAGUAR forage harvesting portfolio with new headers and intelligent automation designed to maximize throughput, improve crop quality and help operators get the most from every harvesting window.
The ORBIS 12000 is a new 16-row corn header engineered specifically for CLAAS JAGUAR 1000 series forage harvester. Designed to keep the industry's highest-capacity forage harvester operating at peak productivity, the ORBIS 12000 delivers smooth crop flow, exceptional throughput and the flexibility to perform across a wide range of crop conditions.
Also joining the JAGUAR 1000 series lineup is the DD 8400 Direct Disc header, featuring a 27.5-foot working width for efficient whole-crop harvesting. The header delivers excellent ground following and consistent crop flow to deliver clean cutting performance while maximizing forage quality and machine productivity.
CLAAS is also introducing CEMOS AUTO KNIFE CONDITION, an intelligent automation system that continuously monitors harvesting conditions and determines the optimal time and number of sharpening passes needed to maintain peak knife performance. By automating the sharpening process, the system helps reduce knife wear and fuel consumption while maintaining consistent chop quality and maximizing harvesting capacity. The result is greater productivity and more consistent performance throughout the harvest season, regardless of operator experience.
Added intelligence for combine harvesting
New CLAAS combine harvesting accessories, and precision technologies have been designed to help producers maximize throughput, protect grain quality and make more informed decisions.
Leading the lineup is the ROVIO 5 Series, a corn head designed and manufactured exclusively by CLAAS. Engineered to integrate seamlessly with LEXION and TRION combines, it features a redesigned picking system, larger intake auger and integrated horizontal choppers that deliver smoother crop flow, increased throughput and cleaner residue management across a wide range of harvest conditions. The head is offered in 12-, 16-, and 18-row models with 30 in. row spacing.
READ NEXT: CORN SILAGE HARVEST: TIMING, PACKING REQUIREMENTS FOR MAXIMUM BUTRIENT RETENTION
To complement to the ROVIO 5 head, both CLAAS combine lines in 2027 offer an electronic machine optimization system designed exclusively for corn crops. CEMOS Corn continuously optimizes combine performance as conditions change throughout the day. The intelligent automation system automatically adjusts machine settings for corn to help maximize grain quality, minimize grain loss and maintain peak harvesting efficiency, allowing operators to spend less time making manual adjustments and more time focused on the harvest.
Once the grain has entered the machine, the new NUTRIMETER GRAIN system--available on LEXION series combines--provides operators with real-time insights using advanced transmissive near-infrared (NIR) technology. Without stopping the combine, operators can continuously measure moisture, protein and other key crop characteristics. The information is automatically captured within CLAAS connect, providing valuable harvest data that supports grain marketing, crop management and future agronomic decisions.
Hay and forage innovation
CLAAS is also expanding the middle range of its hay and forage implement offering with three new VOLTO T series tedders with working widths ranging from 25 feet 3 inches to 35 feet 5 inches and the proven MAX SPREAD crop concept, engineered to deliver faster, more uniform crop drying through gentle crop handling, excellent ground following and high-output performance. The latest model offering includes the 25-foot, 3-inch VOLTO 800 TH, the 28-foot, 6-inch VOLTO 900 T, and 35-foot, 5-inch VOLTO 1100 T.
The latest models offer a new power train with hermetically sealed rotor gearboxes, a new rotor wheel mounting with a reinforced rotor shaft and new spreading angle adjustment for angles of up to 18 degrees. The range boasts reduced hydraulic requirements, KENNFIXX couplings for all hydraulic connections and PERMALINK HD finger clutches passed down from larger models.
By helping producers preserve forage quality while improving field efficiency, the latest VOLTO models complement the company's growing lineup of harvesting solutions designed to maximize throughput, crop quality and overall productivity from the first cut through harvest.
These new harvesting technologies complement the next generation of CLAAS equipment, reflecting the company's continued investment in helping producers meet the growing demands of modern agriculture.
"Every product we've introduced was engineered with one purpose in mind: helping our customers do more," Ogle said.
"More acres in a day. More confidence in every decision. More value from every harvest. That's what made for more means, and that's the standard we're committed to delivering."

Designed to keep the industry's highest-capacity forage harvester operating at peak productivity, the ORBIS 12000 delivers smooth crop flow, exceptional throughput and the flexibility to perform across a wide range of crop conditions.

Also joining the JAGUAR 1000 series lineup is the DD 8400 Direct Disc header, featuring a 27.5-foot working width for efficient whole-crop harvesting. The header delivers excellent ground following and consistent crop flow to deliver clean cutting performance while maximizing forage quality and machine productivity.

CLAAS is also introducing CEMOS AUTO KNIFE CONDITION, an intelligent automation system that continuously monitors harvesting conditions and determines the optimal time and number of sharpening passes needed to maintain peak knife performance. By automating the sharpening process, the system helps reduce knife wear and fuel consumption while maintaining consistent chop quality and maximizing harvesting capacity. The result is greater productivity and more consistent performance throughout the harvest season, regardless of operator experience.

Added intelligence for combine harvesting

New CLAAS combine harvesting accessories, and precision technologies have been designed to help producers maximize throughput, protect grain quality and make more informed decisions.

Leading the lineup is the ROVIO 5 Series, a corn head designed and manufactured exclusively by CLAAS. Engineered to integrate seamlessly with LEXION and TRION combines, it features a redesigned picking system, larger intake auger and integrated horizontal choppers that deliver smoother crop flow, increased throughput and cleaner residue management across a wide range of harvest conditions. The head is offered in 12-, 16-, and 18-row models with 30 in. row spacing.

READ NEXT: CORN SILAGE HARVEST: TIMING, PACKING REQUIREMENTS FOR MAXIMUM BUTRIENT RETENTION

To complement to the ROVIO 5 head, both CLAAS combine lines in 2027 offer an electronic machine optimization system designed exclusively for corn crops. CEMOS Corn continuously optimizes combine performance as conditions change throughout the day. The intelligent automation system automatically adjusts machine settings for corn to help maximize grain quality, minimize grain loss and maintain peak harvesting efficiency, allowing operators to spend less time making manual adjustments and more time focused on the harvest.

Once the grain has entered the machine, the new NUTRIMETER GRAIN system--available on LEXION series combines--provides operators with real-time insights using advanced transmissive near-infrared (NIR) technology. Without stopping the combine, operators can continuously measure moisture, protein and other key crop characteristics. The information is automatically captured within CLAAS connect, providing valuable harvest data that supports grain marketing, crop management and future agronomic decisions.

Hay and forage innovation

CLAAS is also expanding the middle range of its hay and forage implement offering with three new VOLTO T series tedders with working widths ranging from 25 feet 3 inches to 35 feet 5 inches and the proven MAX SPREAD crop concept, engineered to deliver faster, more uniform crop drying through gentle crop handling, excellent ground following and high-output performance. The latest model offering includes the 25-foot, 3-inch VOLTO 800 TH, the 28-foot, 6-inch VOLTO 900 T, and 35-foot, 5-inch VOLTO 1100 T.

The latest models offer a new power train with hermetically sealed rotor gearboxes, a new rotor wheel mounting with a reinforced rotor shaft and new spreading angle adjustment for angles of up to 18 degrees. The range boasts reduced hydraulic requirements, KENNFIXX couplings for all hydraulic connections and PERMALINK HD finger clutches passed down from larger models.

By helping producers preserve forage quality while improving field efficiency, the latest VOLTO models complement the company's growing lineup of harvesting solutions designed to maximize throughput, crop quality and overall productivity from the first cut through harvest.

These new harvesting technologies complement the next generation of CLAAS equipment, reflecting the company's continued investment in helping producers meet the growing demands of modern agriculture.

"Every product we've introduced was engineered with one purpose in mind: helping our customers do more," Ogle said.

"More acres in a day. More confidence in every decision. More value from every harvest. That's what made for more means, and that's the standard we're committed to delivering."

articles.article_title: OpenAI Wants to Talk About The Federalist Papers
articles.heading: OpenAI Wants to Talk About The Federalist Papers
articles.summary: The AI giant is worried about what all-powerful bots could mean for our constitutional rights.
articles.content:
OpenAI Wants to Talk About The Federalist Papers
The AI giant is worried about what all-powerful bots could mean for our constitutional rights.
Late last month, OpenAI launched a rather grand mission: nothing less than defending individual political freedom in an age of all-powerful machines. The company’s “Strategic Futures” team has styled itself, in a sense, as inheriting the task of America’s Founding Fathers: “We labor in service of the ideals of free expression and individual liberty that are enshrined in the humble parchment of the U.S. Constitution,” Dean Ball, the team’s leader, wrote in a new OpenAI blog post. (The post opens with a quote from James Madison in The Federalist Papers.)
Ball worries that advanced AI could radically concentrate power in the hands of those who control it, displacing labor in ways that disempower humans. In an extreme scenario, governments will have no need to listen to their citizens if there are robots to wage wars and omniscient software to run the bureaucracy. Ball is interested in studying what new political institutions might be needed to avoid this fate.
Many Americans—a majority of whom express distrust toward the AI industry, outrage about data centers, and fears about their job security—already seem to be feeling this loss of agency very deeply. And the AI boom has already generated enormous amounts of wealth in just a handful of tech companies—including OpenAI itself. To say the least, it’s paradoxical for one of the most influential companies in the world’s most powerful industry to decry the AI-enabled concentration of power. So I reached out to Ball to understand more about his unease about the industry he works in, and how he wants to see the United States adapt to AI.
Ball, who studies AI policy, is something of a minor celebrity in the industry. Last year, he joined the White House as an AI adviser and helped write the Trump administration’s AI Action Plan, a policy road map for the technology. He eventually departed, seemingly on good terms, from the administration before publicly lambasting it during its dispute with Anthropic earlier this year. Then, in July, he joined OpenAI. “My view is that we basically have transformative AI in the world now,” Ball told me. “You’re living in a world that is being transformed. It is happening.”
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
Matteo Wong: You write that concentration of power through AI could upend the basic human freedoms enshrined in the U.S. Constitution. Can you elaborate on how?
Dean Ball: Fundamentally, political power is the geographically bounded ability to wield the monopoly on legitimate force and violence. Doing so has heretofore required the cooperation of a great many human beings. You needed militaries, you needed people in those militaries, and you needed people to keep those militaries fed and supplied. And you needed people to pay for all of that through taxation. So people had a seat at the table because, in some sense, everything is being provided by them.
Now you have to assume that robotics is going to advance soon in the same way that general digital intelligence has. Maybe it will take longer than I think. But at that point, the ability to project violence no longer requires people. And it is also conceivable that AI might generate sufficient revenue that the government would not need to rely on taxing people.
If you look at the politics of AI, I think Americans are smart and have a sense that their seat at the table might be getting smaller. They’re right to be scared.
Wong: You’re talking about concentration of power in the government, but generative AI is a technology developed in the private sector. There is potential for a rare and even unprecedented concentration of power in industry. What risks does that pose?
Ball: You’re not trying to avoid all concentration of power, but to balance it. If this era gives rise to corporations that have a tremendous amount of power in the world, I think that’s good—so long as those organizations are governed. In other words, so long as the government that oversees them grows in lockstep.
People tend to assume that AI residing in private hands is inherently a concentration-of-power risk. But I think that an extremely well-run, government-owned superintelligence lab is a bigger concentration-of-power risk than a polycentric world where there are many superintelligences made by different, competing companies overseen by a government. Monopolies are the concern.
Wong: As far as private concentration of power goes, there are arguably now two frontier labs, your employer and Anthropic. The market doesn’t seem to be providing many checks on them.
Ball: I think it’s a fiercely competitive market right now. And China, of course, is delivering highly capable open-source models. It’s possible this is going to commodify the products that OpenAI and Anthropic offer. I don’t agree with that, but you can’t dismiss it as a crazy outcome. OpenAI’s mission is to deliver artificial general intelligence safely to the world. If that means we’re more like a utility than we are like a big, fancy tech company, so be it.
Wong: This brings us to the core of your essay. If today’s political institutions and market dynamics are not up to the task of protecting human freedom during an AI era, what must change?
Ball: There are AI regulations that I think are sensible to pass. States have passed hundreds of laws about artificial intelligence, and those things are not satisfying the demands of people. What we will need is new political institutions that give us a way of talking about the rate of acceleration in our society.
I’m imagining a federal body could dictate the ratio that an AI lab is allowed to spend on internal deployment of models to do automated AI research. You could say that, this month, you’re going to be allowed to use 45 percent of your compute for that, and next month, it’ll be 47 percent or 52 percent or some other number. That might slow the rate of AI development, but then a company could use that extra compute to lower costs for consumers. Then this dial for AI development would also become a mechanism with the dual effect of slowing or increasing the rate of technological diffusion.
The closest structural analogy that we have is probably interest rates, which is a kind of hyper-parameter on the economy that policy makers can tune. The Federal Reserve is an institution in and of itself, and on top of that, there is an enormous apparatus that exists, including a bond market, interest-rate traders, analysts, media commentary, political oversight in the form of Congress. All of that taken together, in my view, would constitute the institutional complex. That’s a type of political institution. I’m not saying we need to create a new branch of government or something.
Wong: That makes sense regarding the pace of development and diffusion. I’m not totally following how such a measure ties back to your concerns about human freedoms.
Ball: It’s one example of an institution that would give people a sense of meaningful political control over the technology. However, I do not think that the optimal outcome is one in which we take a vote on every single aspect of technological change. I’m not really a fan of data-center moratoria, but I understand that the American public is pulling a lever, and they think it is the one lever they have.
Wong: What role can OpenAI, Anthropic, and the rest of the industry play in trying to imagine these institutions and bring them into existence?
Ball: I think the AI industry has actually been pretty good stewards, all things considered. No surprise that I’m saying this, because I’m from the AI industry, but there’s a reason that I am working in it. I would not say that every frontier AI company always has performed at 100 percent, by no means. But in the future, we may approach points where more costly things have to occur. The AI industry might have to do things that are not in its interest.
Wong: Does your research agenda extend to economic freedoms—that is, how AI could affect the economy and distribution of wealth?
Ball: The main thing we know how to do on that front is to invest in technological innovation and try to grow the economy by making new things possible.
Wong: I think a lot of people would look at past products and technologies that have come out of Silicon Valley and think that what those enabled was a tremendous concentration of wealth and influence in a small number of companies—
Ball: I’m not going to grant you that characterization of Silicon Valley. Has everything been perfect? Absolutely not. But my goodness, people have access to tremendous riches of information now; you can cause food to appear at your doorstep, which would have seemed like magic to the vast majority of humans who have ever lived.
Wong: I could also point to the gig economy and the economics of Amazon and argue that those have not been good for a lot of people, including those who labor to make all that “magic” happen. It’s not magic.
Ball: No one’s saying it’s magic. I’m saying it’s hard work. I was getting gas in rural Virginia recently, and when a woman came in wearing an Amazon vest, everyone congratulated her on the big new job. She was proud, and I don’t think we should belittle people for that.
And by the way, people like you, Matteo—not to demonize you—will speak out of both sides of your mouth on this. On the one hand, you’ll talk about how the gig economy is dehumanizing, and blah blah blah. But then the second anyone tries to introduce any autonomy into that and have, say, drone deliveries instead of people biking all around cities delivering meals, you’ll say, My God, you’re taking away the work from this gig economy.
I’m less than thrilled by our current world, like everyone. But the existence of wealth is good. Innovators capture a shockingly small amount of the value that they create in society. If OpenAI is a fantastically successful company 10 years from now, a generational company, my bet is that we will capture a single-digit fraction of the value that AGI creates in this world. Wealth is not some resource that we divide up; it’s something we create. That’s the magic.
Wong: But wealth is also something that’s divided up. One could alternatively look at generative AI and think of it as a particularly wealth-concentrating technology. To ask again, is wealth distribution something your team is thinking about?
Ball: I don’t think we should invent a solution in search of a problem. So we shouldn’t invent some elaborate mechanism of wealth redistribution if today’s tax system works out. But we also have to prepare for a world in which that isn’t true.

articles.article_title: 11 Questions for Evaluating Security Technology at GSX 2026
articles.heading: 11 Questions for Evaluating Security Technology at GSX 2026
articles.summary: Security leaders can use the GSX show floor to look beyond product features and assess operational value, interoperability, supportability and long-term fit.
articles.content:
11 Questions for Evaluating Security Technology at GSX 2026
Walking the GSX show floor provides an opportunity to see hundreds of security technology offerings in a very short time. The challenge isn’t finding interesting products. It’s determining which ones can meaningfully improve your security operations and fit into the larger technology and organizational environment in which they must function.
That requires looking beyond features.
Today’s security technologies increasingly operate as parts of larger systems of systems. AI-enabled products can provide new forms of detection, analysis and situational awareness. Specialized products can add capabilities to existing systems without requiring their replacement. Integration can combine technologies into greater capability, while orchestration can establish how technologies, information, people and workflows function together to achieve operational objectives.
At the same time, acquiring and deploying technology does not automatically make an organization ready to put it fully to work. Operational readiness, supportability, cybersecurity, privacy, governance and lifecycle management all affect the value ultimately obtained.
With those perspectives in mind, here are some questions worth taking onto the GSX show floor.
Questions to ask
1. OPERATIONAL VALUE. What specifically will your solution enable our security organization to do more effectively that we cannot do — or cannot do well — today?
Product demonstrations naturally focus on features and functionality. Bring the conversation back to operational improvement. Ask what changes for security personnel, security operations and the organization when the technology is put to work.
2. RISK SCENARIOS. What specific security risk scenarios does your solution address, and how does it change detection, assessment, response or recovery for those scenarios?
A useful answer should go beyond listing product functions. Ask what happens today without the capability, what happens with it, and how the difference improves the security outcome.
3. OPERATIONAL READINESS. What must we have in place — people, processes, training, configuration, information and assigned responsibilities — to put this technology fully to work?
Technology deployment and technology operationalization are not the same thing. A successful installation can still fall short of its potential if the organization isn’t prepared to operate and sustain the resulting capabilities.
For more on this distinction, see my recent SecurityInfoWatch article, “Operationalizing Security Technologies.”
4. ORGANIZATIONAL CAPABILITY. What sustainable organizational security capability will this technology help us establish or improve?
Look beyond what the product itself can do. Consider what the organization will become capable of doing consistently because the technology, people, processes and information have been put together effectively.
5. NATIVE INTEROPERABILITY. What other technologies does your solution interoperate with natively, and what information and functions can they exchange without custom integration work?
A specialized product doesn’t have to be an isolated product. A Natively Interoperable Point Solution can provide highly specialized functionality while being designed from the outset to participate in a larger multi-vendor technology environment.
Ask what works out of the box, what requires configuration, and what requires middleware, custom development or professional services. Don’t stop at “We have an API.”
6. ORCHESTRATION. How can your technology participate in coordinated workflows involving other technologies, information and people?
Can events or information from the product trigger actions in other systems? Can other systems trigger actions in this one? Ask the vendor to describe a complete operational workflow rather than simply naming systems with which the product integrates.
Integration combines systems into greater capability. Orchestration establishes how technologies, information, people and workflows function together to achieve operational objectives.
For more on that distinction, see “Why Orchestration is the Next Step Beyond Integration.”
7. EXISTING SYSTEM VALUE. How can your solution add capabilities to technologies we already have rather than requiring their replacement?
Many organizations have substantial investments in deployed physical security technology. New technology should be evaluated not only for what it can replace, but also for what additional capabilities it can bring to what is already there.
This question can be especially important when evaluating specialized AI analytics, identity and access technologies, sensing technologies, cloud services and other focused offerings.
8. OPERATIONAL SUPPORTABILITY. How easily can our staff and integrator configure, monitor, troubleshoot and recover the solution?
Ask to see the audit trails, event logs and diagnostic tools available for troubleshooting. For integrations, can you determine whether information was sent, received and acted upon as intended? Can configurations be backed up and restored? Can a known-good configuration be recovered after a failure or problematic change?
Also ask: Do you have a publicly available product knowledge base that I can examine? Look for configuration, integration, cybersecurity, troubleshooting and lifecycle-management guidance.
An integration isn’t fully supportable if you can’t readily determine what happened when it doesn’t work as expected.
9. AI OPERATIONAL IMPACT AND GOVERNANCE. Where AI is involved, what does it actually improve, and what must we do to govern its use?
Ask what AI improves: detection, situational awareness, decision-making, response time, operator workload, reporting or some other operational outcome. Then ask who develops and maintains the AI models, how updates are validated, what information the AI uses, and what human oversight is required.
The important question isn’t simply, “Does it use AI?” It is what the AI contributes and what responsibilities come with using it.
10. CYBERSECURITY, PRIVACY AND DATA GOVERNANCE. What protections and controls are built into the product, and what responsibilities remain with us?
Ask about identity and access controls, encryption, digital certificates, security updates, vulnerability management and product security documentation. For systems that collect, analyze, retain or exchange sensitive information, ask what privacy controls are available and how data retention, access, sharing and deletion can be governed.
Don’t settle for “Our product is secure” or “We support privacy.” Ask to see the controls and documentation.
11. LIFECYCLE AND SCALE. What will it take to manage and sustain this technology across our intended deployment over its useful life?
Ask how devices and applications are inventoried, configured, monitored, updated and supported at scale. How are firmware and software updates handled? How long will cybersecurity patches and product support be provided? What happens as the deployment grows from a pilot to dozens, hundreds or thousands of devices, users or sites?
A technology that is easy to demonstrate or pilot may be very different to own at enterprise scale.
Look beyond the product
GSX exhibitors have limited time to demonstrate increasingly capable technologies, so naturally their presentations focus on what their products can do. Your job is to consider something larger: what can your organization accomplish with them?
