11 Questions for Evaluating Security Technology at GSX 2026

Walking the GSX show floor provides an opportunity to see hundreds of security technology offerings in a very short time. The challenge isn’t finding interesting products. It’s determining which ones can meaningfully improve your security operations and fit into the larger technology and organizational environment in which they must function.

That requires looking beyond features.

Today’s security technologies increasingly operate as parts of larger systems of systems. AI-enabled products can provide new forms of detection, analysis and situational awareness. Specialized products can add capabilities to existing systems without requiring their replacement. Integration can combine technologies into greater capability, while orchestration can establish how technologies, information, people and workflows function together to achieve operational objectives.

At the same time, acquiring and deploying technology does not automatically make an organization ready to put it fully to work. Operational readiness, supportability, cybersecurity, privacy, governance and lifecycle management all affect the value ultimately obtained.

With those perspectives in mind, here are some questions worth taking onto the GSX show floor.

AI delivers the greatest value when it helps security teams make sense of information, communicate shared understanding and translate decisions into consistent action.

Questions to ask

1. OPERATIONAL VALUE. What specifically will your solution enable our security organization to do more effectively that we cannot do — or cannot do well — today?

Product demonstrations naturally focus on features and functionality. Bring the conversation back to operational improvement. Ask what changes for security personnel, security operations and the organization when the technology is put to work.

2. RISK SCENARIOS. What specific security risk scenarios does your solution address, and how does it change detection, assessment, response or recovery for those scenarios?

A useful answer should go beyond listing product functions. Ask what happens today without the capability, what happens with it, and how the difference improves the security outcome.

3. OPERATIONAL READINESS. What must we have in place — people, processes, training, configuration, information and assigned responsibilities — to put this technology fully to work?

Technology deployment and technology operationalization are not the same thing. A successful installation can still fall short of its potential if the organization isn’t prepared to operate and sustain the resulting capabilities.

For more on this distinction, see my recent SecurityInfoWatch article, “Operationalizing Security Technologies.”

4. ORGANIZATIONAL CAPABILITY. What sustainable organizational security capability will this technology help us establish or improve?

Look beyond what the product itself can do. Consider what the organization will become capable of doing consistently because the technology, people, processes and information have been put together effectively.

5. NATIVE INTEROPERABILITY. What other technologies does your solution interoperate with natively, and what information and functions can they exchange without custom integration work?

A specialized product doesn’t have to be an isolated product. A Natively Interoperable Point Solution can provide highly specialized functionality while being designed from the outset to participate in a larger multi-vendor technology environment.

Ask what works out of the box, what requires configuration, and what requires middleware, custom development or professional services. Don’t stop at “We have an API.”

6. ORCHESTRATION. How can your technology participate in coordinated workflows involving other technologies, information and people?

Can events or information from the product trigger actions in other systems? Can other systems trigger actions in this one? Ask the vendor to describe a complete operational workflow rather than simply naming systems with which the product integrates.

Integration combines systems into greater capability. Orchestration establishes how technologies, information, people and workflows function together to achieve operational objectives.

For more on that distinction, see “Why Orchestration is the Next Step Beyond Integration.”

7. EXISTING SYSTEM VALUE. How can your solution add capabilities to technologies we already have rather than requiring their replacement?

Many organizations have substantial investments in deployed physical security technology. New technology should be evaluated not only for what it can replace, but also for what additional capabilities it can bring to what is already there.

This question can be especially important when evaluating specialized AI analytics, identity and access technologies, sensing technologies, cloud services and other focused offerings.

8. OPERATIONAL SUPPORTABILITY. How easily can our staff and integrator configure, monitor, troubleshoot and recover the solution?

Ask to see the audit trails, event logs and diagnostic tools available for troubleshooting. For integrations, can you determine whether information was sent, received and acted upon as intended? Can configurations be backed up and restored? Can a known-good configuration be recovered after a failure or problematic change?

Also ask: Do you have a publicly available product knowledge base that I can examine? Look for configuration, integration, cybersecurity, troubleshooting and lifecycle-management guidance.

An integration isn’t fully supportable if you can’t readily determine what happened when it doesn’t work as expected.

9. AI OPERATIONAL IMPACT AND GOVERNANCE. Where AI is involved, what does it actually improve, and what must we do to govern its use?

Ask what AI improves: detection, situational awareness, decision-making, response time, operator workload, reporting or some other operational outcome. Then ask who develops and maintains the AI models, how updates are validated, what information the AI uses, and what human oversight is required.

The important question isn’t simply, “Does it use AI?” It is what the AI contributes and what responsibilities come with using it.

10. CYBERSECURITY, PRIVACY AND DATA GOVERNANCE. What protections and controls are built into the product, and what responsibilities remain with us?

Ask about identity and access controls, encryption, digital certificates, security updates, vulnerability management and product security documentation. For systems that collect, analyze, retain or exchange sensitive information, ask what privacy controls are available and how data retention, access, sharing and deletion can be governed.

Don’t settle for “Our product is secure” or “We support privacy.” Ask to see the controls and documentation.

11. LIFECYCLE AND SCALE. What will it take to manage and sustain this technology across our intended deployment over its useful life?

Ask how devices and applications are inventoried, configured, monitored, updated and supported at scale. How are firmware and software updates handled? How long will cybersecurity patches and product support be provided? What happens as the deployment grows from a pilot to dozens, hundreds or thousands of devices, users or sites?

A technology that is easy to demonstrate or pilot may be very different to own at enterprise scale.

articles.article_title: Humanoid Robots and China’s Vision of the Future
articles.heading: Humanoid Robots and China’s Vision of the Future
articles.summary: China’s humanoid robots are more than a showcase of state ambition. They reveal how differently we interpret visions of the technological future depending on who builds them.
articles.content:
The robots lined up on the track. For a moment, it looked almost like an ordinary athletics meet. Then the race started. The machines lurched forward, their metal legs struggling to keep their balance as they sprinted toward the finish line. One of them, a Chinese humanoid robot called Tiangong Ultra, finished the 100 meters in 8.64 seconds – faster than Usain Bolt’s human world record.
The scene took place this August at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, where more than 2,000 robots competed in 51 events. Some ran and boxed. Others performed household chores or industrial tasks. Some simply fell over. It was part sporting event, part technology demonstration, and part vision of the future.
And the way that future was described was revealing. In Western coverage, the event was often framed as a spectacle, a demonstration of Chinese state power or even propaganda.
Chinese state media had a different emphasis. The focus was less on the event itself and more on what the robots might eventually do: work in factories, move through warehouses, assist in homes or become part of everyday life.
Neither interpretation is necessarily wrong. Beijing clearly wants to showcase China’s technological progress, and the World Humanoid Robot Games was designed to do exactly that. But the difference in emphasis is striking. The same robots can be seen as a technological achievement, an industrial strategy, or a piece of political theater. Reducing the event to the latter risks missing what is happening on the technological side.
China’s humanoid robotics industry is not simply a governmental display. The country has invested heavily in the sector, and Chinese companies are developing robots for factories, logistics, healthcare, and other commercial applications. The Robot Games are part of that broader strategy. They are designed not only to show what robots can do, but also to test how they might be used outside the laboratory.
That does not make the games any less political. Beijing has made technological development a national priority, and events like this clearly serve that ambition. But political purpose and technological progress can exist at the same time. Calling the event propaganda makes it easier to stop looking at the technology itself. The political message then becomes more important than what is actually being built.
China is not the only place where technology comes with a vision of the future. In the United States, Silicon Valley has been selling such visions for years. Autonomous cars, AI assistants and humanoid robots have all been presented not simply as products, but as glimpses of a different way of living and working. Tesla, for example, presents its Optimus robot as part of a broader technological transformation that brings artificial intelligence into the physical world.
These visions are necessarily speculative. They are shaped by commercial interests, investors, and the desire to convince people that a technology will matter before it has fully arrived. Yet imagined futures from Silicon Valley are rarely described as propaganda. They are framed as innovation or ambition.
Both Chinese and Western technology companies sell visions of the future. But those visions are not always interpreted in the same way. This is where the idea of Sinofuturism becomes useful. The term describes China as a source of its own technological future. China is not only adopting new technologies but also developing its own ideas about what life with them could look like.
This is visible in the way Chinese officials and companies talk about humanoid robots. They are not presented only as machines that can run faster or lift more. They are supposed to take over unsafe and undesirable jobs, assist people in their homes, or care for the elderly. The future they describe is one where robot technology becomes part of how society works.
That future may be exaggerated. Some of the promises may never materialize. But even if some of them fail, they show how Chinese companies and officials imagine technology changing everyday life.
Of course, China uses technology to promote its own political goals. But why does this so often become the main way Chinese technology is understood? When a Chinese company develops a humanoid robot, coverage often focuses on what Beijing wants to achieve with it. When a Western company develops one, the focus is more likely to be on what the technology might make possible.
That difference matters. Technology is never completely separate from the society and politics around it. But if we treat China’s technological ambitions mainly as political messaging, we risk missing something else: Countries and companies do not just adapt to the future. They shape it through the technologies they develop and invest in. China is also trying to shape what its own future will look like.
The robots in Beijing may have been part of a political message, but the companies that made them have their own ambitions for the future. The technology is still developing, and many of the presented robots were far from ready for everyday use. That does not make the vision behind them irrelevant.
The robots showed one possible version of what Chinese technology could become. Seeing that future only as propaganda risks missing what is actually changing.

articles.article_title: $25M federal grant to upgrade technology, expand high-speed internet for rural health clinics
articles.heading: $25M federal grant to upgrade technology, expand high-speed internet for rural health clinics
articles.summary: A major investment has been announced that will modernize Michigan healthcare.
articles.content:
$25M federal grant to upgrade technology, expand high-speed internet for rural health clinics
MICHIGAN (WNEM) - A major investment has been announced that will modernize Michigan healthcare.
The Trump Administration is investing $25 million that will go towards new technology and an expansion of telehealth.
The money from the federal Rural Health Transformation program will support more-connected health systems, along with remote patient monitoring in rural communities across the state.
More than $16 million will help rural healthcare providers upgrade their technology and digital systems to better coordinate care, and around $9 million will improve high-speed internet to deliver healthcare in those areas.
The money is part of the larger overall funding being rewarded to Michigan for the fiscal year.

articles.title: Ulta’s use of Flock technology causes upset online
articles.description: Ulta’s use of Flock technology causes upset online retaildive.com
articles.description_html: Ulta’s use of Flock technology causes upset online  retaildive.com
articles.article_title: Ulta’s use of Flock technology causes upset online
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's retail industry news
articles.summary: The retailer drew attention on social media this week for its use of automated license plate readers at some locations as the technology has drawn widespread public criticism.
articles.content:
Social media users flooded Ulta Beauty’s Instagram posts this week sharing their frustration about the company’s work with surveillance technology provider Flock after a campaign by activist organization UltraViolet went viral.
Ulta Beauty uses automated license plate readers from Flock in some of its store locations, a source familiar confirmed to Retail Dive.
The technology is deployed at less than 1% of Ulta’s storefleet nationwide, which has a total of around 1,500 locations. The cameras do not use facial recognition, the source told Retail Dive.
Flock has garnered widespread public criticism of its technology in recent months, with vandalism of the license plate readers growing. Some local and state governments are reconsidering the installation of Flock's technologies.
Ulta did not respond to questions about when its relationship with Flock began. Flock did not respond to Retail Dive’s questions about its relationship with Ulta.
Retail crime remains a focus for industry groups, with the National Retail Federation and Retail Industry Leaders Association pushing for federal legislation to combat organized theft.
Flock lists organized retail crime as a use case for its technology on its website, saying that companies can “add known offenders to LPR custom hotlists and get alerted immediately when they enter” parking lots.
In a blog post from April of last year, Flock highlighted how its license plate reader cameras helped in the arrest of suspects by the Fairfax County Police Department in Virginia linked to organized retail crime at multiple Ulta stores.
Flock's AI chatbot on its website describes Ulta as “one of Flock Safety's retail partners, utilizing our technology to help identify repeat offenders and prevent fraud,” when asked if the beauty retailer is a customer.
Ulta's director of organized retail crime, Rory Stallard, noted the retailer had seen increased violence in stores after the COVID-19 pandemic, according to a recap post from Flock Forward’s August 2025 event.
“We were looking for technology that would help us bridge the gap and collaborate [with law enforcement],” Stallard said, according to Flock’s blog post from Aug. 14 of last year. “It really centered around our company culture and protecting our associates and our guests. So, by taking some of the things that we were doing and leveraging some of that technology to help us solve crimes faster, we can eliminate some of these bad actors from being in our store, we can prevent [crime], and we can try to be more proactive versus reactive. Flock really fit the bill for some of the things that we wanted to be able to do.”
Stallard also attended a Flock Forward conference last month, per a now-deleted LinkedIn post where he expressed appreciation for the event's opportunity to network with law enforcement and private sector connections.
Flock updated its terms and conditions in August amid growing public criticism over the use of its technology across the U.S.

articles.title: Maui Council panel advances license plate reader bill, delays facial recognition technology measure
articles.description: Maui Council panel advances license plate reader bill, delays facial recognition technology measure Maui Now
articles.description_html: Maui Council panel advances license plate reader bill, delays facial recognition technology measure  Maui Now
articles.source: |  Maui Council panel advances license plate reader bill, delays facial recognition technology measure
articles.article_title: Maui Council panel advances license plate reader bill, delays facial recognition technology measure | Maui Now
articles.heading: Maui Council panel advances license plate reader bill, delays facial recognition technology measure
articles.summary: Maui County Council members voted 7-1 in committee Thursday to put safeguards how local law enforcement uses automatic license plate reader technology, but they deferred action on a second bill addressing facial recognition technology that is not yet deployed by the Maui Police Department.
articles.content:
Maui Council panel advances license plate reader bill, delays facial recognition technology measure
Maui County Council members voted 7-1 in committee Thursday to put safeguards on how local law enforcement uses automated license plate reader technology, but they deferred action on a second bill addressing facial recognition technology that is not yet deployed by the Maui Police Department.
The action by the Disaster Recovery, International Affairs and Planning Committee, chaired by Council Member Tamara Paltin, came a day after dozens of Maui residents urged council members to ban or sharply restrict police use of facial recognition and license plate reader technology, maintaining that two bills meant to regulate the tools don’t go far enough and that unregulated camera networks are already watching island residents.
The committee’s vote came with a single dissent from Council Member Gabe Johnson. Council Member Yuki Lei Sugimura was absent and excused.
On Wednesday, the committee spent two-and-a-half hours hearing public testimony on Bill 112 and Bill 113 before recessing without taking action. Of the dozen people who testified, nearly all opposed the bills as written, with several calling for the county to ban the technologies outright rather than regulate their use.
Council Member Keani Rawlins-Fernandez said she doesn’t support Bill 112, especially since facial recognition technology is not being used in Maui County. She said she would prefer a measure prohibiting Maui County’s use of that technology, “disallowing it just so it’s clear what our position is.”
She said that, with all the public concerns about the bill, it would be better to “super pump the brakes on it and just say ‘no.’ “
Bills’ intent
Bill 112 would require Maui County law enforcement officers to use facial recognition technology only in connection with a documented criminal investigation, with limited access to designated and trained personnel. The bill would mandate that any match the technology produces be treated only as an investigative lead rather than proof of identity. The bill would also bar use of the technology for immigration enforcement, civil traffic infractions or to monitor people regarding their race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability or those engaged in lawful protest, worship or other First Amendment-protected activity.
The bill allows facial recognition technology’s use without prior documentation in cases where there’s an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury to a person. Afterward, required documentation needs to be completed within 24 hours of its use.
Bill 113 would prohibit the sale of automated license plate reader data and require that county contracts for the camera systems bar vendors from using the data for purposes outside the contract.
Paltin introduced both bills and told the committee she worked with the Maui Police Department to amend her original drafts. She said the measures were rushed onto the agenda ahead of the South Maui Community Plan discussion and that a third, related bill on data retention still needs work before it can be introduced.
Police: No facial recognition in use, no sale of data
Lt. Taylor Kamakawiwoʻole of the Maui Police Department told the committee the department does not currently use facial recognition technology.
Under Bill 112, he said, any future use would require a documented case number before a data search could run, and a match generated by the software could never by itself establish probable cause or serve as grounds for an arrest.
“A trained person has to confirm the identity, and an independent investigation has to corroborate before it means anything,” Kamakawiwoʻole said. “The national failure cases all came from investigations treating a lead as proof. That is what this bill prevents.”
On automated license plate readers, Kamakawiwoʻole said the cameras only capture plate characters, a vehicle image and the time and location—they do not identify drivers. Alerts are generated only when a plate matches a “hot list” of stolen vehicles or vehicles connected to Amber Alerts or custodial-interference cases, he said, and every query requires a case number and a written reason logged before the search.
“We do not sell any of the data, and we never will,” he said, noting Bill 113 would make that a flat prohibition with no business exception.
Officer Aaron Mark added that the system’s optical character recognition can misread plates and that officers treat every alert as a lead requiring in-person verification, not an automatic stop.
Managing Director Josiah Nishita told the committee the county has no contracts with Flock Safety, the private camera vendor whose devices have drawn national scrutiny, though he said he could not rule out that the company operates under another name.
“To our knowledge and understanding, none of those camera systems or technology are being in use by any of the departments,” Nishita said.
On Thursday, Maui police reported no pending surveillance technology contracts. However, Lt. Christina Bonacorsi told council members the county already executed a contract with Motorola in 2025 for 400 radios for the command central aware program that came with 27 license plate reader cameras. Police said there are a few other cameras left over from a pilot program, bringing the total currently in use to 32.
A subscription licensing fee is about $150 to $200 per camera per year, she said. The county doesn’t and wouldn’t use Flock cameras because the system isn’t a secured government server, Bonacorsi said.
Kamakawiwoʻole said the license plate reader cameras are posted at major, highly traveled intersections and information is stored on SD cards. The technology is used for public safety, he said. Information gathered from the camera can tell officers where and when a possibly stolen vehicle was last seen and in what direction it was headed.
“The way we look at [automated license plate reader] cameras is, instead of posting officers on the corners of every street looking out for these vehicles that are traveling you know we have tools, another set of eyes and that will alleviate and save a lot of manpower,” he said, adding that it’s difficult to fill vacant positions in the department, which is an ongoing problem for “every police department, every sheriff’s department” nationally.
Recently, in Monroe County, Michigan, commissioners voted to end the county sheriff’s use of 40 Flock Safety license plate reading cameras, according to a story posted online by WXYZ TV, an ABC news affiliate. Residents had concerns over system accuracy and complained of “unconstitutional surveillance.”
Residents describe a bigger surveillance buildout
Much of the public testimony went beyond the two bills to describe what several testifiers called a broader, already-underway surveillance buildout on Maui that the county has not fully disclosed.
Sheila Walker of Maui Meadows told the committee she opposes installing surveillance cameras owned or operated by private companies. “There is a difference between investigating a crime and routinely tracking people who are simply living their lives,” she said.
Jake Carton, testifying on behalf of Maui Indivisible, argued the bills regulate only a fraction of a larger system.
“We can’t save the forest by talking about two trees,” he said. “We can’t fix a messed-up development by regulating two hammers,” he said, adding that the group has obtained records showing a nondisclosure agreement between the county and a Motorola subsidiary that installs camera equipment.
“These two bills are trying to do an impossible thing, make it look like we have protections against police and county spy abuse, but still not undermine the spy project that council funded,” Carton said.
Heather Hirchson expressed skepticism about the government’s ability to regulate surveillance of citizens.
“We know that regulating only two spy tools will not bring sanity or real guardrails to Maui County’s mass spy project,” she said. “That’s why scores of counties and cities and towns across the US have shut these projects down in the past year. They’re not just regulating a few tools; they’re abandoning and banning the tech. It’s also not just happening in liberal and progressive places. It’s happening in conservative, MAGA-heavy areas.”
Robert Bence said he’s opposed to both bills as written. He called for Bill 113 to be amended to prohibit the acquisition, operation and expansion of license plate reading systems by county agencies and to require the decommissioning of existing systems. He asked for a similar ban on facial recognition technology in Bill 112.
Bence said the committee was hearing from one side, law enforcement, which is making a case for use of the tools; and that the bills are framed as reining in facial recognition and license plate readers when, in fact, the legislation authorizes and legitimizes their use.
“It’s pretty much Orwellian, if anybody hasn’t read his book,” he said, referring to George Orwell’s 1949 novel “1984,” which depicts a totalitarian state led by an all-seeing “Big Brother.”
Stacey Alapai, testifying on both bills, said she supports the underlying intent but doesn’t support “escalating mass surveillance on our island or using surveillance tech for community policing.”
“My preference would be to stop funding these cameras and take them down,” she said.
Alapai also told the committee that a check of a public camera-mapping website turned up 37 cameras identified as Flock Safety or Motorola devices on Maui, mostly along state highways, and asked how the Police Department was receiving suspected stolen vehicle hot-list photos if the county has no vendor contract—a discrepancy the committee did not resolve Wednesday.
Martin Hamilton cited an American Civil Liberties Union study finding facial recognition error rates below 1% for white men but nearly 35% for women with darker skin, and asked the department to clarify how any future database would be built.
“How is the database being used?” he asked. “Like, how would it know what my face is? Is it pulled from another database? . . . How would you get data on people’s faces?”
Livit Callentine, a longtime Wailuku resident, connected the spending to Maui’s wildfire recovery and called expanding an “unvetted islandwide tracking grid without ironclad binding regulations a direct threat to the privacy and safety of our community.”
“As Maui navigates a painful, historic disaster recovery process, spending $1.7 million on an invasive mass surveillance network is a stark misallocation of resources,” she said, also citing a Washington Post investigation that found dozens of law enforcement officers nationally had misused license plate camera networks to track and stalk former partners. “These taxpayer dollars must be prioritized for urgent local infrastructure, emergency evacuation routes and housing, not for turning Maui County into a corporate monitored and surveillance state.”
Legal concerns and proposed fixes
Prosecuting Attorney Andrew Martin told the committee his office supports the bills’ intent but cautioned against language in Bill 112 that he said could improperly limit how courts interpret probable cause and reasonable suspicion—constitutional standards he said are for judicial, not legislative, determination.
Martin also recommended replacing a provision allowing delayed documentation during an “imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury” with the broader legal term “exigent circumstances,” a change that would apply to both bills.
“That’s a term that more broadly I think encompasses all possible circumstances and tracks what is widely used by the court as the term that defines that particular exception to the warrant requirement,” he said.
The committee later amended Bill 113 to include Martin’s suggested change.
“Exigent circumstances” is a legal term referring to situations urgent enough that law enforcement can act without first getting a warrant, because waiting to get one would create a real risk of harm to someone, destruction of evidence or a suspect escaping.
Is the juice worth the squeeze?
Johnson, who voted against the cameras bill, said he’d prefer an outright ban or moratorium on camera and artificial intelligence use in traffic enforcement or public spaces, telling the committee, “I don’t think the juice is worth the squeeze.”
Johnson credited Maui police with achieving a 14% reduction in crime and doing an “excellent job,” but he said “I live on Lānaʻi and I know a thing or two about heavy handed uses of power, and I’m a proponent of a light touch instead of a heavy hand.”
“I know the department can be capable of keeping people safe, as well as respecting privacy rights, and there is a balance that I would hope we all would achieve,” he said.
What’s next?
Bill 113 moves on to the full Council for first reading, while Bill 112 remains on hold indefinitely.
However, council members agreed that more information and public education is necessary.

Maui Council panel advances license plate reader bill, delays facial recognition technology measure

Maui County Council members voted 7-1 in committee Thursday to put safeguards on how local law enforcement uses automated license plate reader technology, but they deferred action on a second bill addressing facial recognition technology that is not yet deployed by the Maui Police Department.

The action by the Disaster Recovery, International Affairs and Planning Committee, chaired by Council Member Tamara Paltin, came a day after dozens of Maui residents urged council members to ban or sharply restrict police use of facial recognition and license plate reader technology, maintaining that two bills meant to regulate the tools don’t go far enough and that unregulated camera networks are already watching island residents.

The committee’s vote came with a single dissent from Council Member Gabe Johnson. Council Member Yuki Lei Sugimura was absent and excused.

On Wednesday, the committee spent two-and-a-half hours hearing public testimony on Bill 112 and Bill 113 before recessing without taking action. Of the dozen people who testified, nearly all opposed the bills as written, with several calling for the county to ban the technologies outright rather than regulate their use.

Council Member Keani Rawlins-Fernandez said she doesn’t support Bill 112, especially since facial recognition technology is not being used in Maui County. She said she would prefer a measure prohibiting Maui County’s use of that technology, “disallowing it just so it’s clear what our position is.”

She said that, with all the public concerns about the bill, it would be better to “super pump the brakes on it and just say ‘no.’ “

Bills’ intent

Bill 112 would require Maui County law enforcement officers to use facial recognition technology only in connection with a documented criminal investigation, with limited access to designated and trained personnel. The bill would mandate that any match the technology produces be treated only as an investigative lead rather than proof of identity. The bill would also bar use of the technology for immigration enforcement, civil traffic infractions or to monitor people regarding their race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability or those engaged in lawful protest, worship or other First Amendment-protected activity.

The bill allows facial recognition technology’s use without prior documentation in cases where there’s an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury to a person. Afterward, required documentation needs to be completed within 24 hours of its use.

Bill 113 would prohibit the sale of automated license plate reader data and require that county contracts for the camera systems bar vendors from using the data for purposes outside the contract.

Paltin introduced both bills and told the committee she worked with the Maui Police Department to amend her original drafts. She said the measures were rushed onto the agenda ahead of the South Maui Community Plan discussion and that a third, related bill on data retention still needs work before it can be introduced.

Police: No facial recognition in use, no sale of data

Lt. Taylor Kamakawiwoʻole of the Maui Police Department told the committee the department does not currently use facial recognition technology.

Under Bill 112, he said, any future use would require a documented case number before a data search could run, and a match generated by the software could never by itself establish probable cause or serve as grounds for an arrest.

“A trained person has to confirm the identity, and an independent investigation has to corroborate before it means anything,” Kamakawiwoʻole said. “The national failure cases all came from investigations treating a lead as proof. That is what this bill prevents.”

On automated license plate readers, Kamakawiwoʻole said the cameras only capture plate characters, a vehicle image and the time and location—they do not identify drivers. Alerts are generated only when a plate matches a “hot list” of stolen vehicles or vehicles connected to Amber Alerts or custodial-interference cases, he said, and every query requires a case number and a written reason logged before the search.

“We do not sell any of the data, and we never will,” he said, noting Bill 113 would make that a flat prohibition with no business exception.

Officer Aaron Mark added that the system’s optical character recognition can misread plates and that officers treat every alert as a lead requiring in-person verification, not an automatic stop.

Managing Director Josiah Nishita told the committee the county has no contracts with Flock Safety, the private camera vendor whose devices have drawn national scrutiny, though he said he could not rule out that the company operates under another name.

“To our knowledge and understanding, none of those camera systems or technology are being in use by any of the departments,” Nishita said.

On Thursday, Maui police reported no pending surveillance technology contracts. However, Lt. Christina Bonacorsi told council members the county already executed a contract with Motorola in 2025 for 400 radios for the command central aware program that came with 27 license plate reader cameras. Police said there are a few other cameras left over from a pilot program, bringing the total currently in use to 32.

A subscription licensing fee is about $150 to $200 per camera per year, she said. The county doesn’t and wouldn’t use Flock cameras because the system isn’t a secured government server, Bonacorsi said.

Kamakawiwoʻole said the license plate reader cameras are posted at major, highly traveled intersections and information is stored on SD cards. The technology is used for public safety, he said. Information gathered from the camera can tell officers where and when a possibly stolen vehicle was last seen and in what direction it was headed.

“The way we look at [automated license plate reader] cameras is, instead of posting officers on the corners of every street looking out for these vehicles that are traveling you know we have tools, another set of eyes and that will alleviate and save a lot of manpower,” he said, adding that it’s difficult to fill vacant positions in the department, which is an ongoing problem for “every police department, every sheriff’s department” nationally.

Recently, in Monroe County, Michigan, commissioners voted to end the county sheriff’s use of 40 Flock Safety license plate reading cameras, according to a story posted online by WXYZ TV, an ABC news affiliate. Residents had concerns over system accuracy and complained of “unconstitutional surveillance.”

Residents describe a bigger surveillance buildout

Much of the public testimony went beyond the two bills to describe what several testifiers called a broader, already-underway surveillance buildout on Maui that the county has not fully disclosed.

Sheila Walker of Maui Meadows told the committee she opposes installing surveillance cameras owned or operated by private companies. “There is a difference between investigating a crime and routinely tracking people who are simply living their lives,” she said.

Jake Carton, testifying on behalf of Maui Indivisible, argued the bills regulate only a fraction of a larger system.

“We can’t save the forest by talking about two trees,” he said. “We can’t fix a messed-up development by regulating two hammers,” he said, adding that the group has obtained records showing a nondisclosure agreement between the county and a Motorola subsidiary that installs camera equipment.

“These two bills are trying to do an impossible thing, make it look like we have protections against police and county spy abuse, but still not undermine the spy project that council funded,” Carton said.

Heather Hirchson expressed skepticism about the government’s ability to regulate surveillance of citizens.

“We know that regulating only two spy tools will not bring sanity or real guardrails to Maui County’s mass spy project,” she said. “That’s why scores of counties and cities and towns across the US have shut these projects down in the past year. They’re not just regulating a few tools; they’re abandoning and banning the tech. It’s also not just happening in liberal and progressive places. It’s happening in conservative, MAGA-heavy areas.”

Robert Bence said he’s opposed to both bills as written. He called for Bill 113 to be amended to prohibit the acquisition, operation and expansion of license plate reading systems by county agencies and to require the decommissioning of existing systems. He asked for a similar ban on facial recognition technology in Bill 112.

Bence said the committee was hearing from one side, law enforcement, which is making a case for use of the tools; and that the bills are framed as reining in facial recognition and license plate readers when, in fact, the legislation authorizes and legitimizes their use.

“It’s pretty much Orwellian, if anybody hasn’t read his book,” he said, referring to George Orwell’s 1949 novel “1984,” which depicts a totalitarian state led by an all-seeing “Big Brother.”

Stacey Alapai, testifying on both bills, said she supports the underlying intent but doesn’t support “escalating mass surveillance on our island or using surveillance tech for community policing.”

“My preference would be to stop funding these cameras and take them down,” she said.

Alapai also told the committee that a check of a public camera-mapping website turned up 37 cameras identified as Flock Safety or Motorola devices on Maui, mostly along state highways, and asked how the Police Department was receiving suspected stolen vehicle hot-list photos if the county has no vendor contract—a discrepancy the committee did not resolve Wednesday.

Martin Hamilton cited an American Civil Liberties Union study finding facial recognition error rates below 1% for white men but nearly 35% for women with darker skin, and asked the department to clarify how any future database would be built.

“How is the database being used?” he asked. “Like, how would it know what my face is? Is it pulled from another database? . . . How would you get data on people’s faces?”

Livit Callentine, a longtime Wailuku resident, connected the spending to Maui’s wildfire recovery and called expanding an “unvetted islandwide tracking grid without ironclad binding regulations a direct threat to the privacy and safety of our community.”

“As Maui navigates a painful, historic disaster recovery process, spending $1.7 million on an invasive mass surveillance network is a stark misallocation of resources,” she said, also citing a Washington Post investigation that found dozens of law enforcement officers nationally had misused license plate camera networks to track and stalk former partners. “These taxpayer dollars must be prioritized for urgent local infrastructure, emergency evacuation routes and housing, not for turning Maui County into a corporate monitored and surveillance state.”

Legal concerns and proposed fixes

Prosecuting Attorney Andrew Martin told the committee his office supports the bills’ intent but cautioned against language in Bill 112 that he said could improperly limit how courts interpret probable cause and reasonable suspicion—constitutional standards he said are for judicial, not legislative, determination.

Martin also recommended replacing a provision allowing delayed documentation during an “imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury” with the broader legal term “exigent circumstances,” a change that would apply to both bills.

“That’s a term that more broadly I think encompasses all possible circumstances and tracks what is widely used by the court as the term that defines that particular exception to the warrant requirement,” he said.

The committee later amended Bill 113 to include Martin’s suggested change.

“Exigent circumstances” is a legal term referring to situations urgent enough that law enforcement can act without first getting a warrant, because waiting to get one would create a real risk of harm to someone, destruction of evidence or a suspect escaping.

Is the juice worth the squeeze?

Johnson, who voted against the cameras bill, said he’d prefer an outright ban or moratorium on camera and artificial intelligence use in traffic enforcement or public spaces, telling the committee, “I don’t think the juice is worth the squeeze.”

Johnson credited Maui police with achieving a 14% reduction in crime and doing an “excellent job,” but he said “I live on Lānaʻi and I know a thing or two about heavy handed uses of power, and I’m a proponent of a light touch instead of a heavy hand.”

“I know the department can be capable of keeping people safe, as well as respecting privacy rights, and there is a balance that I would hope we all would achieve,” he said.

What’s next?

Bill 113 moves on to the full Council for first reading, while Bill 112 remains on hold indefinitely.

However, council members agreed that more information and public education is necessary.

“There are cameras everywhere, whether they belong to us or not; everybody has one in their back pocket,” Council Member Nohelani Uʻu-Hodgins said. “I have cameras in my house. You cannot come to my house without me knowing that you came to my house.”

She said she appreciates the willingness of the Maui Police Department to work with the Council on the issue.

“I would like a little bit more time to understand how this really applies to us all,” she said.

Council Chair Alice Lee said the Council has a busy schedule through the rest of this year, and she suggested taking up the facial recognition measure next year.

Paltin said she spoke to Maui Police Chief John Pelletier, who said he “doesn’t want people who aren’t police to overtake what the police capabilities are.”

“Time and education are worthwhile for not just us but the county as a whole, including our residents,” she said, adding that it’s necessary to strike a balance.

“We don’t want criminals to have access to more information than our police have access to, but we also want to make sure our police are held accountable,” Paltin said.

articles.content:
Nearly 600,000 active job postings point to continued demand for tech talent
DOWNERS GROVE, Ill., Sept. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Technology occupation employment increased in August and employer demand for new tech talent remained strong, according to analysis by CompTIA, the leading global provider of vendor-neutral technology training and certifications.
Tech occupation employment, which includes tech professionals working across all industry sectors, increased by 86,000 workers in August, CompTIA's analysis of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) #JobsReport data shows.1
The employment picture within the technology sector moved in the opposite direction. Tech companies reduced staffing by about 14,700 positions, inclusive of both technical and non-technical positions. The latest data may reflect the impact of layoffs disclosed in recent months by US-headquartered tech companies.
Demand for AI skills continues to accelerate, with active job postings requiring AI-related capabilities surpassing 320,000 openings in August, a 4.5% increase from July, according to CompTIA's analysis of data from Lightcast.2 The increase aligns with new CompTIA research that indicates employers are moving beyond AI experimentation and increasingly incorporating AI into business operations, creating demand for workers who can apply AI tools, manage AI-enabled workflows, and support AI-driven initiatives.3
More broadly, employer demand for technology talent remains healthy. There were nearly 600,000 active technology occupation postings during the month, with 42% representing newly advertised positions.4 Growth in tech support, infrastructure, project management and cybersecurity roles suggests employers remain focused on strengthening core technology functions while expanding emerging capabilities.
Professional, scientific and technical services, manufacturing, and administrative support services generated the highest volumes of new technology job postings. Several industry sectors, including retail, wholesale trade, and educational services, also recorded month-over-month gains, underscoring the widespread need for technology talent across the economy.
The "CompTIA Tech Jobs Report" is available at https://www.comptia.org/en-us/resources/research/tech-jobs-report/.
About CompTIA
CompTIA, Inc. is the leading global provider of vendor-neutral training and certification products in the information technology (IT) space. Over four million CompTIA certifications have been awarded to current and aspiring technology workers, business professionals, government and military personnel, career changers, students and others. Working in partnership with thousands of academic institutions, governments, training providers and workforce development organizations, CompTIA uses best-in-class learning solutions, industry-recognized certifications and career resources to help job seekers reach their full potential and employers develop skilled technical talent. Learn more at https://www.comptia.org/.
Contact
Steven Ostrowski
CompTIA
[email protected]
630-678-8468
1 Monthly occupation level data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics tends to experience higher levels of variance and volatility.
2 Labor market data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and employer job postings from Lightcast may be subject to backward revisions.
3 "Corporate AI Adoption," August 2026.
4 Active job postings include new postings added by employers in the latest month and open postings carried over from previous months.
SOURCE CompTIA

Update on Technology Use in Classrooms: Prioritizing Connection and High-Quality Learning
Dear Cambridge Public Schools Families,
We are eager to welcome your children back with grades 1st through 12th and Post Grad reporting tomorrow, Tuesday, September 1st and preschool and Kindergarten students joining us on Thursday, September 3rd.
The start and end times for all schools are linked here.
Last week I had the privilege to address an estimated 2,000 Cambridge Public Schools employees at our annual district colloquium, the focus of which was on building stronger trust and partnerships with the families we serve. Building trust requires clear communication about the opportunities and challenges we face. For CPS, like all school systems, that includes determining how to most effectively incorporate new technologies into our students’ education.
On this final day of summer vacation for our students, I wanted to share with you some brief details and thoughts on how we are approaching these challenges as a school system:
Foundational Beliefs:
Learning is fundamentally a human endeavor, and the core of any strong school community are the relationships that exist between educators and students and among students with their peers. When technology is appropriate for a specific instructional purpose, the Cambridge Public Schools is committed to ensuring it is used in intentional and developmentally appropriate ways to enhance students’ educational experiences.
Technology can neither substitute for nor supersede the critical elements of social development students enjoy in their schools. CPS will continue to value play, independent exploration, physical movement, peer to peer and student to educator engaging conversations, reading, writing, creative work, and the interpersonal interactions which should make up a part of every one of the 180 school days that begin tomorrow.
Screen Time Usage:
Last spring the Cambridge Public Schools completed a comprehensive analysis of technology use by CPS students. That analysis indicated that the majority of screen time to which students are exposed is guided by specific and meaningful educational goals. This year, across all CPS schools, the district has instituted explicit grade level guidance to ensure technology use is always grounded in intentional instructional strategies to deepen learning and foster high-quality educational experiences. These guidelines prioritize hands-on learning and human connection, ensuring digital tools enhance rather than replace the face-to-face experiences essential for student growth.
Healthy Habits and Tech Limits:
School is about developing the abilities, skills and knowledge necessary to operate in the world. This certainly includes navigating modern day technologies, but there are also times when the absence of specific types of technology results in more impactful educational experiences. One example of a technology limitation is the strict prohibition on cell phone access during the school day. During a school day that is typically only six hours and thirty minutes, educators are charged with creating an environment of engagement, in-depth learning and meaningful connections between students. Prohibiting access to cell phones is intended to help students stay present and to ensure educators’ focus is on providing substantive instruction.
Additional grade and age-specific guidelines and practices are in place to support these goals. Each of which is designed to ensure age-appropriate and developmentally sound practices that affirm the human-centered core of high-quality elementary and secondary education.
At Home Habits and Family Support:
During the 2026 - 2027 school year, students and caregivers will have the chance to participate in programs focused on developing boundaries and at-home practices to establish a healthy relationship between children and technology, including information about the inherent dangers of social media. The impact of technology on children’s development extends well beyond the school day. We are eager to partner with families to support you in navigating both the opportunities and the challenges of the rapidly-changing environment.
To that end, CPS has made modifications to our practice around distributing take-home technology devices, specifically Chromebooks. At the elementary level, schools will provide devices only upon a specific request by a family based on particular needs of that child’s household. For secondary students (6th grade) families may opt-in to having their child’s Chromebook travel to and from school. From 7th through 12th grade, families who prefer their child’s Chromebook remain at school must opt-out of the take-home designation.
Establishing Boundaries on Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Currently CPS operates under AI guidance developed in part through the work of an AI working group composed of educators, staff and district leaders. Revised guidance related to generative AI will be published in October.
Both the current and developing AI guidance represent proactive efforts to safeguard academic integrity and authentic learning:
- PreK through Grade 5: Generative AI is generally prohibited and blocked through district filtering. Exceptions are very limited with direct supervision by educators and with ongoing communication to caregivers.
- Grade 6 through Grade 8: Generative AI use by students will continue to be significantly restricted to a limited number of applications with specific educational purposes. As is true at the elementary level, schools will communicate with the families how and when students are given the opportunity to use this technology as well as the instructional objectives underlying those opportunities.
- Grades 9 through 12: High school students may only use specific, district-approved AI applications (e.g., Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Canva) for explicit educational purposes consistent with their teacher’s expectations. When permitted, students must fully disclose AI assistance, verify the accuracy of the output, and remain entirely responsible for the integrity of the work they submit.
CPS will also be providing additional opportunities for professional learning for educators to build greater AI understanding so that we may better support the development of students’ media literacy. As these resources are made available, we will be sure to communicate them clearly with families so we can partner together to meet the challenges and maximize any potential benefits for our students.
Preserving the Integrity of the Learning Process:
For every assignment students are asked to complete in school, the objective is to help them to develop an ability, a skill set or a knowledge base that will be useful later in their academic careers and post-secondary lives. This is true from the social and emotional foundation and literacy fluency we focus on at the elementary level, to the most sophisticated and complex tasks in the later stages of high school. When technology enhances this learning, it can be a great tool. But in instances in which a form of technology would diminish the impact or depth of a student’s educational experience, its use will be restricted.
As an organization, the Cambridge Public Schools is committed to continuous learning and improvement. We will continue to strive to support our educators and engage with the families of our students, all in service of creating the most optimal learning environments possible for all students.
Thank you for your partnership in this work. We are looking forward to a great school year.
Sincerely,

David Murphy
Superintendent of Schools

  • PreK through Grade 5: Generative AI is generally prohibited and blocked through district filtering. Exceptions are very limited with direct supervision by educators and with ongoing communication to caregivers.
  • Grade 6 through Grade 8: Generative AI use by students will continue to be significantly restricted to a limited number of applications with specific educational purposes. As is true at the elementary level, schools will communicate with the families how and when students are given the opportunity to use this technology as well as the instructional objectives underlying those opportunities.
  • Grades 9 through 12: High school students may only use specific, district-approved AI applications (e.g., Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Canva) for explicit educational purposes consistent with their teacher’s expectations. When permitted, students must fully disclose AI assistance, verify the accuracy of the output, and remain entirely responsible for the integrity of the work they submit.

CPS will also be providing additional opportunities for professional learning for educators to build greater AI understanding so that we may better support the development of students’ media literacy. As these resources are made available, we will be sure to communicate them clearly with families so we can partner together to meet the challenges and maximize any potential benefits for our students.

Preserving the Integrity of the Learning Process:

For every assignment students are asked to complete in school, the objective is to help them to develop an ability, a skill set or a knowledge base that will be useful later in their academic careers and post-secondary lives. This is true from the social and emotional foundation and literacy fluency we focus on at the elementary level, to the most sophisticated and complex tasks in the later stages of high school. When technology enhances this learning, it can be a great tool. But in instances in which a form of technology would diminish the impact or depth of a student’s educational experience, its use will be restricted.

As an organization, the Cambridge Public Schools is committed to continuous learning and improvement. We will continue to strive to support our educators and engage with the families of our students, all in service of creating the most optimal learning environments possible for all students.

Thank you for your partnership in this work. We are looking forward to a great school year.

Sincerely,


 

David Murphy

Superintendent of Schools

articles.article_title: Normet’s new centre in Finland to drive underground mining technology
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: The centre is focused on fostering advancements in autonomy, robotics, software development and other technologies.
articles.content:
Normet has opened a new technology centre in Pirkkala, Finland, to expedite the future of underground mining.
The facility is intended to bolster research, development and testing capabilities for technologies aimed at improving safety, productivity and sustainability in underground mining operations.
The new centre is focused on fostering advancements in autonomy, robotics, software development and other digital technologies.
As mining operations extend to deeper levels and face more challenging conditions, these technologies become crucial in enabling remote and autonomous functionalities that can minimise human exposure to hazardous environments.
Normet conducts more than 95% of its business outside Finland and has a presence in roughly 50 locations across 30 countries.
Normet president and CEO Ed Santamaria said: "Today is an important milestone for Normet. This investment expands our technology development and testing capabilities and reinforces our commitment to staying at the forefront of innovation in underground mining.
"Customer demand for advanced mining technologies continues to grow, and this centre will help us accelerate the development of solutions that improve safety, productivity and sustainability underground."
The company manufactures mining equipment in Chile, Finland and India. Demand for its products is supported by global trends such as the green transition, urbanisation and increased investment in critical minerals.
The facility will also serve as a venue for customer demonstrations, highlighting autonomous functions, tele-remote operation and battery electric equipment.
Pirkkala was chosen for its location within a prominent ecosystem known for electrified mobile work machines and mining technology.
Santamaria further added: "We have already hired more than 50 people in Finland this year to support our growth, particularly in manufacturing, and we expect this new centre to create additional high-value technology roles in the future."
In April 2025, Normet secured a contract to provide an ancillary underground equipment fleet for South32's Hermosa project, located in a mining district in the Patagonia Mountains of southern Arizona, US.
"Normet's new centre in Finland to drive underground mining technology" was originally created and published by Mining Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

articles.content: Arn Net reports that ConnectWise is focusing on rebuilding trust and investing in new technologies following a cyberattack believed to be carried out by a nation-state actor. CEO Manny Rivelo emphasized the importance of transparency in the aftermath of the breach, which affected a small number of customers using its ScreenConnect solution.ConnectWise experienced a security incident in the past year, suspected to be linked to a sophisticated nation-state actor targeting its ScreenConnect solution. While the breach impacted a limited customer base, its effects were felt globally by partners. CEO Manny Rivelo stated that transparency and clear communication were paramount in addressing the situation, acknowledging that no system is entirely immune to zero-day attacks.The company has since focused on mitigating vulnerabilities within its environment to prevent similar incidents from having a significant impact. This includes enhancing security through governance, systems, and controls, and adjusting product functionalities to improve safety, even if it means adding extra steps for users. ConnectWise is also investing in technology stack consolidation, agentic functionality, and establishing local data centers and hiring new employees in the Australia and New Zealand region to support its partners.Source: Arn Net

articles.description_html: Technology is taking off, but medical care starts with art  KETV
articles.article_title: Technology is taking off, but medical care starts with art
articles.heading: Technology is taking off, but medical care starts with art
articles.summary: UNMC medical illustrator combines art and technology to improve patient care
articles.content:
Technology is taking off, but medical care starts with art
UNMC medical illustrator combines art and technology to improve patient care
Bill Glass, a medical illustrator at UNMC, uses his artistic skills and technology to enhance medical education and make procedures safer.
Article:
Doctors and researchers at the University of Nebraska Medical Center (UNMC) are using technology and art to advance medical care.
Bill Glass, a medical illustrator at UNMC, creates detailed illustrations and animations of human anatomy to focus attention on critical information. "We know what to leave in and what to take out to focus your eye on the important information," Glass said.
Glass has been an artist for decades, specializing in drawing human anatomy. "This would probably take me 3 to 4 hours, this is a skull," he said, describing his process.
Ten years ago, Glass joined UNMC, recognizing the potential of technology and innovative teaching methods to transform medical care. "A faculty can request a project, and we have a committee that meets and prioritizes which projects we will pursue," he said.
Glass creates animations tailored for professors to use in class and simulations of surgeries to ensure doctors are aligned in their approach. "I can adjust what colors I assign to the different levels of gray so I can visualize different pieces of the anatomy," he said.
His work makes learning easier and medical procedures safer. "Those are some of the most rewarding parts of our job, to see the direct impact," Glass said.
Despite the rapid advancements in technology, Glass emphasized that it all starts with art.

articles.title: TCU Lab to Test, Research Wearable Technology Across Industries

articles.description_html: TCU Lab to Test, Research Wearable Technology Across Industries  Texas Christian University
articles.article_title: TCU Lab to Test, Research Wearable Technology Across Industries
articles.heading: TCU Lab to Test, Research Wearable Technology Across Industries
articles.summary: Texas Christian University's Department of Fashion Merchandising launched the Athlete Equipment and Materials Design Lab, a new research and testing space focused on the products people depend on in extreme and demanding environments.
articles.content:
TCU Lab to Test, Research Wearable Technology Across Industries
The clothes we wear do more than complete a look. They help control body temperature, manage sweat, protect the skin and support how people move, work and perform every day.
This fall, Texas Christian University’s Department of Fashion Merchandising launched the Athlete Equipment and Materials Design Lab, a new research and testing space focused on the products people depend on in extreme and demanding environments. Reaching far beyond the College of Fine Arts, the facility will support projects connected to athlete performance, rehabilitation, wearable health technologies, protective equipment and NASA-inspired soft goods research. Future work may also include recovery products, wound care materials, adaptive equipment and smart integrated gear for military personnel, first responders and industrial workers.
“We didn't build an academic research lab,” said Charles Freeman, professor and chair of fashion merchandising and director of research and creative scholarship in the College of Fine Arts. “We built an industry lab. We want students to walk into their first job and recognize the equipment because they've already used it here.”
The work has broad interdisciplinary applications. From athletes training in Texas heat to first responders in protective uniforms, military personnel in extreme conditions and astronauts preparing for space environments, the lab will help answer a practical question: how can the materials closest to the body help people perform better and stay safer?
“People often think of fashion as what they see in stores,” Freeman said. “But clothing does much more than that. It creates the environment around the body. How a garment handles heat sweat, movement and protection affects comfort, recovery, performance and safety.”
Beyond the Runway
Designed as part of TCU's continued investment in research and innovation, the lab
brings industry-level testing capabilities to campus and gives students, faculty and
partners a place to study how apparel, equipment and wearable materials perform in
real conditions.
Inside the lab, researchers will test how materials manage sweat, heat, movement, friction, pressure and exposure to water. The goal is to better understand how the products people wear can support the body in everyday life and in high-stress/high-demand environments. The university recently announced a new certificate and research partnership focusing on textiles and soft-goods engineering.
“How we interact with our clothing throughout the day — whether we're sitting on the couch watching TV, saving lives or traveling to space — matters because clothing helps protect the human body,” Freeman said. “That's really the science of what we do, and it broadens people's perspective of what fashion truly is.”
Built for Collaboration
The lab was designed as a shared space for researchers, students and industry partners
working on problems that connect the body, materials, movement and performance. It reflects
TCU’s continued investment in interdisciplinary research and gives faculty across
campus a new way to test the products and materials used in sports, health, work and
extreme environments.
The facility is already supporting projects with the Roach Institute for Athlete Engineering, which was made possible by a $10 million gift from the Roach Foundation of Fort Worth.
“At the Roach Institute, we’re interested in the entire ecosystem that influences human performance, and what someone is wearing is a major part of that,” said Jim Weinstein, director of the Roach Institute. “This lab gives us the ability to connect what we measure in the human body, movement, heat strain, fatigue and performance, with what is happening in the materials and equipment closest to it. That opens up an entirely new level of research for athletes, first responders, military personnel and others performing in demanding environments.”
Reuben Burch, vice provost for research, said that building a good research enterprise is like establishing departments in an organization. The new lab complements the work at the Roach Institute.
“We brought a new capability to Texas that wasn’t here before, and now it’s at TCU. So, we can expand beyond human performance and into the equipment and materials that all athlete personas will wear. This is the kind of research, invention and creation that people can continue to expect from TCU.”
The new lab is also working with TCU’s engineering, physics and kinesiology programs.
“I’ve been pleasantly surprised at the level of collaboration I've experienced since coming to TCU, said Graci Finco, assistant professor of kinesiology in the Harris College of Nursing & Health Sciences. “Our Limb Loss & Difference Lab has already begun several collaborations with both Charles and the Roach Institute to improve care and performance for people with limb loss and limb difference. I’m excited for what we are building together at TCU with other academic and industry partners.”
Research that Starts with Students
Faculty also anticipate the lab will play a central role in TCU’s new Ph.D. program in advanced soft goods and textile systems launching in 2027 by giving doctoral students access to applied research, product testing and industry-facing projects. It will also expand opportunities for undergraduate research, giving students the chance to work alongside faculty with real-world applications. Students will use the same tools found in industry while contributing to work connected to athlete performance, health, safety, product development and wearable technology.
For Freeman, the investment represents more than a new facility. It reflects the growing role of the College of Fine Arts in TCU’s research mission and the value of giving students access to applied research early in their academic careers.
“Investments like this demonstrate TCU’s commitment to becoming a leading R1 institution,” Freeman said. “Most importantly, they give our students the opportunity to ask big questions, solve real problems and take their ideas all the way to the finish line.”

articles.title: Defense Innovation Days Charts Course For Faster Technology Deployment
articles.description: Defense Innovation Days Charts Course For Faster Technology Deployment Ocean News & Technology
articles.description_html: Defense Innovation Days Charts Course For Faster Technology Deployment  Ocean News & Technology
articles.article_title: Defense Innovation Days Charts Course For Faster Technology Deployment
articles.heading: Defense Innovation Days Charts Course for Faster Technology Deployment
articles.summary: SENEDIA's 12th Defense Innovation Days brought together more than 400 defense industry leaders in Rhode Island to address workforce shortages, autonomous underwater vehicle technology, and strategies for deploying critical defense technology faster. Speakers included senior military officials, lawmakers, and private sector executives focused on strengthening the US defense industrial base.
articles.content:
The Alliance for Defense Tech, Talent, and Innovation yesterday concluded its 12th Defense Innovation Days, New England’s signature national security event that attracted more than 400 of the most important decision makers and innovators in the defense industry. Across a dozen speakers and panels, attendees received practical procurement advice and guidance on how the sector can collectively accelerate development and deploy critical technology to the field faster.
“From cutting edge submarines to state-of-the-art autonomous underwater vehicles, Ocean State companies and workers are essential to building the tools, technologies, and manufacturing capacity that keeps America safe. I’m pleased to welcome national security experts and industry leaders from all over to Rhode Island for SENEDIA’s twelfth annual Defense Innovation Days summit. This forum is an opportunity for industry leaders to connect with Rhode Island-based companies, help showcase their capabilities, and create new partnerships that will benefit the state’s economy and America’s security,” said Senator Jack Reed, Ranking Member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. “I’ve worked hard to ensure Rhode Island is a critical defense hub, and I appreciate the outstanding contributions of SENEDIA for hosting this event, strengthening the state’s defense workforce, and helping to sustainably grow Rhode Island’s defense industry.”
Distinguished speakers joining Reed at the sold-out event represented decades of experience in the private and public sectors and armed services, including the Honorable Michael Cadenazzi, Assistant Secretary of War for Industrial Base Policy; Ian Easton, Associate Professor at the China Maritime Studies Institute, US Naval War College; RDML Kelly Ward, Director, Strategic Effects, Commander US Naval Forces Europe/Africa, Commander, Task Force 66 (CTF-66); BG Chris Hackler, Deputy Commanding General, US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command; and CAPT Matthew Lewis, Acting Deputy Director of In-Service Submarines and Industrial Base.
Remarks were also provided by key state and federal leaders such as Rhode Island Governor Dan McKee and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI). Panels included Strength Through Partnership, moderated by Gloria Berlanga, Vice President of Business Development at Rhode Island Commerce; Unmanned Vehicle Technology, moderated by CAPT Colin Corridan (Ret.), former US Navy DCO, Task Force 59, along with RDML Ward and CMDR Thomas Wieland, Deputy Sector Commander, USCG Sector Southeastern New England; a panel on Naval Undersea Warfare Center Division Newport, moderated by three-time Defense Innovation Days speaker Marie Bussiere, NUWC Newport’s Technical Director; and BG Christopher M. Burns, US Army (Ret.), senior advisor VALENS Global.
Key takeaways from this year’s event:
- The US defense industrial base is facing a critical workforce shortage, which requires intervention at every stage and entry point of the pipeline, from early career exploration and education to armed services to later stage professional development.
- The complexity of the current threat landscape demands greater urgency in developing technology and solutions and in building a culture of experimentation and flexibility to get those tools into the hands of warfighters more quickly.
- While Defense Innovation Days always explores challenges and opportunities in national security, this year’s event put practical guidance at the center and highlighted a continued effort to make it easier to do business in the industry and with the Department of War.
“New England is at the center of defense innovation, but as our impressive Defense Innovation Days speakers reinforced, we must do more and move faster to grow the workforce pipeline and foster greater collaboration across the supply chain,” said Stephen Guertin, Executive Director of SENEDIA. “I’m grateful to our speakers, sponsors, and guests, and especially to the hardworking team at SENEDIA, for making this event a success and creating meaningful opportunities for defense businesses and national security leaders to work together in service of our country.”
