articles.content:
- GOOG +1.59%

- EOSE -3.05%

- EOS-USD +0.99%

- EOS +0.74%

MN8 Energy, Eos Energy Enterprises, Inc. (NASDAQ: EOSE ), and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL )'s Google announced a collaboration on September 2 to deliver new, clean, around-the-clock energy resources to the PJM grid in support of growing demand in the region. For Eos, this deal marks an important validation point for its long-duration battery technology.

In response, Stifel analyst Stephen Gengaro reiterated a Buy rating on the stock with a $9.00 price target. The analyst views the Eos-Google collaboration positively despite the initial project being small.

Google Adds Credibility to EOS

EOS will provide a 10MW/ 100 MWh Z3 battery to provide long-duration energy storage as part of an integrated solution supporting data centers. AI data centers are creating demand for power sources that go beyond the shorter-duration energy storage resources and deliver dependable capacity across more hours of the day.

EOS's system is a step in this direction, offering 10 hours of storage and enabling solar power to remain available for substantially longer periods. According to Nathan Kroeker, Chief Commercial Officer at Eos, the company's work with Google is focused on deploying long-duration storage and solving real grid reliability challenges.

EOS operating backdrop also serves positively. For the second quarter, EOS generated a revenue of $68.8million, up 351% year-over-year, while backlog reached a record $807 million. The company also highlighted a commercial opportunity pipeline of $24.6 billion, as of June 30, 2026.

These numbers, together with the new collaboration with Google, point to growing interest in Eos's technology, which may in the future lead to scaling revenues and growing orders for EOS.

Small and Years Away

While Gengaro views this Google deal positively, the analyst also pointed out that the initial project is small and scheduled to start operating in 2030. The solar component of the project is likely to start in 2028, lithium-ion storage will follow in 2029, while the long-duration storage component of the project isn't expected to begin operations until 2030.

Besides this, the company itself remains far from profitability. For the second quarter, gross loss for EOS stood at $48.8 million, compared to $31.0 million in the prior-year period. Gross margin was negative 71%, even though it did improve 132 percentage points year over year and 7 percentage points sequentially.

The headline revenue growth coming from Q2 also has a concentration risk. Almost $55 million, or roughly 80% of Q2 revenue, came from a pre-existing project. The project was contributed to Frontier Power USA upon closing, while the project and FPUSA represented 49% of backlog volume at quarter end.

Management also reported tightening full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $300 million to $350 million, from the prior range of $300 million to $400 million.

Hedge Funds are Building Positions

Recent filings from Insider Monkey's database shows hedge fund interest building for both EOS and Alphabet. For the second quarter, 45 hedge funds held positions in EOS, up from 33 in the prior quarter. Meanwhile, 275 hedge funds held positions in Alphabet, up from 265 in the prior quarter.

Hudson Bay Capital Management held an estimated 13.68 million shares in EOS at the end of Q2, while Electron Capital Partners also increased its position by 25% to 6.68 million shares.

Overall, the EOS-Google-MN8 collaboration serves as a positive for all three companies, particularly Eos. For EOS, the deal can be seen as a potential technology-validation point rather than an event that can radically transform its financial outlook. Provided all goes well, Google could become evidence that EOS's long-duration storage holds strategic importance in the data-center power market.

While we acknowledge the potential of EOS and GOOGL as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. articles.heading: Plan A Technologies Acquires AI Assessment Technology To Expand Technical M&A Due Diligence
articles.summary: Plan A Technologies has acquired a stealth AI assessment tool designed to strengthen its technical M&A due diligence capabilities.
articles.content:
Plan A Technologies has acquired a stealth AI assessment tool designed to strengthen its technical M&A due diligence capabilities.
Plan A, which provides AI and software engineering services and technology advisory capabilities, said the proprietary technology will help its teams analyze complex technology environments more quickly and identify risks, patterns and opportunities that traditional assessment tools may miss.
The company works with private equity firms, strategic acquirers, enterprises and private investors evaluating technology-intensive transactions.
Its technical due diligence work assesses areas including the quality of underlying technology, scalability, integration complexity, modernization requirements, security risks and the level of investment that may be required after an acquisition closes.
The newly acquired technology adds an AI-powered analytical layer to Plan A’s existing approach, which includes expert interviews, manual code reviews, architecture analysis, documentation reviews and commercial code-scanning products.
Plan A expects the technology to be particularly useful for evaluating large and fragmented technology ecosystems and identifying patterns or anomalies that conventional approaches may overlook.
The tool’s creator, Serhii Melnychuk, has joined Plan A Technologies as an architect and will lead its integration and future development.
The acquisition fits within a broader strategy of building and acquiring proprietary technology to augment Plan A’s engineers, architects, data specialists and technology advisors.
Beyond M&A due diligence, Plan A develops custom software, proprietary AI agents and agentic systems, modernizes legacy applications, builds data platforms, manages cloud migrations and integrates enterprise systems.
The company has completed more than 500 product deployments worldwide.
KEY QUOTES:
“Good technical due diligence isn’t about producing a longer list of issues. It’s about distinguishing ordinary, fixable technical debt from something that can fundamentally change the cost or risk profile of a transaction. We help our clients to understand what is really happening underneath the surface of a technology platform and translate that into business implications. Technical due diligence has traditionally relied on expert interviews, manual code review, architecture analysis, documentation, and commercially available code scanning tools. Plan A will continue to use all of those approaches, but this new technology will help us analyze exceptionally large and fragmented technology ecosystems with greater speed and consistency while looking for patterns or anomalies that conventional approaches may miss. AI is not a substitute for senior technical judgment. The advantage comes from combining AI with people who have spent years building, scaling, fixing, integrating, and evaluating real production systems. That combination allows us to ask better questions and give our clients a more complete picture of what they’re actually buying.”
Slav Kulik, Co-Founder of Plan A Technologies
“I wanted to build something that could help experts do their job more effectively and connect signals scattered across different systems. It’s incredibly exciting to see how Plan A integrated my tool into its broader approach and is bringing it to clients around the world.”
Serhii Melnychuk, Architect at Plan A Technologies and Creator of the AI Assessment Technology

articles.heading: LAUSD drops hammer on AI technology in schools with shocking decision to board members
articles.summary: The biggest twist, the school board itself never approved the moratorium.
articles.content:
LAUSD drops hammer on AI technology in schools with shocking decision to board members
- Los Angeles Unified School District has imposed a moratorium on student use of generative AI for the current school year without board approval.
Los Angeles Unified just pulled the plug on student use of generative AI, and some school board members apparently didn't see it coming.
The district has imposed a moratorium for the current school year, blocking students from using generative AI on district devices until further notice.
The surprise decision surfaced this week as a board committee began examining AI use in schools.
The biggest twist, the school board itself never approved the moratorium.
Senior district administrators imposed it on their own authority, saying the move was made in the spirit of the board's unanimous June vote to limit student screen time.
Under that policy, students have no access to screens until second grade, with permitted screen use expanding as children get older.
Board member Kelly Gonez said she believed the district was still operating under its previous AI policy, which allowed older students to use the technology after completing instructional units on digital literacy and responsibility.
"I, even as a board member," was "under the expectation that we were still operating under last year's policy," Gonez said during the inaugural meeting of the district's new Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee. "The fact that it's different today, this school year, is important."
"Breaking news here in the committee," she said.
Board Member Nick Melvoin was also caught off guard.
He did not object to the temporary ban itself, but questioned why such a major decision had not come from the board.
"If the policy is we're not going to allow students [to] use generative AI for the meantime, then we should publicize that," Melvoin said during the inaugural meeting of the district's new Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee. "But also, that didn't really come from the board, so I'm of two minds on that right now … just expressing some discomfort."
The LAUSD move came as New York City announced its own AI crackdown.
The city will bar student-facing generative AI tools, including chatbots and prompt-based tutors, from preschool through eighth grade during the current school year.
The restriction affects nearly 600,000 students, while limited AI use will remain permitted in high schools.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced the New York policy.
At least 37 states have issued AI guidance for schools, but educators nationwide still lack a single definition of AI literacy or a consensus on how the technology should be taught.
Generative AI can produce new material by drawing on patterns in existing data.
But it can also generate wrong answers or take over work educators expect students to do themselves, including writing papers.
Some AI tools can even make those assignments look more student-written by adding errors or current slang.
LAUSD isn't banning all AI.
Non-generative tools can still be used for education, including adaptive learning systems that change question difficulty based on performance and speech-recognition programs that assist with reading fluency or dictation.
AI can also help with text-to-speech, speech-to-text, live captioning and translation when academically appropriate.
Students can still Google things, too.
But Google's "AI Mode" has been switched off on student accounts and devices, preventing students from having an AI conversation or asking follow-up questions.
Search pages may still display short AI-generated summaries.
"Google is working on a technical update that would allow administrators to turn that feature off completely," a district spokesperson said.
LAUSD is facing a severe financial crisis, with county officials warning it could completely run out of operating cash by November 2027.
To avoid a state takeover and balance its books, the district has launched a three-year stabilization plan aimed at slashing $3.5 billion in spending through massive staff layoffs and school cuts by June 2029.

LAUSD drops hammer on AI technology in schools with shocking decision to board members

  • Los Angeles Unified School District has imposed a moratorium on student use of generative AI for the current school year without board approval.

Los Angeles Unified just pulled the plug on student use of generative AI, and some school board members apparently didn't see it coming.

The district has imposed a moratorium for the current school year, blocking students from using generative AI on district devices until further notice.

The surprise decision surfaced this week as a board committee began examining AI use in schools.

Students have no access to screens until second grade, with permitted screen use expanding as children get older. MediaNews Group via Getty Images

The biggest twist, the school board itself never approved the moratorium.

Senior district administrators imposed it on their own authority, saying the move was made in the spirit of the board's unanimous June vote to limit student screen time.

Under that policy, students have no access to screens until second grade, with permitted screen use expanding as children get older.

Board member Kelly Gonez said she believed the district was still operating under its previous AI policy, which allowed older students to use the technology after completing instructional units on digital literacy and responsibility.

Board member Kelly Gonez said she believed the district was still operating under its previous AI policy. MediaNews Group via Getty Images

"The fact that it's different today, this school year, is important," Gonez said. Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

"I, even as a board member," was "under the expectation that we were still operating under last year's policy," Gonez said during the inaugural meeting of the district's new Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee. "The fact that it's different today, this school year, is important."

"Breaking news here in the committee," she said.

Board Member Nick Melvoin was also caught off guard.

He did not object to the temporary ban itself, but questioned why such a major decision had not come from the board.

Board Member Nick Melvoin was also caught off guard. Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

"If the policy is we're not going to allow students [to] use generative AI for the meantime, then we should publicize that," Melvoin said during the inaugural meeting of the district's new Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee. "But also, that didn't really come from the board, so I'm of two minds on that right now … just expressing some discomfort."

The LAUSD move came as New York City announced its own AI crackdown.

The city will bar student-facing generative AI tools, including chatbots and prompt-based tutors, from preschool through eighth grade during the current school year.

The restriction affects nearly 600,000 students, while limited AI use will remain permitted in high schools.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced the New York policy.

New York City will bar student-facing generative AI tools, including chatbots and prompt-based tutors. Luiz C. Ribeiro for New York Post

At least 37 states have issued AI guidance for schools, but educators nationwide still lack a single definition of AI literacy or a consensus on how the technology should be taught.

Generative AI can produce new material by drawing on patterns in existing data.

But it can also generate wrong answers or take over work educators expect students to do themselves, including writing papers.

Some AI tools can even make those assignments look more student-written by adding errors or current slang.

Students can still Google things, too. MediaNews Group via Getty Images

LAUSD isn't banning all AI.

Non-generative tools can still be used for education, including adaptive learning systems that change question difficulty based on performance and speech-recognition programs that assist with reading fluency or dictation.

AI can also help with text-to-speech, speech-to-text, live captioning and translation when academically appropriate.

Students can still Google things, too.

Search pages may still display short AI-generated summaries. PhotoGranary – stock.adobe.com

But Google's "AI Mode" has been switched off on student accounts and devices, preventing students from having an AI conversation or asking follow-up questions.

Search pages may still display short AI-generated summaries.

"Google is working on a technical update that would allow administrators to turn that feature off completely," a district spokesperson said.

LAUSD is facing a severe financial crisis, with county officials warning it could completely run out of operating cash by November 2027.
To avoid a state takeover and balance its books, the district has launched a three-year stabilization plan aimed at slashing $3.5 billion in spending through massive staff layoffs and school cuts by June 2029.

articles.content:
Fourth lithium technology accelerator cohort named
The Venture Center announced this week the fourth cohort of the Arkansas Lithium Technology Accelerator (ALTA), the nation’s first accelerator dedicated to lithium and battery supply chain innovation.
The three-week program will take participating companies across Arkansas, connecting them with lithium producers, researchers, investors, manufacturers, economic development leaders and other strategic partners working to advance the state’s growing lithium and energy technology ecosystem.
Running through September, Cohort Four will kick off Tuesday, Sept. 8 in Magnolia for the first week and move from Little Rock and Northwest Arkansas in weeks two and three, giving participating companies direct exposure to the people, infrastructure andresources shaping Arkansas’ emerging lithium economy.

– Arcam: An MIT-founded battery materials company focused on making lithium iron phosphate battery recycling economically viable.

“We’re extremely pleased with the technical excellence and the market traction of our fourth cohort, who are definitely maintaining the high standards set by their predecessors,” added Arthur Orduña, executive director of The Venture Center.

articles.title: Why Credo Technology Sank This Week
articles.description: Why Credo Technology Sank This Week The Motley Fool
articles.description_html: Why Credo Technology Sank This Week  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: Why Credo Technology Sank This Week | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: Why Credo Technology Sank This Week
articles.summary: Credo delivered impressive triple-digit growth, but margin pressure led to a violent sell-off amid a high valuation.
articles.content:
Shares of AI networking up-and-comer Credo Technology (CRDO -0.64%) sank this week, falling 29.5% through Thursday trading, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence.
Credo delivered its first fiscal quarter 2027 earnings results this week, and while the headline numbers technically beat analyst expectations, the stock plunged due to some less-than-perfect margin figures. Even after this week's plunge, Credo trades at a high valuation, so anything less than a big beat and raise beyond bullish expectations was probably bound to be met with a pullback.
NASDAQ: CRDO
Key Data Points
Credo's financial results take off, even as the stock reverses
In its fiscal first quarter, Credo grew revenue 114.7% to $479.0 million, while adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings per share rocketed 130% higher to $1.20. Both figures actually beat expectations. Management also guided for strong quarter-over-quarter revenue growth in the current period, which also came in well above expectations.
So, what was the problem? Well, Credo trades at a very high valuation. Heading into this week, its market cap was around $45 billion, relative to its current revenue run rate of about $2 billion. Even though Credo is growing at a triple-digit rate and revenue will be higher in the year ahead, the early week valuation was still about 18 times the upcoming year's revenue estimate of $2.49 billion.
Credo does generate relatively high margins on its specialized networking equipment, but the past quarter's gross margins also saw some pressure. GAAP gross margins fell to 64.5%, down from 68% last quarter and 67.4% in the year-ago quarter. While adjusted gross margins were within the range of the prior quarters, there was apparently a big uptick in stock-based compensation that investors didn't like. The current quarter's guidance also forecasts an even lower GAAP gross margin, so the trend is going the wrong way.
Credo is an AI winner, but not a cheap stock
After its 30% drawdown this week, Credo trades at around 26 times this year's adjusted earnings estimates. That's a very reasonable valuation, given Credo's strong AI-oriented growth outlook.
However, investors should be cognizant that the adjusted earnings estimates exclude stock-based compensation, which is a real cost because it dilutes shareholders. Last quarter, GAAP net income was just a little more than half of non-GAAP income. So, investors should probably regard Credo's true forward earnings multiple as something closer to 50 than 26. In that light, Credo may be seen as more fully valued. That being said, if Credo can maintain triple-digit growth figures beyond next year or something close to it, this past week's pullback could be seen as an opportunity to buy.

articles.title: Inside the $9.5 Trillion Forex Market: Tag Markets on How Technology Is Changing Access
articles.description: Inside the $9.5 Trillion Forex Market: Tag Markets on How Technology Is Changing Access GeekWire
articles.description_html: Inside the $9.5 Trillion Forex Market: Tag Markets on How Technology Is Changing Access  GeekWire
articles.article_title: Inside the $9.5 Trillion Forex Market: Tag Markets on How Technology Is Changing Access
articles.heading: Inside the $9.5 Trillion Forex Market: Tag Markets on How Technology Is Changing Access
articles.summary: Foreign exchange is so embedded in the global economy that most people encounter it without thinking about the market behind… Read More
articles.content:
Foreign exchange is so embedded in the global economy that most people encounter it without thinking about the market behind it. A company paying an overseas supplier, an investor hedging currency exposure, a bank managing liquidity, and a trader speculating on a currency pair are all participating in the same vast system.
In April 2025, average daily turnover in the global foreign exchange market reached about $9.5 trillion, according to final data from the Bank for International Settlements. That was roughly 27 percent higher than three years earlier. The US dollar remained dominant, appearing on one side of nearly 89 percent of all FX trades.
Those numbers reveal something important about Forex. Retail trading is only one small part of a market built around international finance, investment, hedging, funding, and institutional risk management.
The market is also more varied than the currency charts familiar to individual traders.
Spot transactions, where currencies are exchanged at current market prices, accounted for about 31 percent of global turnover in April 2025. Outright forwards, which can be used to lock in an exchange rate for a future date, represented about 19 percent. FX swaps remained the largest individual category, accounting for roughly 42 percent of turnover.
Much of this activity exists because currencies create exposure whenever money moves across borders. A multinational company receiving revenue in one currency while paying expenses in another may want to reduce uncertainty. Asset managers investing overseas can face similar concerns. Banks continuously manage flows between currencies as part of their broader financial operations.
Technology has changed how participants connect to this market.
The institutional FX market remains dominated by large financial firms, but electronic execution is now deeply embedded in its structure. BIS research found that electronic trading represented 59 percent of FX execution in April 2025. Digital platforms can connect participants to multiple sources of pricing and allow large volumes of information and orders to move quickly across markets.
The same technological progression has widened access at the retail level.
A modern Forex brokerage translates a complex global market into an environment where individual clients can view prices, select instruments, manage accounts, and place trades through digital interfaces. The technology between the user and the wider market is therefore an important part of how retail access works.
Tag Markets has built its brokerage around that idea.
Rather than treating market access as the entire product, the company has invested in technology and infrastructure around how clients learn, choose accounts, and decide how they want to participate. Its proprietary CopyX technology is one example. Clients can review available traders and strategies, examine previous results, and choose whether they want qualifying trading activity replicated automatically in their own accounts.
Independent trading remains available for people who prefer to analyze markets and make their own decisions.
Education is another part of the model. Through its Forex education platform, Tag Markets provides clients with video courses, written learning material, and live training sessions at no additional cost. The value of those resources is not that education can remove market uncertainty. It cannot. Their role is to give clients more context before they decide how they want to approach trading.
The distinction matters in a market as large and complex as foreign exchange.
The $9.5 trillion daily figure can make Forex sound like one enormous trading arena, but the reality is a network of different participants with different motives. Banks may be managing liquidity. Corporations may be hedging future payments. Investment firms may be adjusting international portfolios. Individual traders may be expressing a view on how one currency will move against another.
Technology connects these participants in different ways, but it does not make their objectives identical.
Understanding the structure of the market therefore matters before focusing on the trading interface. The EUR/USD price on a screen is the visible edge of a much larger system shaped by interest rates, global capital flows, central bank policy, commercial activity, and changing demand for currencies.
Brokerages such as Tag Markets face a technology challenge: make access more usable without making the underlying market appear simpler than it is. Platforms can improve speed. Copy trading can create another participation model. Education can make information easier to reach. None changes the fact that currencies move in response to forces far larger than any individual trader.
A useful starting point for understanding modern Forex is simple: technology has made the market easier to access, but access is not the same as understanding. The more digital the trading experience becomes, the more valuable it is to know what sits behind the screen.

articles.title: Texas Schools Embraced Technology, but What Is the Cost?
articles.description: Texas Schools Embraced Technology, but What Is the Cost? Texas Scorecard
articles.description_html: Texas Schools Embraced Technology, but What Is the Cost?  Texas Scorecard
articles.article_title: Texas Schools Embraced Technology, but What Is the Cost?
articles.heading: Texas Schools Embraced Technology, but What Is the Cost?
articles.summary: Texas schools pour millions into digital instructional materials each year, yet new research is raising concerns about whether more screen time actually benefits students.
articles.content:
Texas public schools have been expanding the use of laptops, tablets, online curricula, and digital assessments for the past decade. But as lawmakers restrict student cellphone use, a broader question is arising of whether the state should continue treating school-issued technology as a central instructional tool.
According to research from the Texas Public Policy Foundation’s Matthew McCormick, during the 2025-26 school year, $364 million was disbursed from the Instructional Materials and Technology Allotment. Of that money, $247 million went toward online or electronic materials. In addition, $18.6 million went toward laptops and tablets.
The spending reflects a policy shift that began in 2011 when the 82nd Texas Legislature expanded the Instructional Materials and Technology Allotment (IMTA) to allow public schools and charter schools to use state funds for educational technology, including digital instructional materials and classroom devices.
The state’s transition to online STAAR testing and the COVID-19 pandemic further accelerated the use of one-to-one student devices.
That investment has drawn growing scrutiny over whether digital instruction delivers better academic results. Research suggests that increased use of screens does not necessarily translate into better academic output.
Students can perform worse when reading from screens than from physical materials, with one study cited by McCormick finding a difference equivalent to roughly two-thirds of a grade level.
“For too long, the proliferation of technology in Texas public schools has gone unexamined,” wrote McCormick. “Far from delivering the promised revolution in education, educational technology has produced lackluster results while importing novel and unavoidable harms into the classroom.”
The concerns with technology in classrooms are not limited to academics.
Common Sense Media reported in 2022 that 31 percent of surveyed teens had viewed pornography while at school, with 44 percent of those who viewed it during the school day saying they had done so on a school-owned device.
Lawmakers across the country have begun to push back.
During its 2026 legislative session, Utah passed a law prohibiting screen time for students in kindergarten through third grade, with exceptions for computer literacy courses and standardized testing.
Texas has taken a narrower approach.
So far, the state’s approach has focused primarily on personal devices rather than school-issued instructional technology.
In 2025, the Texas lawmakers passed House Bill 1481, requiring school districts to prohibit students from using personal communication devices during the school day.
The Texas Education Agency was allocated $20 million in state grant funding to help schools implement the law.
In 2025, State Sen. Lois Kolkhorst introduced Senate Bill 966, which would have directed the Department of State Health Services and the Texas Education Agency to study the public health effects of digital learning, including its impact on student mental health and academic performance.
With Texas already restricting personal devices in schools, the question now is whether the state will stop at cell phones.
McCormick suggested that lawmakers could revoke the 2011 expansion that allowed the IMTA to be used for technology as one avenue of curtailing the explosion of digital learning.
Additionally, school districts currently seek voter approval for taxpayer-backed bond debt to issue student devices. McCormick recommended disallowing this as an acceptable bond purchase.
“If legislators want to provide effective instruction to Texas students while ensuring their safety and protecting their mental health, they must break schools’ addiction to technology,” concluded McCormick.

articles.summary: Gameplan announced that as of July 31, 2026, its Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals Certification, listed under certification code GAMEP001, appears within Florida's Information Technology career pathway and is identified for eligible students through 10th grade, subject to final State Board of Education approval.Developed in collaboration with Epic Games, the Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals certification is delivered exclusively through Gameplan, which serves as the credential's independent assessment
articles.content:
Information Technology credential could give eligible Florida schools a funded pathway to introduce real-time 3D skills to students through 10th grade

MIAMI, FL / ACCESS Newswire / September 3, 2026 / Gameplan, an education technology company helping schools connect student interest in gaming and technology with career-ready skills, today announced that its Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals Certification is listed on Florida's 2026-27 Career and Professional Education, or CAPE, Industry Certification Funding List, pending final approval by the Florida State Board of Education.

Gameplan announced that as of July 31, 2026, its Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals Certification, listed under certification code GAMEP001 , appears within Florida's Information Technology career pathway and is identified for eligible students through 10th grade, subject to final State Board of Education approval.

Developed in collaboration with Epic Games, the Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals certification is delivered exclusively through Gameplan, which serves as the credential's independent assessment delivery and administration partner.

"Teachers have been asking for an industry credential for years, and now educators have the Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals Certification that they can build a program around," said Steve Isaacs, Director of Secondary Education at Epic Games. "We're excited to offer the certification that gives students a way to turn game development, digital art, and animation projects into a real-world credential that they can present to colleges and employers. With our partner Gameplan, it's now approved in 9 states and on Florida's CAPE list, unlocking CTE funding for schools teaching Unreal Engine. "

If granted final approval, the certification would give eligible Florida schools and districts an opportunity to provide students with industry-connected instruction in 3D design, interactive technology, and Unreal Engine while potentially generating supplemental state funding when qualifying students successfully earn the credential.

"Being listed on Florida's CAPE Industry Certification Funding List represents an important step toward making advanced technology education more accessible to students across the state," said Rasmus Sandström, CEO of Gameplan. "Students are already highly interested in gaming, game design, 3D design, and immersive technology. With final approval, schools would have another way to transform that interest into structured learning, practical skills, and a recognized credential that can support students as they explore future education and career pathways."

What Final CAPE Approval Would Mean for Florida Schools

Florida's CAPE program connects education and workforce development by encouraging schools to offer programs that lead to approved industry certifications and prepare students for continued education and future careers.

Pending final approval, Gameplan's Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals certification is listed as a CAPE Basic Non-Articulated credential with a proposed funding and accountability value of 0.1 for eligible student earners.

If approved, the 0.1 value would be used within Florida's education funding formula when calculating applicable supplemental funding associated with eligible student credential attainment.

For Florida schools and districts, successful certification attainment could:

- Generate supplemental state funding for eligible student earners

Generate supplemental state funding for eligible student earners

- Support applicable college and career acceleration and school accountability measures

Support applicable college and career acceleration and school accountability measures

- Strengthen or expand career and technical education programs

Strengthen or expand career and technical education programs

- Provide students with a CAPE-listed technology credential

Provide students with a CAPE-listed technology credential

- Create an accessible entry point into 3D design and interactive technology pathways

Create an accessible entry point into 3D design and interactive technology pathways

The proposed listing identifies the certification for eligible students through 10th grade. With final approval, schools would be able to introduce these skills earlier and give students more time to continue into advanced courses, projects, certifications, and career-connected learning experiences throughout high school.

"Florida schools could soon have an opportunity to introduce students to real-time 3D technology earlier, within a structured pathway that can grow with them throughout high school," said Chris Aviles, Director of Education at Gameplan. "Final approval would help educators connect the technology students are excited about with meaningful projects, an attainable industry certification, and skills that apply across game development, media, simulation, and other rapidly evolving fields."

Building Foundational Unreal Engine Skills

Unreal Engine is a real-time 3D creation tool used across industries including game development, film and television production, architecture, automotive design, simulation, and immersive experiences.

Gameplan's Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals program is designed for classroom implementation and introduces students to essential concepts through structured, project-based learning. Students develop foundational technical skills while completing practical work that can contribute to a portfolio and prepare them for more advanced coursework.

Gameplan provides ready-to-teach curriculum, educator resources, student progress tracking, assessment tools, and certification preparation, while also serving as the exclusive delivery platform for the Unreal Engine 3D Fundamentals certification exam.

articles.content:
The fourth cohort of Arkansas Lithium Technology Accelerator will soon begin the three-week accelerator program, which will give the companies exposure to people, infrastructure and resources throughout Arkansas.
ALTA is the nation’s first accelerator dedicated to lithium and battery supply-chain innovation. The inaugural program occurred in July 2025.
This newest cohort’s companies are ACT-ion Battery Technologies, Princeton Critical Minerals and Arcam.
“ALTA is about more than developing individual leaders, it’s about driving economic growth through statewide partnership and innovation,” said Sarah Thomas, innovation program manager at The Venture Center.
Standard Lithium and the University of Arkansas are partnering again with the Venture Center for this accelerator.
ALTA is also supported this year by many statewide business and community sponsors, including ExxonMobil, Tetra Technologies, Corzan, Rose Law Firm, Ghidotti Communications, Blue Flame Minerals, the Arkansas State Chamber of Commerce and Terra Volta.
The program launch will take place at 4 p.m. Sept. 8 at Southern Arkansas University in Magnolia.

articles.content:
GILLETTE, Wyo. — The Campbell County Board of Commissioners discussed road work, building demolition, technology upgrades and courthouse security during its meeting.
Commissioners approved the consent agenda and county vouchers, along with budget transfers for several county departments for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. The transfers included the Assessor’s Office, Children’s Development Services, Emergency Management, Library, Parks and Recreation, Public Health and the Sheriff’s Office.
The board also went over upcoming dates, including the Labor Day courthouse closure, a Public Land Board meeting at the Camplex and the 9/11 Commemorative Ceremony.
Commissioners discussed the Bishop Road Mill and Overlay Project, which was awarded to Croell Inc. for $884,775. Croell was the only company to submit a bid. The project is also expected to include a $200,000 change order to add a leveling course to help smooth the road.
The board also approved a $72,558 contract with Norton Construction to demolish the Erickson House at the airport. The work will include removing concrete basement walls and septic tanks and capping the private well. The Sheriff’s Office asked to use the building for about a week of training before demolition begins.
Another major discussion centered on an upgrade to the audio and visual system in the commissioners chambers. The county approved a $474,332.11 sole-source agreement with Forte to replace the outdated system, which has also been overheating.
Commissioners questioned the cost of the 115-inch TVs included in the project. They also discussed adding live closed captioning to meet Americans with Disabilities Act requirements that take effect in spring 2027. The agreement passed 4-1 with Ford voting against.
The board also discussed plans to improve security at the courthouse. The county, courts, Sheriff’s Office and Public Works Department will work together to apply for a $344,700 state grant. The county would provide a $300,000 match.
The proposed security work includes a screening station in the first-floor lobby, panic buttons, alarms, stairwell door sensors and a remodel of the clerk’s office.

articles.summary: A Marquette county middle school is getting students involved with campus projects.
articles.content:
Career and Technology Education programs gain traction with younger people, NICE Community Schools says
ISHPEMING TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WLUC) - The trades are always in need of younger talent. That’s why schools in the U.P. have been putting extra emphasis on introducing students to Career and Technical Education, or CTE, opportunities.
Nearly three years ago, NICE Community Schools invested $1.5 million to renovate its career and technology education facilities.
With another school year starting up, the school says interest in the trades is skewing younger.
Middle school students at Aspen Ridge Middle School are making concrete impacts in their community through CTE courses. They have built trails on campus grounds, maintained wetlands and harvested maple syrup.
John Jessen, a CTE instructor, says NICE has put a lot of resources into the program.
“We’re really blessed in this district that our district really supports Career and Technical Education, and that’s evident by all of our renovations that we’ve done, all of our new programs and all the, all the things that we’re doing here,” Jessen says.
High schoolers can then get affiliated credits with Northern Michigan University or other institutions just by taking high school courses.
NICE Community Schools Superintendent Bryan DeAugustine says students find opportunities with either universities or companies right after graduating.
“And we’ve even had students who’ve gone from graduation right to working on our buildings with local contractors. So doing things like pouring footings, helping with welding and electrical work, it’s really been amazing. And I think it’s a great opportunity for our students,” DeAugustine says.
DeAugustine says investing in these needed trades early can bring great results down the line.

articles.title: Massachusetts' first heat resilience officer eyes data, technology for statewide response to extreme heat
articles.description: Massachusetts' first heat resilience officer eyes data, technology for statewide response to extreme heat StateScoop
articles.description_html: Massachusetts' first heat resilience officer eyes data, technology for statewide response to extreme heat  StateScoop
articles.article_title: Massachusetts' first heat resilience officer eyes data, technology for statewide response to extreme heat | StateScoop
articles.heading: Massachusetts’ first heat resilience officer eyes data, technology for statewide response to extreme heat
articles.summary: Katie Schlick, Massachusetts's first heat resilience officer, eyes data & technology for statewide response to extreme heat
articles.content:
Massachusetts’ first heat resilience officer eyes data, technology for statewide response to extreme heat
Massachusetts’ first heat resilience officer is looking to data, mapping technology and emergency communications to help the state better prepare and respond to extreme heat, a growing threat that has historically received less attention in the Northeast.
Katie Schlick, who took the role in August, will lead coordination across state and local governments and work with communities to prepare for rising temperatures, protect public health and reduce the impacts of extreme heat.
Gov. Maura Healey announced Schlick’s appointment last month at the state’s Clark University, home to the Human-Environment Regional Observatory Program, which studies how communities experience environmental change and how local planning can reduce climate risks. Massachusetts and Arizona are the only two U.S. states to appoint statewide heat officers to combat rising extreme temperatures.
“Extreme heat is becoming more common, more intense and more dangerous in Massachusetts,” said Healey. “We need to be ready for what that means for our families and communities. This new role will lead our work to prepare for extreme heat and make sure we’re doing everything we can to keep Massachusetts and our residents safe.”
In an interview, Schlick said her initial priority will be building the data infrastructure needed to understand how extreme heat is affecting communities, critical infrastructure like utilities, public health and the state’s economy. That could include combining data on heat-related illnesses and deaths with information about housing, cooling access, transportation, schools, agriculture and vulnerable populations.
StateScoop: How does it feel to step into this brand new role that hasn’t existed in Massachusetts before?
Katie Schlick: I think it’s really exciting and, as a young person working in climate, it’s been really motivating and inspiring to see one of our elected leaders in Gov. Healey showing real leadership and taking what we know to be a real risk to the public health and safety of the people across Massachusetts, but also across the United States and globally, and turning that that into action.
SS: I would love to know the catalyst for creating this role. Beyond rising temperatures and how they’re impacting everything from infrastructure to agriculture to education to healthcare, extreme heat has been ubiquitous for some time. Why do you think it took the state so long to recognize this need?
KS: I think that what we’re really seeing is that extreme heat is showing up in every corner and every community of the state, in our built environment, our natural environment and ecosystems, that’s affecting our economy, our infrastructure, roadways and our communities. In Massachusetts, it’s true that the state has warmed by more than three and a half degrees over the past century or so, and most of that warming has occurred since the ’90s. And we’re expecting those numbers to double or triple in the next couple of decades. We know that globally and nationally, extreme heat is the number one killer and kills more people than floods, fires, and hurricanes combined, which is really staggering. New research from Boston University found that those deaths are almost certainly an undercount, and actually we could be looking at more than a factor of five greater numbers of heat-related deaths in the United States. The governor sees this as a real threat to the people of Massachusetts, but also an opportunity to pull more people into the fold and move towards solutions. My job is really to connect those different dots across researchers, regional planning agencies, and local governments who have already been leading the charge in figuring out how to tackle extreme heat, and we need more data to do it.
SS: You mentioned building a better data infrastructure to connect these historically siloed state and local agencies, so everyone has access to the same type of underlying foundation. What role do you see technology — like heat sensors, radar, lidar, GIS mapping, satellite imagery — playing as you move forward and think about making Massachusetts more resilient?
KS: What Arizona has stood up, one of the first things that they tackled was getting down this data infrastructure so that they could track more closely these heat-related illnesses and heat-related deaths. One of the approaches that we see very early on is we need to get our arms around the full challenge all across the economy. What are the impacts to our crops and food security in the state? When you think about our built environment, you know how many homes have access to cooling infrastructure. How many folks have the ability to actually turn on their air conditioning on the hottest of days? Do they have access to a cooling center? Do we have safe transportation to get them there? Heat can buckle roadways and cause all sorts of slowed mass transit systems… Can we look at all these impacts and put numbers to them? Because when we can quantify it, then we can direct resources and partnerships to strengthen and fill those gaps. Then we can look at the technologies that we have to map, to visualize, to track and to present that information and communicate it.
SS: What are some of the challenges or obstacles you anticipate running into as you move forward with connecting all of these historically siloed agencies?
KS: Part of the challenge will be in standing up this very holistic data infrastructure. I’m really focused on making sure that we have the fullest understanding possible of the problem, cutting across all of these agencies, in every corner of the state. So that in and of itself I think will be a heavy lift. I also want to make sure that we are as inclusive of all our different vulnerable populations and the different geographies across the state. There’s also a kind of communications challenge, just in the sense of getting people to think about and see the opportunity in Massachusetts being a proactive leader on an issue like extreme heat. It’s obviously generally thought of as a cold-weather state, and I’m from New England, and I know how much snow we get up here. I know growing up in Connecticut, there was always more snow in the Boston area than there was in Connecticut. Our infrastructure was built to withstand snow and really icy temperatures, and our buildings are built to keep the heat in. And our government structures are built to activate in a cold-weather scenario. We just need to start rethinking now that we are seeing increasingly long heat seasons and an increased number of unhealthy heat days. We are seeing in the data that we are just not as prepared to handle that. But we know this is preventable.
There’s some really interesting social science research that talks about the gap between what we perceive as our risk from extreme heat versus what our actual exposure risk is from extreme heat. That gap is the greatest in our northern states. So I think this role will be really critical in helping to close that gap. This work is about getting into the weeds of all these different government levers that we can pull on the new technologies we can deploy: getting more heat pumps out there, shoring up our electric grids that it’s more reliable and more affordable, protecting our workers indoor and outdoor, protecting our kids, our youngest and our oldest populations, but it’s also going to be about making sure everyone is aware of the risk and knowledgeable about the resources they can utilize to keep themselves safe even on the hottest and the smokiest of days.
SS: How are you going to measure progress your office is making over time?
KS: I’ve been very excited to kind of read the broader framing of just how important it is to get this data infrastructure down as early on as possible, so that we can get a real understanding of where we need to direct our resources based on where the greatest need arises. So part of the metrics is going to be really understanding again across all these different state sectors and different vulnerable populations. I hate to just say ‘quantify,’ because it’s more than that. There’s so many lived experiences attached to all this. You may have workers who are working at a lower productivity level because the human body is not meant to work in those kinds of conditions; what is the economic cost as a result of that? When you look at the different heat-related, heat-caused illnesses and deaths, making sure that our medical examiners know how to classify that so that we have the data to report on it. In our school systems, how many of our schools have air conditioning now? It’s also understanding the number of people that we’re reaching through our heat alerts. When we hear a storm is coming, we all watch the news. We all learn the guidance and what you’re supposed to do. Do we have a similar kind of communications educational infrastructure set up on these unhealthy heat days? There’s this amazing program in North Carolina, which I’m familiar with from my work at the U.S. Climate Alliance, where they have helped municipal governments stand up heat action planning and tabletop exercises in their communities, so that not just at the state level where you’re thinking about this in terms of your emergency management planning and hazard mitigation planning, but that’s embedded in all of your your local infrastructure and regional infrastructure. So I think we’ll be working really closely there.
SS: I’m glad you mentioned your previous work in the U.S. Climate Alliance, because I wanted to ask you what lessons you have learned over the course of your career that you’re bringing with you into this one.
Katie Schlick: Being on the first-ever White House climate team, I think that there I really saw how we can bring this whole-of-government systems approach to tackling climate change to life. With the Biden-Harris administration, it was very much focused around cutting across climate, equity, jobs, and justice, and we had literally a director hired for every sector of the economy, whether it was transportation, or ag lands, or resilience, or having a whole team dedicated to environmental justice. One of the biggest things I took away from my two years there was how much you can get done when you throw that weight of government behind you and when you have leadership that’s really pushing for change and advocating in every room they’re in. Having worked then across state government this past year and a half with the U.S. Climate Alliance, I also have a huge understanding for the role of state government. It’s a systems-level thinking, but it’s also just a real understanding of the capacity of government to do good, and that’s something that I think we need to be leaning into. We have to hold on to how much we can do and how government can help us solve really big problems like climate change, like extreme heat impacts on our communities. So I’ll be bringing an ability to do some bigger-picture visioning of what a more heat-resilient Massachusetts can and will look like.

In Massachusetts, it’s true that the state has warmed by more than three and a half degrees over the past century or so, and most of that warming has occurred since the ’90s. And we’re expecting those numbers to double or triple in the next couple of decades. We know that globally and nationally, extreme heat is the number one killer and kills more people than floods, fires, and hurricanes combined, which is really staggering. New research from Boston University found that those deaths are almost certainly an undercount, and actually we could be looking at more than a factor of five greater numbers of heat-related deaths in the United States. The governor sees this as a real threat to the people of Massachusetts, but also an opportunity to pull more people into the fold and move towards solutions. My job is really to connect those different dots across researchers, regional planning agencies, and local governments who have already been leading the charge in figuring out how to tackle extreme heat, and we need more data to do it.

SS: You mentioned building a better data infrastructure to connect these historically siloed state and local agencies, so everyone has access to the same type of underlying foundation. What role do you see technology — like heat sensors, radar, lidar, GIS mapping, satellite imagery — playing as you move forward and think about making Massachusetts more resilient?

KS: What Arizona has stood up, one of the first things that they tackled was getting down this data infrastructure so that they could track more closely these heat-related illnesses and heat-related deaths. One of the approaches that we see very early on is we need to get our arms around the full challenge all across the economy. What are the impacts to our crops and food security in the state? When you think about our built environment, you know how many homes have access to cooling infrastructure. How many folks have the ability to actually turn on their air conditioning on the hottest of days? Do they have access to a cooling center? Do we have safe transportation to get them there? Heat can buckle roadways and cause all sorts of slowed mass transit systems… Can we look at all these impacts and put numbers to them? Because when we can quantify it, then we can direct resources and partnerships to strengthen and fill those gaps. Then we can look at the technologies that we have to map, to visualize, to track and to present that information and communicate it.

SS: What are some of the challenges or obstacles you anticipate running into as you move forward with connecting all of these historically siloed agencies?

KS: Part of the challenge will be in standing up this very holistic data infrastructure. I’m really focused on making sure that we have the fullest understanding possible of the problem, cutting across all of these agencies, in every corner of the state. So that in and of itself I think will be a heavy lift. I also want to make sure that we are as inclusive of all our different vulnerable populations and the different geographies across the state. There’s also a kind of communications challenge, just in the sense of getting people to think about and see the opportunity in Massachusetts being a proactive leader on an issue like extreme heat. It’s obviously generally thought of as a cold-weather state, and I’m from New England, and I know how much snow we get up here. I know growing up in Connecticut, there was always more snow in the Boston area than there was in Connecticut. Our infrastructure was built to withstand snow and really icy temperatures, and our buildings are built to keep the heat in. And our government structures are built to activate in a cold-weather scenario. We just need to start rethinking now that we are seeing increasingly long heat seasons and an increased number of unhealthy heat days. We are seeing in the data that we are just not as prepared to handle that. But we know this is preventable.

There’s some really interesting social science research that talks about the gap between what we perceive as our risk from extreme heat versus what our actual exposure risk is from extreme heat. That gap is the greatest in our northern states. So I think this role will be really critical in helping to close that gap. This work is about getting into the weeds of all these different government levers that we can pull on the new technologies we can deploy: getting more heat pumps out there, shoring up our electric grids that it’s more reliable and more affordable, protecting our workers indoor and outdoor, protecting our kids, our youngest and our oldest populations, but it’s also going to be about making sure everyone is aware of the risk and knowledgeable about the resources they can utilize to keep themselves safe even on the hottest and the smokiest of days.

SS: How are you going to measure progress your office is making over time?

KS: I’ve been very excited to kind of read the broader framing of just how important it is to get this data infrastructure down as early on as possible, so that we can get a real understanding of where we need to direct our resources based on where the greatest need arises. So part of the metrics is going to be really understanding again across all these different state sectors and different vulnerable populations. I hate to just say ‘quantify,’ because it’s more than that. There’s so many lived experiences attached to all this. You may have workers who are working at a lower productivity level because the human body is not meant to work in those kinds of conditions; what is the economic cost as a result of that? When you look at the different heat-related, heat-caused illnesses and deaths, making sure that our medical examiners know how to classify that so that we have the data to report on it. In our school systems, how many of our schools have air conditioning now? It’s also understanding the number of people that we’re reaching through our heat alerts. When we hear a storm is coming, we all watch the news. We all learn the guidance and what you’re supposed to do. Do we have a similar kind of communications educational infrastructure set up on these unhealthy heat days? There’s this amazing program in North Carolina, which I’m familiar with from my work at the U.S. Climate Alliance, where they have helped municipal governments stand up heat action planning and tabletop exercises in their communities, so that not just at the state level where you’re thinking about this in terms of your emergency management planning and hazard mitigation planning, but that’s embedded in all of your your local infrastructure and regional infrastructure. So I think we’ll be working really closely there.

SS: I’m glad you mentioned your previous work in the U.S. Climate Alliance, because I wanted to ask you what lessons you have learned over the course of your career that you’re bringing with you into this one.

Katie Schlick: Being on the first-ever White House climate team, I think that there I really saw how we can bring this whole-of-government systems approach to tackling climate change to life. With the Biden-Harris administration, it was very much focused around cutting across climate, equity, jobs, and justice, and we had literally a director hired for every sector of the economy, whether it was transportation, or ag lands, or resilience, or having a whole team dedicated to environmental justice. One of the biggest things I took away from my two years there was how much you can get done when you throw that weight of government behind you and when you have leadership that’s really pushing for change and advocating in every room they’re in. Having worked then across state government this past year and a half with the U.S. Climate Alliance, I also have a huge understanding for the role of state government. It’s a systems-level thinking, but it’s also just a real understanding of the capacity of government to do good, and that’s something that I think we need to be leaning into. We have to hold on to how much we can do and how government can help us solve really big problems like climate change, like extreme heat impacts on our communities. So I’ll be bringing an ability to do some bigger-picture visioning of what a more heat-resilient Massachusetts can and will look like.

articles.content:
California and the Australian state of Queensland ink new partnership to accelerate climate resilience, agricultural technology, and innovation
What you need to know: California and Queensland are developing a new partnership to advance agricultural innovation and climate resilience
SACRAMENTO – California Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis and representatives from Governor Newsom’s administration recently welcomed Premier and Minister for Veterans David Crisafulli, Member of Parliament for the Government of Queensland, Australia, to ink a new memorandum of cooperation focused on agricultural innovation, biotechnology, and productivity.
As world leaders in agricultural production, Queensland and California are deepening opportunities to advance climate action on working lands and further innovation in agricultural technology and farm productivity.
Australia and Queensland are not only important partners for California, but share similar ambitions on climate, agriculture, and trade. This partnership provides the foundation for California and Queensland to leverage opportunities for our respective economies and further resilience on our working lands.
Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis
The historic visit marks a new chapter in the partnership between California and Queensland. The partnership will collaborate on agricultural innovation, biotechnology and productivity through cooperation on:
- Research and innovation
- Commercialization and industry engagement
- Trade, investment and market development
- Skills and capability development
- Government collaboration
Under this partnership, the California Department of Food and Agriculture and the Queensland Department of Primary Industries will create an action plan to implement the objectives of the memorandum of cooperation.
In California, this memorandum of cooperation aligns with the state’s investment in the Jobs First California AgTech Alliance and the Farms, Food, Future (F3) initiative. The state’s AgTech Alliance brings together founders, growers, and industry leaders to scale proven technologies, create career pathways for agricultural workers, and strengthen regional partnerships. F3 is supporting agriculture in California’s Central Valley by developing new ag technology, enhancing sustainable farming practices, and supporting workforce development. Together, these complementary initiatives enhance innovation, ag tech, and workforce development across the state.
In Queensland, the government has launched the Sowing the Seeds of Farming Innovation Fund, a $AU30 million investment fund to advance long-term agricultural production by supporting commercially focused innovation.
The visit also marked California and Queensland’s shared commitment to supporting the success of the upcoming Los Angeles 2028 and Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
As hosts to back-to-back Games, California and Queensland have a unique opportunity to deepen our partnership, share best practices, and build a lasting legacy that extends well beyond 2032.
How we got here
California has long been a key player on the international stage — from taking joint action on climate change to identifying new pathways and partnerships for sustained economic growth. During the Newsom Administration alone, California has formed over 70 international partnerships that lay critical groundwork for our continued economic success, while prioritizing workers and businesses that benefit from these new opportunities.
Golden State and global partnerships
- United Kingdom (2026): California and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum of understanding to tackle climate change and promote sustainable development together. The memorandum of understanding builds on an already strong history of cooperation, and focuses on areas for collaboration including clean energy technologies, climate resilience, decarbonizing transportation, and protecting the natural environment.
- Chile (2025): California and Chile signed a memorandum of understanding regarding exchanging information, developing best practices, and cooperating on methane emissions reduction. Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, and the partnership between California and Chile opens up new opportunities for both partners to cooperate on methane reduction in waste, agriculture, and energy sectors.
- Colombia (2025): California and Colombia signed a partnership to advance joint efforts on forest conservation, methane reduction, climate resilience, and clean energy development. The memorandum of understanding deepens coordination on protecting the Amazon, strengthening biodiversity, and expanding nature-based climate solutions that support sustainable and equitable economic growth.
- Nigeria (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with Nigeria on sustainable urban transportation, green ports, low-carbon transportation fuels, climate adaptation, methane detection and abatement policies, greenhouse gas emissions and air quality, and academic exchange and university partnerships. The partnership will build upon our shared commitment to sustainable growth, accelerate the transition to zero-emission transportation, and expand opportunities for the next generation.
- Brazil (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with the Brazilian federal government to scale up cooperation on climate, clean energy, cutting pollution, and job-creating climate opportunities. This new partnership, announced in September 2025, will advance market-based carbon pricing programs, expand clean transportation, including zero-emission vehicles and low-carbon fuels, and strengthen air quality management through enhanced monitoring and regulatory controls. The partnership also focuses on conserving 30% of lands and coastal waters by 2030, including nature-based solutions and biodiversity protection. In 2025, California also advanced a partnership with the State of Pará to strengthen cooperation on wildfire prevention and response — enhancing forest monitoring, identifying areas most at risk, and sharing research and expertise to improve firefighting and emergency management.
- Kenya (2025): California signed a partnership focused on cutting pollution and supporting trade. The partnership advances medium- and long-term low-carbon development, policy research, development, and innovation in sustainable land use and urban planning that reduces long commutes and urban sprawl, while promoting integrated land use and transport systems.
- Noord-Holland (2024): California and Noord-Holland signed a Letter of Intent advancing next-generation air mobility — from drones to zero-emission aircraft. Joint innovation missions are producing pilot projects that inform California’s Advanced Air Mobility Implementation Plan and readiness for major global events.
- Australia (2023): California signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Australia that helped inform the country’s first-ever vehicle emissions standards through input from the California Air Resources Board. The California Public Utilities Commission and California ISO have also advised Australia on electricity market reform to better align incentives for renewable energy.
- British Columbia (2023): California and British Columbia signed a memorandum of understanding on mutual wildfire assistance that is delivering results. British Columbia sent incident management experts to support California’s Palisades Fire in 2025, while CAL FIRE deployed personnel during British Columbia’s 2025 fire season. These exchanges established a lasting framework for cross-border wildfire support.
- China (2023): California signed five Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with China’s National Development and Reform Commission, the provinces of Guangdong and Jiangsu, and the municipalities of Beijing and Shanghai to advance cooperation in cutting greenhouse gas emissions, transitioning away from fossil fuels, and developing clean energy.
- Denmark (2021): California and Denmark signed a memorandum of understanding to collaborate on groundwater mapping, leak detection, and water efficiency, which has modernized California’s data systems and informed key state programs, like the Airborne Electromagnetic Survey. Danish technologies and expertise have helped strengthen drought and water-supply resilience statewide.
- Mexico (Baja California & Sonora): California signed Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with the Mexican states of Baja California and Sonora to advance zero-emission freight corridors, clean ports, and battery manufacturing — strengthening North American supply chains and workforce readiness. Joint forums have already produced new research collaborations and training programs advancing clean-tech.

articles.description: Gulf County Sheriff plans to keep utilizing license plate reader technology WJHG
articles.description_html: Gulf County Sheriff plans to keep utilizing license plate reader technology  WJHG
articles.article_title: Gulf County Sheriff plans to keep utilizing license plate reader technology
articles.heading: Gulf County Sheriff plans to keep utilizing license plate reader technology
articles.summary: The sheriff says the use of the technology on non-state right-of-ways remains uninterrupted.
articles.content:
GULF COUNTY, Fla. (WJHG/WECP) - The Gulf County Sheriff’s Office announced on Thursday it will continue to use license plate reader technology. However, the sheriff stated that they will comply with the governor’s request to remove cameras from the state right-of-ways.
Sheriff Mike Harrison said the cameras have been very useful in solving crimes. He stated that they will continue to use the technology until it isn’t available on state highways.
The sheriff also said the use of the technology on non-state right-of-ways remains uninterrupted.
“Gulf County is a fiscally constrained county with limited law enforcement resources. These systems greatly extend our ability to provide coverage across the entire county. Removing them will make our job more difficult and will take away a valuable tool we use every day to protect our citizens,” said Sheriff Harrison.
Sheriff Harrison said that he plans on working with the Florida Sheriffs Association and other law enforcement agencies across the state regarding the use of the technology.

articles.article_title: Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project
articles.heading: Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project
articles.summary: ETIPP works alongside coastal, remote, and island communities that are seeking to improve the resilience, affordability, and reliability of their energy systems.
articles.content:
The U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project (ETIPP) works alongside coastal, remote, and island communities that are seeking to improve the resilience, affordability, and reliability of their energy systems. ETIPP helps these communities overcome the unique geographical and logistical challenges that limit their access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy resources.
This multi-year, cross-sector technical assistance program applies a tailored approach to each participating community. Leveraging the experience and expertise of its partner network—a broad coalition of local stakeholders, regional organizations, national laboratories, and DOE offices—ETIPP helps communities proactively identify and implement solutions that suit their particular needs.
ETIPP offers two tracks: strategic energy planning (four to eight months) and deep-dive technical assistance (12 to 24 months) for specific energy projects. Selected communities receive support for a project scoping phase, followed by energy planning and analysis projects that:
- Address the community's energy priorities, goals, challenges, and opportunities.
- Advance the community's ability to implement strategic, whole-systems solutions.
- Develop replicable approaches that can add value in neighboring communities, or those with similar characteristics.
In addition to direct funding, communities participating in ETIPP can expect substantial in-kind support from partnering national labs in the form of energy analysis, planning, and, where appropriate, support for leading-edge technology solutions. ETIPP regional partners also provide general program guidance and education.
ETIPP uses the Energy Technology Innovation Initiative's (ETI's) proven framework to find solutions to community energy challenges and share best practices and innovations. The program has supported 95 projects since its inception in 2020.

Learn More About ETIPP
ETIPP is managed by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR). For more information about the program, application process, participating communities, and additional resources, visit NLR’s ETIPP website, or contact ETIPP@nlr.gov with questions.

articles.summary: E-Tech is committed to maintaining our role as the global leader in applied energy research and innovation by funding efforts designed to lower the cost of energy for Americans, enhancing national security and the reliability of the grid, using AI to expediate innovation, commercialization and TRLs and leading the world in next generation energy systems.
articles.content:
The Office of Energy Technology (E-Tech) funds research, development, and deployment for technologies that enhance America’s energy networks, reduce energy costs, and strengthen national security.

In addition to funding, E-Tech collects and disseminates essential data and forges partnerships with government and industry stakeholders to accelerate the commercial deployment of new technologies with applications in energy, manufacturing, and transportation.

articles.heading: Xpect Solutions buys Amivero to bulk up AI, automation capabilities
articles.summary: The deal bulks up Xpect's national security portfolio, as the NewSpring-backed company builds out its mission tech stack.
articles.content:
Xpect Solutions buys Amivero to bulk up AI, automation capabilities
The deal bulks up Xpect's national security portfolio, as the NewSpring-backed company builds out its mission tech stack.
Xpect Solutions is adding artificial intelligence, automation, software development and other mission-focused capabilities through the acquisition of Amivero.
The company didn’t disclose the financial terms of the deal. The addition of Amivero is another step for NewSpring Holdings backed Xpect to build a technology company focused on the national security market.
“Xpect’s strategy has always been about building the capabilities our customers need to solve their most important mission challenges,” said Yusuf Abdul-Salaam, CEO of Xpect Solutions.
Xpect’s strategy has focused on four technical disciplines: enterprise IT, cybersecurity, digital modernization, and data and AI. Amivero adds complementary capabilities and customer relationships.
Its expertise includes AI and automation, fraud operations, digital identity and software development will be added to Xpect’s strengths in network modernization, zero trust, cyber operations, physical security, cloud, DevSecOps and mission-focused data solutions.
Together, the company will accelerate research and development and investment in repeatable solutions to help federal customers modernize and scale mission-critical systems, Xpect said in its announcement.
Over the last year, Xpect has pulled in $40 million in unclassified prime contracts. Its biggest customer is the FBI, according to USASpending.gov.
Amivero had about $32 million in unclassified prime contracts. Much of its work goes through the General Services Administration. The Homeland Security Department is its next biggest customer.

articles.title: Ohio Telecom Association rebrands as the Ohio Broadband & Technology Association
