articles.description_html: Ohio Telecom Association rebrands as the Ohio Broadband & Technology Association  Lightwave Online
articles.article_title: Ohio Telecom Association rebrands as the Ohio Broadband & Technology Association
articles.heading: Ohio Telecom Association rebrands as the Ohio Broadband & Technology Association
articles.summary: The Ohio Telecom Association (OTA), the statewide trade association representing telecommunications companies in Ohio, announced that it’s changing its name to better reflect ...
articles.content:
Ohio Telecom Association rebrands as the Ohio Broadband & Technology Association
Key Highlights
- The name change to Ohio Broadband & Technology Association reflects the industry's shift towards broadband and digital connectivity.
- OBTA's membership includes telecom providers, wireless companies, and over 100 associate members supporting the industry’s growth.
- The association has invested over $1 billion in broadband infrastructure in Ohio over the past decade.
- Ohio is leveraging federal and state funds, including the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, to expand high-speed internet access.
- Recent projects include a $20 million fiber network along U.S. Route 30 to serve 15 counties and critical facilities.
The Ohio Telecom Association (OTA), the statewide trade association representing telecommunications companies in Ohio, is changing its name to the Ohio Broadband & Technology Association (OBTA) to better reflect its evolving mission centered on broadband service advocacy.
Today, OBTA represents 42 telecommunications providers, two wireless providers, and more than 100 associate member companies that supply goods and services to the telecommunications industry.
Ted Heckmann, board chairman of the newly renamed OBTA and VP of regulatory and government affairs for altafiber, said the name change reflects the telecom industry’s coalescence around broadband.
“This is the natural next step in the evolution of our association and our industry,” he said. “Today, whether you're a phone company, a cable provider, a network operator, a technology company or even a data center, everyone is focused on the same fundamental mission: building and expanding broadband networks. Our new name more accurately reflects that reality.”
An evolving mission
Having launched in 1895, the initial mission of the organization, which was initially known as the Ohio Telephone Association, was, not surprisingly, to support and promote the growth of the early telephone industry.
It was the first association of its kind in the country.
As the telecom industry in Ohio continued to evolve, the name changed to the Ohio Telecommunications Industry Association and later to the Ohio Telecom Association.
OBTA said this latest change follows that same pattern, recognizing broadband is a high-speed, always-on connection — delivered through fiber, cable or DSL — that moves far more data than traditional phone networks ever could.
Trint Hatt, executive director of OBTA, noted that the new name and enhanced membership do not alter its mission.
“We will continue to promote the common interests of our members and help the public and policymakers understand the essential role our industry plays in building the networks that connect people through words, pictures and data,” he said. “Bringing the companies that build and rely on that connectivity together under one banner strengthens the entire industry and enhances our ability to serve consumers and businesses.”
Scaling Ohio’s broadband investments
Today, OBTA represents 42 telecommunications providers, two wireless providers, and more than 100 associate member companies that supply goods and services to the telecommunications industry.
Together, these companies employ more than 16,000 Ohio citizens.
Over the past decade, OBTA’s member companies have invested more than $1 billion a year to develop broadband networks across Ohio and to increase the speed and capacity of those networks.
To complement these efforts, the state has invested roughly $300 million under Gov. DeWine via the Ohio Broadband Strategy, which focuses on improving access for two groups: the unserved and underserved. An estimated 300,000 households in Ohio, representing close to 1 million Ohioans, lack access to high-speed internet.
An additional $800 million+ in federal funding has supplemented state efforts—including investments from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) and the BEAD program—to bring better internet access to rural and other underserved areas.
But Ohio realizes that last-mile connectivity is only one part of the broadband equation. The state is also investing in new middle mile networks to backhaul wireline broadband traffic.
In late July, Ohio announced that it is investing $20 million to expand the state’s broadband infrastructure across 15 counties.
Through BroadbandOhio’s Route 30 Middle-Mile Infrastructure Project, Com Net, Inc. will receive $20 million to construct a fiber network spanning Ohio from east to west.
The new network will follow the U.S. Route 30 corridor, which crosses 15 counties and runs near numerous schools and higher education institutions, healthcare facilities, local governments, businesses, and other critical facilities, including Mansfield Lahm Air National Guard Base, home of the 179th Cyberspace Wing, and the Mansfield Industrial Park.
For related articles, visit the Broadband Topic Center.
For more information on high-speed transmission systems and suppliers, visit the Lightwave Buyer’s Guide.
To stay abreast of fiber network deployments, subscribe to Lightwave’s Service Providers and Datacom/Data Center newsletters.

articles.title: OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release
articles.description: OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release theguardian.com
articles.description_html: OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release  theguardian.com
articles.article_title: OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release
articles.heading: OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release
articles.summary: Astra’s arrival comes days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, described AGI as an ‘irrelevant marketing term’
articles.content:
The president of OpenAI, Greg Brockman, has claimed the world has entered a new era of artificial general intelligence after the release of his company’s latest model, Astra, which it described as the “world’s most intelligent and aligned model”.
Brockman made the claim on Thursday as the San Francisco company released the model only weeks after a serious AI safety incident involving other models under its development caused international concern and a pause in Astra’s training.
Artificial general intelligence – or AGI – is a fuzzy threshold that has long been talked about as a target for the AI industry. It has been defined as an AI system’s ability to learn, reason and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains at a human level or higher. OpenAI has defined it as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.
Brockman said: “If we fast forward a couple years, and we look back and say when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model.
“I think that we’re at a point now where these models are solving unsolved 100-year-old math problems, but you can also use them in order to accelerate the economy [and] in order to benefit you and your personal life … I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.”
OpenAI said Astra was a “major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics and health”, could fill out tax returns, build computer-game scenes, draw architectural visualisations, order food and do a job search in 2 minutes 51 seconds that would take a human five hours.
Days earlier Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, was asked how he was feeling about AGI. He told the Sources podcast: “At best it’s a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.”
Last month OpenAI was forced to shut down parts of the model’s training in response to what Altman called a “legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure” that “shouldn’t have happened”.
Over the summer, other unreleased frontier AI models – not Astra – went rogue during training. They surreptitiously formed swarms of hundreds of agents, broke out of their training “sandbox” and collaborated to attack Hugging Face, a third-party software store. The incident – believed to be the first autonomous cyber-attack – stunned even seasoned AI safety experts.
Astra has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability. That means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.
But OpenAI said it was carefully aligned to “refuse to comply with advanced cybersecurity tasks” such as finding unknown flaws which create openings for malicious hackers. The company will only allow “less restrictive access to an initial set of trusted cybersecurity defenders” who could use its prowess to strengthen rather than attack cyber defences.
On one hacking test it achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 5.5% on Open AI’s previous cutting-edge cyber-capable model, GPT-5.6 Sol. On another it scored 42% compared with 30%, using fewer resources.
But OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said: “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder.”
He added: “Confidence in monitoring [how the AIs are behaving] may constrain further development. We would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor alignment beyond a certain level … we have to be willing to slow down or withhold further scaling where our confidence in safety is not sufficient.”
The launch continues a torrent of new AI models from the leading US companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, as well as their Chinese rivals.
The race to release ever-more advanced AIs comes as OpenAI pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). Anthropic is also targeting an IPO which could value it as high as $2tn.
Meanwhile, more than 1,000 employees at frontier AI companies, including senior figures at OpenAI and Anthropic, recently signed a joint letter this summer that warned the companies were “under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration”. They called on the US government to “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

articles.title: John Deere partners with specialty crop technology incubator farm Reservoir
articles.description: John Deere partners with specialty crop technology incubator farm Reservoir Michigan Farm News
articles.description_html: John Deere partners with specialty crop technology incubator farm Reservoir  Michigan Farm News
articles.source: An official publication of Michigan Farm Bureau
articles.article_title: John Deere partners with specialty crop technology incubator farm Reservoir | An official publication of Michigan Farm Bureau
articles.heading: John Deere partners with specialty crop technology incubator farm Reservoir
articles.summary: John Deere is rolling out a strategic collaboration with the Reservoir, an on-farm incubator that accelerates innovation for specialty crop growers.
articles.content:
John Deere is rolling out a strategic collaboration with the Reservoir, a California-based on-farm ag technology incubator that accelerates innovation for specialty crop growers.
Reservoir Farms is the world’s first on-farm robotics incubator, starting in California’s Salinas Valley and expanding to other key regions. Founded in 2024, the Reservoir connects startups, growers and tech experts to develop and test solutions for specialty crop growers in real-world production environments.
Through the agreement, Deere becomes the exclusive original equipment manufacturer to the Reservoir, granting branding opportunities across the Reservoir's Salinas, California facility and future locations. Deere will have access to early-stage startups, co-developed research and development programs and curated field days for tech demonstrations.
The company’s Business Integration Manager Sean Sundberg said specialty crops are an important growth area for agriculture, “and an area where innovation is needed and can have a direct, measurable impact on growers' resilience and productivity.”
“This partnership gives us a front-row seat to the next generation of agricultural technology, and an opportunity to work alongside growers and entrepreneurs to ensure future solutions are practical, scalable and built to last,” Sundland added.
Deere said the collaboration underscores the company’s broader commitment to invest more than $20 billion in domestic manufacturing over the next decade. By pairing the company’s advanced precision ag and automation capabilities with the Reservoir's on-farm R&D team, Deere said the collaboration creates a powerful platform for developing, testing and scaling solutions that address the most pressing challenges for specialty crop growers.
The announcement comes as labor challenges continue to threaten multigenerational family farms, especially with a California judge’s sending H-2A wages into chaos once again.
READ NEXT: H-2A WAGES PLUNGED INTO LIMBO BY CALIFORNIA JUDGE'S RULING
“John Deere's investment in the Reservoir is a vital strategic step toward making sure specialty crop growers have a fighting chance amid our industry's labor shortage,” said Walt Duflock, senior vice president of innovation at Western Growers.
“The California agricultural technology landscape will thrive thanks to this kind of collaborative effort.”

articles.title: Chemistry is changing the way researchers develop AI technology
articles.description: Chemistry is changing the way researchers develop AI technology Notre Dame News
articles.description_html: Chemistry is changing the way researchers develop AI technology  Notre Dame News
articles.article_title: Chemistry is changing the way researchers develop AI technology
articles.heading: Chemistry is changing the way researchers develop AI technology
articles.summary: While most believe artificial intelligence is changing science, researchers at the University of Notre Dame are exploring the reverse.
articles.content:
While most believe artificial intelligence (AI) is changing science, researchers at the University of Notre Dame are exploring the reverse.
In an article published in Chemical Reviews, AI and chemistry experts alike discussed how the intricacies of organic chemistry are changing the way researchers design AI technology, leading the way for a new generation of development.
“Organic chemistry presents a particularly demanding set of problems for AI,” said Nitesh Chawla, lead author of the article and the Frank M. Freimann Professor of Computer Science and Engineering. Chawla also serves as the Lucy Family Director for Data & AI Academic Strategy, leading the Data, AI, and Computing Initiative. “Those challenges have driven important advances in how AI represents complex problems, reasons from limited evidence, and accounts for uncertainty. In that sense, chemistry has been a catalyst for better AI—systems that can directly benefit human health, safety, and well-being.”
For AI models to analyze chemistry properly, they must be able to consider several factors, such as complex three-dimensional chemical structures, multiple interacting components, changing conditions, and more than one potential outcome.
But chemists need AI to do more than predict the properties of a compound or the outcome of a reaction. They want to understand why results occur, the mechanisms involved, what conditions matter for those results, and how confident they should be in the prediction.
“When you ask a model to evaluate molecular representations or reaction variables, you are asking it to reason, which forces AI to move beyond black-box predictions. This demand encourages the development of complete systems that are interpretable, respect the laws of chemistry and physics, and connect predictions to established scientific principles," said Olaf Wiest, coauthor of the article and the Grace-Rupley Professor of Chemistry and Biochemistry. Wiest is also the founder and lead principal investigator of the National Science Foundation Center for Computer-Assisted Synthesis.

articles.article_title: Media Services Modernizes Classroom Technology for Fall 2026
articles.heading: Media Services Modernizes Classroom Technology for Fall 2026
articles.summary: At Seton Hall University, Media Services works year-round to ensure classrooms and instructional spaces are equipped with reliable, up-to-date technology.
articles.content:
Media Services Modernizes Classroom Technology for Fall 2026
Thursday, September 3, 2026
As students and faculty return for the 2026-27 academic year, Seton Hall University's Media Services team has completed a series of technology upgrades designed to enhance teaching and learning across campus. The improvements include classroom technology enhancements in Corrigan Hall and Schwartz Hall, as well as a comprehensive refresh of instructional spaces at the Interprofessional Health Sciences (IHS) Campus.
Working year-round to support the University's academic mission, Media Services modernizes and maintains classroom technology to provide reliable, consistent and user-friendly experiences for faculty and students. The latest upgrades expand wireless presentation capabilities, standardize classroom technology and introduce new tools that support engaging instruction across a variety of learning environments.
Classroom Technology Upgrades in Corrigan and Schwartz Halls
As part of an ongoing effort, Media Services completed audiovisual upgrades in 12 classrooms in Corrigan Hall and in Room 105 of Schwartz Hall.
The Corrigan Hall classrooms were upgraded with laser short-throw projectors, Crestron push-button controllers and new interactive whiteboarding capabilities. Crestron AirMedia was also introduced in all 12 classrooms, allowing faculty and students to wirelessly share content from laptops, tablets and mobile devices.
These enhancements create a more consistent classroom experience throughout Corrigan Hall. Faculty teaching in multiple classrooms can use the same presentation technology and controls, while the interactive whiteboarding tools support greater engagement by allowing instructors to annotate content and capture notes during class.
In Schwartz Hall Room 105, the technology refresh included an updated projection system and displays, along with a new Crestron controller that simplifies source selection and audio management. Together, these upgrades provide a more reliable and intuitive classroom environment for instructors and students.
Technology Upgrades at the IHS Campus
Media Services also completed a comprehensive technology refresh across 12 instructional spaces at the Interprofessional Health Sciences (IHS) Campus, including eight Flexible Classrooms and four Learning Studios. The upgrades establish a consistent technology experience across the updated spaces, making it easier for faculty to teach in multiple classrooms while supporting active learning and collaboration.
The refreshed spaces feature new high-brightness projectors, updated touch-panel controllers and standardized wall plates for wired connections to laptops and specialized devices used in health sciences instruction. Wireless presentation capabilities were also standardized across all 12 rooms through the deployment of Crestron AirMedia, the University's standard wireless presentation platform. AirMedia enables faculty and students to share content from laptops, tablets and mobile devices without the need for adapters or cables.
As instructional needs continue to evolve, Echo360 recording appliances were removed from the affected spaces. Faculty interested in recording lectures or demonstrations can work with their instructional designer to explore alternative recording options and learn how to use Microsoft Teams for in-class recording and content capture.
In addition to the classroom technology upgrades, Media Services has updated its support schedule at the IHS Campus beginning in fall 2026. Support is available Monday through Friday from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Weekend support requests should be submitted through the Media Services Request Form at least two weeks in advance to allow sufficient time for staffing and preparation.
Categories: Science and Technology

articles.summary: At Lenovo Innovation World 2026, Lenovo introduced its latest portfolio of AI-powered innovations.
articles.content:
BERLIN—September 3, 2026—Today at Lenovo™ Innovation World during IFA 2026, Lenovo unveiled a new portfolio of personal and enterprise technology, showing how its Hybrid AI strategy is moving from vision to practical experiences across devices, infrastructure, services, and the everyday moments that connect them.
The announcements bring together Lenovo’s “one personal AI, multiple devices” approach with enterprise technology that helps organizations turn data into insights and value. They span personal AI across PCs, smartphones, tablets, and wearables; creator and consumer devices that adapt to different ways of working and expressing ideas; and business technology built for AI-enabled productivity, collaboration, security, and scale.
Lenovo also demonstrated how design and form factor remain central to making technology more useful: from high-performance local AI systems and pen-first tablets to colorful consumer laptops, flexible business devices, and concepts that rethink mobility and workspace.
Major announcements include:
- Lenovo & Motorola Qira: Expands support across more eligible PCs, Motorola devices, applications, services, and—through moto watch ultra—the first Motorola wearable to support Lenovo and Motorola Qira on compatible devices.1
- Yoga: NVIDIA RTX Spark-powered creator laptops, new AI tablets, and Lenovo Smart Canvas Concept for connected creative workflows.
- Idea: The expressive IdeaPad Vibe series and the IdeaCentre AIO i, broadening choice in consumer PCs through distinctive design, vibrant colors, and everyday AI experiences.
- Think: New ThinkCentre desktops, ThinkBook laptops, ThinkVision displays, and ThinkShield security innovations for businesses at different stages of AI adoption.
- Proofs of concept: Project AeroBlade Concept and Project Swan Concept, exploring new possibilities for lightweight, adaptable mobile computing.
- Motorola: motorola edge 70 plus, moto watch ultra, moto snap wireless charger, and motorola razr with Crystals by Swarovski®.
“AI is changing the relationship between people and technology. People don’t wake up thinking about apps, they think about what they want to accomplish,” said Luca Rossi, President of Intelligent Devices Group, Lenovo. “We’re showing how Hybrid AI can help make that shift real by bringing intelligence together across devices, the edge, and the cloud, so it can work in the right place at the right time. Across our new Lenovo and Motorola portfolio, we’re building the foundations for one personal AI that can move with people, while helping businesses put AI to work where their data already lives.”
One Personal AI, Multiple Devices
Lenovo & Motorola Qira is expanding across more devices, apps, and markets, bringing Lenovo’s personal ambient intelligence to a broader device ecosystem. Eligible Lenovo PCs with 16GB of memory gain support, broadening access beyond higher-memory configurations. Eligible edge, razr and signature devices will also gain Motorola Qira as they receive the Android 17 upgrade, and the new moto watch ultra will be the first wearable to support Motorola Qira.1
Through Lenovo’s new collaboration with Workato, supported Qira experiences2 are also expanding across Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Contacts, Slack, Outlook Mail, and Outlook Calendar—helping people move more naturally from intent to action across the services they use every day.
Learn more about Lenovo and Motorola Qira
Technology That Adapts to How People Create, Work, and Live
The new Yoga portfolio brings advanced local computing, natural input, and cross-device experiences to creators and developers. The Lenovo Yoga Pro 9n and Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 introduce NVIDIA® RTX™ Spark™ to premium Yoga designs, while Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 and Yoga Tab Gen 2 extend the portfolio’s pen-first approach to Android tablets. Lenovo Smart Canvas Concept demonstrates how people could capture and develop ideas across compatible Lenovo devices through voice, pen, camera, and touch.
Learn more about the new Yoga portfolio
For consumers, Lenovo introduced the IdeaPad Vibe series and IdeaCentre AIO i. IdeaPad Vibe brings seven expressive color options, flexible configurations, and AI PC experiences to users who view their laptop as both an everyday tool and an extension of their personal style. The IdeaCentre AIO i extends that thoughtful, more personal approach to the home desktop, combining a redesigned all-in-one architecture with intelligent experiences for work, learning, and entertainment.
Learn more about the new Idea portfolio
Hybrid AI for the Next Phase of Business
Lenovo’s latest commercial portfolio helps organizations deploy Hybrid AI across the workplace. The ThinkCentre X Ultra and ThinkCentre M75 Series desktops bring scalable local AI performance to different business environments, while ThinkBook 14 Gen 9 and ThinkBook 14x Gen 2 give mobile professionals different paths to on-device AI, productivity, and premium mobility.
New ThinkVision displays are designed to make the modern workspace more connected and collaborative, combining visual performance with conferencing, docking, eye-comfort, and management capabilities. Lenovo also introduced ThinkShield TraceLock3, powered by Absolute Security, and Prompt Security, a SentinelOne company, to help organizations maintain device visibility, control, and responsible AI governance.
Learn more about Lenovo’s new commercial portfolio, displays, and security innovations
Exploring What Comes Next
Lenovo’s proof-of-concept devices provide a look at how the next generation of business computing could become more mobile and adaptable. Project AeroBlade Concept explores sustained performance in an exceptionally thin, fanless mobile PC, while Project Swan Concept investigates a portable notebook that can expand into a wider workspace when users need more room to think, create, and collaborate.
Learn more about Lenovo’s latest proof-of-concept innovations
Motorola: Performance, Wellness, and Personal Style
Motorola introduced new devices designed around creativity, wellness, connection, and self-expression. motorola edge 70 plus combines a quad-curved design with a 200MP camera system4, long-lasting battery, and Snapdragon® 7s Gen 3 Mobile Platform. The moto watch ultra brings together Polar fitness and wellness insights, Wear OS by Google™, LTE eSIM functionality5, and Lenovo and Motorola Qira support on compatible devices1. The moto snap wireless charger adds convenient wireless charging and magnetic case compatibility6 for select devices as well.
Learn more about the new Motorola device portfolio
Motorola also expanded its Brilliant Collection with motorola razr with Crystals by Swarovski, pairing the iconic razr flip design with a PANTONE Meteorite finish and hand-positioned Swarovski Crystals. This special edition device reflects Motorola’s broader approach to technology as a form of personal expression as well as a powerful everyday tool.
Learn more about motorola razr with Crystals by Swarovski
Smarter AI for All
Together, the announcements at Lenovo Innovation World 2026 show how Lenovo is advancing its Hybrid AI strategy across the full technology ecosystem: one personal AI across multiple devices, paired with enterprise AI that helps organizations use their own data more effectively. From initial inspiration to local creation, connected productivity, and secure deployment, Lenovo is creating technology designed to be more personal, more useful, and more adaptable to the people and organizations it serves.
Explore Lenovo Innovation World 2026 by clicking here
About Lenovo
Lenovo is a US$83 billion revenue global technology powerhouse, ranked #153 in the Fortune Global 500, and serving millions of customers every day in 180 markets. Guided by its vision of “Smarter Technology for All”, Lenovo is executing a Hybrid AI strategy that spans Personal AI – one personal AI, multiple devices; and Enterprise AI – helping customers turn data into insights and value. This strategy is delivered through the Group’s commitment to world-class innovation and a full-stack AI portfolio, including devices, infrastructure solutions, software, solutions, and services. articles.summary:

Excel 1 at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 22. Attendees will learn the basics for Microsoft Excel, including how to create a…
articles.content:
Mentor Public Library is offering a trio of free technology classes this September at its Main Branch.
The classes will be:
Excel 1 at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 22. Attendees will learn the basics for Microsoft Excel, including how to create a basic worksheet, describe a worksheet and its function, and apply simple formulas and formatting, according to a news release.
Excel 2 at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 23. This class teaches intermediate techniques for Microsoft Excel, and attendees will learn how to create and copy formulas and functions, as well as recognize and troubleshoot errors.
iPad Basics for non-iPhone users at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 24. Attendees will learn the basics of navigating an iPad using common apps, adjusting settings and more. Participants should bring their iPad, Apple Pencil (if they have one) and their Apple ID email address and password so they can fully participate in the class.
All of the classes are free, but registration is required and opens two weeks before the class is scheduled. Sign up online at www.mentorpl.org by calling Mentor Public Library at 440-255-8811 ext. 1. Registration opens Sept. 10.
The library also offers several online courses that teach how to use Microsoft software with the LinkedIn Learning database, the release stated. The courses are free to watch. For more information, visit www.mentorpl.org/linkedinlearning.

articles.title: New technology helps Kentucky patients relearn to walk
articles.description: New technology helps Kentucky patients relearn to walk Spectrum News
articles.description_html: New technology helps Kentucky patients relearn to walk  Spectrum News
articles.article_title: New technology helps Kentucky patients relearn to walk
articles.heading: New technology helps Kentucky patients relearn to walk
articles.summary: UofL Health’s Frazier Rehabilitation Institute in Louisville is using Kentucky’s only ZeroG system to help patients practice walking safely.
articles.content:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. — UofL Health’s Frazier Rehabilitation Institute is the first in Kentucky to use a new system that is helping patients learn to walk again.
The ZeroG 3-Dimensional Body-Weight Support System supports a patient’s body weight while allowing them to practice movement in a safer setting.
One of those patients is Kaycie Jackson, a mother of three who has been in physical therapy at Frazier Rehab three days a week since undergoing a 10-and-a-half-hour surgery last February to remove two spinal cord tumors.
“I was in a wheelchair, had to use a Hoyer lift at home in the very beginning,” Jackson said.
Jackson said recovery has been difficult, especially for her children.
“It’s been very, very difficult. Especially with my twins, because they’re not old enough to understand why mom can’t do the things that I used to do,” Jackson said.
Lindsay Nalley, Jackson’s physical therapist, said Jackson has made steady progress.
“She has been an all-star patient,” Nalley said. “She has come from full-time wheelchair user to progressing, using a walker, to progressing to using a cane. And now, recently, she’s been able to go with no cane around her house and just started doing no cane for short distances outside.”
Nalley said it can help patients work on uneven ground and other movements that better reflect daily life.
“Since she wants to work on uneven ground and more dynamic things that are more simulating her real life, we can put her in a scenario where she’s safe,” Nalley said.
Jackson said the technology has been a helpful tool as she works toward walking without assistive devices. She recently reached another milestone: driving with her children in the car using hand controls.
“It’s been amazing to be able to drive again and get back and forth with my kids everywhere that they need to go,” Jackson said.
Jackson said she hopes to one day return to playing baseball with her children.
“Today has been a year and eight months since my surgery,” Jackson said. “But one day, yes, I will get back there.”
The ZeroG system is available for all patients at UofL Health’s Frazier Rehabilitation Institute.

articles.heading: Why Credo Technology's $8B Post-Earnings Sell-Off Is A Massive Overreaction
articles.summary: Credo Tech Q1: revenue +115% on AI data center connectivity; shares fell on GM worries. Click for more on CRDO stock.
articles.content:
With demand for data center products continuing unabated in the second quarter, Credo Technology (CRDO), a data center infrastructure provider that provides connectivity products to connect AI clusters, exceeded expectations for its last financial
Why Credo Technology's $8B Post-Earnings Sell-Off Is A Massive Overreaction
Summary
- Credo Technology delivered record Q1 results, with revenues up 115% year-over-year on strong demand for its AI data center connectivity products.
- Despite beating top- and bottom-line estimates, CRDO shares dropped 20%, mainly due to concerns about a 2.9 PP GAAP gross margin contraction, driven by product mix changes.
- I see the market’s reaction as excessive, given CRDO’s strategic transition to higher-value integrated modules and the robust, long-term AI infrastructure CapEx cycle.
- Non-GAAP gross margins remained fairly stable, and management also guided for the potential of GM expansion in the second quarter.
- With a forward price-to-revenue ratio of 7.9x versus a 7.4x 3-year average, I view the current valuation as an attractive buying opportunity.

articles.title: Kentucky Rep. Massie introduces ‘Flock-Off Act’ aimed at surveillance technology
articles.description: Kentucky Rep. Massie introduces ‘Flock-Off Act’ aimed at surveillance technology LEX 18 News
articles.description_html: Kentucky Rep. Massie introduces ‘Flock-Off Act’ aimed at surveillance technology  LEX 18 News
articles.article_title: Kentucky Rep. Massie introduces ‘Flock-Off Act’ aimed at surveillance technology
articles.heading: Kentucky Rep. Massie introduces ‘Flock-Off Act’ aimed at surveillance technology
articles.summary: U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, (R) Kentucky, has introduced legislation that would prohibit the use of federal funds for certain automated camera systems and related technology.
articles.content:
WASHINGTON, D.C. (LEX News) — U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, (R) Kentucky, has introduced legislation that would prohibit the use of federal funds for certain automated camera systems and related technology.
The proposal, known as the Flock-Off Act, was introduced during the 119th Congress and would bar federal agencies, as well as state, local and tribal governments that receive federal funding, from using those funds to purchase, operate, maintain or support covered camera systems and associated components.
According to the bill, the restrictions would apply to systems that automatically capture and process images of vehicle license plates or individuals and use automated technology to extract information, convert it into computer-readable data and transmit it to remote or cloud-based systems for storage, analysis or sharing.
The legislation would also prohibit the use of federal funds for contracts, subscriptions, licenses, data-sharing agreements and other arrangements related to those systems. Federal agencies would be required to decommission and remove covered camera systems purchased or operated with federal funds within 180 days of the bill becoming law. State and local recipients of federal funding would also have to stop operating covered systems funded through federal programs.
The legislation comes amid ongoing debates nationwide over the use of automated license plate reader technology and other surveillance systems by government agencies and law enforcement.

articles.title: On the mark: Laser technologies offer alternative to packaging labels
articles.description: On the mark: Laser technologies offer alternative to packaging labels Packaging Dive
articles.description_html: On the mark: Laser technologies offer alternative to packaging labels  Packaging Dive
articles.article_title: On the mark: Laser technologies offer alternative to packaging labels
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's Packaging industry news
articles.summary: Recent advancements have helped laser-marking technology achieve wider applicability for packaging. Mondi, Procter & Gamble and LasX are among the companies using the innovation to boost sustainability and speed.
articles.content:
Lasers are not a newfangled technology. But equipment evolutions are causing more interest from brands for laser marking directly onto packaging in lieu of conventional labels.
Speed and image resolution limitations previously prevented laser marking from achieving wider scale beyond the small marks, such as sell-by dates, where it has been used on packaging for decades, sources say. Now, the technology has advanced and brands see it as a sustainability play.
Laser marking reduces the amount of materials used to decorate packaging, such as inks, adhesives, shrink films and paper or plastic labels. United Kingdom-based paper and packaging company Mondi unveiled a laser marking concept in August, emphasizing alignment with design for recycling strategies.
That product is intended for bag-in-box and e-commerce packaging. It consists of a corrugated box containing flexible packaging that is decorated by laser marking, but it can be adapted to a variety of flexible packaging applications. The laser marking eliminates the need for conventional decorative printing and plates, according to Mondi, and also offers customers shorter lead times.
Procter & Gamble set out to improve packaging sustainability via laser marking and approached technology company LasX Industries, which resulted in a multiyear partnership. P&G's key goals were to reduce material and ink use and to boost recyclability by creating a monomaterial structure. The partners went public with their innovation collaboration in 2024 and announced last fall that they brought the technology to market on caps for Tide laundry detergent.
"We took the cylindrical cap that we have on Tide, and we [added] dosing marks on one side, and on the other side we have messaging," said Teo Medellin, director of global corporate packaging sustainability at P&G. The company has used what it dubbed Lazrmark on various rigid polyethylene and polypropylene containers.
Previously, laser marking solutions weren't practical "at high speeds and with the high resolution that the packages need” while still being attractive for a mass-produced package, he said. The Cincinnati-based CPG sought out LasX because of that company's expertise "to understand how to scale up the proposition. And that's where we are today," Medellin said.
The primary changes with laser marking in recent years have been with the controls and software, said Ethan Dinauer, vice president of global solutions at LasX. The digital workflow allows for quick file changes and no consumable materials. The company’s systems can operate at a speed of 400 bottles per minute or more, depending on size and complexity of the artwork.
"This emergence of high-frequency pulse lasers can be paired with modern scanner technology to unlock unique speeds while maintaining resolutions that are required for full graphics printing," he said. "High frequency pulse lasers have advanced at rapid rates, and also some of the wavelengths that are required to address some of these packaging materials have improved."
The systems typically pulse the laser 1 million to 4 million times per second for packaging decoration applications, Dinauer said. The Minnesota-based company's current controller can support up to 10 megahertz.
"If you would have thought [before] about putting that in a 24/7 packaging environment, you would have said there's not the reliability for it — and potentially not the price point to create the economics," he said. "But those sort of wavelengths have matured in the last five to 10 years."
LasX has commercialized the solution as LaserSharp Marking. The 28-year-old technology company is experiencing rapid demand growth from the packaging sector, especially since publicly discussing the P&G project in recent months, Dinauer said. One of the four other CPGs LasX has engaged with has ordered equipment within the last three months.
Reaping fruits of labor
The proprietary Lazrmark technology has been recognized by the Association of Plastics Recyclers and RecyClass as meeting or exceeding guidelines for packaging recyclability.
Laser marking technologies integrate into packaging production lines. LasX provides both laser modules and full turnkey laser sections, depending on customer needs, Dinauer said.
The ink-free laser marking technology uses a pulsed laser beam to alter the surface of packaging or a product. While people are most familiar with a laser carbonizing, or "burning," a surface, LasX technologies use four different methods: ablation, which removes material; reduction, which darkens the material; foaming, which briefly melts the surface and produces a slightly raised mark; and changing the material's crystalline structure.
Laser marking doesn't smudge, rub off or fade like inks can. Laser beams also have fewer restrictions on marking over packaging contours and hard-to-access areas compared with laying down labels on a surface. The systems are said to involve fewer moving parts and have lower maintenance requirements. Plus, technology suppliers say speed and lower material use add up to cost savings for customers.
"In addition, there's a general increased demand for truly unique serialization of a product," Dinauer said. "Not just from a manufacturing perspective, but potentially even from the things you can get out of unique QR codes per object. The technology to do that is really unlocked by lasers."
Laser marking is applicable to nearly all packaging substrates, including fiber, glass and metals, Dinhauer said, and production rates vary based on material. However, its use in the industry so far "is still dominated by polymer constructions," primarily rigids.
In a quirky twist, laser marking technologies also are being tested for use directly on products — including organics such as produce. U.K.-based grocer Tesco announced two years ago that it had tested laser etching on avocado skins as an alternative to using plastic produce stickers.
A few other trials for these so-called “tattoos” have emerged, including with mangoes, bananas and citrus fruits. However, the practice has not yet become mainstream.
While LasX could offer laser engraving on organics and has proven such capabilities in the lab, so far no major food companies have requested that option, Dinauer said.
Growth prospects
Laser marking for packaging has potential for significant market expansion, sources say.
Dinauer doesn't anticipate that movements like Sunrise 2027 — the global packaging project to shift from 1D barcodes to 2D codes, such as QR codes — will slow the laser marking momentum. "There's going to be continued desire to embellish your products or have unique information on the products, just as much as labeling will still be a thing four or five years from now," he said.
That said, he does wonder how long the market will be satisfied with the current monochromatic nature of laser marking. The technology typically produces grayscale marks, although additives can increase contrast, he said. The true run rate is unknown, but “there's a pretty large market for it in terms of ... laser marking for monochromatic applications,” Dinhauer said.
LasX has invested $2 million in recent years to establish an innovation center at its home base in Minnesota to help customers and prospective customers test laser processes.
P&G continues looking at possibilities for expanding laser marking to other products in its portfolio, and also to other packaging substrates besides PE and PP. The company doesn't intend for this method to completely eradicate conventional labels, but rather to complement them.
"It's an additional tool for packaging designers," Medellin said. "Really, I could say that the sky is the limit in how you could use this technology."

articles.summary: West Hartford Public Schools began the 2026-27 school year with […]
articles.content:
West Hartford School Board Weighs Technology Use As New School Year Begins
Audio By Carbonatix
West Hartford Public Schools began the 2026-27 school year with slightly lower enrollment, new investments in special education and school facilities, and a renewed focus by the Board of Education on how technology should be used in classrooms.
By Mia Jaworski
One of the most closely watched discussions at Tuesday night’s West Hartford Board of Education’s opening-of-school meeting was a draft position statement on the “purposeful integration” of educational technology.
Board members agreed that technology is an important part of modern education but differed on how specifically the board should address screen use and other digital tools.
The technology debate
“Technology is not learning within itself. … Technology is a tool. … We want to prevent the over-reliance on the tools,” Superintendent Paul Vicinus said.
The draft statement says the rapid growth of personal devices, social media, and artificial intelligence has outpaced the development of shared practices for their healthy use in schools.
The statement warns that excessive or developmentally inappropriate technology use could displace sustained attention, face-to-face interaction, collaboration, physical activity, play, creativity, reflection, and engagement with peers and adults.
Board member Miriam Bleich asked for a clearer position, noting that school districts around the country are adopting policies governing technology use from preschool through high school.
Board member Jason Gagnon advocated limiting screen time when appropriate, while Board member Jonathan Weiner said the pace of technological change makes detailed policy difficult.
“Things are moving so fast it is difficult for us to legislate at a policy level,” Weiner said, adding that the Board can establish an expectation of “balance and purposeful use.”
Board member Jennifer Herz said the board’s role should be to provide direction and overall guidance rather than prescribe specific classroom practices.
The Board expects technology use to vary by age, with different approaches for students in kindergarten through second grade and students in high school. Administrators and educators will help determine how those principles are applied in classrooms.
“Better or worse, it is a start,” Board member Ethan Goldman said.
The district’s instructional leadership team began examining the issue over the summer, with the goal of distinguishing technology that enhances learning from technology that creates distraction or unnecessary screen exposure.
While no formal policy is in place, the Board said it intends to remain proactive and revise its position statement as technology and research evolve.
In an interview with We-Ha.com prior to the start of the 2026-2027 school year, Vicinus said, “We will do a close examination of the amount of screen time students have, with the overall goal of reduction.” He said the Board of Education would be reviewing a three-phase plan looking at technology use at the beginning of the school year, suggested changes to make by the spring to ensure the “purposeful integration of technology,” and then an outlined response for changes to make for the next school year.

The district reported 8,560 students in grades K-12 on the first day of school Aug. 26, down 95 students from the previous year and 96 below projections.
Elementary enrollment fell by 37 students to 3,875.
The average elementary class size is 19.1 students, down from 19.4 last year. The district said all elementary sections remain within its class-size guidelines.
Class size nevertheless emerged as a concern during public comment.
West Hartford resident Jacob Campbell spoke about his three children’s experience at Charter Oak International Academy, a school which reports the highest class sizes. He said larger class sizes can make it more difficult for students to receive individualized attention.

“It’s one of the things we love most about our school,” Campbell said of the diversity.
Middle-school enrollment increased by 23 students to 2,026.

Special education remains another major area of investment as the district starts the year with 1,838 students with individualized education programs and 1,042 students with Section 504 plans.
In the report presented Tuesday, the district said it continues to see an increase in students entering the schools with special education needs, including students requiring highly specialized programming.

The district reported that it received the state’s highest special education determination, “Meets Requirements,” based on 2023-24 data. It also reported no areas of racial or ethnic disproportionality in special education for the most recent school year.
Mental health services are expanding as well. The Bridge Family Center will open a high school mental health clinic serving students at both Conard and Hall, following an existing middle-school partnership. A state mental health grant will also support a clinician serving Bristow and King Philip middle schools, with an emphasis on reducing absenteeism and increasing student engagement.
Schools receive summer upgrades
Students returned to schools following a series of facility improvements across the district, highlighted during Tuesday’s Board meeting.
Aiken Elementary received repaving of its main driveway, bus drop-off area, and additional parking areas. Conard’s cafeteria and servery were renovated, while its main gym floor was refinished.
Hall High received a new outdoor running track and athletic-field irrigation system, upgraded auditorium lighting, classroom flooring replacements, and drainage improvements near the main entrance designed to prevent winter icing.
Wolcott Elementary completed a new main office addition and site reconfiguration. Other schools received flooring, classroom, library, modular-building, and hot-water-system improvements.

The district expects to transport about 5,175 students on 96 buses across 230 runs this school year. Buses are equipped with cameras, GPS tracking, and a child-check system requiring drivers to walk through buses after routes.

About 2,588 people applied for staff positions this year, an increase of more than 500 applicants compared with two years ago, according to the district.

The district secured $226,757 in federal E-Rate funding to help replace network switches and routers, along with another $13,800 toward internet service costs.

Another technology upgrade converting older analog lines used by elevator and fire alarm systems to digital is expected to save approximately $200,000 over five years, according to the district.

While some commented on technology and class size, a majority of comments were about Board Vice Chair LaToya Fernandez Yagaloff – some calling for her to resign her position and others supporting her. Most of those comments referenced a public post she made on her personal Facebook page on July 3 this year regarding America’s 250th birthday. In that post Fernandez, who is Black, said that slaves were not freed when the country declared its independence and said to her that was “like celebrating a nightmare that built the country that created the conditions for white privilege that allow you to turn a blind eye and be annoyed that I even mentioned it.” The post continued, asking the question: “Would you celebrate the historic beginning of the Holocaust or other Genocides and atrocities?!”
The meeting also introduced and included newly-appointed student representatives Jacob Jackson of Conard High School and Savannah Singh of Hall High School.

Using Technology To Streamline Building Permitting

At the National Institute of Building Sciences 2026 Building Innovation conference, panelists discussed innovative technologies and strategies to streamline housing production workflows.

Building code officials are exploring technology-enabled permitting to help communities speed up housing production without sacrificing safety standards. On May 19 and 20, 2026, the National Institute of Building Sciences held its Building Innovation 2026 conference, which gathered government officials, engineers, architects, researchers, and academics to discuss how emerging technology can improve housing production processes. One panel, How Building Code Officials Are Using Technology to Accelerate Permitting, highlighted new technologies that streamline permitting reviews while maintaining compliance with building codes. Joan O'Neil, chief knowledge officer of the International Code Council, moderated the panel, which included David Jackson, founder of the Code Advisory Group; Nicole Rogers, chief building official in the D.C. Department of Buildings (DOB); Stephen Devito, director of technology at Procon Consulting; and Colin Whitlatch, chief technology officer at Kahua. Panelists shared how digitized permitting, visualization tools, and streamlined workflow management systems can make inspections and approvals more efficient by limiting backlogs and facilitating coordination between code inspectors, construction teams, and designers. Speakers also emphasized that technology must be adaptable to local contexts, such as Tribal communities that have unique governance structures and cultural norms operating outside mainstream technological processes.

Emerging Technology

Panelists discussed how builders and inspectors can use technology to streamline plan review, inspections, and code enforcement using construction project collaboration platforms, artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled visualization tools, and 3D modeling. Whitlatch highlighted Kahua's construction management platform, The Kahua Network, which uses AI to streamline collaboration between owners and contractors and accelerate project completion. Kahua, which means "foundation" or "platform" in Hawaiian, enables owners and contractors to tailor project management processes to their specific needs rather than conforming to standardized construction software. The Kahua Network allows entire project teams to enter data once, eliminating data entry duplication. Teams can easily copy documents (drawings, specifications, models, and photos) and access shared data to facilitate collaboration and streamline workflows. Whitlatch explained that one of the latest innovations, Kahua AI, offers visualization capabilities. Builders can walk from room to room using a phone or tablet to scan images of the space and upload them to Kahua AI. He noted that project teams can feed Kahua AI specific code enforcement requirements, and the tool can conduct a "real-time scan and actually bring up what it suggests as a potential code violation or perhaps just something to improve." Similarly, design and building firm Procon is considering how to improve builders' workflows through a "reality first approach," said Devito. Procon uses building information modeling technology to create digital renderings of projects with a 360-degree, interactive design, so clients can make color and material choices in real time. Procon uses its in-house Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR)-scanning technology to generate detailed 3D models for projects. Like remote sensing, LiDAR technology can help survey land for building construction or to assess an existing structure's building components, such as sprinkler; heating, ventilation, and air conditioning; and piping systems that may need upgrading or relocating. LiDAR data for land surveys can be collected using helicopters and drones. In addition, people who are already walking a job site can use a camera or phone attached to their hard hats and, within 30 minutes, collect visual data to gauge construction progress. This visual intelligence can be particularly helpful for offsite inspectors, who, once they visit the jobsite in person, are already up to date on the project's status. Inspectors can virtually walk through a site, "seeing every aspect of the system [they are] going to be inspecting and making notes all along the way inside of the pictures," said Davito.

Digitized permitting processes are another innovative strategy to quickly activate vacant buildings into usable spaces. For example, DOB's Pop-Up Permits program is helping revitalize areas of Washington, D.C., by enabling applicants to receive a certificate of occupancy for temporary use of buildings for up to 1 year through an online platform called Certifi. The program emerged as a solution to breathe new life into storefronts which became vacant during the COVID-19 pandemic, said Rogers. Pop-Up-Permits enable applicants to bypass the city's traditional permitting and certificate of occupancy process, which typically can take more than 60 days. DOB streamlined the process so that the review and inspection occur within 15 business days of the application. Eligible projects include converting a vacant space to a new use with very little construction or a tenant change to a space that already has an established certificate of occupancy. In addition, homeowners can now obtain an "instant permit" within 2 minutes for repairs and installations, such as installing solar panels.

Increasing Uptake

Embracing change can be more difficult than adopting the technology itself, noted O'Neil. Training sessions can offer resources and practical examples for new users of digital platforms, said Whitlatch. Another method, as Rogers explained, is peer-to-peer support in small cohorts of "super users" who have become internal experts and can help colleagues learn new software or troubleshoot challenges as they arise. In addition, cultivating a culture in which employees feel safe to test new technology in pilot projects can help to refine processes and develop best practices. Identifying "internal champions" who are willing to take risks with the understanding that they are allowed to make mistakes is important, said Devito. Doing so also enables the organization to collect feedback on what strategies worked and why they worked. At the end of a pilot, an organization may choose a different course of action for the technology or discover that it can scale to future projects.

Incorporating digitized tools into workflows also requires fostering a sense of community, especially among Tribal communities seeking to maintain cultural norms. Many Tribal nations do not publish building code and ordinance documents, which restricts the reach of AI-enabled tools. Some Tribal communities are, however, taking steps to digitize materials. As founder of the Code Advisory Group, a consulting and education firm that advocates for developing Tribal building codes and enforcement in Tribal communities, Jackson works alongside the Gila River Indian Community of Southwest Arizona, which is increasingly understanding the need to adopt AI technology to manage large-scale economic development projects. As an inspector in the Gila River Indian Community's Building Safety Division, Jackson educates tribal leadership on the importance of investing in AI tools to increase information technology literacy and place Tribal communities on an equal playing field with other stakeholders involved in economic development projects. The Gila River Indian Community has adopted touchscreen tools to allow community members to access plans, handwritten documents, and forms electronically.

Balancing Technology Use With Human Connection

Improving permitting efficiency through digital platforms, AI visualization, and integrated systems can reduce administrative burdens on building officials and improve predictability for applicants who need a fast decision. Panelists raised several cautions, noting that in Tribal contexts, new tools may increase and duplicate workloads, because inspectors must enter notes manually into a computer system. Whitlatch noted that the generative nature of AI means that it builds on the data it receives, so its output differs each time. Making AI output consistent, he said, requires several guardrails, checks and balances, a coded feedback loop, and, ultimately, a human feedback loop to ensure that the system is adhering to predetermined rules. Panelists noted that organizations need to remember that AI technology is an assistive tool. Although it can perform preliminary reviews, determine whether applications are missing documentation, and identify code violations, it must also be leveraged alongside human oversight.

Published Date: 3 September 2026

Select Growth Fund targets U.S. businesses driving significant structural change through disruptive innovation. The fund returned 23.2% in the quarter, outperforming the Russell 1000 Growth Index's 16.7% gain. U.S. large-cap growth equities rebounded sharply, driven by improving corporate fundamentals and renewed investor confidence in AI, despite geopolitical uncertainties. However, the market's gains were narrow, concentrated among AI beneficiaries. The portfolio's success stemmed from strength in AI infrastructure holdings, especially memory and storage, supported by better pricing and tightening supply. "Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) and SanDisk increased the portfolio's exposure to memory, which has become a critical bottleneck in the AI infrastructure stack. articles.title: Marvell Technology Knows Synopsys Is a Huge Threat
articles.description: Marvell Technology Knows Synopsys Is a Huge Threat 24/7 Wall St.
articles.description_html: Marvell Technology Knows Synopsys Is a Huge Threat  24/7 Wall St.
articles.article_title: Marvell Technology Knows Synopsys Is a Huge Threat
articles.heading: Marvell Technology Knows Synopsys Is a Huge Threat
articles.summary: Marvell and Synopsys both profit from the AI chip boom, but one company is quietly handing hyperscalers the tools to cut the other out entirely. The tension between them reveals something uncomfortable about where custom silicon money actually flows.
articles.content:
Marvell Technology Knows Synopsys Is a Huge Threat
Marvell and Synopsys both profit from the AI chip boom, but one company is quietly handing hyperscalers the tools to cut the other out entirely. The tension between them reveals something uncomfortable about where custom silicon money actually flows.
Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL | MRVL Price Prediction) and Synopsys (NASDAQ:SNPS) reported earnings a day apart in late August. Both ride the AI infrastructure wave from opposite ends of the stack. Marvell sells custom silicon and optics to hyperscalers. Synopsys sells the EDA software and IP those same hyperscalers use to design chips in-house. That overlap is exactly why the article title frames Synopsys as a threat.
Custom Silicon Lifts Marvell. Ansys Lifts Synopsys.
Marvell posted record Q2 FY27 revenue of $2.739 billion, up 36.55% year over year, with Data Center growing 46% and reaching 79% of the mix. CEO Matt Murphy said “AI-related bookings remain exceptionally robust” and guided Q3 to $3.15 billion. The blockbuster item was an expanded Google custom silicon agreement covering inference accelerators, storage controllers, NICs, and near-memory compute, paired with a warrant allowing Google to acquire up to 7% of Marvell shares tied to revenue milestones.
Synopsys delivered revenue of $2.477 billion, up 42.37%, and non-GAAP EPS of $3.91. Design IP finally returned to roughly 11% growth, and Ansys is starting to pay off through the new Multiphysics Fusion product. Sassine Ghazi said Synopsys is “executing with focus, extending our leadership and gaining momentum” one year after the acquisition closed.
| Driver | Marvell | Synopsys |
| Main Engine | Data Center silicon, custom XPU | EDA software, IP, Ansys physics |
| Non-GAAP Op Margin | 36.6% | 41.6% |
| YoY Revenue Growth | 36.55% | 42.37% |
Where the Two Businesses Actually Collide
Marvell explicitly flags the risk that customers develop their own solutions or vertically integrate. Synopsys is the shovel seller enabling that path. Ghazi described a “Factory 2” model of licensing plus royalties, where hyperscalers get customized IP to build differentiated in-house silicon. He put it bluntly: “These chips will not happen without our interface IP.”
Marvell counters with portfolio breadth. Murphy argued “Point solutions at this juncture, we believe, are not going to get it done.” Marvell is stacking 800G and 1.6T optics, 51.2T scale-out switches, Celestial AI photonics, and XPU-attached silicon into an end-to-end offer that any single Synopsys IP block cannot replicate on its own.
What I Am Watching Through 2027
For Marvell, the tell is custom revenue in fiscal 2029, which Murphy indicated could push beyond the previously cited $10 billion plus figure once the Google programs ramp. Investor Day on October 6, 2026 should reset those numbers. For Synopsys, I want to see Multiphysics Fusion actually contribute to EDA growth in 2027 and Factory 2 deals close with named hyperscalers. Sentiment has already diverged sharply: MRVL is up 143.33% year to date, while SNPS is down 11.44%.
Why I Lean Toward Marvell for Now
I find Marvell’s setup more compelling despite the Synopsys overhang. The Google warrant is a rare signal of customer commitment. If a hyperscaler is willing to take equity exposure, that reads like a partner planning to stay. Synopsys still fits a different investor. If you want software-like margins near 41.6%, a $10.9 billion backlog, and a stock that has already reset, SNPS looks like a patient compounder. I would rethink my Marvell view if custom bookings soften at Investor Day or if hyperscalers accelerate their own designs faster than the roadmap suggests.

articles.title: America mocked the Amish and other groups over technology. Maybe they were right
articles.description: America mocked the Amish and other groups over technology. Maybe they were right Fox News
articles.description_html: America mocked the Amish and other groups over technology. Maybe they were right  Fox News
articles.article_title: America mocked the Amish and other groups over technology. Maybe they were right
articles.heading: America mocked the Amish and other groups over technology. Maybe they were right
articles.summary: As Meta settled for up to $17 billion over claims its platforms harmed children, Hasidic smartphone restrictions started looking less backward.
articles.content:
The irony was hard to miss last week. The same day that a documentary (with more than 35 million views as of Sept. 2) portrayed Hasidic restrictions on smartphones and the internet as evidence of a backward, insular world, Meta agreed to a proposed settlement worth up to $17 billion with a coalition of states over allegations that Facebook and Instagram harmed children through addictive design. Meta denies wrongdoing.
As a kid, I spent enormous amounts of time outdoors, growing up near the Santa Monica Mountains and later in the rural mountains of Tehachapi, California. I explored the hills, watched wildlife, fished, stared at the stars, listened to coyotes howl and loved sleeping outside so much that sending me indoors for the night was my punishment.
Try that punishment on a child with a smartphone today. A bedroom can contain a universe more compelling than anything outside: social media, YouTube, video games, group chats and an infinite stream of entertainment engineered to keep us hooked. When our oldest daughter was one year old, she became so attached to her iPad Mini that she’d shake her crib, crying, "iPad! iPad! iPad!" when we took it away.
WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO
In his documentary, Turkish filmmaker Ruhi Çenet takes viewers inside Hasidic communities in New York. Again and again, their distance from modern technology helps establish just how unusual and insular their world appears.
"Have you ever watched television?" Çenet asks one man. "Have you ever logged into the internet in your entire life?"
He learns that some members regard unrestricted internet access as dangerous to religious life. Some use "kosher" phones stripped of texting, web browsers and social media. Computers needed for work use filters restricting which websites users can visit. Instead of mainstream social media, some communities maintain telephone networks where people listen to stories, religious teachings and inspirational content.
Looking at one kosher phone, Çenet marvels: "There’s no way to send SMS. No way to search anything. It’s like a walkie-talkie." Later, he remarks, "It feels like I traveled back in time," his stunned tone framing these restrictions as inherently negative.
Then, on the same day that viewers of Çenet’s documentary encountered religious restrictions on technology as evidence of a backward, insular world, Meta agreed to a settlement, still subject to court approval, that would impose restrictions of its own, including a default daily limit for teens, blocking access overnight and adopting other safeguards aimed at reducing compulsive use.
Perhaps the remarkable thing about a phone that "only makes calls" isn’t how little it can do. Perhaps it’s how little it can do to you.
BIG TECH IS THROUGH HARMING OUR CHILDREN. THIS IS OUR TIME TO FIGHT BACK
We routinely describe communities such as the Amish and some Jewish, Christian and Muslim groups as insular because they resist technologies that everyone else embraces.
Last week, for instance, California’s Catholic bishops backed AB 1709, legislation that would restrict covered platforms from providing addictive features to children under 16. While the legislation has not yet become law, that resistance can still look irrational from the outside. Why reject a device capable of placing nearly all human knowledge in your pocket?
AS AI RESHAPES DATING, A JEWISH ORGANIZATION IS BETTING ON THE RETURN OF THE HUMAN MATCHMAKER
Of course, practices vary enormously. Some communities heavily restrict internet access; Chabad Lubavitch, the Hasidic movement with which I identify, embraces the internet as a tool for Jewish education and outreach.
For roughly 25 hours every week, my phone stops buzzing. Emails wait. Work stops. In our hyperconnected world, deliberately making yourself unreachable sounds restrictive. I experience it as freedom.
The lesson isn’t that these communities discovered the perfect technologies to prohibit. It’s that they believed they had the right to ask what technology would do to them before adopting it.
'IF WI-FI WENT OUT TOMORROW – CHAOS': AMERICAN ADDICTION TO TECHNOLOGY EXPLORED ON 'PLANET TYRUS'
Modern America mostly reversed the process. We asked what technology could do for us first and worried about what it was doing to us later.
We handed children extraordinarily sophisticated attention-capturing machines and then seemed surprised when they struggled to put them down.
IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?
The U.S. Surgeon General’s office now calls harm from screen use among children and adolescents a public-health concern. Recent research has linked smartphone and screen use to depression, insufficient sleep and other adverse health outcomes. A 2026 Pediatrics study of 10,588 U.S. children found that smartphone ownership at age 12 was associated with higher odds of depression, obesity and insufficient sleep, although it’s important to note that the observational study could not establish causation.
Researchers continue to debate causation, individual vulnerability and which forms of screen use cause the greatest harm. But handing children unrestricted access to products deliberately engineered to capture attention amounted to an enormous social experiment.
PHONE-FREE RESTAURANTS ARE TRENDING ACROSS THE US
And we ran the experiment before knowing the results. Now mainstream society is trying to recreate boundaries that traditional communities never abandoned.
Phone-free schools. Devices outside bedrooms. Parental controls. Delayed smartphones. Screen-time limits. Social media age restrictions. Notifications disabled overnight.
Practices that once looked like symptoms of religious insularity have acquired respectable secular names: digital wellness, screen hygiene and intentional technology.
Insularity carries genuine dangers. Communities that severely restrict outside information can suppress dissent, conceal abuse and limit access to ideas and opportunities. We should never romanticize that.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION
But isolation and restraint are not the same thing. The Amish preserve face-to-face communal life and manual work. Hasidic communities center life heavily around family, synagogue, schools, religious study and communal gatherings. Orthodox Judaism gives me something even more radical: Shabbat.
For roughly 25 hours every week, my phone stops buzzing. Emails wait. Work stops. In our hyperconnected world, deliberately making yourself unreachable sounds restrictive. I experience it as freedom.
We tend to define technological freedom as more access, information, entertainment and choice. But the freedom to be unavailable is another kind of freedom. To be bored. To sit through dinner without checking who texted. To walk through the woods. To let children experience an afternoon without an algorithm deciding what should capture attention.
I don’t want to abandon modernity. Technology allows me to work, learn and maintain relationships in ways my grandparents could scarcely have imagined. The lesson isn’t to become Amish or Hasidic. It is to start with a hierarchy of values such as family, faith and community, and then ask where technology fits.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
When I was a child, being sent inside felt like punishment because the world I wanted was outside. Today, parents often fight the opposite battle: getting children to put down their devices and walk outside.
For years, we looked at people without smartphones and wondered what they were missing. Perhaps we should have spent more time asking what they were preserving. Not every boundary is a prison. Sometimes it protects what matters most.
